News.title: Top children’s doctor killed after man snuck through window and attacked family as they slept with kids in next room
News.content:
Next

A CHILDREN’S doctor and medical director was stabbed to death in his bed and his wife critically injured in a horrifying attack by an intruder.

Dr Idris Evans, 46, was killed in his home in Edgewood, Pennsylvania, at around 12:30am on Thursday after a man entered the property through an open window.



The pediatric critical care physician and his wife awoke in their third-floor bedroom to find a man wearing only underwear attacking them with a kitchen knife, court documents seen by CBS News reveal.

Evans’ wife was seriously injured in the frenzy, but was able to alert their children, aged eight and 12, who were sleeping in the next room, to flee.



Elijah Hemingway, 32, has been arrested and charged with criminal homicide, aggravated assault, burglary and criminal trespass.

Evans, who was the medical director at UPMC Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh, and his wife were rushed to a hospital in critical condition but the doctor died of his injuries.

She told investigators how the intruder was muttering about “being God” as he launched the terrifying attack, per the criminal complaint.

The pair “fought back the best of their ability,” she said, and during the struggle, despite suffering from multiple stab wounds, she screamed at their children to run to a neighbor’s house for safety.

She too was able to escape and call the police.

“It was a very violent scene,” Allegheny County Assistant Superintendent Victor Joseph said at a press conference.



“The bedroom furniture was broken, mirrors broken. It was a very graphic scene.”

As the investigation continues, officials said a motive for the attack remains unclear but that there are questions over if the two men knew each other.

The doctor’s wife told police that she remembered her husband saying “Elijah” when addressing the alleged attacker.

“We do not know if there was any pre-existing relationship,” Joseph said.

“The woman did not know this male. We are trying to determine if the two males knew each other.”



After Evans and his wife were rushed to hospital, officers discovered Hemingway behind a property near the house with cuts to his hands.

He was detained and taken to hospital for treatment.

Cops say that in an interview, he claimed Evans had invited him to the property hours beforehand and that he and his wife attacked him.



Officials said that he was unable to give any evidence or details supporting this claim.

His latest arrest comes just a week before he was due back in court for a burglary in Pittsburgh earlier this year for which he was released on nonmonetary bond.

Meanwhile, the community at Evans’ hospital has been rocked by the tragedy, saying they are “deeply saddened” by his death.

“Dr. Evans was a dedicated caregiver and valued member of our hospital and university communities,” UPMC said.

“Our thoughts are with his family, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time. We ask that their privacy be respected.”



Meanwhile, police have asked people to be mindful about what they share about the incident.

“We are a small and close-knit community and we are sure that many of you may be feeling shaken today,” cops said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“You may be sad, angry, anxious, distracted, or just having a hard time making sense of what happened.”

They have asked people to refrain from posting rumors, speculation, graphic details, and any photographs about the tragedy.

News.title: Tragic details heard in death of Noah Woods, 3, who drowned in lake after ‘leaving play area through gap in a fence’
News.content:
Next

TRAGIC Noah Woods was found dead in a lake after leaving a playground “through a gap in the fence”, an inquest has heard.

The three-year-old vanished after running off from a playpark on September 15, sparking a massive frantic search.



Noah, who was partly deaf and non-verbal, had been with his granddad before disappearing from the under 5s playground in Brantham, Suffolk.

Hundreds of locals joined the search for the little boy.



A day later, cops confirmed his body had been found in a large fishing lake near the park.

The Met Police had deployed specialist divers to search Decoy Pond, a fishing lake about 0.2 miles away from the park where Noah vanished.

Volunteers who had helped with the search effort sobbed as they comforted each other after the briefing.

Noah’s dad previously paid tribute: “There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.



“It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation, you have all taken Noah into your own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound.

“A heartfelt thank you to everyone in our community (even far and wide) who came together to search for our boy.

“The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives.”



He added: “This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that’s what we kept telling ourselves the whole time.

“Noah, you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much, it has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short 3 years you were with us.”

Speaking after the tragic find, Superintendent Tom Pearse said: “First and foremost our thoughts are with Noah’s family and all who knew him.



“As a parent myself, I completely understand why people would want to help and such a response is one that typifies the strong sense of community and the heart-warming nature of Suffolk people that make the county such a special place.

“I am sure you appreciate the family now need time, space and privacy and I thank you for your understanding in this.”

News.title: Britain risks growing divide on adopting AI as small firms face missing out, study shows
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN risks creating an artificial intelligence divide as small firms face missing out unlocking new growth, a new study shows.

Research found that 44 per cent of small and mid-market firms use AI with another four in ten firms expecting to adopt it in the next five years.



But only a small fraction of those firms, some 6 per cent, have reached the stage where its changing their day-to-day business of decision-making and customer experience.

The Natwest findings reveal that nearly a third of firms, sone 29 per cent, are using AI in its earliest stages which linits their ability to grow.



The findings show that companies with more than 100 workers are twice as likely to use the new technology as smaller firms.

The gap between the firms highlights a growing divide for revenue streams.

Those firms at an early stage report saving of between 1 per cent and 10 per cent of working time – those at a more advanced level show average savings of 61 per cent to 70 per cent.

The study reports that 95 per cent of firms at that advanced stage report higher revenue – compared to 29 per cent for those in the early stages of adopting AI.

AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said: “Putting AI to work can help businesses save time, raise productivity and unlock new opportunities for growth.

“We must make sure firms of every size have the skills and confidence to move beyond experimentation and adopt the technology safely and successfully.



“Government will play its part, but businesses, banks and technology companies all have a role too. NatWest’s support will help more businesses make AI work for them.”

Seb Burnside, Chief Economist at NatWest said: “The opportunity from AI is not confined to the UK’s major technology centres.

“With size and scale a much stronger predictor of AI adoption, the regional growth story will be shaped less by where a business is based and more by the conditions around it – its access to skills and expertise, the confidence of its leaders and the strength of its local industrial base.

“Every nation and region has the potential to benefit, but turning that into growth will depend on creating the right local environment for businesses of all sizes to adopt AI successfully.”

News.title: Xi hails friendship ‘forged in blood & fire’ as Trump gifts tyrant bald eagle after revealing he ‘loves good granite’
News.content:
Next

DONALD Trump gifted Xi Jinping a bald eagle sculpture and revealed the Chinese leader “loves good granite” during their elaborate White House dinner.

The two presidents heaped praise on each other at the lavish banquet – where Xi said Beijing-Washington relations were “forged in blood and fire”.



This strong connection between the US and China was born during the fight against Japan in World War Two, Xi said at the meal last night.

The Chinese leader added “ping pong” diplomacy – the exchange of table tennis players in the 1970s which eased Cold War tensions – had further deepened their bond.



Trump also commended Beijing, and toasted to a future of “harmony, peace and success” between China and the US.

Tech giant CEOs, billionaire tycoons and top Trump officials attended the extravagant feast.



Several protesters outside the dinner were arrested as they shouted at guests arriving for the high-profile event.

Xi was also gifted a stunning bald eagle statue, the national symbol of the US.



Trump said: “The bald eagle is the national symbol of the United States and an embodiment of the free and soaring spirit of America.

“And we hope it will find a nice place, a wonderful place, in Beijing.”

The US president said the gift was made “by an extraordinary American artist” and “designed in personal collaboration with Melania and myself”.



In one priceless clip, Trump highlighted Xi’s “great interest” in granite.

He told reporters: “We had a great meeting – and he has a great interest in granite.

“He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”



He also invited Xi into his unfinished ballroom, which he said was not yet ready.

Trump said the Chinese leader and his wife could be the first people to enter the room as a “special treat”.

“Anybody who wants to walk into a construction site that’s nice and clean and sparkling, it’s our honour to have you do so,” he said.

The ballroom is still one year away from completion.

Xi thanked his hosts for receiving him and his wife with “meticulous care and consideration”, making them “feel truly at home”.



He said the two leaders were “making history in our bilateral engagements”.

Xi said: “We agreed to build a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability.

Among the several tech titans were Apple‘s Tim Cook, OpenAI‘s Sam Altman, Google‘s Sundar Pichai, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, and Nvidia‘s Jensen Huang.

Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg was also at the banquet, as well as Jeff Yass, the US billionaire who owns a share of TikTok.

The menu, which showcased American ingredients with a Chinese twist, included yellow squash, wild mushrooms, and crispy pancetta for the first course.



Diners were then presented with sesame-crusted sea bass, braised bok choy and aubergine.

For dessert, the chefs prepared vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit and an accompanying ice cream “made with harvested White House honey”.

The meal was the culmination of Xi’s three-day visit to the US – his first Washington trip in over a decade.

During this week’s high-stakes talks, the two leaders discussed AI, Iran, Ukraine and Taiwan.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

But experts warn despite the warm exchange of words, it is still unclear whether much progress has been made on any of these issues.

News.title: Town ‘under siege’ by bloodthirsty bears as rampaging beasts maul at least six people to death in just one month
News.content:
PROWLING BEASTS Town ‘under siege’ by bloodthirsty bears as rampaging beasts maul at least six people to death in just one month







Next

A REMOTE town is “under siege” by bloodthirsty brown bears with six people mauled to death in just one month.

From creeping through bedroom windows to ambushing forest foragers, predatory bears are terrorising the town of Podtyosovo in Siberia’s Krasnoyarsk region.



Locals have been left gripped with fear as more and more people die, leaving them wondering who among them will be the next victim.

The vast frozen plains of Siberia are home to nearly 308,000 free-roaming brown bears and while fatal human interactions have been historically rare, there has been a noticeable increase this summer.



Krasnoyarsk was plunged into lockdown earlier this month when two grandmas were killed and dismembered in two separate vicious bear attack just hours apart at the remote town of Podtyosovo.

Pensioners Galina Teterina, 73, and Zoya G, 67, had both gone out to pick mushrooms in Russia when they were ambushed by the animal.

It is believed the bear killed and buried Zoya before Galina came to the same spot just hours later.

A state of “high alert” was ordered in the aftermath of the double-murder due to “the increasing number of bear sightings within the city limits”.



The attack was closely followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who was walking through the forest.

Earlier this month, two people were also killed while foraging for wild berries in a remote forest along the Lena River.

And just last week, a 66-year-old mother-of-eight was killed by a brown bear after it broke into her home and dragged her to her death.



She – Lyudmila Prokofievna – is among the six people dead in the area and one of 14 fatalities recorded in Russia this year.

Russian authorities have now committed to investigating the recent spike in deaths in the Krasnoyarsk region.

They will identify any potential negligence in failing to control the bear population or in failing to prevent the animals from entering populated areas.

Investigative Committee of Russia of the Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia regions argue local officials have “failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people.”

Moscow, however, rejects the idea that the number of bear attacks across Russia has increased, stating that it has remained relatively stable at around 20 to 30 a year.



But for those living in the region, the danger is very much real.

In a neighbouring area in August, a bride-to-be was ripped from her tent and killed just hours after she had been proposed to.

Snezhana Korolyova, 29, was mauled to death at her romantic camping trip in the Altai Mountains of Russia in southern Siberia.

The newly-engaged couple were awoken to the beast tearing apart their tent around 1am before it “hauled the screaming woman away”.

The Altai Republic prosecutor’s office opened an inquiry into the woman’s death.



It is understood gamekeepers and Russian cops shot in the air but did not aim at the beast despite “having the opportunity to kill it” due to shooting restrictions in the area.

Since 1990, Russia’s brown bear population has increased from 130,000 to almost 308,000 by 2026, Russia’s natural resources ministry said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Authorities have reportedly killed more than 530 bears who were considered to be aggressive across Russia since spring.

Experts believe the increased sightings of bears at populated areas is primarily due to a lack of their primary food source – nuts, berries, and mushrooms.

News.title: Brit climber, 28, plunges 200ft to his death near summit of popular mountain in Spain
News.content:
Next

A BRITISH climber has plunged 200ft to his death after hiking up one of the highest mountains in northern Spain.

The mountaineer, 28, was reportedly just 65ft from the summit of Torrecerredo when he lost his life.



Emergency services raced to reports of a fall where someone had “possibly died” at around 1.30pm on Thursday.

A responder said that the alert was for “a person had fallen 40 to 60 metres and had possibly died”.



One hour later, a rescue doctor confirmed the climber’s death in the horror mountaineering accident.

Emergency services said the medic “had to remain at the scene, guarding the body” for an extra hour while a police helicopter arrived to take the body away.

The remains were transported to La Morgal “where funeral services were waiting”, according to officials.

It is not currently clear who raised the alarm or whether the Brit had been travelling with friends or family.

Local reports differ on whether the climber had been just about to reach the summit of the 8,690ft mount or whether he had been clambering down.

It follows the death of British woman who fell more than 1,650ft in a tragic mountaineering accident.



The woman, 42, plunged to her death in front of her partner while hiking the slopes of the Pyrenees in northern Spain.

She fell from the Balaitus Peak, while crossing a popular hiking route known as the Great Diagonal.

Her 53-year-old partner was unharmed in the horror accident in the Huesca region.



One month earlier, another British mountaineer was found dead in Spain after making a terrified SOS call.

The 61-year-old told emergency responders he was “lost and exhausted” when he made his last call around 7pm yesterday.

He had travelled to the famous Picos de Europa mountain range in the north of Spain.

The Brit was found in the Moeno canal, according to sources from the 112 Emergency Center of Castilla y León.

And in April, two people were killed by falling rocks at a world-renowned climbing spot in Spain.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

They had been practising rock climbing in Montserrat, around 30 miles north-west of Barcelona.

Part of a group of seven climbers, both died in hospital after the accident.

News.title: Couple left with horror face injuries & broken bones after savage bear attack as beloved dog dies saving them
News.content:
HERO DOG Couple left with horror face injuries & broken bones after savage bear attack as beloved dog dies saving them







Next

A COUPLE were left with severe face injuries after a horror bear attack with their hero French bulldog being killed as it saved their lives.

Jeff and Mallory Wilson were mauled by a bear after it lashed out at them in their own garden in California.



Their beloved “sweet indoor lap baby” French bulldog Cassie barked when she heard a commotion in their garden on September 19.

As Jeff opened the garden door at their home in Trinity County to check on the mysterious noise, a huge bear leapt out from behind the patio furniture.



The wild beast then mauled Jeff, knocking him to the floor.

Mallory rushed outside only to be the next victim of the bear’s vicious attack, suffering from serious injuries to her face and body.



Jeff sustained two broken ribs and several bite wounds.

During the brawl, the bear had clamped down on Cassie with its mouth.

The couple threw chairs and patio heaters at the beast eventually causing it to drop their dog from its jaws.

They rushed maimed Cassie to emergency surgery to treat multiple severe bite wounds and deep cuts along her spine.



Despite the pup starting to walk and drink water again on her own two days later, Cassie died of her injuries just three days after the attack.

Jeff believes that the bear was frightened from being cornered between their house’s small fence and open gate.

Rachel Moscon, who has been the couple’s friend for 20 years, set up a GoFundMe Page to raise money for Jeff and Mallory’s recovery from a “devastating and unprovoked” bear attack.



She said: “Cassie was a deeply loved member of their family and in the moment Jeff needed her most, this little dog courageously put herself between him and a bear.”

Mallory told Redheaded Blackbelt: “She was never meant to be a hero, she was not our guard dog.

“She was just our sweet indoor lap baby.”

The couple had built their lives to be surrounded by nature and have years of experience living and working alongside wildlife, according to Rachel.

She added: “[They] take precautions to peacefully co-exist with the animals that share their land.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“They are passionate animal lovers, which has made this extraordinarily rare encounter and the loss of Cassie heartbreaking on so many levels.”

Their GoFundMe page has raised $11,239 (£8,489) at the time of this writing with a target of $16,000 (£12,086).

News.title: Legendary explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, ‘illegally kept in care homes under fake names by his wife’
News.content:
WHERE IS HE?

WHERE IS HE? Legendary explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, 82, ‘illegally kept in care homes under fake names by his wife’







Next

SIR Ranulph Fiennes is being illegally kept in care homes under fake names by his wife, it is claimed.

The legendary explorer, 82, has not been seen in public for two years, having been allegedly “unlawfully deprived of his liberty” by spouse Louise Millington-Cotes.



Pals are said to be concerned for Sir Ranulph’s welfare, claiming Ms Millington-Cotes, 59, is refusing to let them visit him or know where he is, according to the Daily Telegraph.

It’s alleged one of the care homes where the retired explorer has lived reported a number of concerns about his wellbeing to authorities, including contacting the police.



The care home owner also wrote to the Office of the Public Guardian (OPG) to raise concerns about unorthodox medicinal arrangements.

And have also queried the “do not resuscitate” document Ms Millington-Cotes allegedly provided.



Earlier this year a care watchdog found Sir Ranulph – who was diagnosed with Parkinson’s – was being deprived of his liberty unlawfully.

Several friends and family members are now contemplating a legal challenge to Ms Millington-Cotes’ guardianship, the Telegraph reports.



Sir Ranulph married Ms Millington-Cotes after the death of his first wife Virginia Fiennes from cancer in 2004.

He became a father for the first time shortly after they married. Their daughter Elizabeth is now 20.

Concerns over his whereabouts emerged after the former explorer failed to attend a Royal Geographical Society gala evening celebrating his life on October 23 2024.

He instead appeared in a brief pre-recorded video – and has not been seen in public since.

It’s alleged Sir Ranulph spent time at a care home in London last year where his wife allegedly asked visitors to sign non-disclosure agreements before they could see him.



He was later moved to care facilities in Wales and Cheshire.

Ms Millington-Cotes is reported to have employed a private carer to look after him and supply medication instead of registering him with a GP.

But it’s alleged she failed to ensure a deprivation of liberty safeguards was in place – with one care home owner then contacting the Care Inspectorate of Wales.

The watchdog concluded in January Sir Ranulph was “deprived of his liberty unlawfully” as no authorised deprivation was enacted that “reflects the current residence and restrictions in place”.

It concluded the former explorer is “under continuous supervision and control” and “is not free to leave and is not able to consent to care, treatment and accommodation”.



Sir Ranulph is recognised by the Guinness Book of World Records as “the world’s greatest living explorer”.

Born in Windsor in 1944, he is a former member of the British Army’s elite Special Air Service (SAS).

He is the only living person to have completed a surface circumnavigation of the Earth along its vertical polar axis.

Over a prolific career spanning several decades, he has led more than 20 major expeditions across the globe.

Care Inspectorate Wales, the independent regulator of social care, said: “Care Inspectorate Wales is committed to promoting the safety, wellbeing and rights of people who receive social care services across Wales.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“It would not be appropriate for us to comment on an individual’s personal circumstances or care arrangements.”

The Sun was unable to contact Ms Millington-Cotes.

News.title: 'The future is Birkenhead' - how a neon-pink sign about an underdog town came true
News.content:
In the winter of 2020, a four-letter slogan appeared in five-foot-tall pink neon letters on the front of a former nightclub – ‘THE FUTURE IS BIRKENHEAD’.

“We came up with the slogan originally because we thought it was tongue-in-cheek,” its architect, Craig Pennington says now. “But then we put it on a t-shirt we thought no-one would wear, and we sold 100 of them. Sometimes the world wants to tell a different story about Birkenhead. But that underdog story is part of us – the ugly cousin over the water. The confidence is the point.”

Just six years later, it may not be written in pink neon, but the future *is* Birkenhead. The town on the left bank of the Mersey has just been shortlisted for UK Town of Culture. “We used ‘The Future is Birkenhead’ as the strap-line on the pitch,” Craig says. “And now we can say we are a town of culture. We are to Liverpool what Brooklyn is to New York, where all the most interesting things are happening.”

Birkenhead’s original ambitious entrepreneurs, the Laird family – whose boilerworks and shipyards once generated the wealth that built the handsome Hamilton Square, and the world’s first municipal park, with Europe’s first street tramway running between them – would recognise the spirit of the new community builders.

‌



The former site of Rocky’s nightclub has been transformed by Craig and his team into the Future Yard, a state-of-the-art, carbon-neutral live music venue and arts hub, which draws bands from around the world and punters not just from across the water but all over the North-West.

Why The Mirror is launching Britain Talks - and how you can take part READ MORE :

View 4 Images (R) Craig Pennington with members from the Left Bank Collective (Image: CHRIS NEILL)

“To make this work, Future Yard has to be better than Liverpool,” Craig says. “For people to bother to get on a train, it’s got to be truly amazing.” Future Yard would be remarkable enough, but it’s only one of scores of ambitious creative projects aimed at turning culture on its head in a town both built and scarred by the looming shipyards.

The Left Bank Collective – which led the culture bid – is a good guide, including Start Yard, which provides start-up space, Make CIC which runs community creative hubs, and Make It Happen, which leads sustainable regeneration via everything from social supermarkets to ‘citizen stewards’ who help with planters, litter picks and community picnics. “We want to be the golden thread that connects people in the local area,” says CEO Amy Butterworth.

‌



A short walk away, Craig’s fellow iconoclast brother Lee and his colleagues have transformed an old tenement block into ‘Joy’. A joyful, soulful building that wouldn’t be out of place as a boutique hotel, it’s actually aimed at rebuilding the mental health of local people who, too often, are at the bottom of every one of the indices of deprivation.

Joy bills itself as “a mental health support, social action, arts and culture third space” that fosters “love and human connection”. “Our aim is to build the most progressive mental wellness space in the country, changing the NHS in a positive way and setting a national example of how we can work differently,” says Lee, who runs Open Door, a charity reimagining mental health through belonging.

When I visit, Birkenhead has just been diagnosed as the most depressed constituency in England, with roughly one in four adults recorded as having depression. Nearby Wallasey came in third. Unsurprising, perhaps, when local clinicians say there’s a 12-year difference in life expectancy on different sides of the M53, which divides the Wirral.

View 4 Images Future Yard in Birkenhead is a state-of-the-art, carbon-neutral live music venue and arts hub

‌



Joy is about turning everything on its head and recognising mental health provision as it stands is not working. “We look different at Joy, because want people to think, ‘what on earth is this place’?” Lee says. “We want to intrigue people enough that they want to explore. That’s what retail does - why not mental health?

“People might come for a sound bath, for candle painting, the chatter cafe. We are all about health by stealth – and we aim to be more playful than services usually are. That’s not to say we don’t deal with very serious things – suicide prevention, self harm, disordered eating, trauma and young people in care – but we want to take a playful, colourful, relaxed approach where appropriate.”

Inside, Joy is host to a whole range of mental health provisions from NHS services to art therapy to counselling, while offering a community cafe, and a place for weddings, afternoon raves and local events. “By all moving in together, we don’t know what will happen,” Lee says. “But we know if things live together new things and new impacts happen.”

Central to Joy’s offer is a pioneering mental health triage project called ‘Branch’, an online mental wellbeing hub for children and young people in Wirral. Most of all, Lee says, “we are bringing people on a journey. We can’t just land here and not speak the language of the things around us, but also we want to challenge the experiences of the place.”

‌



Tomorrow, the Mirror will be part of a special event in Birkenhead, ‘Connected Places, Stronger Futures’, celebrating the renaissance of the Merseyside underdog – as part of a collaboration with UCL Policy Lab, Lloyds Bank Foundation, Open Door Charity and Future Yard. The event, connected to the Labour Party Conference across the water, coincides with a new report from UCL Policy Lab, Demos and the ‘Nation of Neighbours’ advisory group, of which Lee is a member.

View 4 Images Rachel Smith, Alex Shears, Lee Pennington, Liam Comer and Jenny at Joy in Birkenhead (Image: CHRIS NEILL)

‘Becoming a Nation of Neighbours - The political story for neighbourhood renewal, told from the ground up,’ tells a compelling story of how community organisations can rebuild trust and connection in civic space. Community organisations, it says, are not just an informal welfare system and a space where people get a genuine say, but provide “the everyday, face-to-face connection that underpins a healthy, trusting information ecosystem in an age of division and disinformation.”

The way to start a “hope loop”, the report says is for the state to “invest in, listen to, and share power with the people and organisations already doing the work of holding local life together.” From the top of Joy, where counselling rooms made from shipping containers will soon sit in the rich canopy of the local plane trees, it’s possible to see most of Birkenhead unfolding under the rain clouds.

‌



“That’s the largest concentration of grade-one listed buildings in one area outside London,” Lee says, looking down. In the near distance is the Priory on which Birkenhead was founded by canny monks who spotted a business proposition ferrying people across the Mersey.

“All of us in the Left Bank Collective do genuinely have the spirit of 150 to 200 years ago, looking for gaps and opportunities, and building a future that gets us back to where we should have been if we’d kept on going,” says Chris Lee, from Start Yard, which re-inhabited a former Camel Laird transport depot.

For everyone in the Collective, the mantra is experiential change – that by going out and spending time with people, and experiencing something new and different, people and places can change their futures. “At Future Yard, we believe that by using the power of music, we can fundamentally change what a place means,” Craig says. “We can reimagine what our town actually is.”

News.title: Romance scams on the rise with huge surge in Gen Z victims as age warning issued
News.content:
Romance scams on the rise with huge surge in Gen Z victims as age warning issued

A UK bank report that romance scams are up by nearly a quarter year-on-year, with younger victims typically meeting fraudsters on dating apps and social media now a big target

View 3 Images A leading UK bank has recorded a steep increase in romance scam reports over the past year (Image: Getty Images)

A huge jump in reports of romance scams over the past year has seen a surge in swindlers successfully targeting more and more Gen Z victims.

‌



The frauds reported by Lloyds Banking Group saw a 24% hike when customers between September 1 2025 and August 31 2026 were compared with those in the previous 12 months. While there was a particularly large increase in reports among younger adults, older victims typically lost more money.

‌



Reports involving victims aged 18 to 24 surged by 59% over the period, while those involving victims aged 25 to 34 also increased particularly sharply, by 39%. In the most recent 12-month period analysed by Lloyds, more than half (55%) of money lost to romance scams came from victims aged over 65.

‌



Victims aged 75 to 84 lost an average of £9,051, the highest average of any age group, and 19% more than the previous year. The average loss across romance scam victims generally fell by 20% to reach £4,078, Lloyds said.

View 3 Images Younger victims often met fraudsters on dating apps and on social media (Image: Getty Images)

Dating app Bumble slammed after ditching signature 'women-first' chat rule READ MORE :

Dating apps and social media platforms were common places for younger victims to have met scammers, while, among over-50s, traditional dating websites and social media platforms were among the places they had encountered criminals.

‌



Liz Ziegler, fraud prevention director at Lloyds, said “Romance scammers don’t care how old someone is. They look for opportunities to build trust, create an emotional connection, then turn that relationship into a request for money.

“We speak to customers every day who believed they had found a genuine relationship, only to discover that the person they trusted was only interested in money.

“Victims can be left dealing not only with a financial loss, but also the distress of learning that the relationship and future they had imagined were never real. The rise in reports from younger adults shows anyone building friendships or relationships needs to recognise the warning signs.

‌



View 3 Images Reports from victims aged 18 to 24 surged by almost 60 per cent (Image: Getty Images)

“Many people assume younger adults are less likely to fall victim because they are confident online, but being digitally savvy does not make someone immune to fraud.

“If someone you’ve recently met starts asking for money, take a step back and speak to someone you trust. A genuine relationship should never depend on money.”

‌



Patrick Hurley, ombudsman director at the Financial Ombudsman Service (FOS), said: “Being the victim of a fraud or scam can be deeply distressing and sadly for many people the financial implications can be life-changing.

“Romance scams particularly can leave an emotional scar and the impact on victims is often significant. If consumers are unhappy with their financial provider, they should first raise a complaint with the business.

“If they don’t believe that has resolved the issue, they can get in touch with us and we’ll see if we can help.”

News.title: B&M 10p-to-use gadget 'keeps you warm at home' without turning central heating on
News.content:
B&M 10p-to-use gadget 'keeps you warm at home' without turning central heating on

The item offers an affordable option to heat individual rooms during the UK's cold autumn and winter months

View 3 Images The heater is available to buy in stores (Image: Getty )

As temperatures start to plummet across the UK, households are searching for affordable ways to keep warm without overspending. For many families, switching on the central heating can feel like a financial burden.

‌



Yet discount retailer B&M has unveiled a wallet-friendly solution with its £20 Blaupunkt Three Bar Oscillating Halogen Heater. The compact device has been slashed in price, dropping from £24 to £20. It could prove perfect for those who want to heat individual rooms rather than their entire home.

‌



Experts, including Martin Lewis, recommend focused heating as one of the most efficient ways to control energy bills during the colder months, and the Blaupunkt model offers precisely that at a remarkably low running cost.

‌



Based on current Ofgem energy price cap figures, operating this 1200W heater on its maximum setting costs around 31p per hour. For milder conditions, users can select lower settings to further reduce costs, reports the Liverpool Echo.

Running a single bar at 400W costs just over 10p per hour. Meanwhile, the medium 800W setting costs roughly 21p per hour.

View 3 Images Blaupunkt Three Bar Oscillating Halogen Heater (Image: B&M)

‌



Halogen heaters are generally considered extremely efficient as they deliver immediate, direct warmth. Unlike conventional fan heaters that circulate warm air, halogen bulbs emit infrared radiation that directly heats objects and individuals positioned in front of them.

While it is not designed to replace a full home heating system, B&M says its budget-friendly option offers a quick, simple and affordable supplement for home offices, living rooms or bedrooms. The heater measures 36 x 26 x 48cm and weighs 1.3kg.

B&M says: "Heat your home with the Blaupunkt Halogen Heater – the cost-effective, quick and easy solution for a cosy home. This hologen heater is a powerful and effective domestic appliance, providing heat quickly when you need it most.

‌



"Blaupunkt electric heater boasts a clean and sleek design, in a contemporary grey colour. Save money on energy bills by heating only the rooms you need, with an electric heater from B&M."

Running the B&M Blaupunkt Three Bar Oscillating Halogen Heater will set you back between 10.44p and 31.33p per hour, depending on which heat setting you select. These figures are based on the current average UK Ofgem Energy Price Cap standard variable electricity rate of 26.11p per kWh.

‌



From 1st October 2026, the Ofgem price cap will nudge up slightly to 26.32p per kWh, pushing the maximum hourly running cost to approximately 31.58p at the highest setting.

View 3 Images Blaupunkt Plug-In Fan Heater (Image: B&M)

Shoppers can browse the full range of heaters on the B&M website, though online ordering is not available. To purchase, customers will need to head to their nearest store, and can check local stock availability using the retailer's handy online postcode tool.

Article continues below

B&M is also selling a Blaupunkt Plug-In Fan Heater for £15. The store says: "A compact and convenient heating solution designed for smaller spaces, this fan heater plugs directly into a wall socket with no trailing cables, helping to keep rooms neat and clutter-free."

News.title: Millions of UK drivers in line for share of £56million compensation - how to claim
News.content:
Millions of UK drivers in line for share of £56million compensation - how to claim

Those who bought or leased new cars or vans from 37 brands between October 18, 2006 and September 6, 2015 could be due payouts

View 2 Images Millions of drivers could be due compensation (Image: Getty Images)

Millions of UK drivers are in line for a share of almost £56million in compensation over money lost from inflated car delivery charges.

‌



It comes after the European Commission fined international shipping companies €395million (£340million) in 2018 for fixing prices for the transport of vehicles.

‌



It was alleged that five companies co-ordinated prices, divided up customers between them and exchanged commercially sensitive information.

‌



The Commission ruled: "Instead of competing, they gave each other a free hand on certain routes or with certain customers, by deliberately quoting high prices or not quoting at all in tenders by carmakers."

The Competition Appeal Tribunal (CAT) has now approved plans to distribute £55.87million in compensation to consumers and businesses that were affected as a result.

Drivers urged to implement 60mph rule as motoring change introduced today READ MORE :

View 2 Images Drivers who bought or leased new cars or vans from 37 brands between 2006 and 2015 could be due payouts (Image: Getty)

‌



Those who bought or leased new cars or vans from 37 brands between October 18, 2006 and September 6, 2015 could be due payouts. The motor brands include Ford, Vauxhall, Volkswagen, Peugeot, BMW, Mercedes, Nissan, Toyota, Citroen, Renault, Honda, Hyundai, and Kia plus 24 other major vehicle manufacturers.

Individual payouts for consumers and businesses will start at £25 for the first vehicle, while those with more than one affected vehicle stand to receive an additional £5 for vehicles two to six and at least £2.50 for each extra eligible vehicle.

Get the best deals and tips from Mirror Money WHATSAPP GROUP: Get money news and top deals straight to your phone by joining our Money WhatsApp group here. We also treat our community members to special offers, promotions, and adverts from us and our partners. If you don’t like our community, you can check out any time you like. If you’re curious, you can read our Privacy Notice. NEWSLETTER: Or sign up to the Mirror's Money newsletter here for all the best advice and shopping deals straight to your inbox.

‌



There are a few different ways the compensation can be paid, including a bank payment, Nectar points and donations to charities.

Former Which? consumer expert Mark McLaren urged consumers to sign up to receive the compensation. Drivers can sign up at www.cardeliverycharges.com/register.

He said: “Signing up now is the best way to be first in line for compensation. With everything now fully approved, the distribution of settlement monies can be distributed later this year.

‌



“Those already signed up will be contacted as soon as the distribution is open and will be directed to our online claim form to get back the money you’re owed. We’ve done everything we can to make this process as easy as possible for those affected.

“This settlement has been secured on behalf of consumers and businesses who were overcharged for new vehicles, because of hidden agreements between companies they’d never heard, which secretly cost them money. They now deserve to get that money back.”

Businesses who bought new vehicles for their own use are also eligible, including car rental, delivery, construction, maintenance, and fleet management companies.

Article continues below

Government institutions across the UK are also owed compensation, with tens of thousands of vehicles purchased or leased by public sector organisations and local authorities in the relevant period.

News.title: TV doctor gives ashwagandha 'evidence' warning and verdict on viral supplement
News.content:
TV doctor gives ashwagandha 'evidence' warning and verdict on viral supplement

Dr Amir Khan, a regular on ITV's Lorraine and This Morning said 'we don’t have the evidence'

View Image Dr Amir Khan spoke out about ashwagandha (Image: noappointmentpodcast/instagram)

An NHS GP has spoken out about a supplement which has gained massive popularity to deal with stress - and is taken by many going through the perimenopause. Dr Amir Khan, who is a regular on ITV shows Lorraine and This Morning appeared on the No Appointment podcast to talk about ashwagandha.

‌



Ashwagandha is an evergreen shrub (Withania somnifera) used in traditional Ayurvedic medicine to help the body manage stress. Ashwagandha is popular because modern wellness consumers widely use it as an adaptogen to manage stress, lower cortisol, and improve sleep.

‌



Dr Khan said: “Ashwagandha is another plant-based supplement that has been used in traditional Indian and Chinese medicine to help with stress particularly. We don’t have the evidence to say ashwagandha can help with stress.”

‌



Podcast host Cherry Healey said: “I’m really surprised. I thought you were going to say that there was because it’s done so many things. Lots of people with perimenopause swear by it.”

But Dr Khan replied: “If it works for you, continue to take it. A lot of ancient traditional medicine, you know, we don’t have the large randomized control trials that give us the evidence, but that if it works for you, then it works for you. But we don’t have any hard evidence that ashwagandha can reduce your stress levels. But if you like it and you enjoy it, take it.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Cherry asked: “Is it that because it’s ancient and it’s kind of already on the shelves, big pharma companies or people funding the research, I just can’t be bothered with that particular one because it doesn’t have that star quality?”

Dr Khan said: “I think that’s a possibility. I certainly do. But I do think there has been some studies in to Ashwagandha to look into it and they just haven’t produced the results that we were hoping for. Um, and with any supplement like like Ashwagandha or anything there is a chance it can interact with medication. It can cause side effects. So, you’ve got to be really careful about these things too.”

Harvard Health said: “Some evidence suggests that ashwagandha affects levels of the stress hormone cortisol. This may help regulate the body’s cardiovascular, nervous, and immune systems. Ashwagandha’s effects are thought to come from withanolides, compounds that seem to affect pathways that regulate inflammation, interactions between the nervous system and the endocrine (hormone-producing) system, and the body’s response to stress.”

‌



In terms of stress Harvard said Some research suggests that ashwagandha might help reduce feelings of stress and anxiety. In a randomized trial lasting one month, people who took ashwagandha capsules daily reported better well-being. Many said that they had more energy and focus. They reported sleeping better, too.

BBC expert key repair advice for anyone with washing machine in kitchen READ MORE :

For sleep Harvard said: “There’s less research on ashwagandha and sleep. But a handful of small trials suggest that the remedy could be beneficial. In one study, participants who took 120 mg of ashwagandha extract daily for six weeks had greater improvements in sleep compared with those who took a placebo.

“Another trial looking at adults with insomnia showed similar results: compared with those who got a placebo, the ashwagandha users fell asleep faster, had better sleep quality, and felt more alert when they woke up.”

Article continues below

In terms of side effects Harvard said data for use beyond 3 months was ‘limited’. It said: “Some people who take ashwagandha may have mild side effects. These can include loose stools, nausea, or drowsiness. In rare instances, ashwagandha has also been reported to cause liver injury, impaired liver function, or both.”

Ashwagandha may also interact with medications used to treat

News.title: David Beckham nets £40MILLION thanks to string of big money World Cup deals
News.content:
David Beckham nets £40MILLION thanks to string of big money World Cup deals

David Beckham cashed in on his global fame with a host of commercial deals around the World Cup to help profits at his brand arm leap nearly 50% last year

View 3 Images Sir David Beckham, knighted by King Charles last year, has built to his estimated £1.2billion fortune with a new dividend bonanza from his brand business (Image: Getty Images)

Superstar David Beckham has netted another £40million as a key part of his business empire notched-up a record year.

‌



Newly released accounts show the former England football captain raked it in from a string of lucrative commercial deals in the run-up to this summer’s FIFA World Cup.

‌



Profits at DRJB Holdings, which looks after the Becks’ brand, jumped nearly 50% to £50million last year. That triggered a bumper dividend for Golden Balls, who still owns 45% of the business., and has since bagged another £21million payout from the firm.

‌



It caps another stunning year for Sir David, which was knighted by King Charles last November and who was confirmed as Britain’s first billionaire sportsman earlier this year.

He also received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in June this year to acknowledge his role in boosting football’s profile in the United States.

The Day Alex Ferguson Changed Football: Celebrate 27 Years of United Greatness READ MORE :

View 3 Images David Beckham's World Cup linked deals included crisps brand Lay's

‌



The Sunday Times Rich List estimated his and wife Victoria’s fortune at nearly £1.2billion, with their wealth having surged from £500million a year ago.

The one major setback for the couple has been son Brooklyn Beckham’s feud with his parents. The amateur chef, 27, decided to turn his back on his family and famous parents after a bitter fallout.

He issued a lengthy statement online where he said he had been “silent for years” and accused his family of “trying to endlessly ruin his relationship”.

‌



An important part of Sir David’s fortune comes from trading on his famous name and image. Revenues at DRJB, which was bought by Authentic Brands Group in 2022, rose by a fifth to £84million in 2025 thanks to “new commercial partnerships and product launches, creating significant momentum ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup”.

Big money deals struck in the run-up to the tournament in North America and Mexico included with fast food giant McDonald’s, communications heavyweight Verizon, and PepsiCo’s crisps brand Lay’s.

Beckham, 51, already has commercial tie-ups with everyone from Bank of America to fashion firm Hugo Boss, with whom he launched a eyewear collection.

Article continues below

View 3 Images One big disappointment for Sir David and wife Victoria has been a public falling out with son Brooklyn (Image: Dave Benett/Getty Images for Hug)

Corey Salter, chief executive of entertainment at Authentic, said: “The recent financial performance has again demonstrated why David Beckham is one of the most powerful global brands in sport, lifestyle, entertainment and much more. It’s been an outstanding year, from new partnerships to important philanthropic campaigns and overall brand growth.

“What these results show is that behind the Beckham brand is a strong and highly effective team within Authentic, set up with the financial discipline and strong fundamentals to continue to grow profitably through 2026 and beyond.”

News.title: Aldi cuts price of Christmas chocolate tubs from today to 'lowest on market'
News.content:
Aldi cuts price of Christmas chocolate tubs from today to 'lowest on market'

Shoppers can stock up now ahead of Christmas

View 3 Images A branch of Aldi

Aldi has cut the price of two iconic Christmas chocolate tub favourites to £3.85 each, making them the cheapest on the market.

From today, shoppers can pick up Quality Street (500g) and Cadbury Heroes (475g) for under £4 in Aldi stores nationwide. The tubs are 40% cheaper than Sainsbury’s, saving shoppers £2.65 on the same product. Even with a Nectar card, Sainsbury’s Cadbury Heroes tub is still 22% more than Aldi’s.

The deal lands as early festive planners look to spread the cost of Christmas, with the price drop on the tubs starting from today - so shoppers can stock up early.

‌



View 3 Images The retailer is known for its bargains

The deal is not currently available in Scotland.

‌



Heroes, Celebrations, Roses and Quality Street tubs are already stacked high across supermarkets. The weight for Cadbury Heroes and Roses is down from 550g a year ago meaning that shoppers are getting around 13% less in the tubs than in 2025.

Last year, Morrisons sold 550g of Quality Street, Heroes and Roses for £7. Celebrations were 500g but still cost £7, although varying More card offers were available across the season. News.title: BBC expert key repair advice for anyone with washing machine in kitchen
News.content:
BBC expert key repair advice for anyone with washing machine in kitchen

Appearing on BBC Morning Live, Dave Fishwick told a view about what to do with the 7 year old machine

View 2 Images Dave Fishwick gave washing machine advice (Image: BBC)

A BBC expert has given advice for anyone who has a washing machine in their kitchen or utility room. Appearing on BBC Morning Live, Dave Fishwick told host Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton what to do if you’re in a dilemma about what to do if it goes wrong.

‌



Gethin said that viewer John had got in touch on what to do about his 7-year-old washing machine which has gone wrong - and if it should be repaired - or replace. Mr Fishwick said that it all depends on the cost of the repair - and also suggested that there was another option - finding a local independent shop.

‌



He said: “So, if it’s a minor cost for the repair much much less than half price, then it’s worth having a go. I mean, the secondhand washing machine’s out there, but you it’s worth having a go at fixing it. I mean, in this case, his bearings had gone. Now, bear in mind as well that a month later, 3 months later, whatever, the washing machine’s still done seven years.

‌



“It’s only the bearings that’s been changed. But I love the idea of going to an independent washing machine place where he can speak. but speaking to somebody, negotiating a deal, you’ll find something with a few scratches on it maybe last year’s model.”

Mr Fishwick said the core function was key - without extra electronics - but he explained that if people do buy new, they should make sure they get an A rated one for power as washing machines can used a lot: “You don’t need Bluetooth. You don’t need to know the time in 24 countries or be watching the telly on it. But what you do need is you need to wash your underpants. Get your y fronts in there so it’ll do the job. You don’t need Bluetooth.”

Gethin asle: “Also, if you are what other things to think about if you are buying a secondhand like well if you’re changing it like energy efficient.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Mr Fishwick said: “Yes, you’re looking at prioritising. So, you need to prioritise an A rated machine. Energy efficient. That’s going to save you a fortune on bills. It’s going to make such a difference. And washing underwear has never been so cheap.”

Meanwhile a new study released this week showed nearly nine in 10 adults in Britain have taken at least one step to cut back on water use in the past month, a survey suggests, as many areas of the country remain officially in drought despite recent rainfall.

‌



A summer of record-breaking heat and persistent dry weather has left reservoir levels well below average, besides damaging crops, harming wildlife and disrupting this year’s harvest.

View 2 Images BBC Morning Live hosts Gethin Jones and Helen Skelton (Image: BBC)

Around 30 million people in England remain affected by hosepipe bans. Some 88% of respondents to a survey by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said they had taken at least one step to cut water usage in August.

‌



The figure was highest among people aged 70 and over, at 92%, falling to 90% for those aged 50 to 69, and 85% for both 16 to 29-year-olds and 30 to 49-year-olds.

The most popular action was not leaving a tap running (reported by 65% of all survey respondents), followed by waiting until the washing machine or dishwasher is full before switching it on (55%), using less tap water in the garden (48%) and taking shorter showers (42%).

The proportion of adults who reported using less tap water, including hosepipes, in the garden was notably higher in August (48%) than in July (36%).

‌



A smaller percentage of respondents said they had collected rainwater in a water butt (25%) and taken fewer showers or baths (24%).

The ONS survey was carried out between August 5 and 30 and is based on responses from a representative sample of 3,530 adults aged 16 and over in Great Britain.

Most of England and all of Wales remain officially in drought, the exceptions being the North East, North West and Yorkshire.

Article continues below

Reservoir storage in England currently stands at 56%, nearly 20 percentage points below the average for this time of year, the Environment Agency said.

News.title: Families failed by decision to bail sex offender to flat near playground, victims commissioner says
News.content:
Victims and their families were "grossly failed" by the court system that bailed a sex offender and repeatedly allowed him to return to his home overlooking the playground he targeted, London's victims' commissioner said.

Zafer Dogan, 32, of Enfield, north London, was jailed on Thursday for two years and four months for taking thousands of pictures of children and using AI software to "nudify" them.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today, commissioner Andrea Simon said the case showed "the justice system did not centre victims" and called for a multi-agency review.

The government said the law was clear that bail "should only be used where necessary and proportionate, including to protect victims".

Dogan had pleaded guilty to three counts of making indecent images of a child, which included 900 category C images, 294 category B images and 653 category A images, which are the most serious.

He also admitted possessing extreme pornography, possessing a prohibited image of a child, creating purported intimate images of an adult, obstructing a constable in the execution of their duty and a further two counts of making indecent photographs of a child.

According to the police, he had taken more than 5,000 pictures, many from his bedroom window.

Despite protests from the police and prosecutors, he had previously been bailed back to his flat, forcing one family who had fallen victim to his crimes to move into temporary accommodation.

Simon said: "I think victims and their families were grossly failed by the decision to allow this paedophile to return to an address where he was overlooking a playground near to his victims.

"The case [shows that] the justice system just does not centre victims. To know that the police and prosecutors opposed bail multiple times, but nevertheless, he was returned to the community, is an indication that the capacity pressures on prisons are not being balanced with the impacts that that's having on victims' lives.

"We seem to be lurching from one crisis to another, and victim safety and their rights seem to be put to one side, as the justice system struggles."

News.title: Just how hot and dry was your summer? Use our postcode lookup to find out
News.content:
Where does the data come from?

This lookup uses data from the HadUK Grid dataset (opens in new tab), which is produced by the Met Office Hadley Centre. HadUK Grid is one of the main products used by scientists to monitor and research the UKâs changing climate.

The data for 2026 is provisional, with fewer observations feeding into calculations due to lags in data availability. As such, the precise values could change slightly in future as more data comes available. The historical averages are calculated over a 30-year period from 1991-2020, which matches the standard period used by the UNâs World Meteorological Organization.

The HadUK dataset displays temperature and rainfall data across a uniform grid covering the entire landmass of the UK. The data does not cover the Channel Islands. Every value on the grid is an estimate for the centre point of a 1km by 1km grid box, the most detailed climate data publicly available for the UK. The values are created using observations from land-based weather stations across the country, and by taking into account additional factors such as altitude, terrain and distance from the coast to scientifically âfill in the gapsâ between weather stations.

What do we mean by your area?

Weâve matched every active postcode in the UK to its nearest 1km by 1km grid cell in the HadUK dataset.

The results displayed for your area represent a mean average of that grid cell and the surrounding grid cells to your location. For most areas, this represents a 5km square centred on your postcode. Along irregular coastlines and on small islands, the nearest grid cells are chosen to match the shape of the coastline or island, but no cells are further than 7km away.

This approach aims to avoid sharp jumps between neighbouring locations which may occasionally arise due to uncertainties in the data, while still making use of the most detailed dataset available to capture local weather conditions across the UK's varied geography.

What does your areaâs weather data represent?

The average temperature represents the mean average of the selection of grid cells across the month or season.

The maximum temperature is the mean average of the daily maximums recorded across all nearest grid cells for the month or season; the minimum temperature is the mean average of the daily minimums.

The rainfall is the total amount of rain for the month or season, averaged across the selection of grid cells.

To calculate the number of days above the heatwave threshold, we first averaged the daily maximum temperature for each grid cell with its nearest grid cells on every day. Using the Met Officeâs heatwave thresholds (opens in new tab), we determined how many maximum daily temperatures exceeded the threshold for your location, based on the centre of your grid cell. Your areaâs heatwave threshold may be approximate if your postcode is near a county boundary.

This is not the same as the number of days spent in an official heatwave, where the threshold has to be met or exceeded for at least three consecutive days.

Acknowledgements

Methodology support from Dan Hollis, Amy Doherty and Oli Claydon, UK Met Office.

News.title: Brain tumour diagnosis cut from weeks to hours with rapid new test
News.content:
A rapid new test for brain tumours that the NHS has started using can slash the time it takes for an accurate diagnosis from up to eight weeks to two hours.

The test, which is used by doctors to diagnose which type of tumour a patient has, should mean patients can start treatment including radiotherapy and chemotherapy sooner, and are spared weeks of uncertainty.

Steve Palmer, 55, from Nottingham, is among those to benefit from the new technology - and it meant surgeons were able to get his result while they were still operating to remove his tumour.

"Getting that quick diagnosis removed weeks of anxiety," he told the BBC.

NHS England said that the genomic test, which works by quickly analysing the genetic code of a sample of the tumour, will be piloted in specialist centres around England.

There are around 150 different types of brain tumour ranging from slow-growing to aggressive cancers, each of which can respond differently to treatment.

Steve was diagnosed with a brain tumour after he collapsed at the gym, and the test revealed it to be a grade 4 glioblastoma.

"It wasn't the result I wanted to hear but it means I can get on with the next phase of treatment and recovery, and get on with fighting whatever it is I've got to fight," he told the BBC.

Consultant neurosurgeon Stuart Smith, who led Steve's operation at Queens Medical Centre, part of Nottingham University Hospitals NHS Trust, told the BBC the test "seems almost magical."

"The diagnosis of brain tumours relies on molecular and genetic analysis but it can take up to six to eight weeks to get the full information back. Here it is done while we are still operating."

Diagnosing the type of tumour while the patient is still on the operating table could impact how surgeons operate. Smith explained: "For some tumour types, which are curable, surgery needs to be as radical as possible to remove every last bit of tumour that we can find.

"Other types, sadly, are too aggressive, and beyond what surgery can remove, so we would be more cautious in order to lower the risk of causing damage to the brain."

News.title: What to expect from Burnham's first Labour conference as PM
News.content:
Andy Burnham had plenty to say about where the government - and the country - was going wrong at last year's Labour conference in Liverpool.

But that was at a fringe meeting on the sidelines of the main event.

Now, as Labour leader and prime minister, he is the main event - and it is down to him to show party members and the wider public that he has some answers.

Earlier this week, he said his debut leader's speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role".

"People are going to know the direction I want to take this country and I will set it down quite clearly," he told reporters en route to the UN General Assembly in New York.

An internal No 10 note has set out the broad themes he will explore when he takes to the stage in Liverpool on Tuesday - including setting out long-term solutions to build a belief that the future can be brighter.

The slogan for this year's conference is "Hope Again".

So in his speech he is likely to point to his forthcoming 10 Year Plan for the UK â which, he says, will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As for the specifics of what he will say, some of it will be very familiar to anyone who was listening to his conference fringe speech 12 months ago.

News.title: Anti-migrant activist charged after dinghy slashed in Channel
News.content:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been charged with criminal damage after a video appeared to show him slashing at a dinghy in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, has also been charged with failing to disclose the PIN to his phone, Hampshire Police said.

He has been remanded in custody and is due to appear at Basingstoke Magistrates' Court via videolink on Friday, the force added.

Several hundred people had gathered outside a police investigation centre in Basingstoke on Thursday evening believing Thomas was inside.

The demonstration, which seemed to pass off peacefully, began shortly before 18:30 BST. Protesters stood on the road outside the building and could be heard chanting "free DT".

The crowd began to disperse at about 21:45 BST after they learned of the charges against Thomas.

News.title: Police force says staff information could be 'compromised' after cyber-attack
News.content:
A police force in south Wales says it has suffered a cyber-attack which has caused disruption to some non-emergency systems and could have led to staff information being "accessed or compromised".

Dyfed-Powys Police said the incident was identified on 14 September, and an investigation had been going on into the circumstances surrounding it.

The force said it remained fully operational and its response to emergency incidents had not been affected, adding that while online and email contact services were unavailable for a period, these had now been restored, and 999 and 101 service had not been affected.
