News.title: FA could have prevented our son's death, say parents of striker Billy Vigar
News.content:
"You swing from sadness to anger because you just feel it could have been prevented."

That is the view of Camilla Vigar, whose son Billy, a former Arsenal academy player, died a year ago today from a "significant brain injury", five days after colliding with a concrete wall surrounding a pitch.

The 21-year-old striker was playing for Chichester City at Wingate and Finchley FC in north London.

In their first broadcast interview since their son's passing, the Vigar family accuse the Football Association of doing "nothing" after previous similar incidents.

"[Billy] had his whole life ahead of him. He was 21 years old and he lost it playing football when he didn't need to," she told BBC Sport.

"I personally feel that the FA could have stopped Billy losing his life because they had so many warnings."

They give the example of amateur footballer Ben Hiscox, who died in 2015 after colliding with a clubhouse near Bristol.

After the coroner warned the FA about the risk of future deaths, padding was added to Stoke Gifford United's clubhouse and the run-off between it and the pitch was increased.

The Vigars also point to the life-changing injuries sustained by Alex Fletcher in 2022.

Fletcher fractured his skull when colliding with concrete barriers next to the pitch at Bath City's ground, and was forced to retire in 2024.

The FA conducted a review of clubs after that incident.

"As far as I'm aware, nothing was done with that information and it just sat there. One of the clubs as far as I'm aware that was highlighted as being one of the high-risk clubs was Wingate [and Finchley], where Billy then lost his life," said Camilla Vigar.

When asked by the BBC what was done with the information it had gathered, the FA provided no comment.

News.title: Watch: UN delegates walk out of Netanyahu speech
News.content:
Dozens of United Nations delegates walked out of the hall Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was due to deliver a speech in.

Addressing the UN's General Assembly in New York, Netanyahu described those walking out as "moral cowards". Those who remained and felt similarly should leave, he said.

The Israeli delegation could be seen cheering Netanyahu in support.

Israel has faced condemnation for its actions in Gaza and Lebanon. A UN commission of inquiry has previously accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza - Israel has strongly rejected the accusations.

The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Israel responded by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,920 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry.

News.title: Miliband tells Iran minister UK will not tolerate 'hostile activity' on British soil
News.content:
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi that the UK will "not tolerate intimidation, threats or hostile activity on UK soil".

The ministers met face-to-face at the UN General Assembly in New York City.

The Foreign Office said Miliband spoke to his counterpart about "the UK's unwavering resolve to combat threats from Iranian-linked groups in UK soil, including attacks on the British Jewish community", and discussed war in the Middle East and a British couple detained in Iran.

There was no immediate comment from Araghchi. The Islamic Republic News Agency reported the men met and "discussed bilateral ties and international developments during their talks".

Miliband's comments follow an arson attack on four Jewish community ambulances in Golders Green in March and other incidents.

The BBC understands that British intelligence chiefs were initially keeping an open mind as to whether the Iranian state or organisations working for it had a role in the Hatzola ambulance attack and other attacks against Jewish communities during 2026.

They later concluded that secret intelligence pointed to Iran or its proxies being involved in the attack.

In July, a small power plant in the UK was also shut down due to a cyber attack, which the Telegraph reported , externalwas carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also spoke to his counterpart about the country's war with the US, telling Araghchi that Iran should choose "de-escalation and diplomacy instead of prolonging the war" and stressing the importance of reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

In February, the US and Israel attacked Iran, killing the country's supreme leader.

Iran responded by launching strikes on Israel and neighbouring Gulf Arab states which host US military bases. It also effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, impacting the global economy.

On Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told the UN General Assembly that any deal would have to include an end to the US blockade stopping Iranian ships from using the waterway.

Responding to US President Donald Trump's threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if a deal is not reached soon, Pezeshkian said his country will never "bend the knee".

"The resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying," he said.

There was no immediate comment from the US, whose delegation walked out of the chamber at the start of Pezeshkian's address.

The Foreign Office said Miliband also used Thursday's meeting to raise the detention of British couple Lindsay and Craig Foreman in Iran.

The couple, who are from East Sussex, have been detained for more than 20 months after being arrested while passing through the country on a motorcycle journey.

In February, the Foremans were each sentenced to 10 years in jail on espionage charges, which they deny.

In Miliband's discussion with the Iranian foreign minister, he reiterated the call for them to be immediately released and stressed that their welfare remains a priority for the government, the Foreign Office said.

News.title: Drumcree parade decision expected to be announced
News.content:
The parade by Portadown District Orange Order is due to start at 13:00 BST at Drumcree church on Sunday and finish at Carleton Street in the town centre by 14:30.

A total of 60 people would march along the road in silence, without any bands.

The last time the commission considered the parade route, it re-routed the march, but that decision in June was later quashed in court as proper procedures had not been followed.

The commission's decision, known as a determination, was explained in a nine-page document.

A lengthy explanation is expected to accompany the latest determination.

The decision could face a legal challenge. The reasons behind the determination are likely to be outlined in detail.

Final submissions were made this week by the Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition as well as all of the major political parties in Northern Ireland.

The police were also consulted about the planned parade.

The Police Service of Northern Ireland says it has activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday.

The Parades Commission, led by Professor Evelyn Collins, has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court.

A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office.

News.title: One person taken to hospital after barracks fire
News.content:
One person has been taken to hospital after a fire broke out at the military barracks accommodation block in Catterick Garrison.

North Yorkshire Fire and Rescue Service said multiple crews were sent at 19:48 BST on Thursday where the blaze was found to be "well alight".

The service said the person was taken to hospital with smoke inhalation while fire crews remained on scene until 02:43 BST.

It said on-site personnel kept a watching brief overnight and a fire investigation was due to take place.

Along with firefighters from North Yorkshire, additional resources were sent from several other stations.

Unverified videos and images shared online show flames and smoke rising up from a building as bystanders watch.

The BBC has asked the Ministry of Defence for comment.

Hipswell and Colburn councillor Kevin Foster had earlier told local media: "My immediate concern is for the safety and wellbeing of everyone at the camp, including our military personnel, their families and the emergency services responding to the incident."

News.title: 'I was living out my dream career in football – tumours mean I need to leave'
News.content:
It was May 2025 and life was good for Premier League and Fifa assistant referee Dan Robathan.

In fact, he was flying high.

Years of climbing the football ladder had paid off and he was running the line at the FA Cup final between Crystal Palace and Manchester City.

But just months after this career highlight, symptoms Dan thought were sciatic nerve pain and wear and tear were revealed to be benign tumours in his spine, which needed to be operated on immediately.

"I saw a neurosurgeon who told me I had two tumours, initially I thought it was one, but it was two," Dan tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It was compressing nerves, there was a chance it could affect a motor nerve which means it could affect function in my leg.

"I needed to go home, lay down and not move. I did that for 15 days, my life turned upside down overnight."

BBC Newsbeat met Dan at a football pitch in Norwich, close to where he lives, where he revealed the struggles he has had in trying to regain his fitness and mobility.

News.title: Greek PM urges Burnham to return Elgin Marbles permanently
News.content:
The Greek prime minister has called on Andy Burnham to find the "political will" to send the Parthenon sculptures back to Greece.

Kyriakos Mitsotakis wrote in the Guardian that returning the classical treasures, also known as the Elgin Marbles in the UK, would "send a powerful signal" but would require "courage".

The sculptures have been on display in the British Museum since the 19th Century, though Greece has long disputed the legality of their removal.

Mitsotakis and his government have previously held talks with the British Museum about the sculptures, but the two have so far failed to reach an agreement, with Greek authorities seeking their permanent return.

The Greek PM used the recent fanfare generated by the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry to the British Museum to restate his country's claim to the Elgin Marbles.

"Nobody would seriously contemplate cutting what survives of the tapestry in two and displaying half in London and half in Bayeux, and claiming this was an adequate way to understand it," he wrote on Thursday, external.

"Yet that is exactly what happened to the Parthenon sculptures."

His comments come after British Museum director Nicholas Cullinan suggested that the recent arrangement struck between the UK and France, after decades of rejected requests to borrow the medieval embroidery, offered hope of a deal with Greece over the Elgin Marbles.

Mitsotakis said he was "surprised at the recent suggestion from the museum that the Bayeux Tapestry loan might provide a template for an agreement over the Parthenon sculptures", adding: "I do not believe it does."

"Greece cannot accept any arrangement that would require it to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the sculptures, or a scheme that would mean we 'borrow' parts of our own monument," he wrote.

Instead, he urged Burnham to stand by his previous comments on the sculptures and find a way of returning them for good.

This would be a "decisive step", Mitsotakis said, that would "reunite the sculptures and transform a historic dispute into a unique act of cultural friendship".

Back in 2023, several years before he returned to government and became prime minister, Burnham said the sculptures should be returned to Greece with "no strings attached".

For years, he supported a change in the law to allow for this. But last month, he told the Financial Times that "ultimately it's an issue for the British Museum", adding that "legally that's where that issue rests".

News.title: Betty the 'cold-stunned' turtle set for Azores release
News.content:
A rare loggerhead turtle found "cold-stunned" after coastal storms is preparing to return to the sea after seven months of recovery and rehabilitation.

Named Betty by her carers, the turtle was mistaken for "debris" on Dunwich beach in Suffolk by a member of the public in February who called the British Divers Marine Life Rescue (BDMLR).

She was transferred to Hunstanton Sea Life Centre in Norfolk, where a second loggerhead turtle, called Olive, has been under care since December. Both will travel to the Azores later this month for release.

Katie Robertson, display supervisor at the centre, said: "The moment they finally get released is going to be an emotional time for us."

Both turtles were found cold-stunned - when temperatures rapidly decline and the struggle to find warmer waters can make them lethargic and experience decreased circulation.

The condition can be fatal.

News.title: UK 'moving closer' to flying cars, says air taxi boss as assembly centre opens
News.content:
Futuristic air taxis that take off like helicopters will be built at a new facility that is the first of its kind in the UK.

Bristol-based company Vertical Aerospace has announced a new aircraft assembly centre at Cotswold Airport, near Kemble in Gloucestershire, describing it as a "once-in-a-generation opportunity".

The Valo aircraft currently being developed and tested there are electric, carry four passengers and can fly up to 160km (100 miles) with no operating emissions, the firm said.

Minister for Reindustrialisation Blair McDougall said the new facility would "help turn British innovation into British manufacturing".

Vertical's CEO Stuart Simpson said: "We're getting really close to this idea of flying cars, flying taxis.

"Opening our aircraft assembly centre is an important step in Vertical's transition from prototype developer to aircraft manufacturer."

News.title: British rapper Yung Filly to face rape retrial in Australia next June
News.content:
British rapper Yung Filly will face a rape retrial in Australia next June after a jury failed to reach a verdict during an earlier trial.

In July, a jury acquitted the 31-year-old - whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos - of three counts of rape, one of assault and one of strangulation but found him guilty of two assault charges. No decision was reached for three rape charges, which he has denied.

A fan, aged 20 at the time, alleges Barrientos repeatedly raped and assaulted her in his hotel room in Perth, Western Australia, after a 2024 concert.

The court previously heard that Barrientos and the woman had consensual sex before she alleged it turned violent and he refused to stop.

On Friday, Perth's District Court set 15 June as the start date for the retrial which is expected to last eight days.

Barrientos was not required to appear in court and is understood to have returned to the UK after the court granted him permission to leave Australia as part of his bail conditions.

Sentencing for the two assault charges that the jury found Barrientos guilty of in July will take place after the retrial.

Barrientos, who was born in Colombia and brought up in the UK, is known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad.

He has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows.

Three-year-old Noah Woods, who was found dead in a lake following a huge search in Suffolk, had left a play area “through a gap in the fence”, an inquest in Ipswich heard.

A desperate search was launched on 15 September for Noah, who police said was non-verbal, partially deaf and undergoing an assessment for autism. The three-year-old went missing in Brantham, Suffolk when separated from a relative near a playground.

More than 24 hours after his disappearance, police confirmed that dive teams had recovered a child’s body from a lake known locally as Decoy Pond, which was later identified as the three-year-old boy.

The inquest for the three-year-old was formally launched on Friday morning at Suffolk Coroner’s Court in Ipswich.

open image in gallery Noah Woods, three, played at a playground before he went missing on Tuesday (Suffolk Police/PA) ( PA Media )

Around 1,300 volunteers turned out to help find Noah, and search efforts were supported by the National Police Air Service, HM Coastguard, Suffolk Fire & Rescue Service, and Suffolk Lowland Search & Rescue.

Suffolk Police confirmed that the body of a child had been found and the discovery was being treated as unexplained but not suspicious.

Noah’s father paid tribute to the three-year-old in the days following his death, calling him “the sweetest and most innocent little boy” in a post on social media.

“As I’m sure you have all seen, the body that was found in Decoy Pond is our little Noah,” he said. “There are no words to describe the pain of this loss, we are all absolutely heartbroken, Noah was the sweetest and most innocent little boy, with nothing but love to give, and we are going to miss him so very much.”

open image in gallery A tribute was paid to Noah Woods on the big screen ahead of the Everton v Ipswich Town Premier League match at the Hill Dickinson Stadium, Liverpool (Peter Byrne/PA) ( PA Wire )

He added: “It seems he has made an impact across the whole nation, you have all taken Noah into you’re own hearts, with all the overwhelming help, we were all just trying to bring him home to us safe and sound.”

Noah’s father thanked volunteers and authorities for their compassion during “the darkest time of our lives.”

“The compassion shown by all of you will never be forgotten by us, and brought us comfort and strength at the darkest time of our lives,” he said. “This was the most heartbreaking outcome for us, we were just hoping that he would be hiding somewhere obvious where someone could find him, that’s what we kept telling ourselves the whole time.

“Noah, you will be loved forever, you will never be forgotten and we miss you so so much, it has been a privilege to be your parents and be able to have packed so much love in the short 3 years you were with us.”

A tribute to the three-year-old was also shown on the big screen ahead of the Everton v Ipswich Town Premier League match, while players wore black armbands in his memory. More than £100,000 has been raised to support Noah’s family.

This is a breaking news story. More to follow.

Pope Leo XIV told members of the press on Friday that they were welcome to accompany his trip, highlighting the vital role journalists play in covering public figures amid efforts by the Trump administration to restrict U.S. media access to the White House.

Speaking to reporters aboard his flight to France at the start of a four-day visit, Leo was asked by a CNN reporter about the Trump administration’s attempt to bar CNN alongside other outlets. He reassured the traveling press that they were welcome on his plane.

"I am very happy that here, you are all welcome," he said.

open image in gallery Pope Leo XIV told reporters they were welcome to cover him as he responded a question about the Trump administration’s attempt to bar U.S. media from the White House ( AFP/Getty )

On Thursday, a judge granted CNN, MS NOW and Politico a reprieve to resume coverage.

Leo also apologized for missing the opportunity to speak with journalists on his previous international trip, when an Iberia charter breakdown in the Canary Islands led him to travel home solo on a private jet, bypassing his traditional airborne press conference.

Leo told the reporters traveling with him that he had "nothing to do with" deciding to accept the Spanish king’s offer to use his private plane to return to Rome. More than 70 journalists and members of the Vatican delegation waited several hours at Tenerife airport for a replacement flight.

open image in gallery Flyers hang in the White House briefing room in Washington, DC, on September 21, following Trump's media ban ( AFP via Getty Images )

Leo addressed the press pool's frustration when he walked to the back of the plane to greet them.

"A special mention I would like to make for those of you who were traveling with me when we returned to Rome from Spain," he said. "I want to apologize personally for an incident, that I had nothing to do with, but which I know left a number of you unhappy with the fact that we couldn’t have the flight back together back to Rome."

News.title: Is it really unprofessional to bring an iced coffee to a job interview?
News.content:

We believe quality journalism should be available to everyone, paid for by those who can afford it. Your support makes all the difference. Read more

Every now and again, a trivial question pops up online that causes debate at both metaphorical and literal water coolers. Three years ago, it was how often (and why) men were thinking about the Roman Empire. The latest conundrum to get tongues wagging is a far more corporate query: would you take an iced coffee into a job interview? It might seem like an innocuous question but everyone on the internet has a firm view.

Caitlin Wehniainen, a corporate recruiter who frequently shares work advice aimed at Gen Z on TikTok, kicked off the conversation by sharing her concerns that young people had been doing exactly that. Iced lattes, iced americanos; we can only hope not a frappuccino with whipped cream and a caramel drizzle.

In Wehniainen’s opinion, the move is way too laid back. “It looks like this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day,” she said. “It looks a little too casual to me.”

Much in the same way millennials were mocked for their “girl boss energy” and avocado toast obsession, Gen Z have previously been the butt of the joke for their informal approach to office culture: eg saying “ok diva” to colleagues on Slack. But now it turns out this overall aura could be one of the things contributing to scuppering their chances to get through the office door in the first place.

The UK job market for Gen Z is abysmal, with the number of young people not in employment, education or training (NEET) expected to rise to 1.25 million by 2031. And with the competition for available positions bigger than ever it’s no surprise that even the smallest detail about how those rare interviews should unfold pricked up the ears of many thousands of people online. Still, not everyone agrees about the optics of iced beverages and the implications of turning up to an interview with one in hand.

open image in gallery Some young people argue that coffee is no different from drinking water to stay hydrated ( Getty )

“I don’t see the difference between bringing that or a bottle of water,” says 26-year-old audience development editor Nicola, who’s been at the same company since graduating in 2021. “It’s just a drink. If it makes you feel comfortable or calms you down, then why not?”

“For some reason it feels more sophisticated than a bottle or can of a fizzy drink sitting on the table in an interview,” she adds. “And if you were having the conversation remotely, you’d probably have a comforting cup of tea nearby to sip. So, what’s the big deal?”

Helen, a manager in her early 50s disagrees. “If a potential employee turned up with an iced drink in their hand I would consider it to be unprofessional,” she says. “It gives the impression that their focus is elsewhere and they are not serious or focused on the matter at hand, which really should be the interview, the possible job, and demonstrating that they are a good fit for it”.

Although the coronavirus pandemic and remote working practices are often attributed to warping the perception of what’s “office appropriate” among young people, not all those who fall into the Gen Z bracket are of the same casual mindset when it comes to work although the detail might be more nuanced than meets the eye.

Seeing all the controversy and knowing the current state of the job market... I just wouldn’t risk it Emmie Dowling, final year student

Phoebe, who is 28 and actively looking for employment after returning to the UK following a career break to travel, is troubled by the iced portion of the act. “You’re going to be leaving damp patches everywhere if you put it down,” she muses. “The condensation. The sound of the ice. Both of those are unprofessional – but a hot coffee is chic.”

As a millennial afflicted by lifelong clumsiness, my own concern is manoeuvring the cup to shake someone’s hand, the potential for spills, or – god forbid – the sound of a slurp. Frankly, it’s a hurdle of uncertainty I’d rather not face.

Even Nicola, who sees nothing offensive about the coffee per se, admits that she’d never take one to an interview herself. “My hands shake during interviews,” she says of her nerves when trying to impress. “The ice would be such a tell – like holding a maraca,” she laughs.

open image in gallery Green flag: would you slip into a big interview with a matcha latte? ( AFP/Getty )

Career coach and former recruiter Hannah Salton says that taking a coffee to an interview won’t be the thing that fundamentally loses Gen Z a job – but, like how a candidate speaks, dresses or sits, it builds up part of an impression about who they are.

“The person interviewing them might think ‘oh they’re exhausted from partying,’” she says. “Or that they’re not taking the interview seriously – or arrived in a rush.

“A lot of those thoughts will be subconscious – but if other cues align with the impression that someone is not particularly committed, professional or present, then the recruiter might cling to them a little bit more. If these actions fit a pattern, then they’re like mini red flags.

Other times, they’re a blip that’s barely noticed – but it’s just one of those things that’s almost not worth the risk.”

It looks like this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day. It looks a little too casual to me Caitlin Wehniainen, corporate recruiter

Thanks to the current health of the economy, a considerable number of young people do, in fact, agree: “Seeing all the controversy and knowing the current state of the job market... I just wouldn’t risk it,” says Emmie Dowling, a final year student at the University of Exeter.

Salton stresses that the type of beverage here is not, in fact, the issue. “You could apply this to almost any drink apart from water,” she says. “If someone's got a big takeaway cup of Diet Coke, that can still create the impression that they’re not quite prepared.”

Much like wearing jeans to the office – some businesses do, some businesses don’t – it’s smarter not to be too bold before you know the lay of the land. “There’s a big difference in etiquette when you’re interviewing in a small tech startup versus a corporate law firm,” says Salton.

“A coffee is just a small thing that could count against you.”

open image in gallery Chill out: chains like Pret a Manger have reported their iced drink sales can double or triple in warmer months ( Getty )

Notably, taking a coffee to your interview robs the hiring manager the opportunity to offer a drink themselves; a small opportunity to form a connection that could aid a candidate's chances.

But not every employer would mind. “I personally rate the ice coffee,” says Grace Vielma, editor-in-chief at the youth media brand The Tab. “So long as they’re not late because of it.”

Fundamentally, iced coffee is representative of a culture shift still in its relative infancy – the clattering ice cubes were nowhere near as common ten years ago. Now, among UK coffee chains, iced “season” is considered to be between May and September in line with the warmer months, when sales can double or even triple at chains like Pret a Manger.

As such, the iced coffee - or iced matcha - has almost become synonymous with young people and, ever increasingly, Gen Z’s more informal approach to working. This is not the first inter-generational divide represented by food, drink, clothing, language, boundaries or interests, and, inside the office or out, it won’t be the last inter-age social sticking point.

“We’ve got a big workforce at the moment,” says Salton. “And Gen X’s and Millennials will be working for years, so it’s only going to get bigger.

“Every generation is different, with their own opinions, biases, and preconceptions about what’s acceptable, or what’s a bit borderline. It’s not necessarily going to get worse – but it’s not going anywhere.”

But, given the difference in generational outlook in the meantime, some members of Gen Z people might be asking whether, when it comes to getting your foot in the office door in the first place, it’s worth the risk.

The Premier League has joined demands for a radical overhaul at Fifa, warning that the governing body's management structure is currently "not fit for purpose".

Fifa president Gianni Infantino has faced intense criticism and calls to step down since details surfaced on 28 July regarding a private investment plan for a commercial entity, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run its events.

While opposition across three continents forced the withdrawal of the FFE proposal, European governing body Uefa insists it no longer has confidence in Infantino and will seek a credible alternative candidate to oppose him in next year's presidential vote.

Although Infantino promised reform this week, executives from four leading European competitions, including Premier League chief Richard Masters, co-signed a statement reading: "It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within Fifa, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference."

open image in gallery Premier League chief Richard Masters has co-signed the statement ( PA )

The reference to political meddling concerns Fifa's handling of Folarin Balogun, whose one-match suspension was frozen to allow the United States forward to play against Belgium in the World Cup round of 16. Although Fifa's disciplinary panel enacted the stay, US president Donald Trump stated he had personally telephoned Infantino to request a "review" of the ruling.

The joint declaration - issued on Friday morning alongside Spain’s La Liga, Germany’s Bundesliga and Italy’s Serie A - advocates for formal checks and balances. This includes creating a permanent committee of associations, leagues, clubs and player representatives holding veto power over the international calendar, competitions, employment and core assets.

Warning against Fifa's "relentless expansionism" which "affects everyone", the leagues pointed out: "Around one per cent of the world’s professional players take part in the Fifa World Cup, while the remaining players and their clubs stop competing when domestic leagues come to a halt,"

The statement added: "Yet when Fifa takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us – for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause – the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process.

open image in gallery Infantino issued a defiant statement on Instagram earlier this week ( Reuters )

"A Fifa governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."

In an Instagram post on Thursday, Infantino insisted he has "never been more determined and committed" to doing "what is right for the game", adding: "There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another."

Uefa has requested an independent external inquiry into the FFE scheme and sought document disclosures through US courts, potentially leading to a Swiss criminal complaint if Infantino is shown to have undervalued FFE at $20 billion.

Fifa rejected Uefa’s legal filings as a "smear campaign".

It’s very rare for a Netflix miniseries to be brought back for a new season – but that’s exactly what’s happened to The Beast in Me, the psychological drama starring Claire Danes and Matthew Rhys.

Weeks after Rhys won an Emmy for his role in the show, Netflix has announced it’ll bring the show back for a second run, despite being originally intended to be one completed series. The series was nominated in the Limited Series category at the Emmys.

The Beast in Me follows Aggie Wiggs, a Pulitzer Prize-winning writer whose world is dangerously rocked by her new neighbour, Nile Jarvis, a famous business magnate who was suspected of killing his wife. Danes will return in season two.

open image in gallery Claire Danes will return for a new season of ‘The Beast in Me’ ( Netflix )

Episodes were written by Gabe Rotter, a protégé of X-Files creator Chris Carter, and 24 and Homeland producer Howard Gordon, who tapped up Danes to star in the series. Gordon and his fellow season one producer, Daniel Pearle, will showrun season two.

At the time of the show’s release in November 2025, Gordon told Deadline a follow-up season was possible, adding: “I do think that there’s certainly room for another chapter.”

At the series’ New York City red carpet premiere, Rhys shared his partner Keri Russell’s reaction to some of the more shocking scenes, quipping to The Independent: “When she saw it, she was like, 'This is tailor-made for you. This is the person you truly are. It's about time the world knew who you are. She saw the beast in me a long time ago and wasn’t that impressed then.”

The actor made history at the Emmys after winning not just for The Beast in Me, but for Apple TV+ series Widow’s Bay. Together with his 2018 lead drama win for The Americans, he is the first male performer to win in all three lead acting categories, which are separated into drama, comedy and limited series.

open image in gallery Matthew Rhys won Emmys for his role in both ‘The Beast in Me’ and ‘Widow’s Bay’ ( Reuters )

"It certainly hasn't sunk, sunk in," Rhys told reporters after winning the trophies. "[I'm] stumbling for words, because I really don't have them at the moment. I really can't quite believe it."

Other shows that started life as limited series on Netflix but had follow-up seasons greenlit are Beef and Untamed.

News.title: Buttler injury derails England chase and sends Sri Lanka series to decider
News.content:
Enter Buttler to play a wonderful counter-attack, whacking Wellalage for four and six and dumping leg-spinner Sachindu Colombage over the rope twice as he raced to 41 off 22 balls.

Buttler was at a crossroads after the T20 World Cup in February. Despite England making the semi-finals, he averaged just 10 in the tournament to complete a third poor World Cup in a row. A break with his family, and a very good Indian Premier League, where he made a crucial technical correction, changed his fortunes.

Matthew Hayden, the batting coach at the Gujarat Titans, asked him whether he was watching the ball closely enough. Buttler discovered that, now 36, he is a right-eye dominant batsman, so with Hayden’s help he opened up his stance to give himself a better view of the ball. A summer rich in runs has followed with an average of 51 for England and a strut back in his body language. The injury has surely ended Buttler’s summer and there are worries that he could be out of the Pakistan ODI triangular tournament next month as well, just to add to the night’s woes.

This was not a vintage England performance. Atkinson made a crucial error on the boundary, dropping a straightforward chance off Kusal Mendis on 17. It kickstarted Mendis, who went on the charge smashing 51 in 24 balls. He put on 137 in 120 balls with Kuminda Mendis. Josh Tongue had an off day going at seven an over and Jofra Archer was given similar treatment, although he bowled better than figures suggest, as anything wayward with pace on the ball was hit away.

Overton was more effective with his cutters and slower balls, while Ahmed did at least bag a couple of wickets, credit for keeping his head after some early rough treatment. Kusal Mendis was given out leg before on 99 but overturned the decision and stroked a four next ball for a deserved hundred.

Thanks for joining me. A global rout in bond markets deepened overnight as traders expect the US to keep raising interest rates.

Japan’s 10-year bond yield surged to 3.08pc on Thursday, its highest level since 1996, as markets responded to stronger than expected US economic data and higher oil prices.

It followed sharp rises in the US on Wednesday, when the yield on 10-year Treasuries – a benchmark of global borrowing costs – surged as high as 5.12pc, up from 4.96pc. It was the biggest jump since the “liberation day” tariff turmoil in April last year.

Bonds were sent into turmoil as traders bet that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates three times by April next year in an effort to bring down inflation. Money markets suggest there is a 70pc chance of the Fed following this month’s first rate rise in three years with a second in October.

This followed closely watched industry data on Wednesday, known as PMIs, showed US private sector activity jumped unexpectedly to a five-year high in September.

Meanwhile, oil prices spiked 3.9pc on Wednesday to move back above $100 a barrel, risking an inflationary spiral in the world economy.

Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The main driver was a strong batch of PMIs, along with a rebound in oil prices, which both led to mounting speculation about faster rate hikes.” Here is what you need to know.

5 things to start your day

1) US borrowing costs hit highest since 2007 on fears economy overheating | Yield on 10-year Treasuries soars amid inflation concerns as oil prices rise

2) Diesel prices surge as Trump mulls 90-day US export ban | Pump prices could exceed £3 per litre in Britain if Washington imposes ‘catastrophic’ block on exports

3) England’s first new reservoir in 30 years delayed despite drought warnings | Havant Thicket, in Hampshire, will now be completed in 2034, five years after initially planned

4) Timpson customers ask for extra belt holes after weight-loss jabs | Boss of key cutting chain credits Ozempic and Mounjaro after surge in requests

5) Chinese carmaker’s new EV battery will charge in under five minutes | Geely says its latest system is fastest in industry as brands approach ‘physical limit’

What happened overnight

Debt markets were in turmoil after Japanese bond yields hit 30-year highs.

As Tokyo markets reopened after a three-day holiday, the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond yield jumped to its highest level since 1996.

This came after a steep sell-off in the US market overnight. Oil prices remained around $103 a barrel and the dollar held gains after Tehran’s leader vowed to never surrender following a warning by Donald Trump that he could “annihilate” Iran.

Japan’s benchmark stock market, the Nikkei 225 rose 1pc to 65,645.10, as some chipmakers got a boost from the recent interest in AI. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.7pc to 8,702.00.

Hong Kong’s Hang Seng lost 0.3pc to 24,762.39, while the Shanghai Composite dipped 0.9pc to 4,545.09. Trading was closed in South Korea for the Chuseok autumn harvest holiday.

News.title: Zelensky lashes out at EU
News.content:
Volodymyr Zelensky lashed out at the European Union over its moves to weaken sanctions on Russian oligarchs.

In his address to the UN General Assembly, the Ukrainian leader warned that beyond making life “more comfortable” for Russians, “it also gives the war more time for Putin to send poor people into the kill zone. So Russia’s revenues must remain a target.”

His criticism came after France and Luxembourg successfully pushed for sanctions exemptions for Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, Russian oligarchs, on Tuesday.

Kyiv branded the decision “shameful and unjustifiable”. The men are known to share close ties to Vladimir Putin and have net worths of $14bn and $16bn, respectively.

In his fourth address to the UN as a wartime leader, Mr Zelensky said it was paramount that the international community increased pressure on the Kremlin to stop “the madness” of the war spreading.

Under pressure from Donald Trump to halt attacks on Russian energy targets, Mr Zelensky defended his country’s aerial offensive for successfully depriving Putin of revenue for his war.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said.

‘End the war before winter’

Washington has recently attempted to revive the long-stalled negotiations between Ukraine and Russia. On Tuesday, Mr Zelensky implored Mr Trump to help Kyiv end the war “before winter”.

Mr Trump appeared optimistic, suggesting an agreement would happen “more quickly than people understand”.

Sergei Lavrov, the Russian foreign minister, told the UN Security Council on Wednesday that Russia was prepared to negotiate for a lasting peace but would not “pause the war”.

Mr Zelensky sought to remind world leaders that the conflict was not constrained within Ukraine’s borders at a time when the global community was distracted by a myriad of conflicts and crises.

Citing the support of Iran and North Korea for Russia, he warned that Putin’s war kept “spreading further”.

“Putin is always looking for someone who can help him kill more, kill more people for every kilometre of land, take more territory and take another country instead of simply stopping and running his own country,” Mr Zelensky said at the UN.

He noted that fighters from at least 47 countries were helping to prosecute Moscow’s war against Ukraine and urged leaders to prevent their citizens from being dragged into the conflict.

After Mr Zelensky’s address, reports emerged that Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, was on his way to the US where he would meet Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Trump administration representatives.

Sources told Reuters that the meeting would take place in New ‌York on the sidelines of the UN summit.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, also confirmed Mr Trump had invited his Russian counterpart to attend the G20 summit of world leaders in Miami in December.

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

Sports.title: Former England captain Steven Gerrard announces multi-million project for sport hubs in his hometown
Sports.content:
CHANGING LIVES Former England captain Steven Gerrard announces multi-million project for sport hubs in his hometown







Next

LIVERPOOL legend Steven Gerrard has announced a multi-million pound project for state-of-the-art sports hubs in his hometown.

The former England captain, 46, is set to pile money into community centres across Liverpool, including Huyton, where he played as a child.



The ambitious project will see world-class sports and educational facilities built in a bid to inspire youngsters across Merseyside.

Gerrard himself has made a “significant personal investment” to help deliver two major developments as part of the plans.



This includes a sports hub at Childwall Sports and Science Academy in Liverpool and a new centre at King George V Playing Fields in Huyton.

Gerrard’s project will see the creation of six new 3G football pitches and up to 16 padel courts.

Facilities will also be designed for schools and grassroots clubs, expanding access to sport, education and jobs.

The ex-Liverpool captain – who spent 17 seasons with his boyhood club – told how he wanted to “give something back” to the city.



He said: “Liverpool gave me so much growing up.

“I’ve always wanted to give something back to the city where I was born and the place I’m proud to call home.

“I’m investing in these projects because I believe in the difference they can make for young people.

“The ambitions are incredibly exciting. It is also fantastic to announce the plan for Huyton because it is not too far from where I grew up.

“Sport has the power to change lives. It builds confidence, creates opportunity and opens pathways into education, training and employment.



“We’ve seen that through the Steven Gerrard Academy already.

“Padel is one of the fastest-growing sports in the world.

“Bringing it into a school setting alongside world-class football facilities will give young people even more opportunities to get active, develop new skills and discover a sport they might never otherwise have tried.”

Sports.title: Man Utd star Patrick Dorgu goes viral for wild antics on Arsenal’s Martin Odegaard during Norway vs Denmark
Sports.content:
Next

PATRICK DORGU has gone viral for the bizarre way he tried to deal with Martin Odegaard.

Manchester United star Dorgu and Arsenal captain Odegaard faced off in their national team colours as Norway faced Denmark in the Uefa Nations League.



However, in the 70th minute of the clash with the score 2-2, Dorgu inexplicably appeared to try and pants Odegaard.

The 21-year-old was lining up on the right wing for the Danes when Odegaard skipped past him.



But rather than allow the midfielder to continue dribbling towards goal, Dorgu went about tackling him by grabbing the bottom of his shirt and pulling him to the floor.

Dorgu picked up a yellow card for the foul on the 27-year-old, but the incident left fans in stitches on social media.

One said: “What am I watching?”

A second said: “Dorgu wants to take Odegaard’s pants off.”

A third added: “Dorgu wanted Odegaard’s jersey at all costs.”



Another said: “Dorgu had to pull Odegaard for a long time to be able to stop him.”

Sports.title: Hairy Man Utd fan reveals the three words Ruben Amorim said to him after meeting former manager
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED’s hairiest fan has revealed the three words Ruben Amorim said to him at a chance meeting.

The United Strand, real name Frank Ilett, started a challenge on October 5, 2024, that he would not cut his hair until United‘s senior team won five games in a row.



That unfortunately coincided with the sacking of then-boss Erik ten Hag a few weeks later, with Amorim appointed as his replacement.

But what followed would be later described by Amorim as a “disaster season”, with the Red Devils falling to their worst ever finish in the Premier League and losing the Europa League final.



Frank exclusively told SunSport a few months into the challenge he did not expect United to struggle as badly as they did.

And Amorim’s ill-fated spell at Old Trafford plodded on with United not winning back to back league games until October.

Amorim, 41, was then sacked after 14 months in charge at the beginning of January 2026 following his eruption in a press conference calling out the club hierarchy.

Darren Fletcher and then Michael Carrick came in to finish the season, with the challenge looking like it might be completed in February under the latter only for the team to draw against West Ham.

The challenge remarkably remains incomplete two years after it started, with Frank’s wild barnet going viral for how incredible it looks.

But after being invited to the Portugal Football summit, Frank and Amorim ended up meeting.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

While the hairy United fan could have bore a grudge, he shared a picture of them smiling together and revealed what Amorim said to him.

Frank, who now has 1.5 million followers on Instagram alone, captioned his post: “Great to meet Ruben Amorim at the Portugal Football Summit.

“He saw me, pointed to my hair and said ‘sorry about that!’ Still have love for him!”

Frank’s challenge is seeing him raise money for the The Little Princess Trust and MIND UK.

He has raised over £11,400 since the challenge began.



The earliest United can win five in a row this season is October 25.

Sports.title: I’m an ex-Arsenal star who was scared to death of Didier Drogba – playing against Viktor Gyokeres wouldn’t even worry me
Sports.content:
Next

VIKTOR GYOKERES was by far and away Arsenal’s top scorer when they ended their 22-year wait for a Premier League title in May.

But not everyone is convinced he is good enough to be their long-term No9.



Former Gunners left-back Armand Traore was a student of Arsene Wenger and faced some of the English top-flight’s most legendary attackers.

He readily admits that Chelsea legend Didier Drogba scared the living daylights out of him.



And sharing a training pitch with Thierry Henry set the standard for how good an Arsenal striker should be.

After a season of watching Gyokeres, Traore reckons Arsenal are suffering with the Swede up top.

He told SunSport: “I’m not having Gyokeres at all.

“Arsenal would be better off with a striker that takes them in behind to create space to play.

“Gyokeres is like a plug inside a sink so they are forced to go on the outside, but that is easy to counter. That is why they relied on set-pieces a lot last year.”

Mikel Arteta may also need some convincing. The Arsenal boss is yet to start Gyokeres in the league this campaign, with Kai Havertz now the undisputed first choice through the middle.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Havertz may also lack Drogba’s fear factor, even if he partly makes up for it with intelligent play in the final third.

But Traore feels a big, physical frontman like Gyokeres, Traore feels he needs to be giving defenders more to think about.

He explained: “I always liked my strikers to be quite mobile.

“In my experience and my time in football, winning teams have always had a renowned striker, a Harry Kane, a Drogba, a Cantona. Even Jermain Defoe was an absolute joke for a while.



“Gyokeres, I just don’t get that killer instinct that some of these guys had.

“I played against Drogba many times. My lord. He had such an aura. It stinks of, ‘I’m a leader’. I don’t get that with Gyokeres or Havertz.

“If I was to play against Gyokeres I wouldn’t be worried. I was a very, very fast player. He could push it past me but there is no way he is getting past.

“Think of Thierry Henry and Gyokeres, it’s day and night. Try to play against Thierry, either way he goes it’s a problem. These players are a problem. Speed kills and I don’t see that Gyokeres is very quick.”

Traore, 36, retired from football in 2020, but he is gearing up to return to the sporting arena in a completely different discipline on October 22.



The former Senegal international is fighting fellow ex-pro footballer Sebastien Bassong in ‘A Night to Remember III’ – a charity boxing event masterminded by former Arsenal goalkeeper Graham Stack.

Stack and Co have already raised over £200,000 from their first two events, and are looking to surpass half a million.

Keen scrapper Traore said: “I boxed for about a year and a half and then I went into Muay Thai because I wanted to learn how to kick.

“I became more and more obsessed. It has become my new obsession ever since I retired.

“Combat sport has saved my life. In the mental health hole I found myself in, it gave me the structure to keep going. It made me feel unbelievable.”

HARRY KANE has been tipped by England boss Thomas Tuchel to star at the next World Cup — weeks before he turns 37.

The veteran Three Lions captain faces Spain in the Nations League on Saturday night.



And Tuchel said: “No problem, age is just age, it doesn’t matter.

The Wembley clash with the world champions represents the first step towards a home Euros in 2028.

But Tuchel believes Kane, 33, who has scored 85 goals for his country, will carry on through to the 2030 World Cup in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.

“He is so committed to the high press and being involved in every part of the match.

“Be it deep build-up, be it finishing, be it build-up play in the middle block, be it defending.

Kane is just four games away from equalling goalkeeper Peter Shilton’s record of 125 England caps.

Kane hit 73 goals for Bayern Munich and England last term — and is a contender for next month’s Ballon d’Or.

Sports.title: Chelsea in landmark fertility policy: 'Being a player and mum are both possible now'
Sports.content:
Chelsea are used to being the first. While plenty of that has come on the pitch, it is the behind the scenes work that is truly leading the way for female players and women's health.

Now, the Blues are the first team in the WSL to introduced new fertility and maternity policies, giving their players the choice to start a family in whichever way they want to, and the post-natal support to balance the demands of elite sport and motherhood.

The Blues were also the first club in the world to starting tracking menstrual cycles - introduced by Emma Hayes in February 2020 - and how they impact performance. This is the next step in that process.

What is the fertility policy? Chelsea have partnered with Fertility Plus - one of London's leading fertility clinics - to set up a fund accessible to all players in support of their fertility journey.



This includes egg freezing, IVF, smear tests and contraception, as well as counselling and workshops to give players everything they need to make informed choices



It is not an enforced policy and players can access it however they need with support from Chelsea.

What is the Player Maternity policy? The Player Maternity policy covers a wide range of support both during and after pregnancy, including:



- Personalised pregnancy and post-partum recovery support.

- Financial support for a partner or nanny to travel to away fixtures up to one year after a player’s return to playing.

- Enhanced adoption and parental leave policies.

- Wage support and subsidised childcare.

"As a club, it's always been really important for us to support our players the best way possible," Chelsea head coach Sonia Bompastor exclusively told Sky Sports.

"We want to be a club who always supports the players to have more knowledge around different opportunities... it's more for them to be able to make a choice and a decision about what they want for them.

"Every player is different, every individual is different, they have a different journey and you can make a choice based on what you know and what is available for you.

"You don't have to choose anymore between your professional career and your personal life being a mum. Now, both are possible."

Chelsea have partnered with leading London fertility clinic Fertility Plus - and former goalkeeper and commercial manager for the women's team, Carly Telford, has led the way it that collaboration.

She exclusively told Sky Sports: "I've seen first-hand the kind of experiences that women, girls and athletes have when it comes to making choices around fertility and I wanted us to be a leading club in that.

"I wanted to find someone that understood us as athletes first, but also understood us as women and what that comes with. I wanted to find a fertility clinic that offered more than just egg freezing and more than just optional things, but to give choices around hormones, endometriosis, cycle tracking, testing - something all-encompassing around the female body.

Image: Carly Telford is commercial manager for the women's team and a former goalkeeper

"Then what the players do with that is completely up to the individual. That was really important to the club and to the players in terms of having options outside of their careers for how their families or how the individual look at themselves.

"It brings comfort and a thought process that we as a club are looking at them differently and are treating them as people as well as footballers. They will give their whole bodies to this club for the amount of time they're with us and it's an extra option for them to think about themselves.

"It's an important thing to have that every club should be looking at, the league should be looking at, the FA should be looking at in terms of making sure that women have a choice when it comes to their whole body and what that looks like during and after their careers."

Chelsea is one of the best clubs in the world. A lot of people are looking at us, so we should always aim to be the best ones, the pioneers and try to push everyone with us. We want to be the first ones on many things and making sure we help the players in the best way possible, as well as for the future of the game.

'I thought there was only one way for me to becoming a mum and be a footballer'

Bompastor herself has four children with her partner, Chelsea assistant coach Camille Abily. She always knew she wanted to have a family, but a lack of options during her own player career led her to believe there was only one way for her to have children.

"When I reflect on my own story and experience, I didn't really have the choice," she explained. "I wanted to have a really good career as a player and I decided to carry on and to finish maybe a little bit earlier than what I should have done because I also wanted to become a mum and have a family.

"With the knowledge I had in that moment and everything that was available for me, I thought it was almost the only way for me to do that, because when we talk about becoming a mum when you are still an athlete, there are lot of questions to answer.

Image: Sonia Bompastor had her children after her playing career - but says she may have retired earlier than she needed to do so

"It's about the pregnancy, but also everything after that. How can you look after your kid when you are an athlete and you play at the highest level? All these things were really difficult questions for me and I didn't have all the answers.

"Now, to have a club who is able to support the players, bringing them the knowledge, allowing them to talk about that subject is really important for us and giving them different opportunities to become a mum when they decide to. I'm really proud to be the head coach at Chelsea and to offer that opportunity to the players."

'Players are feeling comfortable with new policies'

No Chelsea players have yet revealed their intention to use the new resources available to them which, of course, should remain their own private decisions.

But Telford - who remains close with the squad from her own playing days - gave some insight into how the policies have been received.

She explained: "We touched base with some of the players and I'm lucky enough to be friends with a lot of them, so I leant on a few of them just to see what they felt about what this would look like for them. A lot of the feedback was 'this would be really good, keep us across it'.

"As soon as we knew the deal with Fertility Plus deal was close, we informed the leadership group who then informed the team and since then, we've had a lot of good feedback. The players are feeling very comfortable with it and then how they act upon that based on their own individual needs.

"Any information will confidentially be shared amongst the doctors at Fertility Plus and the doctors within the club and it will stay like that."

Chelsea have had pregnant players before. Melanie Leupolz had a baby in 2022 before returning to play for the club, while Zecira Musovic moved back to Sweden in June 2025 before giving birth later that year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking in 2023 while at Chelsea, Melanie Leupolz told Sky Sports the support offered by clubs to their pregnant players is improving

Telford said their pregnancies made her and the club consider how older players in the squad might be approaching their fertility and future families. For example, former Blues captain Millie Bright recently announced her pregnancy having retired from playing earlier this year.

"The 30-plus-year-olds are probably the last group of women that have had to maybe put those things on hold," Telford hopes.

How the policies work in tandem to offer players options

Ultimately, the two programmes offer players choice in whatever they decide, whether that is to start a family or looking after their gynaecological health. There is a clear link between fertility and maternity care and the two will work in tandem to give the players the support they need.

Bompastor said: "Having a family is something no one can teach you. You just learn to be a mum when you have your first child and even if someone is trying to tell you how you have to deal with the situation, you only learn when you have a baby.

"Having the opportunity to have platforms where you have information you can share with different people who already experienced that is already a big thing.

"Also, giving the support to players after having a baby. They need that because when you are a high-level athlete and you become a mum, those are two full-time jobs and you need that support to be able to do both at your best level.

"All these elements are really important for the players to have, but also for them to know there are different opportunities and they are available for them."

Having the Player Maternity Policy means we're thinking of the whole cycle of them as people and players and we're looking after them in every aspect of their life. That is so important because the more they're thought about as people, the happier they are as footballers and ultimately, we want them to perform all of the time.

'All women should know about their bodies'

While Chelsea's announcements are player-focused, Telford is hoping that the club's profile can help raise the importance of women's health across the board.

She explained: "We want to be followed for the things we're doing around the team that have a wider impact when it comes to women in general and that's the impact that our sport has.

"We're very lucky to play one of the most popular sports in the world and be part of one of the biggest clubs and biggest brands. If we can make businesses, other football clubs and other sports think differently around their women, that is what we want to do.

"As women, we need to take more control of ourselves and have more viewership of what our bodies are doing, what they look like during womanhood and how that changes in terms of genetics, lifestyle, all these things that impact our bodies.

"And it's not just the athletes. They take a bigger toll on their bodies because of what they do, but general womanhood and what that looks like for us, that is the thing that I wanted to echo outside of football.

"I would have loved to have known more about my body for lots of different reasons while I was playing - how I get the best out of it as an athlete, what it's like during menstruation, what it's like in terms of longevity of my cycle and fertility and what that looks like moving forward, the options I then have during my career and what it looks like later on in life and in my career.

"Now they have that, I am really proud of it. I do hope this sparks a big conversation around what that looks like, not just for the future of women's sport, but for the future of women in general."

Sports.title: Why Spain test is 'pivotal' for Tuchel's England project
Sports.content:
England go again. After World Cup heartbreak this summer they kick-off their Nations League campaign against Spain on Saturday at Wembley.

The arrival of the world champions in the capital will be a painful reminder of what England were so close to achieving in North America - and re-exposes the scar, as boss Thomas Tuchel put it - of the mistakes made late on in that semi-final loss to Argentina.

Tuchel has been eager to highlight the positives of England's campaign at the World Cup, insisting the experience and bonds built through the tournament leave the group well placed to kick on and achieve success in the Nations League and then at Euro 2028.

However, while Tuchel retains the firm backing of the FA, who handed him a contract extension through to the end of the European championships prior to the World Cup, Sky Sports News football correspondent Rob Dorsett says the clash with Spain could be key in determining the path ahead.

"It's massive, and for me, it feels like a pivotal moment for Thomas Tuchel," Dorsett told Sky Sports' Peter Smith during a special Essential Football podcast at St George's Park this week.

"If they lose it, then the media will be gunning for Thomas Tuchel and saying, 'Hang on, you couldn't beat Argentina, you can't beat Spain, all right, you won against France, but that was a dead rubber, a meaningless third and fourth place playoff - you're supposed to be the big man who comes in and wins the big games.

"I think there's an awful lot at stake and an awful lot for England to play for."

Tuchel has since suggested he may have to "embrace the chaos" and lean into English football's traditional strengths of more physical, direct play - a sentiment similar to the one he had when he first took charge.

"Tuchel said this when he took the job," explained Dorsett. "Before he got anywhere near taking an England training session, Thomas Tuchel said he thought England's players, when they put on that England shirt, play with fear. And he said, 'my mission is to take the handbrake off'.

"He's now saying the same things again after the World Cup, 18 months into his tenure. I think he knows - and we certainly know - that he put the handbrake on against Argentina and he got it wrong.

"Hearing Anthony Gordon speak in the way that he has, I think will be music to Thomas Tuchel's ears. He'll be very, very relieved that a really important player for England shares his feelings."

Sports.title: Alcaraz felt burnt out after too much exposure on and off the court
Sports.content:
Carlos Alcaraz has admitted feeling burnt out due to being exposed to a lot of commitments before he suffered a lengthy layoff due to an injury sustained in April.

The Spaniard, who won the Australian Open title at the start of the year, was forced to miss more than four months from tennis because of a right wrist injury.

Alcaraz returned at the US Open where he reached the quarter-finals before losing a five-set thriller to American Ben Shelton, which finished at 3.33am local time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the US Open quarter-final between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch this incredible point from the match between Alcaraz and Shelton in New York

Due to the demanding nature of the calendar, the former world No 1 has said he plans to take longer breaks from the game in the future and skip some tournaments.

"With the breaks I cannot plan them in advance," Alcaraz told Sky's Jacquie Beltrao at London's O2. "It depends how I feel mentally and physically.

"The tennis calendar has been super tight. There are more important tournaments and even more Masters 1000 events over two weeks, so it's pretty long. You have to be focused from the first day until the last, plus all the Grand Slams and everything else so it depends on how many matches I've been playing.

"If I'm injured or mentally a bit down I'm going to need those breaks. I realise it will be better to take it before getting injured."
