Alcaraz also revealed he felt physically and mentally exhausted before being forced to miss the French Open and Wimbledon through injury.

"You expose yourself in every tournament, but not only when you go on the court, it's every time you go out for dinner, the people who stop you, the people rolling with the cameras. Sometimes that is hard to deal with when you expose yourself at that level," the seven-time Grand Slam champion said.

"Mentally, it's hard to deal with. That's why sometimes I have to stay at home alone or with my close people around.

"Home is my peace. When I can chill and be myself. With my friends and family."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Alcaraz decided to change his US Open outfit due to a series of nip-slips during his games!

Alcaraz admits he needs a more balanced lifestyle knowing he could return from his intended breaks out of practice.

"Yes, I could be," he added. "That's why I have to plan it in a good period of time. Every time that I go to tournaments I want to be able to enjoy them.

"I don't want to feel like 'I have to go there and play there because I have to' - it's because I want to and that's a really important feeling for me.

"Sometimes things have to be missed and I want to miss tennis sometimes."

Murray: I understand it from the players' perspective

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Naomi Broady, Ryan Harrison and Jamie Murray discuss Alcaraz's future schedule after he admitted he'll be taking more breaks from the ATP Tour

Speaking to Sky Sports Tennis, Jamie Murray said: "I can totally understand it from the players' perspective. The Tour is longer than it's ever been in terms of commitment and days away from home.

"These younger guys have seen how Roger [Federer] and Rafael [Nadal] have elongated their careers - how they finished their careers as well. If they want to play until they're 34, 35, 36, they will probably have to skip tournaments and that's something the Tour needs to consider.

"The Tour is catering for over hundred players and they want to be out there competing."

“The Fifa president has now acknowledged the need for reform, but it is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE – fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within Fifa, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference.” Share

Sports.title: João Félix strike for Portugal enough to sink Wales but Ronaldo fever falls flat
Sports.content:
There was a comic-strip feel to another eventful evening in the kingdom of Cristiano Ronaldo. Where to start? It was the 67th minute when his No 7 went up on the fourth official’s board, the cue to remove the captain’s armband from his left bicep before departing to a universal ovation, but for the pocket of Wales supporters.

The referee, Donatas Rumsas, hurried him off the pitch but Ronaldo, his hair glazed copper, was presumably ruminating on a series of missed chances, a sitter from a few yards at the start of the second half, and his disallowed goal, after skating offside to latch on to a Bruno Fernandes pass. The grandiose “Siu” celebration went to waste, though try telling that to the locals who worship him.

In the end, Portugal began their defence of the Nations League with a narrow victory courtesy of another Al-Nassr forward, João Felix’s deflected first-half strike from the edge of the box beating Danny Ward in goal.

Many of the Wales squad have been lightly raced of late, but they could have snatched a late equaliser when Brennan Johnson hit the crossbar and Rúben Dias desperately denied Lewis Koumas, who again impressed Craig Bellamy. For Wales, this was an exhaustive physical effort and afterwards the head coach, citing his own experiences as a player, referenced how mentally sapping games against elite opposition can prove. “I needed an ice pack on my head,” Bellamy said.

All eyes were on Ronaldo, back playing in Lisbon for the first time since last October, at the José Alvalade Stadium where he made his name as a teenager. The 41-year-old started, as Jorge Jesus promised he would, and despite Ronaldo talking of a new era, different tactics and even a different language, alluding to Jesus’s predecessor Roberto Martínez, this all felt rather run of the mill.

Rúben Neves, another player in Saudi, replacing João Neves in Portugal’s three-man midfield was the only change from their World Cup last-16 exit by Spain in Dallas.

Ronaldo finished with 27 touches, the fewest of any of Portugal’s outfield starters, and looked to the heavens after fluffing the best of the hosts’ chances to extend their lead four minutes into the second half.

View image in fullscreen Cristiano Ronaldo sends a shot wide on a night when good fortune in front of goal eluded him. Photograph: Miguel Lemos/Eurasia Sport Images/Getty Images

Neves put in a delicious cross from the right flank but Ronaldo, unmarked and alone with his thoughts in the six-yard box, shanked the ball over off his left shin. Sunday’s visit to Norway is his next opportunity to edge towards his 1,000 goals target. “I took him out 25 minutes before the end, because I thought it was important to have a fresh player on the pitch,” Jesus said. “I knew that Cris could stay a little longer, five or 10 minutes, but I was going to take him out anyway, I had planned it.” In a previous answer, he added: “Some players who are important were not up to their quality.”

Jesus, who twice managed Benfica and spent three years here in charge of Sporting, knows all about Ronaldo, having spent last season coaching him at Al-Nassr and defended the striker on the eve of this game, describing him as a symbol of Portugal. It is hard to disagree on that front. Ronaldo-mania is omnipresent in Lisbon, chiefly inside the official Portugal stores in Praça da Figueira, the city’s downtown, where you can buy CR7-branded briefs, face masks, action figures, lanyards, Lego, and even a Ronaldo boxset celebrating his time at Sporting.

Bellamy accepted Wales would suffer against a starting XI boasting five Champions League winners and three Ballon d’Or nominees, but began confidently. Bellamy does not have the same quality at his disposal, with Harry Wilson, Wales’s best performer in recent years, and Karl Darlow, these days the undisputed No 1, among those absent through injury. A harmless Ben Cabango header was Wales’s sole effort at goal in the first half and they did not trouble Diogo Costa. “He practically didn’t have to touch the ball,” Jesus said of his goalkeeper.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Ronaldo spurned four decent chances in the first half alone, the best of which was from about 12 yards and left him scuffing his boots in frustration. Then, after a predictably excitable buildup, there was a free-kick flighted into Wales’s yellow wall. He should have done better when Fernandes presented him with his first opening amid huge cheers from the locals, but his touch was rusty and the ball bobbled off his left foot, and he later volleyed wide from an awkward angle.

Wales were valiant. Jay Dasilva was excellent at left-back. Ben Davies, a Wales centurion and always a dependable performer for his country, marshalled the defence on his second appearance of the season, his only minutes for Tottenham coming against a Charlton B team in the Carabao Cup. Ward’s sole appearance was in the same competition for Wrexham six weeks ago.

Portugal racked up 23 shots but recorded only five on target and Wales will take plenty of confidence from this slender defeat. “I’m fully aware of who we were playing and what their value is,” Bellamy said, claiming the value of Portugal’s squad totals £1.4bn. “But the positive I’m coming away with is: I think there’s more [to come from us]. I’m beyond proud. We showed a big heart.”

Sports.title: Raphinha: ‘In my head I was leaving Barça, but a few small words can change you’
Sports.content:
For once, Raphael Dias Belloli puts the brakes on. The man who seems to be in perpetual motion, a footballer forever on fast forward, pauses, goes quiet for a moment and then, softly, utters something that says so much: “I think maybe people saw in me something I didn’t realise was there.” He did not know he was a leader, but he likes it. He did not know he was a captain, but according to his manager he is the “perfect captain”. And he did not know he was a No 9 either, but right now he is the best No 9 there is. In Barcelona or anywhere.

There was a time when Raphinha did not know whether he would be in Barcelona, when, feeling unwanted, he had accepted it was over, but this week he extended his contract to 2030. He will be 33 then: he would like to retire here and they would like him to retire here, too, a legend built on empathy and affection. “This is the best decision the club has made,” said Hansi Flick, the head coach Raphinha says changed his life. Sometimes you cannot get what you want so you have to settle for the best.

The first word Raphinha uses when training has finished and the tape starts rolling at Sant Joan Despí, when he is addressed as the world’s top No 9, is “false”. It comes with a smile; turns out there is nothing false about this 9. Seven games into the league season, the man filling in at centre-forward has scored 12 goals, plus two in the Champions League. The scorers leading the way in Europe’s other top leagues are five behind. No one in Barcelona’s history has started a season like this. And, no, Raphinha says, he has never played there before: “Even as a kid I wasn’t a 9.”

As if it is even about the goals. There may be no one as enjoyable to watch as Raphinha; no one as admirable or important either. The touch at speed is astonishing and there is a wild intensity about everything he does, only it is not wild, he says; it is worked upon, the entire system depending on him. The press defines Barcelona’s identity and it is, Raphinha says, “mechanised”. No, he is not going to reveal how but it begins with him. “As captain, he goes and everyone follows,” Flick says. “We always start with the No 9 and he has that incredible hunger and intensity, the mentality and attitude we need.”

Yet this is not what Raphinha or anyone expected. This summer Robert Lewandowski, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford departed, having contributed 38 league goals between them last season. They were supposed to be replaced by Julián Álvarez but Atlético Madrid refused to sell, leaving Barcelona with no striker. “There was a moment of need,” Raphinha says. “There was no No 9 for the [friendly] against Basel, so I played there.”

Raphinha backs Lamine Yamal to win Ballon d’Or – video

It was not supposed to be permanent, although Flick suspected it might be and was warming to the idea: Barcelona had not given up on Álvarez yet and the coach considered other solutions, including Anthony Gordon. This was better. Raphinha did not score but Barça got five.

“In pre-season we did a few tests: the manager liked what he saw and after Basel he told me a bit about his idea,” Raphinha says. “The adaptation came over the last two years, getting used to coming inside, closer to goal. But we tested [me as] an actual No 9 and it went well. There’s the occasional detail that has to be explained, but I’m OK. Before Elche [on the opening day], he asked if I was comfortable there or wanted to go back to my position. I said it was fine, see how it goes, we can always change back.”

Raphinha scored two against Elche, one against Athletic, two against Rayo and another at Valencia. Against Racing there was a hat-trick and another against Sevilla: right foot, left foot, header. Raphinha showed his old qualities and new, less expected ones: the movement, timing and clinical finishing of a classic No 9, efficiency to go with the intensity. Only one La Liga player has a better shot conversion rate. Against Feyenoord came two more.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha (right) is joined by Lamine Yamal – the player he says he is a ‘big brother to’ – after scoring during the Champions League match against Feyenoord. Photograph: Judit Cartiel/Uefa/Getty Images

Nor is it just about him. The point of Raphinha is that it is not even about him. Only once this season has he not scored, and against Levante he created the first two, then handed over the penalty for Lamine Yamal to add the third. Barcelona have scored five, two, five, five, five, four, seven and three, respectively in winning their first eight games.

Flick had done it again. “I always have and always will say that he changed my mentality, changed me as a person,” Raphinha says.

By 2024, Raphinha was convinced he had no future at Barcelona. His numbers were good: 10 goals and 12 assists in his first season, 10 goals and 13 assists in his second. But Lamine Yamal was emerging and, more importantly, Raphinha did not feel backed, completing 90 minutes seven times in 60 games under Xavi Hernández. It had not escaped his attention that Barcelona thought about selling him; it had not escaped anyone’s attention that they wanted to buy Nico Williams, publicly keen to reunite the pair that tore up the Euros.

Barcelona failed twice, and were all the better for it. A Photoshopped image of Williams in his No 11 shirt on social media hurt, Raphinha admitted. But Flick had arrived and if there is something even more powerful than the desire to prove people wrong, it is the desire to prove people right.

View image in fullscreen Raphinha fires in his team’s fourth goal in the 5-2 win against Rayo Vallecano. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“In my head, I knew I was leaving,” Raphinha says. “That was [mentally] done, that’s the truth. I was in Brazil and Flick called. He said come talk to him before taking a final decision. I met him and he said he trusted in me, that I was going to be important, that the team[’s play] would be good for me. In a moment like that, a few small words can change you. I felt a lot of faith in me. He gave me the confidence to play my football. I got an idea into my head: give everything, your life, regardless of the personal moment you’re in.”

Love won out, even if Raphinha is swift to add: “If you get results people are going to love you; if not, they’re not.” Feeling supported and valued changed everything. His success is a human story, his qualities human ones. He led Barcelona to the league. Flying in from the left, Raphinha scored 34 goals and provided 26 assists in 57 games. Another title followed in 2025-26 and although injuries reduced his contribution, there were 21 goals and eight assists in 33, Flick’s faith gratefully repaid.

His teammates’ faith, too. The dressing room had voted Raphinha as a club captain, third in line. He had not expected it and was genuinely touched. There was something in that moment, in the realisation of how they felt about him, how much they believed in him, that was transformative. Now Flick has named him his first choice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen A jubilant Raphinha with the trophy after winning the Spanish Super Cup against Real Madrid. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

That moment brings pause, thought. “When I saw people had voted for me, it was like a switch had been flipped, a shift in mindset,” he says. “People could see something in me I didn’t realise was there, and that’s changed me. Before being captain, I didn’t know how much I would like it. Having that responsibility has also changed my mentality, helped me. I never thought I’d like being Barcelona captain so much. You feel you matter. It’s an honour. It’s not just wearing the armband.”

He is a natural, as pure a captain as there has been since Carles Puyol – even if he did need to be told. It is there in the relentless example he sets: Raphinha has sprinted the second-furthest distance in La Liga and Gradient Sports has measured only three players with more final-third pressures per 30 minutes out of possession. Raphinha says: “I talk less than most captains but I know people are watching. They think: ‘If this guy’s running like an animal, I have to follow.’. If you talk too much and then don’t do what you have to, people aren’t going to listen.”

Yet what teammates saw in him went deeper, to his very being. Leadership is there in the empathy, kindness and understanding too, in Raphinha returning the support that was good for him, an approach at once collective and individual. He says he can see when Lamine Yamal is drifting from games and how to reconnect him, every celebration shared with the teenager. A clip went round recently in which he quietly tells Gordon not to be afraid. And no clip was more powerful, more eloquent, than the moment when Flick sat on the bench, alone, lost in his thoughts and Raphinha consoled him, drawing him out of his dark place, roles reversed.

View image in fullscreen Fermín López, Raphinha, Lamine Yamal and Anthony Gordon celebrate their team’s third goal against Valencia. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

“The coach-player relationship is the most important in football,” Raphinha says. “From the moment [Flick] arrived, we could talk to him about anything – and anything is anything. That time, I saw him, head down. At first, I didn’t really understand why. I asked what was wrong. He said he felt the team wasn’t playing well. From what I remember, I told him it was OK, we’d won and we would play well again. I prefer a thousand times to win playing badly than lose playing well. Win games, confidence and the football comes.

“What kind of leader [I am] depends on the moment. If I have to be slightly tougher, I can. But I prefer nicer moments, jokes. The last two years have been spectacular so I haven’t had to be the pesado [pain in the arse] often. I know that annoys people but someone has to do it sometimes.”

With a squad like this, especially? Four of Barcelona’s first team were born in 2007. “Buah!” Raphinha says, laughing. “That hurts: it shows I’m closer to the end than starting out at 18, 19, like them. But I’m in spectacular physical shape so [retirement] is some way off. It’s very easy with them. There are young players but they’re very responsible about their career, their lives. Once in a while, you have to [be paternal] because they’re kids. But they understand. If they get told off, they know it’s for their own good. I’ll tell them.”

View image in fullscreen Raphinha, pictured at the Barcelona training complex, is thriving in the role of captain. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Is there something of the father figure in him with Lamine Yamal in particular? “No, no,” Raphinha jumps in. “Big brother, that’s better.” And Lamine Yamal is the star who should win the Ballon d’Or, he says: for his “individual numbers, collective titles, and the magic on the pitch, charisma. There’s no doubt. For me, he has to take the prize, no matter what. Even if I wasn’t Lamine’s teammate, for what he does, the numbers, the titles – and I think titles are important – he’s the candidate. One of one. Of three trophies, he won two with Barcelona. He won the World Cup with Spain.”

Only the Champions League escaped them; for two years Barcelona have come close, and it is their obsession now. “The semi-final against Inter [in 2025] hurt the most,” Raphinha says. “Against Atlético [in the quarter-final in 2026] we could have gone through, we could talk about things that could have gone differently, decisions. But against Inter, we had one foot in the final and to lose that way was hard. We’re a young team – that’s not an excuse – and sometimes you lack the maturity to manage key moments. This season we’re more mature, better prepared. If we carry on like this, with this mentality, we can compete for it all. We have everything.”

Starting from the front with the captain, the leader and the No 9.

Sports.title: Gakpo denies Klopp perfect start as Xavi’s Netherlands rescue draw against Germany
Sports.content:
At least Germany can be sure it will not be dull. Jürgen Klopp had predicted his debut as head coach could be wild, a trait he would accept as long as his team were lively enough. Both transpired in a frayed, pinball-like game whose lack of quality could be forgiven on account of its entertainment levels. The Netherlands more than merited a brilliant late equaliser from Cody Gakpo and by the time those present had drawn breath it felt appropriate that, for all the talk of new dawns, everyone finished back where they had started.

World domination is a far-off prospect for both of these flailing giants on such scrappy, frenetic evidence. But at least those with a stake in this famous old fixture, largely shorn of the spite and spit that defined it of old, could come away feeling something. Restoring those essential sensations of joy, pain and meaning sits at the very top of Klopp’s priorities. Germany looked raw and scattergun for long periods, reined in only by their lack of technical aptitude, but there were signs of an energy that had long been missing.

Nonetheless it was the more understated Xavi, making his own bow in charge of the hosts, who could punch the air in added time after Gakpo volleyed in a wonderful outside-of-the-boot cross from the substitute Ruben van Bommel. It so happens that the 22-year-old Van Bommel is son of the 79-times capped Mark; his grandfather is the former Netherlands manager Bert van Marwijk. An enthusiastic if largely toothless performance from Xavi’s crop was a reminder that the stardust of Van Bommel senior’s day is largely absent now; the equaliser’s conception, though, left lingering promise that the past can birth a brighter future.

“In a parallel world, if someone said you’d get a draw in Holland you’d take that,” Klopp said. “I feel we lost two points because of the time we conceded. But I’m fine with tonight, not more.” His approach to squad management across this four-game Nations League run had been to unveil a sprawling 44-player squad, a handful only passingly familiar even to some seasoned Bundesliga watchers, that would be split between assignments. His plans, and perhaps those of two club managers he must keep onside, were derailed by concerning injuries to Jamal Musiala and Kai Havertz.

The former felt his thigh in the warm-up, Nadiem Amiri taking his place in the starting lineup; Havertz was similarly afflicted early on, departing on the half-hour, and the pair were due to have MRI scans before returning home. “I hope we get the diagnosis tonight, I hope it’s nothing serious,” said Klopp, who expected the pair to at least miss Sunday’s match against Greece.

His team had begun with the intensity demanded before riding their luck, Virgil van Dijk unfortunate not to put one over his old boss when his glancing header was ruled out for a soft foul by Brian Brobbey on Marc-André ter Stegen. The Netherlands were further aggrieved when, with Brobbey lying on the floor near halfway requiring treatment, Joshua Kimmich elected to play on and set in train the move that opened Klopp’s account. The debutant right-back Philipp Treu crossed for Karim Adeyemi to attempt a close-range shot and, from the rebound, Felix Nmecha swept in.

View image in fullscreen Felix Nmecha finds the back of the net from close range to give Germany the lead. Photograph: Dean Mouhtaropoulos/Getty Images

Van Dijk led impassioned home protests, which turned into scuffles between the sides on the far touchline, but no laws had been broken. Germany should have doubled their lead when Adeyemi spooned Nathaniel Brown’s pass horribly high, Klopp reduced to grim laughter at the side, but Xavi’s players took charge thereafter.

“The second half is the way we must play,” Xavi said. “We want to show this ambition, passion and desire.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Ter Stegen, playing at his new Ajax home, frustrated his old Barcelona manager with commendable saves on numerous occasions while looking consistently jittery under set pieces. He should have finally been beaten when Max Meerdink, on for the stricken Brobbey, somehow diverted Denzel Dumfries’s centre wide from a matter of feet.

Germany were brisk but bereft of control in a scruffy but beguiling second period; much of that could be put down to their new broom but it will surely have irked Klopp that the substitute Serge Gnabry, one of his more experienced call-ups, had presented the ball carelessly to Van Bommel before the leveller.

“To develop a way of football you need more than two days,” Klopp said. “We only scratched the surface. We have to go deeper.” For better or worse, this taster was enough to promise a compelling ride ahead.

Sports.title: James Garner keen to live up to ‘mini-Valverde’ tag after late England call
Sports.content:
“It’s a very good comparison,” James Garner says, and he is not kidding. It came from Thomas Tuchel in March after the England manager had watched the Everton midfielder impress on his international debut against Uruguay. He was up against Federico Valverde and Tuchel went big with his praise. Garner was a “mini Valverde”, he said after the 1-1 draw at Wembley.

It was surely too much, despite the prefix that Tuchel attached, yet it was possible to see where he was coming from. Like Valverde, Garner wants to operate in central midfield but he can play at right-back or on the wing. And like Valverde, who they called El Pajarito – or the Little Bird – when he was a kid, Garner can sometimes fly a bit under the radar.

Is Valverde the most underrated player in the game? The more the question is asked, the more the point is lost but there is certainly something there. “You wouldn’t really call him a household name, would you?” Garner says of the Real Madrid player. “But players who have played the game – they know how good he is. I watch a lot of football. I watch all the Champions League games and he always stands out. So yeah, I would go as far as saying that he’s underrated. In my opinion, he’s one of the best midfielders in the world.”

The pros know. And within the game, there is a burgeoning appreciation of Garner, who located such outstanding form at Everton from the turn of the year that he won his first England call-up and was considered unlucky to miss out on the World Cup squad. In the end, Tuchel went with Jordan Henderson and Kobbie Mainoo as the midfield back-ups to Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson. Henderson played six minutes as a substitute during the tournament; Mainoo not at all.

“It was a tough phone call [from Tuchel] because you don’t know whether it’s a yes or a no,” Garner says. “He just said that he could only take a certain amount of players and I’ve missed out this time. I respect his decision and it just makes you hungrier.”

View image in fullscreen James Garner impressed on debut against Uruguay but missed out on the World Cup. Photograph: Alex Davidson/The FA/Getty Images

The 25-year-old is back in the squad for the upcoming Nations League fixtures, albeit as a late call-up after the withdrawals of Rice and Mainoo. Henderson was not picked on fitness grounds. Tuchel recalled Alex Scott and Myles Lewis-Skelly in his original selection and continues to overlook Adam Wharton. Anderson stands as the most established midfielder as Tuchel prepares for the visit of Spain to Wembley on Saturday night. Thereafter, England play Czechia and Croatia away before returning to Wembley to face Czechia.

Garner flew to Bodrum in Turkey on Sunday night for a holiday with his partner and he had just put the key in the hotel room door when he got the call from the Football Association. He flew home on Monday before reporting to St George’s Park on Tuesday. “It was a very short holiday,” he says with a smile. “I’m more than happy to be here now.”

Tuchel also gave a late call to Morgan Gibbs-White, who had just got to Dubai for a family holiday. The Nottingham Forest attacking midfielder made a lighthearted TikTok video in which he and his fiancee mimed Gotta Go My Own Way from High School Musical 2 as he packed up and headed back. Was Garner tempted to do something similar? “No. That’s not me,” he replies.

Garner is no-nonsense. He is laidback company but there is a toughness to him on the pitch, a warrior spirit to go with the intelligence of his game, the technique and range of his passing. Growing up in the Manchester United academy, he played as a centre-half until the age of 15 and his boyhood hero feels appropriate.

“I’ve never actually said this but I used to love Nemanja Vidic,” he says. “I used to love the No 15 [which Vidic wore] and things like that. Then you grow up a little bit more, I became a midfielder and I used to love Lampard, Scholes and Gerrard.”

Garner made the move into midfield with United at a junior tournament. “It was the Nike Cup and our midfielder got injured in the first game,” Garner says. “I’ve always been half-decent with the ball at my feet so they thought: ‘We’ll push him into midfield.’ I had a really good tournament and it just went from there. Albeit when I was with England under-16s and under-17s, I played centre-back.”

He is a student of the game. “I watch all matches and also, as mad as it sounds, I played Fifa for so long,” he says. “I’ve been so indulged in football since I was a kid. My brother is five years older than me, he played and I’ve always been around football. I was lucky enough to come through United’s academy, which is one of the best academies in the world, and I learned so much from a lot of good coaches. I’ve just always had that tactical awareness and maybe that helps me playing different positions.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Garner could not see a first-team pathway at United. They loaned him to Watford for six months, then Forest for 18 months. The writing was on the wall for him in the summer of 2022 when United bolstered their midfield with the signings of Casemiro and Christian Eriksen. His move to Everton for a bargain £9m still rankles with a section of the United support.

View image in fullscreen James Garner has no regrets over leaving Manchester United and joining Everton. Photograph: Gary Oakley/Everton FC/Getty Images

“It was the perfect thing for me to do – 1,000%,” Garner says. “I’ve never been shy of going into a more uncomfortable place, changing scenery or anything like that. I went on loan. I moved down to London and Nottingham. It was about playing games and Everton was the perfect choice. I didn’t want to fizzle into the background and just sit on the bench. I wanted to go to a team where I felt like I had a chance to fight for my position.

“Do I have any regrets about leaving United? No, not really. I am a big believer that everything happens for a reason. Had I stayed I wouldn’t have been where I am today so I am more than happy that I left.”

Garner made a statement on the international stage when he starred for the England under-21s in their European Championship triumph of 2023. He was named in the team of the tournament – as a right-back, which was where he played in the final when England beat Spain 1-0. He hopes to make another against the same nation.

“Spain have got the Ballon d’Or winner in their midfield [Rodri] so to play against someone like that is the ultimate test,” Garner says. “You want to go against the best and see how you fare.”

Sports.title: Israel’s Saied Abu Farchi sent off for corner flag celebration in defeat by Austria
Sports.content:
Israel’s forward Saied Abu Farchi was ⁠sent off as a result of his goal celebration against Austria in ⁠his side’s 3-1 ​Nations League defeat on Thursday.

Abu Farchi headed home in the 55th ⁠minute to bring Israel level after ​Austria had ‌taken the lead ‌through a Romano Schmid penalty before ‌half-time at the Raiffeisen Arena in Linz.

The 20-year-old ran to the corner flag, grabbed it and went down on one knee before continuing his celebration. Some reports suggested Abu Farchi used the corner flag to simulate a gun but he appeared to be mimicking a snooker cue. He has previously posted on social media: “It’s all a celebration of snooker.”

View image in fullscreen Saied Abu Farchi after scoring his side’s equaliser against Austria. Photograph: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP/Getty Images

The ‌referee had booked Abu Farchi four minutes earlier and showed ​him a second yellow card for the celebration, leaving Israel with 10 players.

Austria regained ⁠the lead in the 90th minute through ​Phillipp ​Mwene, who scored via Paul ​Wanner’s cross. ‌Sasa Kalajdzic ​added ​a third in stoppage time with a close-range finish.

Israel’s head coach, Ran Ben Shimon, was quoted by Austrian media as saying: “Abu Farchi celebrates all his goals in this way – you can check that. Perhaps it was my fault that I didn’t tell him he needs to stop. He must learn from this. It is also a big lesson for us.”

The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat in Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina. The buildup had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which the Ireland manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly. The home side saw two shots cleared off the line before the Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhín Kelleher clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrímsson’s side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland, who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday, showed plenty of spirit as they dug in for the second half, but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when the Kosovo captain, Vedat Muriqi, bundled the ball in from close range.

In a Group A4 match, Norway’s ‌Erling Haaland struck twice, including a 74th-minute winner, to edge his team past Denmark 3-2 in Oslo and earn their first competitive win over their opponents.

“It tasted sweet. It feels great to beat our neighbours,” the captain, Martin Ødegaard, said. “There is a lot we could have done better, but ​even when we were put under pressure, we found a way back and responded.”

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland scores to put Norway 2-0 ahead against Denmark Photograph: Ulrik Pedersen/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock

The Danes had powered back from a two-goal deficit and levelled the game on the hour after first-half goals from Oscar Bobb and Haaland had put the hosts 2-0 up. Norway were also left with 10 men in stoppage time after David Møller Wolfe was sent off for receiving a second booking.

There was drama in Belgrade where Greece came from a goal down to snatch a 2-1 victory over Serbia thanks to Tasos Douvikas’s winner deep in stoppage time. Malta came from behind to beat Andorra 2-1 in their League D clash, while Lithuania won 2-0 in Liechtenstein.

Sports.title: Former England player Andy Carroll reveals he was sexually assaulted in 2021
Sports.content:
The former England forward Andy Carroll has revealed in his autobiography he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021. The 37-year-old included the details in his book, Owning It. As a victim of sexual assault, Carroll was automatically granted anonymity.

Carroll revealed the incident took place at his home during a second spell at Newcastle. The offender – a friend of his former partner, who was staying away at the time – was later jailed for three years, with Carroll having testified in court.

The former Liverpool and West Ham striker, who is now a player/co-owner of the National League South club Dagenham & Redbridge, said the incident happened when he was sleeping. He then threw the man out of the house, then knocked him unconscious when he attempted to get back inside.

“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now,” wrote Carroll, who had decided to include the incident in his book “at the very last minute” after discussing it with his partner, Lou Teasdale.

“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not. I avoided my publisher for so long that they probably suspected I got cold feet.

“Scary to talk about but it’s made [me] the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”

Carroll said testifying in court, where the attacker was found guilty of sexual offences and placed on the sex offenders register, was “humiliating and embarrassing and absolutely horrendous”.

The 37-year-old said: “What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football … The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”

Sports.title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Max Rushden
Sports.content:
Disclaimer: I have made a lot of bad TV programmes. I have done quite a few below-average radio shows. Podcasts, there are millions of them – some might say too many – and I’ve done my fair share that won’t go down in history. In between those, I’ve hopefully done some pretty good ones – it’s not for me to say.

I have had good ideas and the odd great one that didn’t make it to air (attention the full-size unreferenced post-Keys and Gray elephant in the Soccer AM studio). I’ve had more awful ones. I’ve hosted shows where I’ve had almost complete editorial control, and ones where I could have been replaced by a performing monkey.

I’ve had to host TV shows at every possible height – sitting on a sofa, on a normal chair, on a normal chair behind a desk, on a bar stool in a pub, on a bar stool not in a pub, and standing up when there was somewhere comfortable to sit just out of shot. I complained a lot, but standing did actually work, Murray.

The point being, I have some experience when it comes to reviewing the opening night of the Disney+ coverage of the Women’s Champions League. The Hangout was hosted by Alex Scott with her fellow former England international Lianne Sanderson, the content creators Tyra Mills and Alex Bailess, and quite inexplicably a golden retriever called Barley Boy, who at the time of writing has 82,000 more Instagram followers than I have – I must work on my reels.

The show included a quiz about Italy, including guess the Italian name for football and what pasta the reporter in Milan is cooking. There’s an incredible still image of the panel staring at a load of farfalle on a big screen normally reserved for team lineups or key match incidents.

The immediate reaction was a mix of bewilderment and fury from seasoned lovers of the women’s game. Kathryn Batte wrote an understandable critique for the Telegraph. The broadcaster Flo Lloyd-Hughes posted on X: “Disney’s new UWCL coverage is the closest we’ve seen to CBBC football (derogatory). I wouldn’t be surprised if we see someone gunged for making a wrong prediction or perhaps Raven will make a cameo. Keep stopping to remind myself this isn’t a dream.”

Consistent with all the criticism is the truth that the men’s Champions League would never be covered in the same way. It is perhaps interesting to ask how the team arrived at the concept. Why replace former pros with content creators, why replace tactical analysis with asking what’s the biggest city in Italy? Why a dog?

The broadcaster Marva Kreel perfectly articulated one of the issues in her own X post: “I think a lot of the problem with the debates in women’s football broadcasting over analysis and punditry v content creation and gimmicky fun, is that in men’s football you can get both – and in different shows. In women’s football you get one show, and so they try to do it all.”

It’s a fair point. I’ve mainly hosted the show before the show – where a dog running around wouldn’t be regarded as a crime against the game. In fact hosting live football is significantly more straightforward than interviewing an indie band about their difficult second album or trying to come up with a three-hour radio show in the middle of the international break. The show Disney tried to make on Wednesday is technically much harder than Super Sunday – but that doesn’t mean it was the right call.

I can understand the thinking. I imagine the bosses told the producers they want to bring in a younger audience. I have been told this before. Exactly how to do that is impossible to work out. Should I stop making references to Jossy’s Giants and Aswad? And Disney could probably argue that most of the criticism didn’t come from young people. It came from people who expect the game to be covered in a certain way.

(From left) Former England international Lianne Sanderson, content creators Alex Bailess and Tyra Mills, and golden retriever Barley Boy. Photograph: Disney+

Disney may be being cynical – people are talking and writing about it. The hardcore will watch anyway. Had they produced more traditional coverage, no one would have said anything. And sometimes you have to try something different. I wouldn’t want to be too critical; Disney may give me a gig one day.

Major broadcasters have less money to make the same amount of stuff – and have had a battle over the past 20 years to work out how to harness social media. I saw it at Sky, where a Facebook livestream filmed on an iPhone in the green room would get as many views as the show itself with the costs of studio/lighting/sound/producers etc.

As a middle-aged man – whose wife accuses him of being a “boomer” – I really dislike the phrase “content creator”; perhaps I’m nervous that eventually they’ll take all my jobs. From what I saw, Bailess and Mills came across as very personable and fun – which was clearly the brief – and you can’t criticise anyone for taking a job. And they bring a following with them – quite how many followers lead to subscriptions is a different question.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

I feel for Scott, who perpetually finds herself in the middle of some sort of culture war. You are entitled to regard her as the greatest or worst broadcaster of her generation – or somewhere in between – as you are with me or anyone else. I know many listeners certainly feel the latter about my abilities.

I found the discourse around the end of Football Focus pretty troubling – people suggesting the show went woke and lost its way when she was appointed. It’s much more accurate to accuse me of turning Soccer AM woke, with my clarinet, lefty snowflake opinions and inability to flirt on live television. But then I’m not a woman and I’m white; generally people just accuse me of turning it shit.

But back to the Hangout. I imagine Scott didn’t suggest having a dog in the studio or having guess the pasta. Perhaps she has a lot of editorial control – I genuinely don’t know. But sometimes as a host you have to do what you’re told and do it with conviction.

The reality of live football coverage is that people are watching because they want to watch the game. If people want comedy, they’ll watch Curb Your Enthusiasm. If Liverpool are playing Real Madrid, the fans will watch it – and either enjoy or endure the coverage. But what you can do as a broadcaster is make it as compelling as possible, and there are different ways of being a good host or pundit.

Live football coverage hasn’t changed dramatically in 50 years. Welcome, team news, managers, bit of tactics or player focus, throw to commentators. Half-time: what did you make of that? Full time: what did you make of that?

The dog did not return for the second night of coverage. I know it would have been a strange and difficult day for everyone involved. They made a show, people didn’t like it and they had to go again the next night. Do you double down, screw the haters, or try to subtly move towards a more traditional setup? It seemed on Wednesday they went for the latter.

You can’t magic up an audience, but you can make people feel like you respect the game, you can do it in an entertaining way without introducing animals, and people will come back and watch you again.

Sports.title: The young star about to break out at your PREM club: From the rapid Zimbabwean signed via Instagram and an 18-year-old flying Gloucester wing, to a Scottish farmer, the 23-stone Italian and Exeter's 'physical monster'
Sports.content:
The young star about to break out at your PREM club: From the rapid Zimbabwean signed via Instagram and an 18-year-old flying Gloucester wing, to a Scottish farmer, the 23-stone Italian and Exeter's 'physical monster'

The new PREM Rugby season kicks off on Friday, and with it comes a chance to shine for a host of talented youngsters.

When defending champions Northampton Saints host Newcastle Red Bulls and Harlequins meet Bath tomorrow night, the usual stars from Henry Pollock to Ollie Lawrence will be front and centre. But there will also be a number of new faces who could catch the eye of rugby fans.

Here, Daily Mail Sport’s Nik Simon and Alex Bywater pick 10 potential PREM stars – one from each club – to watch out for this term…

EDWARD SIGAUKE

Age: 22, Club: Harlequins, Position: Wing

The young Zimbabwean could be one of the feelgood stories of the season. He was playing university rugby in Johannesburg last year and signed for Harlequins after the club’s head of recruitment sent him a message on Instagram.

A quick look through his highlights reel showcases the winger’s raw ability to turn defenders inside out with his speed and footwork.

Idolising Cheslin Kolbe and Darcy Graham, the 22-year-old scored with his first touch in pre-season.

The electric Edward Sigauke of Harlequins scores in pre-season against Edinburgh

SIONE VA'ENUKU

Age: 26, Club: Saracens, Position: Centre

Ever since Manu Tuilagi moved over to France in 2023, English rugby has been on the lookout for powerful centres.

Va'enuku played rugby league for the Sydney Roosters before moving to the UK in 2024. He is English qualified and joined Saracens through the club’s partnership programme with Ampthill.

Following the departure of Alex Lozowski to Sale, the hard-running Tongan, 26, should get his fair share of game time in the PREM.

The hard-running Tongan centre Sione Va'enuku should get plenty of game-time for Sarries this season

ALLAN FERRIE

Age: 26, Club: Newcastle Red Bulls, Position: Flanker

Ferrie is primed to make his top-flight debut at the age of 26 after signing a two-year contract at Newcastle over the summer.

He hails from Scottish farming stock and is a late bloomer in the professional game. Ferrie spent a year playing amateur Shute Shield rugby in Australia before signing for Coventry, scoring 14 tries in 24 appearances.

He is a wildcard recruit for the big-spending Red Bulls but he has already impressed with his powerful, athletic ball carrying.

Newcastle's Allan Ferrie hails from Scottish farming stock and is a late bloomer in the professional game

JAMES PATER

Age: 19, Club: Northampton, Position: Full-back

The emergence of Pater at full-back is one of the reasons Northampton allowed George Furbank to join Harlequins.

Phil Dowson has not spoken so glowingly about a young player since Henry Pollock broke through.

Last season, Dowson said of Pater: ‘James always looks like he has time on the ball. He reads space exceptionally well, he’s strong under the high ball, his passing is top quality, he’s not afraid to carry the ball into contact or take defenders on and he finds gaps you don’t think are there.

'He’s brave defensively, too. He’s calm, unfazed and remarkably composed for someone so young. His ceiling is incredibly high.’

The emergence of James Pater (centre) at full-back is one of the reasons Northampton allowed George Furbank to join Harlequins

FINN CARNDUFF

Age: 22, Club: Leicester Tigers, Position: Flanker

There is a rich history of abrasive forwards coming through the Tigers academy and Carnduff could be the next cab off the rank.

He captained England Under 20s to their World Cup triumph in 2024 but his development has been stalled by injuries.

The 22-year-old is a lineout-jumping flanker who could step up as Leicester’s pack adapts to life without George Martin and Hanro Liebenberg.

Leicester's Finn Carnduff scores against Quins in the PREM Rugby Cup this month. He captained England Under 20s to their World Cup triumph in 2024

ENOCH OPOKU-GYAMFI

Age: 20, Club: Bath, Position: Lock/No 8

This time last year another young Italian in Edoardo Todaro emerged from nowhere to star on the wing for Northampton. Opoku-Gyamfi, 20, is another Azzurri man who could do likewise.

Despite still being a fringe player for his club, Opoku-Gyamfi has already worn the blue shirt of his country at senior Test level.

A sports performance student, he also helped the University of Bath to silverware last season but is set for bigger things now.

Bath’s pack is ageing so head of rugby Johann van Graan needs to bring through fresh blood. At more than 23 stone and 6ft 5in, you can't miss Opoku-Gyamfi!

At more than 23 stone and 6ft 5in, Bath's Enoch Opoku-Gyamfi is hard to miss!

ZACK WIMBUSH

Age: 22, Club: Exeter Chiefs, Position: Centre

At 22, Wimbush has been around the Exeter set-up for a few years now without ever really cutting the mustard.

When he was loaned to spend time with Cornish Pirates, it looked like his time as a Chief might be up. But Rob Baxter has seemingly kept the faith and the way Wimbush set up a try for Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in a pre-season clash with Cardiff showed exactly what he is about.

Wimbush has pace and power. He’s a monster physically.

With Australian superstar Len Ikitau now departed, Exeter need someone to step up in midfield and Wimbush could be that man.

Zack Wimbush has pace and power and is a monster physically. This could be his time

DOM HANSON

Age: 20, Club: Sale Sharks, Position: Scrum-half

Alex Sanderson’s Sharks have signed a plethora of exceptional new talent, mainly up front in the likes of Courtney Lawes, Nicky Smith and Tomas Francis. Centre Joe Marchant is a big arrival, too.

Highly-rated former Chiefs and New Zealand scrum-half Xavier Roe is likely to start at No 9, but in that position Hanson, 20, could well emerge as a surprise package.

He’s been tipped by experienced Sale and England playmaker George Ford to have a big season and Ford is a man who knows his stuff.

Hanson suits a fast-paced game and there might be pressure on Sanderson to deliver exactly that after a turgid, underwhelming campaign last time out.

Dom Hanson could emerge as a surprise package at No9 for Sale this season

JUNIOR DENNY

Age: 18, Club: Gloucester, Position: Wing

The Cherry and Whites have recruited well with the likes of Jac Morgan, Dewi Lake and Jean Kleyn.

But there is real excitement at Kingsholm about the development of 18-year-old wing Denny. He was a stand-out performer for Gloucester at age-grade level last season and in the build-up to the new PREM season, he scored a try on his PREM Cup debut against Bristol.

Anyone who was at that game went home raving about his performance and so too did George Skivington. ‘

Junior did really well,’ said the Gloucester boss. ‘He’s a real one for the future. We’ve got a lot of hope for him. He’s a really good lad, really humble, and wants to work hard and make an impact.’

There is real excitement at Kingsholm about the development of 18-year-old wing Junior Denny

AIDAN BOSHOFF

Age: 20, Club: Bristol Bears, Position: Wing

If it hadn’t been for injury, it is likely Boshoff would have been selected for senior Wales involvement last season by their head coach Steve Tandy.

Louis Rees-Zammit is the Welsh winger at Bristol who gets all the headlines. But Boshoff, 20, is a coming force in the same position.

The mullet-haired Aidan Boshoff, 20, plays on the wing for Bristol and is a coming force

Boshoff got a taste of the PREM last term after impressing for Wales Under 20s and will only get better for that experience.

He has an interesting background, too, having spent much of his childhood in Cape Town and later attending the prestigious Clifton College.

He's hard to miss with his mullet haircut!

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher urges Man United NOT to sack Michael Carrick and give him at least two more MONTHS to turn his struggling team around
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher has urged Manchester United to stick by Michael Carrick despite their poor start to the season. He insists that Carrick should be allowed the full campaign to restore 'calm' to the club before potentially 'passing the baton' to somebody else. United have made their joint-worst start to a Premier League season ever with a mere five points from their opening five games, and some concerning performances thrown in. Gary Neville raised the alarm over what he saw as their 'disgraceful' lack of effort in their 1-1 draw with Fulham at the weekend, but pointed the finger at the players more than his former team-mate. Now Carragher has thrown his weight behind Carrick, telling The Overlap Fan Debate: 'I think it would be ludicrous to get rid of Michael Carrick. 'I don't see Michael Carrick as the Manchester United manager in the long term. I almost feel like he's in there doing a job for the club to get them through a rocky period and then passing the baton on. Jamie Carragher says Manchester United should stick by Michael Carrick despite a tough spell Manchester United have made their joint-worst start to a Premier League season 'If that sounds disrespectful to him, I don't mean it like that. He came in, and Manchester United needed calm, they needed not being a circus, not being a banter club. 'His results have been unbelievable since he's come into the job over the long period. He got the job on the back of that. The fact he got them in the Champions League brings the money. 'Manchester United need to be a Champions League club again. It's not about, wow, we're going to win the league this year. They need another season of just making sure you get the Champions League, and then it'd be a case of bringing in one of the top managers about who could manage a club at that level. 'I don't think the idea of changing Michael Carrick now or at the next international break makes sense. It just needs to be relaxed, just let him get on with it.' Despite a disappointing start to the season, with United 12th in the Premier League, Carrick's overall record with the club is quite strong. He has won 14 of his 24 matches in charge, drawing and losing five each, and last term guided them to third in the table after taking over from the disastrous Ruben Amorim. They recently endured a nightmarish seven-day period with three blows: first a defeat to Manchester City in the derby, then a loss to Brighton after throwing away a two-goal lead in the Carabao Cup, then the draw at Fulham where they lacked cutting edge. Matheus Cunha was only able to score in that game thanks to a wicked deflection off David Affengruber, but they did have 25 shots, which suggests they can be creative. The club has picked up just five points in five games, with some disappointing performances Neville found the performance abysmal, telling Sky Sports: 'I rarely say teams don't make an effort because that's the ultimate criticism. That first 15 minutes of the second half, and generally the first 60 minutes, United were an absolute disgrace. ‘I’ve watched Man United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen. Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort. ‘There needs to be a reset in terms of structure. They don't want to do the ugly part of the game. ‘I've never seen a Manchester United team walk as much as that. Michael (Carrick) needs to stop defending them. 'If they carry on like that, they will concede so many goals week after week. They were lucky to concede one. 'I just see apathy and ambling around the pitch. They can all work harder than that- they're getting outrun in every match.' After Cunha scored a late equaliser – heavily deflected off David Affengruber – to cancel out a disastrous own-goal by team-mate Lisandro Martinez, the forward admitted that United only woke up once Fulham went ahead. ‘In the second half it was like they put in more energy than us,’ he said. ‘We cannot accept this. We always play better after conceding a goal, and it cannot be like this.’

Sports.title: The next 007? Tennis star Carlos Alcaraz channels James Bond in a sharp tuxedo as he returns to London after missing Wimbledon
Sports.content:
The next 007? Tennis star Carlos Alcaraz channels James Bond in a sharp tuxedo as he returns to London after missing Wimbledon

Tennis sensation Carlos Alcaraz channelled his inner James Bond on Thursday night as he donned a black tuxedo at an event in London.

The 23-year-old Spaniard returned to the capital for the Opening Night Gala ahead of the 2026 Laver Cup, and spoke to reporters at the O2 Arena following his US Open campaign.

There, he reached the quarter-final before losing to home favourite Ben Shelton, with the game finishing at 3.30am local time – the latest ever finish to a game at the tournament.

He found himself throwing up in a towel at his first tournament since a four-month absence from tennis due to a wrist injury, but dusted himself down on Thursday to attend the event in London - the scene of the Wimbledon tournament he missed this year.

'With the breaks I cannot plan them in advance,' Alcaraz told Sky at the event. 'It depends how I feel mentally and physically.

'The tennis calendar has been super tight. There are more important tournaments and even more Masters 1000 events over two weeks, so it's pretty long. You have to be focused from the first day until the last, plus all the Grand Slams and everything else so it depends on how many matches I've been playing.

Carlos Alcaraz channelled his inner James Bond as he attended the Opening Night Gala for the Laver Cup

The 24-year-old posed in a tuxedo after returning to action at the US Open following a wrist injury that kept him out for four months

The likes of Arthur Fery (left) Alexander Zverev (third left) and will also be involved in the event

'If I'm injured or mentally a bit down I'm going to need those breaks. I realise it will be better to take it before getting injured.'

Alcaraz took in the attention as he carried out some Bond-style poses, including making a gun sign with his hand.

He will be representing Team Europe at the tournament, but may have his sights on a new career in acting after his appearance in the capital.

'You expose yourself in every tournament, but not only when you go on the court, it's every time you go out for dinner,' he continued. 'The people who stop you, the people rolling with the cameras.

'Sometimes that is hard to deal with when you expose yourself at that level. Mentally, it's hard to deal with. That's why sometimes I have to stay at home alone or with my close people around.

'Home is my peace. When I can chill and be myself. With my friends and family.'

The Laver Cup will take place at the O2 from Friday to Sunday, with Team Europe also including US Open champion Alexander Zverev and former world No2 Casper Ruud.

Team World, meanwhile, includes the likes of Taylor Fritz, Alex De Minaur and Brandon Nakashima.

Brit Arthur Fery has been included as an alternate in the European team.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight leaves Luke Littler furious - as he rages at promoter Eddie Hearn for putting the Battle of Britain on same night as the darts at Ally Pally
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight leaves Luke Littler furious - as he rages at promoter Eddie Hearn for putting the Battle of Britain on same night as the darts at Ally Pally

Luke Littler has spat his dummy out after the Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua fight was scheduled for the same night as the World Darts Championship opener.

The 19-year-old defending champion will play in the curtain raiser of darts' biggest tournament on December 11 at Alexandra Palace in London.

But Joshua and Fury's much-anticipated event will take place on the same night at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium.

In reality the two will only do their ring walks at around 2am on December 12, in order to accommodate an American audience, while Littler would be in action well before midnight.

But The Nuke, a big boxing fan, fumed on Instagram: 'A message to the Hearns (promoters): what is this?

'Opening night of the World Championship (world champion plays on opening night 11th December) and you put one of the biggest fights in Britain on the same night.

Luke Littler has hit out at Eddie Hearn over the Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury fight scheduling

'You had one job' said Littler as he vented in front of his 2.1 million Instagram followers

He then backtracked and claimed he had been joking after receiving a negative reaction

'You had one job.'

A couple of hours later, having received a negative reaction, he added: 'Why's everyone so sensitive it's literally a JOKE cmon guys.'

At least the bout does not coincide with the final of the tournament in early January, when Littler will be hoping to make it three world titles in a row.

He has won more than £3.1million in prize money over the past couple of years according to the Professional Darts Corporation Order of Merit – but that sum is dwarfed by what Joshua and Fury are set to bank.

It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York.

Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff.

The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown.

Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York.

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects

Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight.

Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans.

'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.'

Netflix confirmed on Thursday the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK.

Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation,' alongside an emoji of the British flag.

His promoter Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.'

Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua.

The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil.

Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen.

Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away.

Sports.title: 'The England snub was the wake-up call I needed': OLLIE LAWRENCE on the frustrations of last season, why he's now raring to go, the latest on his Bath contract and how wedding season came at a good time for Johann van Graan
Sports.content:
For a man who wasn’t away with England, Ollie Lawrence had a particularly busy summer.

Six of Bath’s first-teamers – Lawrence included – tied the knot during the off-season, so the squad jetted around Europe to multiple celebrations.

‘There was basically a wedding every weekend, so I think the gaffer (Johann van Graan) had quite a headache trying to organise pre-season fixtures and training,’ Lawrence tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Myself, Will Muir, Beno Obano, Finn Russell, Ted Hill, Will Stuart. There aren’t many left now! It was a packed wedding season.

‘I got married in France at the back end of August, an hour or so north of Bordeaux. We spent a couple of days there. Anthony Watson, Marcus Smith, Cam Redpath and Joe Cokanasiga were groomsmen.

‘Coming back from weekends away, there were a couple of tough pre-season training sessions on a Monday morning but we got through it! We held up our end of the bargain with Johann.

'Everyone’s pretty settled now and the gaffer probably prefers that to all of us being single! I don’t know how different the environment would be if we were, but it’s more like a family vibe at the club now.’

Bath centre Ollie Lawrence had a busy wedding-filled summer but is raring to go ahead of the new season

Lawrence tied the knot with his partner Emily in France. 'Everyone’s pretty settled now and the gaffer probably prefers that to all of us being single!' says the 27-year-old

Lawrence, 27, is hoping to show similar stability on the pitch. Bath missed out on major trophies last season and the centre slipped out of Steve Borthwick’s immediate Test plans.

He had been primed for a British & Irish Lions call-up last year but ruptured his achilles playing for England and was sidelined for more than six months.

‘As a whole, I wasn’t really happy with how last season went for me,’ he says. ‘Coming back from my achilles injury quite quickly, I felt really good. Everything seemed to be going really well but I had a bit of a wobble after the autumn. A few injuries set me back and then I didn’t really feel like I could get rolling after that.

‘I wasn’t really playing to my potential, which was frustrating. A bit of it was physical and a bit of it was probably going through the motions. When I’m at my best, I know I can really be an addition to this side.

'This summer is probably the first time I’ve had a full pre-season in five years and that’s been good for me. Before this, I had a few niggles in my knee and I probably wasn’t accelerating as quickly as I wanted to. Having an off season, letting everything calm down, can help with that.’

Lawrence describes missing out on England selection for the summer’s Nations Championship games with South Africa, Fiji and Argentina as ‘frustrating’.

‘I had a chat with Steve and hopefully I can see some reward from it,’ he says. ‘I wouldn’t say it was a kick up the a**e – I didn’t take it personally. I didn’t deserve to go on that tour.

'I hadn’t played to the level I’ve shown over the last few years, whether that’s for club or country. Maybe it was the wake-up call I needed in terms of realising I needed to get my body back to where it was and firing on all cylinders.’

'I didn’t deserve to go on that tour,' says Lawrence about missing out for selection for England's summer matches against South Africa, Fiji and Argentina

Lawrence suffered an achilles injury during the 2025 Six Nations that ruled him out for six months and it affected his form last season

Ahead of the new PREM Rugby season, England’s top league is shaping up to be more competitive than last year, although Bath remain the biggest threat to Northampton’s title defence.

They have the most valuable squad of players, boasting an international-standard backs division with the potential to take on the biggest clubs in Europe.

Yet their performances petered out last season, losing their home play-off against Exeter after failing to score off a 40-phase stand in the final play. They have lost the ball-carrying clout of Thomas du Toit and Alfie Barbeary, but they have brought in attack coach Mike Prendergast to improve their finishing power.

‘The messaging hasn’t been too dissimilar to previous years,’ says Lawrence, who has also lost his enhanced elite player squad contract with England after falling down Borthwick’s pecking order.

‘Yes, we wanted to win the PREM and the Champions Cup but it wasn’t a bad season for the club. We got to the semi-finals and we had opportunities to win both those games that we lost. We just missed a beat.

‘We’ve had a few coaching changes. We’ve all got the same goal to win the league and there’s going to be a lot more competition, so we just want to get better. Mike came in on the attack and the detail he’s brought has been really good.

‘We discussed the semi-final in the first week and looked at a few bits, then we just parked it. You don’t want to dwell on the past. I didn’t watch the semi-final back but we went through a lot of phases at the end and that’s a prime example.

'It’s nobody’s fault but we just need to be better. We tapered off at the back end of the season and we weren’t putting teams away. We were allowing teams to creep back into games.

‘The main thing is our accuracy and our skill level. Mike knows he’s got a talented group to work with. It’s holding ourselves accountable to our skill accuracy and making sure we pull the trigger when we need to.

'Knowing when the forwards go to work and when we need to get the ball to the backs. There are small cues. There are changes to the maul so it’s utilising that and getting the ball into the backs’ hands when we need to.'

Lawrence wants to hit the ground running with Bath after an injury-hit season last time out

There is plenty to play for. Contract season is upon us and almost all of Bath’s centres – Lawrence, Redpath, Max Ojomoh and Louie Hennessey – are free agents next summer and will be looking to renew terms. The market tends to loosen up in World Cup years, providing players with an extra financial incentive to prove their worth.

‘I’m enjoying my rugby here and I’d love to stay,’ admits Lawrence. ‘As long as the gaffer wants to keep me and (club owner) Bruce Craig wants to keep me then I should be all right. What will be will be.’

Their new season starts today, away to Harlequins, and the finish line feels a long way away. Contracts, trophies and World Cup selection are all on the line. Lawrence might not have been awarded a central contract but Borthwick has been in constant contact.

‘The World Cup is in the back of my mind,’ says Lawrence. ‘Having a full season probably gives you the best chance, but my priority is these first six or seven games for Bath. Start fast, get moving, get some wins on the board and play some good rugby. I might not play the autumn. I might not play in the Six Nations. Who knows?

'But there’s a lot of rugby to be played before the World Cup next year. The main thing for me has been getting back to fitness and enjoying my rugby again.’

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo's night of frustration: Portugal star, 41, has goal ruled out, misses HUGE chance and is subbed off in narrow win over Wales
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo endured a frustrating return to Lisbon as the veteran forward missed a golden chance and had a goal disallowed before being substituted in Portugal's 1-0 win over Wales. Ronaldo, 41, had admitted in the build-up to the Nations League tie that he had considered retiring from international football after Portugal's World Cup exit in the summer. The star has instead opted to continue his international career and captained defending Nations League winners Portugal in Lisbon, where he initially made his name 24 years ago. While Ronaldo led the line in Portugal's first match under new coach Jorge Jesus, his Al-Nassr team-mate Joao Felix scored the opening goal with a deflected effort in the 22nd minute. Ronaldo went close to doubling Portugal's advantage in the early stages of the second half. After pulling away from Wales' defenders, Ronaldo looked set to provide the finishing touch to a Ruben Neves cross from six yards out. Cristiano Ronaldo endured a frustrating night in front of goal as Portugal overcame Wales Ronaldo, 41, missed a golden chance at the start of the second half before finding the back of the net to seemingly double Portugal's lead The star was ultimately left frustated when his effort was ruled out by VAR for offside Ronaldo, however, only proved able to steer a left-footed volley over the bar and ultimately found himself lying frustrated in the goalmouth. His moment then appeared to have arrived in the 58th minute as Ronaldo ran onto a through pass before finishing past Wales' goalkeeper Danny Ward. Ronaldo ran away to the corner flag and performed his iconic celebration, only for his joy to be dampened by a VAR check. Portugal fans jeered and Ronaldo waved his arm in frustration when the goal was ultimately ruled out for offside, with the forward having made his run too early beyond the last defender. His frustrating night came to an end in the 67th minute when he was substituted to a standing ovation, with Goncalo Ramos coming on in his place. Portugal, who had missed several openings to extend their lead, survived a scare when a Brennan Johnson shot hit the woodwork before Lewis Koumas' follow-up was blocked. The hosts would hold on to secure a narrow victory on Jesus' first game in the dugout. Post-match, Jesus explained his decision to substitute Ronaldo, stating that he needed a fresh forward to press from the front. Ronaldo was substituted to a standing ovation in the second half on his return to Lisbon Portugal boss Jorge Jesus claimed he needed a fresh attacker to press up front 'That's what the game dictated, there were 25 minutes left and I needed to have at least one player who was fresh to press the build-up play,' Jesus said. 'I might not have had, technically, in offensive terms, the quality that Cris has to appear and hold the ball, but I knew that Goncalo [Ramos] would provide defensive speed right in our first defensive line, which is important. 'That's pretty much what I did, also because technically he didn't have that many plays. 'But anyway, I'm satisfied with the team.'
