Sports.title: Chaos in the Football League as international call-ups force postponement of matches involving THREE lowest-ranked sides - and key target is missed
Sports.content:
Tighter rules imposed to minimise lower league postponements during international breaks have missed the target with more games off than at this time last year, including those featuring the three lowest ranked teams in the EFL. The League One programme has been ravaged with 16 of the next 24 fixtures off to accommodate national team call-ups. Five games in League Two are also postponed over the next two weekends, including Port Vale against Northampton, who are ranked 90th and 91st. It all seems self-defeating with complaints forever swirling around congested fixture lists and at a time when clubs could feast on greater exposure and bigger crowds without Premier League and Championship action. New criteria were brought in this season enabling clubs to apply for a postponement if they expected at least three players to be on duty for senior, Under-21, Under-20 or Under-19 internationals but only if those players had appeared before the 75th minute in 50 per cent of league games or four of the last five first-team games. This is more stringent than last season, when the limit was also three players but with the qualification rules applied only upon the U21, U20 and U19 – not the seniors – and if players started in 25 per cent of league games or in three of the last five first-team games. The League Two match between Northampton and Port Vale, who lie 22nd and 23rd in the table, is one of several postponed in the EFL due to international call-ups There is a slightly different protocol for goalkeepers, with clubs allowed to request a postponement if both the first and second choice goalkeepers are called up. League One leaders Bradford City are without two goalkeepers with regular number one Jon McCracken in the Scotland squad and Zac Hadi called up by Iraq U23s but Cameron Dawson, McCracken's deputy, is available. Bradford have confirmed their game at Reading will go ahead on Saturday, October 3 but the home game against Barnsley on Saturday has been called off by the visitors, who have Patrick Kelly with Northern Ireland, Tyrese Noslin with Curacao, Jonathan Bland with Wales U21s and Makenzie Kirk with Northern Ireland U21s. Reading's opponents Wycombe will also be without their number one 'keeper Conor Hazard, who is with Northern Ireland. The prospect of two games against teams with deputies in goal may explain some of the thinking behind Reading boss Leam Richardson's decision to play on despite three call-ups from his own squad - Charlie Savage for Wales, Andy Rinomhota for Zimbabwe and Jeriel Dorsett for Montserrat. 'Football is a squad game, and we have confidence in the players available to us, while keeping the fixture in place also helps us avoid adding another game to an already busy schedule,' said Richardson. 'It's better for the supporters too. Saturday afternoon is the ideal time to play football whenever circumstances allow, so we were pleased to keep this one in place.' It is not one dimensional. Some clubs want to play on for their own reasons and like the idea of a break for different reasons. Reading will play on despite having international call-ups and could take advantage of their next two opponents missing their first choice goalkeepers With seven on international duty, five of them first team regulars, it is difficult to see how Luton could be expected to play. This season's changes were made with an eye towards the congested schedules and in the hope of keeping more EFL fixtures on where possible. On a financial level, few clubs in the third tier like to lose Saturday afternoon games which are generally better attended and more lucrative than rearranged evening dates in midweek. But there is an inevitable balance to strike with all managers under pressure to win and reluctant to take the risk with some of their better players unavailable and possibly making selections and substitution decisions with the qualification rules in mind. Crawley Town, rock bottom of League Two, are not playing because of call-ups for winger Dion Pereira with Antigua and Barbuda, left-back Jonny Russell with Northern Ireland Under-21s and goalkeeper Nicholas Michalski with England U20s. Michalski, 19, on loan from Blackburn has been first choice for Crawley since veteran former Arsenal keeper Vito Mannone, 38, was injured in August. In last year's September international break eight of the 12 League One fixtures went ahead with a full set in League Two. In the October break last year there were seven of 12 League One games on and only one game off in League Two. There are different reasons in play. Former Premier League clubs Leicester City and Sheffield Wednesday are in League One this season, with bigger academies and appeal for talented youngsters on loan from the top-flight looking for experience. There is an increase in lower-league players searching out international football via ancestral links. And, for the first time, this year's international break is extended to cover two weekends featuring more games and bigger squads.

Sports.title: How Jurgen Klopp fared on his return: Fresh squad approach pays off and why he will already empathise with club managers as Germany are saved by technology he wants to scrap!
Sports.content:
How Jurgen Klopp fared on his return: Fresh squad approach pays off and why he will already empathise with club managers as Germany are saved by technology he wants to scrap!

Jurgen Klopp missed out on his first win as Germany manager with Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo scoring the stoppage-time volley which denied him.

It was a fine finish from Gakpo and an equally exquisite cross from Ruben van Bommel after Serge Gnabry had given away the ball in the build-up. That ensured the Netherlands, now managed by Barcelona and Spain legend Xavi, avoided losing in Amsterdam.

A draw was the deserved result at the end of what turned into a nasty Nations League clash. The tackles were flying in, though there were two apparent muscular injuries which will have a pair of Premier League managers concerned. Kai Havertz of Arsenal and Brian Brobbey of Sunderland – both of whom have started every league game for their clubs this season – needed substituting. It was while the latter was down injured that Germany controversially scored their opener.

While in charge of Liverpool, Klopp used to find internationals stressful to watch for the very reason of injuries, and so he will have empathy for Mikel Arteta and Regis Le Bris now.

Here is what we learned from this showdown between these two heavyweights.

Jurgen Klopp was denied victory in his first match as head coach of the German national team

His former Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo equalised late on as the Dutch earned a 1-1 draw

TWO PREM STRIKERS INJURED

Arsenal and Sunderland still have time – more than two weeks until their next Premier League fixtures with Leeds and Brighton respectively – but the sight of their strikers having to be substituted here will have sparked immediate fears back in England as one followed after the other.

First, Havertz had to be substituted after 30 minutes. He had been on the receiving end of an ugly foul by Quinten Timber – on another day, VAR might have punished the midfielder whose brother, Jurrien, plays for Arsenal – but that did not seem to be the reason for Havertz’s withdrawal.

It was a few minutes after Timber's challenge that Havertz dropped down, lifting up his shorts to show his strapped left thigh which appeared to be the source of his discomfort.

Then, Brobbey likewise needed substituting after 35 minutes, with the Sunderland striker grabbing his right hamstring and immediately asking to be replaced.

Arsenal forward Kai Havertz was forced off with an apparent thigh problem in the first half

Brian Brobbey gave Sunderland cause for concern after suffering a hamstring injury

DUTCH ANGER AT GERMAN OPENER MISPLACED

It was while Brobbey was down injured that Germany scored their first goal of the Klopp era – and it left the Netherlands incandescent at their opponents for not kicking the ball out of play.

Nadiem Amiri thought about it. The Germany midfielder had possession in the final third but rather than roll it away for a throw-in, he passed to his captain, Joshua Kimmich, to see what he wanted to do. Kimmich played on and from that very attack, Felix Nmecha scored to make it 1-0.

Denzel Dumfries took the greatest exception to what he perceived as a lack of sportsmanship, chasing the Germany players as they ran to the corner flag to celebrate.

Yet it was a perfectly legal opener despite the Netherlands’ complaints. Xavi’s main gripe with this goal should be how his side left Germany’s right wing entirely empty.

Felix Nmecha scored Germany's goal after they continued to play while Brobbey was down

The Netherlands were furious with Germany over what they viewed as a lack of sportsmanship

VAR SAVES KLOPP AND DENIES XAVI

When Klopp departed Liverpool in May 2024, he used his final pre-match press conference to tell us what he really thought of video assistant referees meddling in matches. ‘I would vote for scrapping VAR,’ he said before beating Wolverhampton Wanderers 2-0 in an Anfield farewell.

Yet that very technology saved Klopp here, some 858 days on from the last time he stood on a touchline as a manager. Good job, too, because Germany’s defending for the set-piece from which the Netherlands thought they had opened the scoring was rather embarrassing.

It was 0-0 at the time and came from a corner taken by Tijjani Reijnders. If anyone should know how dangerous Virgil van Dijk is in the air, it is Klopp, and yet Liverpool's central defender was uncontested. Germany were prioritising zonal marking inside their six-yard box. They placed nobody on the 6ft 5in bloke who scored a fair few headers under Klopp at Liverpool. Van Dijk just drifted forwards, headed in, and celebrated.

However, VAR, desperate to get involved, sent the referee to his pitch-side monitor because it was thought Brobbey was blocking Marc-Andre Ter Stegen. The goal was disallowed, and the next time the Netherlands had a corner, Van Dijk found himself being man-marked.

Virgl van Dijk had been denied the first goal of the match when Brobbey was adjudged by VAR to have interfered with Marc-Andre Ter Stegen from an offside position

A NEW ERA UNDER KLOPP

Unlike other managers, Klopp picked 44 players for Germany’s four Nations League fixtures, with half involved versus the Netherlands and Greece this week and the other half reserved for Serbia and Greece next week. Only goalkeeper Finn Dahmen of Augsburg is in both camps.

It smacked of a desire to identify new, fresh, hungry talents. Both squads for this international break carried an average age between 24 and 25, and included 16 uncapped players, and it was in the spirit of giving opportunities that Philipp Treu won his first cap for Germany as a starter.

Right back has been a priority position for Klopp, who would rather not use Kimmich there like his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. Treu is a 25-year-old for Freiburg and largely held his own as the Netherlands pushed for their second-half leveller until the bitter end.

Germany relied on a series of saves from Ter Stegen while Mexx Meerdink, who replaced Brobbey, should have equalised when he missed the gaping goal. In Meerdink’s defence, he was stretching to meet the ball when it was blasted into the six-yard box.

Gakpo eventually ensured this ended in a draw after Van Bommel’s classy cross with the outside of his boot, denying Klopp but giving Xavi cause to celebrate.

Sports.title: 'Game's Gone': Every modern football hatred listed and debated
Sports.content:
VAR, cut socks, soft fouls on keepers, goal music, pre-match handshakes and more - have your say on football's worst traits.

When Manchester United launched the sale of £125 Old Trafford turf cubes this week, there was a shared reaction from the average football fan.

An eye roll, a shake of the head, and the remark of: "Game's Gone".

The phrase has become the by-word reaction of traditional supporters to their frustrations at some of the traits of the modern, multi-billion pound global industry that is the Premier League.

So while we're going to miss the dramatic soap opera of elite English football during this three-week international break, there are definitely some things we will be happy to swerve for a few days.

We've asked our football journalists to nominate some of their modern football pet hates so we can list then, debate them and rank them.

It's quite cathartic. Read on...

Sports.title: Man Utd news LIVE: JJ Gabriel transfer update, Glazers stake decision, INEOS boycott plan latest
Sports.content:
Manchester United still have more than two weeks to go until they are next back in action against Tottenham with the extended international break in full swing

Hello and welcome to Mirror Football 's Manchester United news live blog for Friday, September 25.

JJ Gabriel is still the main topic of conversation at Old Trafford, more than a week on since he expressed his desire to cancel his registration and leave United with immediate effect. The Reds have been left stunned by Gabriel's decision but are still hoping to convince him to stay, despite significant interest elsewhere.

Barcelona and Real Madrid are among the leading contenders to land Gabriel's signature and it's thought he would prefer a move to Spain, rather than joining Bayern Munich or Paris Saint-Germain. If he does chose to remain in England, however, Chelsea is his top option.

Although he is desperate to quit United, Gabriel is not able to leave until the end of the season and cannot be deregistered. He is 16 next month, so can then become eligible to sign a scholarship agreement with United.

Elsewhere, United fans have called for a boycott of INEOS-owned products and companies, as well as any of United's commercial sponsorship deals. Some examples include Betway, CocaCola, Adidas, and DHL.

Stay tuned with the latest from United throughout the day...

Tottenham star Dejan Kulusevski leaves magistrates confused after missing court date

The winger has seen his speeding hearing adjourned until next month

View 2 Images Dejan Kulusevski was unable to attend his sentencing hearing for speeding. (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

Tottenham Hotspur winger Dejan Kulusevski has had his sentencing hearing for speeding adjourned after he was unable to attend. Magistrates delayed the case after being unsure whether he wanted it to proceed without him.

‌



Kulusevski was due to attend on Monday after being caught doing 43mph in a 30 mph limit zone last year. But the BBC reports that, in an email to Barkingside Magistrates' Court, he confirmed he could not attend because he was in training with Spurs.

‌



The 26-year-old already has 18 points on his licence and added in the email that his young family relies on him to drive, as he faces a potential ban. He has accepted that he was speeding, but has argued that most of his offences involve him being just over the speed limit.

‌

Ordering the adjournment, presiding magistrate Mary Miller, said that it was ‘not clear from the email’ whether Kulusevski wanted the hearing adjourned. An adjournment was therefore granted until 19 October.

The Sweden international is closing in on a return to action after more than a year out with a complicated knee injury. His last appearance was in May 2025, in a 2-0 loss to Crystal Palace, meaning he missed all of last season and the summer’s World Cup.

‌



Kulusevski has now returned to full training with his Spurs teammates. He has not been called up to the Sweden squad for the current international break as he continues his progress and eyes a return to action.

Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp provides worrying Kai Havertz update after Arsenal star suffered injury

Arsenal's Kai Havertz was subbed off during Germany's dramatic 1-1 draw with the Netherlands, having been on the end of a high challenge from Crystal Palace star Quinten Timber

View 2 Images Jurgen Klopp has given the latest on Kai Havertz (Image: Lars Baron/Getty Images)

Arsenal star Kai Havertz has undergone a scan after suffering a suspected hamstring injury while playing for Germany. Havertz, 27, had to be taken off in the 30th minute of his country's 1-1 draw away to the Netherlands in their Nations League opener.

‌



The forward had been caught by a high challenge from Crystal Palace's Quinten Timber, the brother of Havertz's Arsenal team-mate, Jurrien. Germany manager Jurgen Klopp confirmed after his team were denied a win thanks to a 92nd-minute equaliser that both Havertz and Jamal Musiala, who felt a twinge in his thigh during the warm-up, would have scans.

‌



"Both will undergo scans tonight," Klopp said after his first game as Germany boss. "They're probably out for us, but I hope they'll be back soon (for their clubs)."

‌



Havertz was only called up for two of Germany's four games this international window, with Klopp deciding to split his squad of 44 players in half. Their next game is at home to Greece on Sunday.

Mikel Arteta will be hoping that Havertz's injury proves not to be serious, with the former Chelsea man having started all five of Arsenal's Premier League games this season, scoring three goals in all competitions. Havertz's form has seen him has successfully dislodge Viktor Gyokeres as Arteta's first-choice striker.

The Gunners have a packed schedule following the international break. Arsenal play nine games in 27 days, including mouth-watering clashes with Bayern Munich and Liverpool.

Arteta's side had a perfect record until Brighton hammered them 3-0 last Saturday. It allowed Manchester City to leapfrog them at the top of the Premier League table.

‌



Havertz's form was key to their strong start. The 27-year-old had an injury-hit season last time out but returned to full fitness towards the end of the campaign, scoring in the Champions League final. "Kai is extremely intelligent, that's his biggest quality," Arteta recently hailed.

Sports.title: 'I was sent home from England duty for sneaking out – but boss let me go to Ibiza instead'
Sports.content:
'I was sent home from England duty for sneaking out – but boss let me go to Ibiza instead'

A former Premier League star has recalled the reaction from his club manager after being sent home for sneaking out on England duty

View 2 Images A former Premier League star has recalled his experience of being sent home from England duty (Image: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images)

Andy Carroll has revealed that he was allowed to head to Ibiza after being sent home from England duty. The striker was one of three U19 call-ups disciplined for sneaking out of the team hotel but got an unexpected reaction from his club manager.

‌



During the early part of his storied career, Carroll starred for his boyhood club Newcastle United and became the most expensive British player when joining Liverpool in January 2011. The 37-year-old is currently with Dagenham and Redbridge, also serving as assistant coach and a minority shareholder at the National League South club.

‌



Carroll has captured attention throughout his playing days but first made waves off the pitch in 2007. The then-18-year-old was on loan at Preston North End from Newcastle and had earned a spot in Brian Eastick’s England U19 squad, though the international break had begun to take a toll.

‌



The former Premier League striker, alongside Chelsea starlets Scott Sinclair and Ryan Bertrand, hatched a plan to leave the hotel. However, he and his team-mates were quickly rumbled and promptly sent home.

Thomas Tuchel can't afford to dismiss Nations League in battle to win back England fans READ MORE :

Wayne Rooney makes 'money' confession as Man Utd icon admits management career could be over READ MORE :

In his new autobiography, Owning It, Carroll wrote: “It was Ryan Bertrand who suggested a few of us go for a walk, while I came up with the idea of heading downstairs with our England tracksuits over our normal clothes so that no one would twig we were going out, before removing our tracksuits by the fire exit and leaving them under the stairs.

“Scott Sinclair got a pen and paper from reception, wrote PLEASE LEAVE THESE ITEMS - BY MANAGER'S REQUEST, and stuck the note to the tracksuits, and we used a rock to hold the fire exit door slightly open, so we could slip back in later.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

"The plan was to go to a couple of bars, not to get hammered, just for a change of scenery, but we'd only got as far as McDonald's when Ryan and Scott's Chelsea team-mate Sam Hutchinson rang to say that the manager knew we were out.

"We sprinted back as fast as we could, entered through the fire exit, noticed our tracksuits were gone - B*******! - and when we got back upstairs, the goalkeeping coach Tony Parks was waiting for us, looking like his dog had died. He sent us straight to the gaffer Brian Eastick, who shouted at us for a few minutes about disrespecting our coaches, our team-mates and the shirt, before telling us that we were being sent home immediately.”

‌



The incident soon came to wider attention, with Eastick commenting on the situation: “I have found it necessary to send three players home for breaking our code of conduct. All the appropriate people have been informed and there will be no further comment at this time.”

View 2 Images Andy Carroll was surprised by Sam Allardyce's reaction to him being sent home from England duty (Image: Jan Kruger/Getty Images)

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



Despite not having had a boozy night out, Carroll was prepared to face a similar reaction from then-Newcastle boss Sam Allardyce upon returning to his parent club. However, the future England manager listened to Carroll’s version of events and allowed him time off, resulting in the striker jetting off to Ibiza.

“I thought I'd never play for England again, and I assumed I'd get a proper coating when I reported for training at Newcastle,” Carroll recalled. “But Big Sam believed my explanation, told me not to worry and said I could have three days off during the international break.

“What a legend. While Scott and Ryan were probably doing laps around the pitch at Chelsea, I was having a ball in Ibiza.”

Article continues below

Carroll was ultimately recalled to the England set-up, eventually earning nine senior caps for the Three Lions and notably scoring in a win over Sweden at Euro 2012. The striker never played under Allardyce during his short stint at St James’ Park but later spent three seasons with the former Newcastle boss at West Ham.

Sports.title: Nations League news: Cristiano Ronaldo frustrated, double injury blow and bizarre red card
Sports.content:
Nations League news: Cristiano Ronaldo frustrated, double injury blow and bizarre red card

The international break means that the Nations League returned for European national teams, with Wales among those in action

View 2 Images Cristiano Ronaldo was left frustrated in Portugal's Nations League clash vs Wales. (Image: Valter Gouveia/Sports Press Photo/Getty Images)

The newly extended international break gives the chance for the Nations League to take centre stage for the next couple of weeks. Thursday night saw the new edition of the UEFA tournament kick off.

‌



International teams are in action up to four times over the next three weeks as they look to grab an early advantage in their respective tables. For England, they start their campaign when they host World Champions Spain on Saturday.

‌



But it was Wales who were among those to be in action on Thursday as they faced Cristiano Ronaldo’s Portugal in Lisbon in their Group D encounter. That was one of nine games to take place.

‌



Arsenal handed Kai Havertz injury blow as forward limps out of Germany match READ MORE :

Man Utd complete Liverpool transfer coup after swooping for Man City youngster READ MORE :

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Here’s a look at what happened as the Nations League returned.

Group B

Netherlands 1-1 Germany

Felix Nmecha gave Germany the lead in the 32nd minute, to give Jurgen Klopp the perfect start as Germany boss. But in a worry for Arsenal, Kai Havertz left the field with an injury after a heavy challenge from Quinten Timber.

‌



Sunderland were also handed an injury worry, with striker Brian Brobbey forced off with a hamstring injury. And there was also some late drama as Liverpool's Cody Gakpo equalised for the Netherlands in the 92nd minute.

Serbia 1-2 Greece

Andrija Zivkovic’s fourth-minute goal for Serbia was the difference between the sides at halftime. Arsenal's Christos Tzolis equalised for Greece in the 74th minute.

Greece then completed the turnaround through Anastasios Douvikas' 95th-minute winner.

‌



Group D

Portugal 1-0 Wales

It was the first competitive meeting between the two nations since the Euro 2016 semi-final.

While all eyes were on Cristiano Ronaldo, it was Joao Felix who was the difference between the two sides at half-time, thanks to his goal from outside the box. The travelling Wales fans had fun aiming an X-rated jibe at a frustrated Ronaldo, serenading him with "you're just a s*** Gareth Bale" after a fairly tame effort at goal.

He thought he'd gotten his own back when he ran through to slot past Danny Ward in the second half. But celebrations were cut short by a VAR check, which showed he was offside, much to his and the home crowd’s annoyance.

‌



He didn’t have the chance to get closer to that 1,000 goal milestone as he was replaced by Ruben Neves just after the hour mark. A popped ball and Wales somehow missing pretty much an open goal, followed, but the visitors were unable to find an equaliser.

Norway 3-2 Denmark

There’s no surprise who was on the scoresheet for Norway, as Erling Haaland made it 2-0 just four minutes after Fulham’s Oscar Bobb had opened the scoring in the first half. Brentford’s Mikkel Damsgaard halved the deficit for Denmark in the 25th minute.

Former Man United striker Rasmus Hojlund equalised for Denmark, but it was that man again to regain Norway's lead and make it 3-2 to Norway in the second half.

‌



David Moller Wolfe was shown a red card for Norway in the fourth minute of added time after receiving a second yellow card.

Haaland’s goals were his 63rd and 64th in 56 international appearances for his nation - pushing him beyond the likes of Brazilian star Ronaldo and Zlatan Ibrahimovic in the all-time international goalscorers rankings -pretty mind-blowing!

View 2 Images Erling Haaland scored a brace in Norway's 3-2 win over Denmark. (Image: Marius Nordnes / Nordnes Foto/Getty Images)

‌



Group G

Austria 3-1 Israel

Romano Schmid scored from the penalty spot just before halftime to give Austria the lead. But Sayed Abu Farchi drew level in the 55th minute.

However, he didn't think through his celebration. Already on a yellow card, he celebrated just a bit too much and was shown a second yellow, leaving his team with 10 men for the remainder of the game.

Israel held on until the 90th minute when Phillipp Mwene scored the winning goal for Austria. Sasa Kalajdzig made it 3-1 in the third minute of added time.

‌



Kosovo 1-0 Ireland

An 83rd-minute winner from Vedat Muriqi condemned Ireland to defeat in a game where they faced 23 shots, compared to their three. Next up for Heimir Hallgrímsson's side is the clash against Israel which has already dominated the news heading into the international fixtures.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Why have the Republic of Ireland's two games against Israel become so controversial?
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will face Israel in a men’s football fixture for the first time since 2005 in this international break, but there have been calls for the two UEFA Nations League games not to be played at all.

Both meetings - the first played in Debrecen, Hungary on Sunday and the second scheduled for the Serbian town of Backa Topola on October 4 - have been overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

Uncertainty over the games going ahead might have subsided, but the tensions between the two nations have not.

Heimir Hallgrimsson, the Republic of Ireland head coach, has been accused of "stupidity and hypocrisy" by the Israel Football Association after last week suggesting his team would be "playing against genocide" when facing Israel, while his players are not ruling out their own protests ahead of the games.

The Athletic examines the key issues ahead of the first meeting this weekend.

Why have these games caused controversy?

This has been a contentious issue rolling down the tracks ever since the 2026-27 Nations League draw was made in February. Group B3 saw the Republic of Ireland pitted against Kosovo, their opening opponents this evening, and Austria, but it was the prospect of facing Israel which created immediate unease.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) had overwhelmingly approved a motion that called on UEFA to ban Israel from its competitions just four months earlier due to violations of the governing body's statutes, including "the organisation of clubs in illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank without the consent of the Palestinian Football Association".

The Nations League draw duly reignited the row. Irish politicians, including the FAI member Joanna Byrne, were quick to call for a boycott of the Israel games in the following days and protests ensued when Qatar visited Dublin's Aviva Stadium for a friendly in May. Tennis balls featuring the Palestine flag were thrown on the pitch by supporters, twice causing brief interruptions.

Image: Tennis balls with a Palestinian flag on were thrown onto the pitch in Dublin during protests in May 2026

The FAI had already confirmed its plans to go ahead with the Israel games by then, and that decision was formally approved at an EGM in July.

That saw only 32 votes in favour of a boycott, with 75 members voting for the games to be played. The FAI had argued that boycotting games would cause "significant and lasting harm to Irish football" due to the likely disciplinary sanctions from UEFA.

A measure of the opposition to the Republic of Ireland facing Israel also came with the acceptance that the "home" fixture would not be played in Dublin. The FAI cited "operational challenges (that) could impact the delivery of the game on home soil" and the decision was eventually made in late June, with the support of UEFA, to move the game to Backa Topola, a small town in northern Serbia, on Sunday week.

No tickets for the game will be made available to Ireland fans.

The FAI has subsequently revealed that a request to see the two nations kept apart in future competition draws has been rejected by UEFA.

"The answer I got was very clear," FAI chief executive David Courell told reporters on September 18. "That would not be possible because Ireland and Israel have never been in direct conflict."

What is the political backdrop?

The Republic of Ireland has consistently outlined its backing for the Palestinian people since the conflict with Israel began almost three years ago, joining Norway and Spain when officially recognising a Palestinian state in 2024. Taoiseach Micheal Martin has also made his stance clear, accusing Israel of committing "genocide" last year in comments reported by the Irish Mirror.

The conflict in Gaza began after Israel responded to attacks by Hamas militants on October 7, 2023, which saw around 1,200 people, mostly civilians, killed in Israel and 250 taken hostage. The war has subsequently seen 73,000 people killed, according to figures from the Gaza Health Ministry and used by the UN.

Strained relations between the Republic of Ireland and Israel have continued this year. Two Israeli government ministers were the subject of travel bans in June, while foreign minister Helen McEntee also confirmed Ireland's intent to limit goods trading with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank this summer.

Image: Taoiseach Micheal Martin

A meeting between the Republic of Ireland and Israel on a football field this weekend has subsequently taken on enormous significance against such a backdrop.

There are similarities in Ireland's political stance with those of Norway, who faced similar calls for a boycott when Israel travelled to Oslo last October. The Norwegian Football Federation (NFF) had aligned itself with its government and said in a statement leading up to Israel's visit that the "tragic humanitarian suffering in Gaza" had made the fixture challenging.

That World Cup qualifier, won 5-0 by Norway, saw thousands take part in a protest march to the stadium.

Who has opposed the games taking place?

Moving a home game 1,500 miles away has not stopped the objections building ahead of the two teams meeting on Sunday. More than 160 Irish sportspeople signed an open letter asking their national team to boycott the Israel games under the banner of the Irish Sport for Palestine Group, who have also run the "Stop the Game" campaign that protested outside of the Irish team hotel in Dublin on Monday.

"This is a significant moment and with this moment you have an opportunity to do the right thing," the letter said.

Kevin Kilbane, the former Republic of Ireland international who holds 110 caps, has also been unequivocal in his views. "The Republic of Ireland should not be playing Israel… not while Israeli forces are committing genocide," he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.">he wrote in a column for the Irish Times.

Amnesty International also issued a fresh statement on Tuesday that said UEFA risked letting football "rubber-stamp apartheid" by allowing Israel's continued participation in its club and international competitions. A spokesperson for the Israeli FA responded to that by saying: "Their obsession with the idea of Israel as a state is incurable, as is their need of attention."

The Irish media, meanwhile, has faced its own dilemmas in the coverage of the Israel games. RTE, the public broadcaster behind Ireland's boycott of the Eurovision Song Contest in the last two years due to Israel's continued involvement, has stripped back its coverage. Contractual obligations will be met, RTE confirmed in a statement, but there would be no studio coverage or commentators sent to either fixture.

Image: Kevin Kilbane, former Ireland international, has spoken out

What have the key stakeholders said ahead of this weekend?

Relations between the two nations have grown increasingly hostile in the last week. Hallgrimsson appeared in front of the media to announce his squad for the upcoming friendlies and made pointed remarks when asked how his players would focus on football.

"We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," the former Iceland head coach told reporters. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel."

The reaction to those words, in a social media post from the Israel FA account, raised temperatures further still. "We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way," it read. "Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach. We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them."

Martin, who was among the world leaders attending the UN General Assembly in New York, was then drawn back into debate on Tuesday. "I think those are unacceptable remarks. They should be withdrawn. Israel can't keep denying what the world knows and what the world understands."

The FAI has not addressed Hallgrimsson's comments publicly, but the Republic of Ireland's head coach said on Wednesday that he had been "grateful for the support" he had received.

"Maybe from a leadership point of view, it was not clever from me to take the attention (away) like this. It's a tricky time for us," Hallgrimsson said in his pre-match press conference ahead of facing Kosovo.

The same extends to his players, too. Dara O'Shea, the Ipswich Town defender, said, according to the BBC, that he and the rest of the players would come together on Friday to "openly discuss" the prospect of a protest ahead of the first Israel game in Debrecen on Sunday.

Image: Dara O’Shea, left, and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson during Wednesday’s press conference

Why are the games being played in Hungary and Serbia?

Hungary has acted as an adopted home for Israel since the start of the conflict. They first played there in November 2023, when resuming their attempts to qualify for Euro 2024 when hosting Switzerland at the Pancho Arena in Felcsut, a small village 26 miles west of Budapest.

Victor Orban, who lost his position as Hungary's prime minister this year, had been a long-standing ally of Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and claimed Hungary to be the "safest country in Europe" for Jews.

The World Cup 2026 qualifiers against Estonia, Norway and Italy were all held in Debrecen, which has also previously hosted European games for Israeli sides Maccabi Haifa and Maccabi Tel Aviv.

The Republic of Ireland's choice of Backa Topola, Serbia, is less clear. Dublin ceased to become an option, even behind closed doors, as the opposition to Israel visiting became clear, which left limited options for relocation.

It needed to be a nation sympathetic to Israel to avoid further protests and Serbia, neighbouring Hungary to the south, has forged strong diplomatic relations. According to the Associated Press, Serbia's president Aleksandar Vucic inaugurated an assembly factory for Israel-made drones last week, with plans for three more production sites.

A switch to Serbia was reliant on UEFA approval and it will be Backa Topola's home of the TSC Arena where this story ends on October 4.

Sports.title: 'Brutal, searing and punishing heat' - Babb on playing for Ireland at USA '94
Sports.content:
While none of the home nations qualified for the 1994 World Cup, the Republic of Ireland did.

It was a second successive appearance at the tournament for the Boys in Green, who were again led by 1966 World Cup winner Jack Charlton.

At Italia '90, the weather had been hot - but at USA '94, it was a different kettle of fish altogether.

The iconic image of Charlton launching an open bottle of water in the direction of Andy Townsend and Tommy Coyne always provides a reminder of that.

Image: Jack Charlton led the Republic of Ireland at Italia '90 and USA '94

He clashed with FIFA over their policy that bottles could not be thrown to the players on the pitch, so took to throwing the contents instead before FIFA later relented and allowed water bags to be thrown.

"They trust me to do what is right for them and I will continue to do it," Charlton said. "We have been right in pursuing this matter and FIFA's change of heart proves that."

Charlton was rarely seen without his white baseball cap that summer. Steve Staunton famously even wore one during the national anthem before the second group game against Mexico.

One of the players in the Ireland squad that summer was Phil Babb. The defender, then 23, had just completed his second full Premier League season at Coventry.

He made his international debut in a 0-0 friendly draw with Russia in March 1994, then played in the next four friendlies leading up to the tournament.

Image: Phil Babb played in all four of the Republic of Ireland's games at the 1994 World Cup

Nothing was set in stone, but he knew he would at least have a decent chance of being included in Charlton's 22-man squad, so started to physically prepare himself.

"A coach at Coventry asked me if I wanted to do anything specific - we ended up doing 12-minute sessions in a sauna!" Babb recalls, with a smile.

"We were doing burpees, press-ups, just trying to acclimatise to that intense heat. We did about six sessions - but I wouldn't recommend it for anyone now!

"I was a fit lad and had played pretty much all the Premier League games Coventry had played that season. I adapted to the heat pretty well, but I know some of the older lads really struggled."

Babb started alongside Paul McGrath in the heart of defence for Ireland's tournament opener at Giants Stadium in New Jersey.

Image: Ray Houghton's stunning strike earned a shock 1-0 win over Italy

That Saturday, they shocked an Italy side that featured Paolo Maldini, Franco Baresi and Roberto Baggio. John Aldridge's stunner sealed a memorable 1-0 win.

It was an achievement made all the more impressive by the fact the Azzurri went on to finish as runners-up - but also given the fact it was played in temperatures exceeding 30C.

"When we walked out onto the field, about two hours before kick-off, you could tell it was going to be absolutely roasting," he recalls.

"You could tell that straight away and we didn't stay out long. I just checked the grass to see which studs I wanted, then I went straight back in. I know some of the lads were walking around and taking the atmosphere in, but I thought: 'This is too hot'.

"I didn't go out for a warm-up with the rest of the lads, either. I stayed in the changing room. It was built for NFL, so they had a 40m sprint track. I warmed up in there and waited until we went out. It was brutal, it was searing, it was punishing.

"It affected everyone's game. You were saturated after just 10 minutes walking onto a pitch, so you had to conserve energy at the right times.

"Recovery was very basic and there was very little ball work because of the demands of the actual games and the fluids you lose. When you're that dehydrated, it's quite difficult. You want a drink, but you don't feel hungry and that is a key part of the recuperation."

Image: Babb, whose Ireland were knocked out by Dennis Bergkamp's Netherlands, joined Liverpool later that summer

Thirty-two years on from that tournament, football has evolved exponentially.

Sports science has taken on a key role in the game and, this summer, is likely to play into the way teams approach games tactically due to the heat. A slower tempo is expected in many.

Charlton was not prepared to facilitate the same in 1994, though.

"We only played one way, so if you tried to go off-piste, Jack would certainly let you know!" adds Babb.

"We had one style of play, with a lone striker. If it wasn't Tommy Coyne, it might have been Niall Quinn up there and we'd be putting long balls up to him, with either willing runners out wide or the midfield bombing on.

"That was the Irish way back then. Tommy ran tirelessly, to the point where he actually collapsed with heat exhaustion on the plane home.

"I think Jack's sports science was a barrel of Guinness in his room and he'd call the lads in and have a pint! I'm sure there's a high calorific content in that, so maybe he was ahead of his time!"

In spite of that, Babb's memories of the tournament are largely positive.

"I enjoyed it, I have to admit! I'd rather play in the searing heat than a wet Tuesday night in Hull," he says.

"I was a fit lad and it was quite easy for me playing alongside Paul McGrath, who was imperious in that tournament. I learned a lot from him and how he conserved his energy.

"I felt I got stronger because I got used to it. I guess our 0-0 draw against Norway would probably attest to the heat and the style of play.

"It all comes down to the individual. Footballers are supreme athletes now and they leave nothing to chance, so I think they'll cope a lot better than we did in the mid-90s."

The methods may have moved on since Charlton was throwing water onto the pitch, but Babb's memories from USA '94 provide a reminder this World Cup will be a battle against more than just the opposition.

Sports.title: Ogbene earns Republic of Ireland draw with Canada
Sports.content:
Chiedozie Ogbene's equaliser ensured the Republic of Ireland continued their good run of results as they drew 1-1 with World Cup co-hosts Canada in Montreal.

Canada went ahead in the 24th minute from an own goal by defender Jake O'Brien, heading a failed clearance into his own net from Stephen Eustaquio's corner.

Ireland were then awarded a penalty in the second half after Cyle Larin - who signed a two-year deal with Southampton earlier in the day - took out Jamie McGrath.

Canada goalkeeper Maxime Crepeau saved Troy Parrott's initial attempt, but Ogbene was on hand to slam home the rebound and tie the game in the 60th minute.

Image: Ireland's Jake O'Brien heads the ball into his own net

Ireland, who failed to qualify for this summer's World Cup, went close to a winner but Crepeau denied a charging run from Mason Melia late on.

The Orlando City goalkeeper missed out on the 2022 World Cup in Qatar after breaking his leg while playing in the MLS Cup final.

Canada, managed by former Leeds boss Jesse Marsch, officially open the World Cup on June 12 in Toronto against Bosnia and Herzegovina, before facing Qatar on June 18 and Switzerland on June 24.

They remain without captain Alphonso Davies, who is still nursing a hamstring injury he sustained while playing for Bayern Munich.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland edge past Qatar in friendly as both sides end with 10
Sports.content:
Captain Nathan Collins headed the Republic of Ireland to a 1-0 friendly victory over World Cup-bound Qatar as both sides were reduced to 10 men.

Collins ensured Ireland got the better of a side managed by his former Wolves boss Julen Lopetegui with an early header.

However, just how the evening might have panned out had Jack Moylan not been dismissed as half-time approached, a sparse crowd inside the Aviva Stadium will never know.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, whose hopes of making it to the World Cup finals were dashed in heartbreaking fashion in March when they lost their play-off semi-final to the Czech Republic on penalties, were in complete control until Moylan's premature exit.

Qatar substitute Almoez Ali suffered the same fate 12 minutes from time.

Image: Jack Moylan was sent off before half-time at the Aviva Stadium

The game was played out against the backdrop of ongoing unease at the forthcoming Nations League clashes with Israel, and play was interrupted on several occasions during the first half as 'Stop the Game' protesters among a crowd of 28,981 repeatedly hurled tennis balls on to the pitch.

Ireland will now head for Montreal and their friendly against World Cup co-hosts Canada on June 6, while Qatar continue their preparations for the finals - they launch their Group B campaign against Switzerland in San Francisco on June 13 - against El Salvador in Los Angeles on the same day.

The Republic took the lead with just five minutes gone when, having been fouled by Ayoub Al-Oui wide on the left, Moylan curled the resulting free-kick on to the head of Collins, who glanced the ball effortlessly past 'keeper Mahmoud Abunada.

Image: Qatar's Almoez Ali was also sent off

There was a brief interruption after the protesters made their presence felt for the first time as Qatar's Pedro Miguel underwent treatment for injury, but once order had been restored, Troy Parrott whipped a first-time shot wide after being picked out by Seamus Coleman.

The Qataris simply could not get anywhere near Hallgrimsson's men and a mid-half drinks break did little to improve matters for the visitors with Abunada having to field Jayson Molumby's deflected 24th-minute shot from distance.

Lopetegui could not hide his frustration on the sideline and only the bravery of defender Ahmed Fathi denied Chiedozie Ogbene a second goal as he attempted to latch on to Liam Scales' header back across goal.

But the home side's night took a turn for the worse on the stroke of half-time when Northern Irish referee Jamie Robinson deemed Moylan's challenge on Jassem Gaber worthy of a red card, much to the Lincoln frontman's clear astonishment.

Image: Former Wolves and West Ham boss Julen Lopetegui is now in charge of Qatar

With defender James Abankwah having replaced Dara O'Shea at half-time, the 10 men found themselves under pressure for the first time on their return, although Coleman very nearly caught Abunada off his line with an audacious 52nd-minute attempt from the right wing.

Edmilson Junior dragged a long-range effort wide two minutes later after Molumby went down in midfield under Fathi's challenge and it took a fine 71st-minute reaction save by Caoimhin Kelleher - his first of the night - to keep out Yusuf Abdurisag's deflected shot.

However, Qatari hopes of salvation were dashed with 12 minutes remaining when Ali struck out at Molumby off the ball on several occasions and was also sent off.

Sports.title: Parrott out of luck as Republic of Ireland draw with North Macedonia
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott had two goals disallowed as the Republic of Ireland played out a stalemate against North Macedonia on the night on which they had hoped to book a trip to the World Cup finals.

Five days after their dreams came to an end for another four years in Prague, Ireland drew 0-0 with the Macedonians in a friendly encounter neither side wanted as the Czech Republic and Denmark fought for the big prize.

Even a third successive home victory for the first time since the 2015-16 campaign would have provided scant consolation for Thursday night's disappointment but Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had to make do with a disappointing draw.

AZ Alkmaar striker Parrott came closest to breaking the deadlock as 37-year-old defender Seamus Coleman received a standing ovation from a crowd of 39,560 at the Aviva Stadium when he was replaced during the second half of what could yet prove to be his final appearance for his country.

Nevertheless, the squad will reconvene for a series of friendlies at the end of the season ahead of next season's Nations League campaign and later Euro 2028 qualification having restored a measure of pride and established a momentum they hope will serve them well when they return to competitive action.

The hosts went on to the offensive from the off, although they were unable to find the final ball to allow either Parrott or Chiedozie Ogbene to threaten.

John Egan could not direct an 11th-minute corner at goal and Ogbene saw his snapshot deflected over three minutes later, but goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher had to parry Enis Bardhi's 21st-minute free-kick after it flicked off the defensive wall, with Bardhi volleying high over after the resulting corner had been only half-cleared.

Macedonia keeper Stole Dimitrievski saved Parrott's 23rd-minute header comfortably after Dara O'Shea and Finn Azaz had sparked a concerted attack, and Azaz failed to make the most of a free-kick two minutes later after he had been tripped just outside the penalty area.

Parrott was played into a promising position by Knight nine minutes before the break, only to miss the target by some distance.

The in-form striker - he scored his sixth goal in three games in Prague - might have done better again two minutes later after Azaz's clipped pass had caused problems for the Macedonian defence but he snatched at his attempt and fired high and wide.

Parrott twice had the ball in the net as time ran down but an offside flag stalled his celebrations on each occasion.

Ireland were unfortunate not to take the lead with 52 minutes gone when Azaz accepted Seamus Coleman's pass and found Parrott, who turned smartly before shooting against the upright.

Azaz curled an effort just wide and Tihomir Kostadinov denied Parrott a clear run on goal as the hosts began to turn the screw but it was veteran Coleman's 61st-minute departure as

Hallgrimsson made changes which attracted the biggest cheer of the night to that point.

Wholesale changes did not help the flow of the game, which rather petered out as the whistle approached, although Ireland substitute Johnny Kenny passed up a glorious opportunity to win it at the end with a weak shot at the keeper.

Sports.title: Szmodics out of hospital and 'on the mend' after collision
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland forward Sammie Szmodics has been released from hospital in Prague after being knocked unconscious during Thursday's World Cup play-off defeat by the Czech Republic.

The 24-year-old, who is currently on loan at Derby from Ipswich, was hurt in a collision with defender Stepan Chaloupek just two minutes after his introduction as an extra-time substitute at the Fortuna Arena, sparking concerned medics to rush to his aid.

Szmodics was carried from the field on a stretcher and taken straight to hospital, where Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson later revealed he would spend the night under observation.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan looks back on the heartbreaking result for the Republic of Ireland who lost their World Cup qualifying play-off against Czech Republic on penalties

A Football Association of Ireland spokesperson said on Friday morning: "Sammie Szmodics was transferred to hospital yesterday having sustained a head injury during extra time of the play-off against Czechia.

"Following further tests and a period of observation, he has been safely discharged from hospital and will continue his recovery under the care of the Republic of Ireland and Derby County medical teams."

Szmodics, who Hallgrimsson confirmed would have taken a penalty in the shoot-out which Ireland ultimately lost 4-3, took to social media to express his thanks to those who had helped him.

He posted on X: "Gutted the way it ended. Fans and boys immense all evening!! Appreciate everyone's messages. And thank you to the medical staff who acted so quickly to help me. On the mend."

Collins: Ireland must build on World Cup near miss

Ireland captain Nathan Collins is confident his side have laid the foundations to qualify for future tournaments having seen hopes of reaching this summer's World Cup finals come to an end.

Collins and his team-mates were agonisingly close to the play-off final when they led the Czech Republic 2-1 in Prague on Thursday evening with just four minutes of normal time remaining.

Image: A dejected Nathan Collins and head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson

However, Czech skipper Ladislav Krejci's late equaliser took the tie to extra-time and ultimately to penalties, where the hosts prevailed 4-3 to extend Ireland's wait for a first return to the big stage since 2002.

Asked about their progression to the play-offs, which was secured by back-to-back wins over Armenia, Portugal and Hungary, Brentford defender Collins said: "I'm not seeing many positives right now because we're in the gutter.

"But what we've created, the environment created with the fans and country, has been special. That's something we need to keep growing, to get even better at.

"That can help us get better on the pitch. We can push that and get fans to more tournaments."

Ireland had hoped to return to the Aviva Stadium on Tuesday for a showdown with either Denmark or North Macedonia for a place in the finals, but the Czechs will now host the Danes, who were 4-0 winners in Copenhagen.

Instead, Heimir Hallgrimsson's side face a friendly against the Macedonians.

Collins said: "The motivation has to be the same. We've to win to keep improving as a team and country. Any game we play at home is a big game."

Sports.title: 'Pain' - Irish heartbreak as Czech Republic win on penalties
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland's World Cup hopes were cruelly and heartbreakingly dashed as Czech Republic came from 2-0 down - to then beat them on penalties.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's side, who went two goals up after 23 minutes in Prague, were four minutes plus stoppage-time away from victory - before Wolves defender Ladislav Krejci headed in a corner to force extra-time.

Ireland were also a handful of penalties away from going through, as penalty saving expert Caomhin Kelleher saved from Mojmír Chytil in the shoot-out to give them a momentary advantage.

But Finn Azaz and Alan Browne both missed their spot kicks, allowing Patrick Schick and then Jan Kliment to win it for the hosts.

As a result, Czech Republic will go on to face Denmark on Tuesday for a spot at the World Cup - as Ireland's wait for a first World Cup appearance since 2002 goes on.

After Wales and Northern Ireland's semi-final exits, it also means England and Scotland will be the only teams from Great Britain and Ireland at the World Cup this summer.

Image: Ireland's players walk off the pitch after defeat

World Cup play-off finals - Europe Bosnia & Herzegovina vs Italy

Sweden vs Poland

Kosovo vs Turkey

Czech Republic vs Denmark

How Ireland threw away their lead

Ireland came flying out the blocks flying in Prague. Four shots in the opening ten minutes, including Nathan Collins crashing a shot off the bar from range, set the tone for a brilliant display - and they got their rewards.

A long throw caused chaos and Nathan Collins was deemed to have been caught slightly late by Vladimir Darida by VAR, who sent referee Glenn Byberg to the monitor for a review.

Troy Parrott, who else, crashed in the penalty for his sixth goal in the last three Ireland matches. And it got better for Ireland four minutes later.

Ryan Manning's corner found Dara O'Shea at the back post and his header across was cleared off the line by Vladimir Coufal - but off goalkeeper Matej Kovar and over the line.

Image: Czech Republic goalkeeper Matej Kovar scores an own goal to give Ireland a 2-0 lead

Ireland were in dreamland but a moment of Manning madness brought the Czech Republic back into it. The defender's needless tug back on Krekci - when the ball was heading out of play - was penalised by referee Byberg, with Patrick Schick pulling one back from the spot.

Ireland did, however, manage to settle the nerves down - right throughout the second half. Despite sustained Czech pressure in the second half, they barely threatened.

It was Ireland who had the better chances after the break, with Jayson Molumby striking the post and Parrott denied by a solid Kovar save at a corner. But then heartbreak struck with four minutes of normal time remaining, as Krejci bundled the ball in at the near post from a set piece.

Krejci could have even won it with the last kick of the game but scuffed his finish, as extra-time came.

Substitute Tomas Soucek missed a glorious chance for the hosts, with Adam Idah was denied a one-on-one chance by a goal-saving challenge from Stepan Chaloupek. Penalties came and the lottery fell in the hosts' favour.

Image: Jan Kliment scored the winning goal in the penalty shoot-out

Hallgrimsson confident in Ireland future despite 'pain'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"One word is pain. I feel pain. I feel pride for the performance of the players. They gave it all. I feel gratitude for all the supporters who supported us through the whole game, even after the loss. I feel pride being a part of that group. Personally, I know all the players will feel pain now. Only pain.

"We take with us that we can play teams higher in the FIFA ranking and can punch above our weight: Portugal, Hungary and here. We can compete with these teams. We came here with three wins in a row, a long time since that happened for this national team.

"So there's growth in this squad. It's maturing. These are been the biggest game most of these players have played. That's encouraging to know we're growing. It's strange to say that after we lost today.

"I know I'm biased in this, all the statistics and metrics of the team have improved. Big games, being on the line, crunch times all the time, we've managed to go through this. It showed the resilience, character of these players, that's why I feel confident going on."

Sports.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua £150m fight is finally CONFIRMED - in Cardiff at 2am on a Friday night in December - and Netflix reveal price it will cost to watch

Anthony Joshua's long-awaited fight with Tyson Fury has finally been confirmed for December 11 at Cardiff’s Principality Stadium – and it will save Joshua around £7.5million in tax.

It is understood each man will pocket around £75m for arguably the biggest bout to be staged on British soil after Joshua’s team, led by Eddie Hearn, succeeded in forcing the promotion’s Saudi backers to scrap plans to stage the showdown in New York.

Hearn initially pushed for Wembley Stadium, but the combination of a roof over the Principality Stadium and the Welsh government’s willingness to bend their late-night curfew swung the fight towards Cardiff. The ring walk is expected to take place around 2am to suit a US-based audience, in line with the demands of Netflix, which will broadcast the heavyweight showdown.

Although the delivery of the fight in Wales will be positioned as a victory for British fight fans, pragmatism around tax was also a key consideration in Hearn’s argument against Madison Square Garden in New York.

As Daily Mail Sport revealed earlier this month, the two fighters would have been taxed around 30 per cent of their purses in America, compared to 20 per cent in the UK, with Joshua particularly unhappy about the prospect of an extra £7.5m being added to his bill. The two-time world champion instead demanded that his contract be honoured, which stipulated a British-based fight.

Boxing supremo Turki Alalshikh said: 'Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury Vs Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans.

'The time for talking is over. Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua. Years in the making. One night to settle it. December 11th. LIVE on Netflix.'

Netflix today confirmed the fight would be available 'at no additional cost' to subscribers. Their general membership pricing starts at £7.99 a month in the UK.

Bookmaker Betfair make Fury the early favourite to win, pricing him at 8/15. Joshua is priced at 13/8.

Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua has been announced for Friday, December 11

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects

Joshua tweeted: 'I am inspiring a generation', alongside an emoji of the British flag.

His promoter Eddie Hearn, who fought relentlessly to keep the fight in the UK, wrote: 'WE DID IT. Forever indebted to the U.K. public for their support of Anthony Joshua. We couldn’t have got this over the line without you.'

Fury's name appearing first on the card for the Battle of Britain will be an early win for the Gypsy King in his constant PR war with Joshua.

The pair had originally been pencilled in to fight on November 20 at Madison Square Garden in New York, but a determined push from Joshua and Hearn saw the contracts re-negotiated to bring the fight back to British soil.

Hearn had been adamant that British fans deserved the opportunity to watch two of the country's biggest sporting stars go head-to-head at home, and fought hard to make that happen.

Fury, too, wanted the fight in the UK, but had been prepared to accept a move to America because of his concerns that the bout could once again slip away.

Now those fears, after ten years of frustration, have been put to bed. The fight will take place in Cardiff, with the later-than-usual start time expected to mean ring walks at around 2am UK time as organisers attempt to satisfy the American audience watching on Netflix.

Wembley had been the preferred venue for the showdown, but the major stumbling block was securing the necessary late-night permit.

With Netflix and Turki Alalshikh keen for the event to cater to viewers in the United States, organisers required a start time significantly later than would normally be permitted at Wembley.

Cardiff, however, was able to secure the required permit - clearing the final obstacle to bringing the fight back to Britain.

Cardiff's Principality Stadium has come out on top to host the fight after weeks of negotiations

The scale of the occasion is already being felt in the Welsh capital, with hotels in Cardiff now understood to be sold out as supporters scramble to secure accommodation for one of the biggest fights in British boxing.

For Joshua, the move represents the culmination of a push to ensure the fight was staged in the UK.

The former two-times world champion and Hearn had been clear that, after years of watching British heavyweight stars travel overseas for major fights, Joshua-Fury belonged in front of their home crowd.

Fury was willing to compromise on the location if necessary, however, with his priority being to finally get the fight over the line.

The roots of Joshua-Fury stretch back more than a decade, to when both men were emerging as Britain's leading heavyweight prospects.

Joshua won Olympic gold at London 2012 before turning professional, while Fury had already made his professional debut in 2008 and was building an unbeaten record of his own.

For years, the prospect of the two eventually sharing a ring became one of British boxing's great hypothetical match-ups.

Fury's stunning victory over Wladimir Klitschko in 2015 elevated him to the summit of the heavyweight division, while Joshua was rapidly closing in on world-title status himself.
