Brisbane, Australia — An OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian national healthcare database in the first known case of AI hacking a government network, the country’s prime minister said Wednesday.

“The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files” of the country’s Medicare statistics database, and even wrote files into it, Anthony Albanese told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.

The disclosure is the latest example of AI agents going rogue and acting in ways beyond what their human handlers intended, and follows calls from top AI industry figures, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, to slow down the pace of AI development.

Albanese said he expressed Australia’s “extreme concern” to Altman in a phone call on Wednesday. Canberra wasn’t aware of a precedent for an AI breach of a government system, he added.

In another development, AI research lab Transluce said Wednesday that it had detecting AI agents going rogue on several occasions going back to at least March –– predating previously known hacking incidents. The targets included a University of New Mexico library and the website of the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, though none of the attempts were successful.

The health database hack

The Australian health database hack occurred when an OpenAI agent conducting research into healthcare spending circumvented blocks to find answers in areas it had no authority to access, Albanese said.

“A forensic investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate is now underway to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected,” he said.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri said the incident occurred in June but that the company was only made aware of it in August as they conducted extensive checks into its AI models’ activity.

“During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend,” Pusateri said.

Albanese said three other government systems may have been impacted, including the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and the Victorian Department of Health.

OpenAI said they found no evidence patient records were accessed in the Medicare breach and that the information included “aggregate health statistics and internal file names.”

The company said it informed the Australian government on September 10. That notification was sent to a public mailbox, Albanese said, leading to a five-day delay in the relevant government minister being advised.

Albanese said he told Altman that “it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.”

“I think OpenAI knows that they need to have better protocols in place,” Albanese told reporters.

Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles announced a taskforce investigation into the latest breach on Thursday local time, while assuring the public that the impact was “relatively minor.”

“No individuals’ medical data was accessed here. The system itself has not been in any way compromised,” he said.

What Transluce found

The rogue activities of AI agents first raised alarm in July, when OpenAI disclosed that during cybersecurity testing, its models created a swarm of AI agents that hacked into AI company Hugging Face’s systems. Many in the industry pointed to that hack as an example of the perils of the rapid pace of AI developments and capabilities.

But the incidents revealed by Transluce on Wednesday showed AI agents apparently going rogue earlier and during much more mundane tasks.

In the three unsuccessful cases it highlighted, AI agents attempted “cyber exploits” against data sources after failing to find the answers they wanted to answer web search tasks through normal means.

In May, agents tried to retrieve a photograph from a University of New Mexico’s collection, but despite sending a “flood” of requests, were unsuccessful, Transluce said. Agents also targeted Data USA later that month trying to get visualization data about the University of Iowa.

In June, agents trying to access statistics from AIHW attempted to “exploit vulnerabilities.” While no non-public data was exposed, the agent bypassed the site’s anti-bot controls, Transluce said. The Australian government acknowledged on Wednesday that the AIHW was among the sites targeted, but said they did not believe there had been a breach.

An OpenAI spokesperson said they were already reviewing “much of the activity described in Transluce’s report” with their own investigations into “misaligned model activity,” a process that could take months, the spokesperosn said.

“We’ve reached out to the University of New Mexico and Data USA and have been in communication with the Australian government about affected government websites,” the spokesperson said, adding that they are prioritizing “the most serious incidents” versus lower-severity activity like AI agents “spamming websites.”

Growing concerns

Open AI’s Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who are among the industry figures to have recently voiced their concern about the rapid pace of AI’s development, both spoke at the UNGA on Wednesday, calling for greater global coordination and international standards for AI development.

Altman urged global leaders to create international standards for “measuring capabilities, assessing risks, determining whether safeguards are sufficient and preserving meaningful human oversight” of the rapidly advancing technology.

Walayat Hussain, an associate professor of information technology at Australian Catholic University in Sydney, said the latest incident, alongside the Hugging Face breach in July, looked like a pattern.

“Today’s AI agents are becoming brilliant at getting things done, but they are still poor at knowing where the line is,” he said. “We cannot rely on AI agents to police themselves, and we cannot ask the companies that build them to mark their own homework.”

Hussain warned that many government systems were not built with sophisticated AI agents in mind.

This article has been updated with additional information.

World.title: The Grand Egyptian Museum among world’s top visited museums after hitting 6.5 million visitors
World.content:
The Grand Egyptian Museum (GEM) topped the list of the world’s most visited museums after welcoming over 6.5 million visitors during its opening months, reflecting the massive global interest in one of Egypt’s most prominent cultural and tourism mega-projects.

This milestone follows the official opening of the GEM on November 1, 2025, attended by numerous world leaders.

As the largest archaeological museum in the world dedicated to a single civilization, the GEM represents a major addition to Egypt’s archaeological and tourist destinations.

According to state documents regarding the economic and social development plan for the fiscal year 2025/2026, this surge in visitors underscores the success of national efforts to support historical and archaeological tourism, strengthening Egypt’s status as the global destination for cultural tourism.

The state’s development plans places the tourism sector among the primary beneficiaries of national growth plans, confirming ongoing government support to upgrade historical tourism and maximize returns from Egypt’s civilizational assets—led by the GEM.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Iran threatens US and Israel with expanding scope of war ‘as far as the the Indian ocean’
World.content:
The military adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, Yahya Rahim Safavi, issued a warning on Thursday regarding the potential renewal of war against Iran, threatening to expand the conflict’s geographical reach by “as far as the the Indian ocean”.

In a video broadcast by the Fars News Agency, Safavi stated: “Our armed forces are planning intelligently and have programs in place for the worst-case scenarios. We possess the necessary combat readiness to confront the enemy. If the United States and Israel attack our facilities and national interests again in any form, the war front will expand this time as well.”

He added: “With the conflict now stretching from the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, this scope could potentially broaden in response to a possible war—reaching as far as the Indian Ocean, or perhaps even beyond.”

Regarding the tactical leverage his country holds, Safavi remarked: “I believe linking territorial waters and the Red Sea to the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab will alter the battlefield. If the Americans initiate a new war, a new front centered around the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab could open up before them.”

Alliance with Yemen’s Huthis and strategic waterways

Safavi further noted that “We and the Yemenis share a common destiny and defend one another; a threat to Yemen is a threat to Iran.” He added that “Ansar Allah [the Huthis] have their own goals and strategy and have made advancements in arms manufacturing.”

The military adviser reaffirmed that Iran will maintain control and management over the Strait of Hormuz.

He pointed out that Tehran had reached a mechanism with Oman regarding maritime traffic through the strait, but alleged that “the US is obstructing it.”

Safavi concluded: “If Washington implements our seven proposed conditions, I believe Iranian officials can consider ship transit mechanisms through the Strait of Hormuz differently. We seek to keep war away from our nation, but if war is forced upon us, we are fully prepared for comprehensive defense.”

World.title: Rapper Wegz apologizes over unintentional Hadith citation in his song
World.content:
Egyptian rapper Wegz sparked widespread debate after incorporating a phrase from a Hadith (a saying of the Prophet Muhammad) into his new song’s lyrics, reopening a broader discussion about the appropriateness of using religious texts in musical work.

The controversy unfolded after it was found the song included the line “Everyone will be judged by their intentions“, which forms part of the well-known Hadith: “Actions are judged by intentions, and each person will awarded according to what they intended.”

This prompted preacher Khaled Zaki to criticize the inclusion of the phrase via a post on his Instagram account.

Wegz inquires about the religious ruling

Responding to the criticism, Wegz clarified that he was unaware the phrase was excerpted from a prophetic Hadith and requested clarification on the religious ruling regarding using such phrases in songs.

“Forgive my ignorance on two counts, Sheikh,” Wegz wrote in his reply. “First, that the sentence comes from a prophetic Hadith; and second, regarding the religious ruling on using a phrase spoken by Prophet Muhammad. If you could reply to me with the explicit text and religious ruling so I can understand better, I would be grateful.”

Wegz affirmed his readiness to alter the song’s lyrics, adding: “The words that are inappropriate to put in a song will be changed immediately. May God guide us and grant us repentance.”

This indicated his intent to remove the controversial line once he learned of its source and received expert guidance.

Fatwa official requests lyrics removal

A Fatwa official at the Egyptian Dar al-Ifta (the official Islamic legal authority), Hisham Rabie, commented on the incident by directing a message to Wegz asking him to delete or modify the segment.

Writing on his official Facebook page, Rabie noted that he had been following the situation regarding the phrase’s inclusion in the song. He emphasized that the sayings of the Prophet hold a sacred status and placing them within an entertainment or musical context may not align with their sanctity.

Rabie stressed that handling prophetic traditions requires reverence and decorum, calling on Wegz to rectify the matter by cutting or altering the phrase while noting that admitting a mistake is a positive step.

He further invited Wegz to visit Dar Al-Ifta to sit down with Fatwa advisers to discuss such matters, reassuring him that the institution’s doors are open for dialogue and that the goal is to offer guidance without targeting art or creativity.

Public reaction

What began as criticism over a religious phrase in a song quickly evolved into a broader discussion about how religious texts should be handled in artistic works.

Wegz’s willingness to amend the lyrics was widely welcomed by his audience, who commended his swift response, acknowledgement of his mistake, and the tolerant, gentle manner in which the religious scholars offered their counsel.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Liberian Leader Demands Two Permanent African Seats On Security Council, Fairer Global Finance System
World.content:
UNITED NATIONS, New York – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai on Thursday night told world leaders that trust in the United Nations has been broken by the uneven application of its founding principles, and called for sweeping reforms of the Security Council and the global financial system to restore it.

By Rodney D Sieh, rodney,[email protected]

Addressing the 81st Session of the UN General Assembly, held under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All,” the Liberian leader said the world is facing “a lingering crisis of legitimacy and relevance that demands urgent attention.”

“Our answer to that fragmentation cannot be less multilateralism,” President Boakai declared. “It must be better multilateralism!”

‘Eighty years of patience is enough’

The President reserved his strongest words for the Security Council, noting that Africa, home to 1.5 billion people and nearly one-third of UN membership, still has no permanent seat, even though 80 percent of the Council’s mandates concern African peace and security.

“Eighty years of patience is enough. The time for structural reform is now,” he said, describing the imbalance as a “historical injustice” that “is no longer tenable.”

Reaffirming Liberia’s support for the Common African Position, President Boakai said Africa demands no fewer than two permanent seats with full rights, including the veto for as long as it exists, plus additional non-permanent seats. “Correcting this imbalance is not a favor to Africa,” he said. “It is necessary to restore the United Nations’ trust, credibility, and legitimacy.”

Security Council seat and the drug war

Speaking as a current member of the Security Council, the President highlighted threats facing West Africa, including transnational organized crime, cyber warfare and narcotics trafficking along maritime routes in the Gulf of Guinea.

He said Liberia’s Joint Security forces are “tightening the vise on transnational drug cartels,” but stressed that no nation can fight global criminal networks alone. He appealed to international partners for targeted support in coast guard surveillance, intelligence sharing and port security technology.

He also called for an immediate end to hostilities in conflict zones, unhindered humanitarian access and stronger investment in preventive diplomacy, arguing that “the cost of preventing a war pales in comparison to the cost of rebuilding a broken society.”

‘Governed by so few’

On the economy, President Boakai said developing nations are being “squeezed by unsustainable debt, shrinking fiscal space, and mounting external shocks” as the 2030 deadline for the Sustainable Development Goals approaches.

He called for structural reform of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund, whose governance, he said, still reflects the world of 1945. “A financial system that decides the fate of billions cannot continue to be governed by so few,” he said.

At home, he pointed to progress under the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development – focused on Agriculture, Roads, Rule of Law, Education, Sanitation and Tourism – citing gains in revenue administration and rural farm-to-market roads. He also said his administration is strengthening accountability, financial management and the fight against corruption.

Climate justice, youth and AI

The President noted that Liberia contributes virtually nothing to global emissions yet suffers coastal erosion, flooding and disrupted farming seasons, while holding 42 percent of the remaining Upper Guinean Rainforest. He urged industrialized nations to honor their climate financing pledges and put loss-and-damage mechanisms into operation.

He called for investment in STEM education and digital skills for Africa’s youth, more than 60 percent of whom are under 25, reaffirmed Liberia’s commitment to equality for women and girls, and joined calls for binding rules on artificial intelligence, particularly in warfare. “Innovation must protect human development, not automate human destruction,” he said.

From San Francisco to today

Recalling that Liberia was one of only four African nations to sign the UN Charter in 1945, President Boakai presented the country’s journey from civil war to constitutional democracy as proof that “institutions can be rebuilt.”

He opened his address by congratulating Khalilur Rahman on his election as President of the 81st Session, thanking outgoing President Annalena Baerbock, and saluting Secretary-General António Guterres as he prepares to end his tenure.

“Let us leave this Assembly committed to a United Nations that not only deliberates on crises but also resolves them,” he concluded.

World.title: Liberia: Kwarbo vs. Coleman: The Drug Van Order that Nobody Owns
World.content:
A statement attributed to detained former Highway Patrol Chief Wadell Kwarbo says IG Gregory Coleman ordered him to escort the drug van. His family denies he made it, and the IG calls it part of a four-month disinformation campaign.

MONROVIA — A few days ago, Wadell Kwarbo’s father appeared on Spoon FM with an account of what his detained son had allegedly told him before he was taken into custody.

By Rodney D. Sieh

According to the father, a senior officer had called Kwarbo and instructed him to escort a shipment of drugs. At the time, he did not publicly identify the officer.

This week, however, a name emerged.

A statement attributed to Kwarbo, the former chief of the Liberia National Police Highway Patrol Division who remains detained at the Monrovia Central Prison, identified Police Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman as the officer who allegedly made the call.

“Police IG Gregory Coleman ordered me to escort the van. He instructed me to escort the drugs with my patrol vehicle (RL-141). And I acted on his order,” Kwarbo was quoted as saying on Spoon FM.

The statement reportedly went further, calling for his telephone records and written statement to be made available.

“Let them get my call log. My call log can be subpoenaed through the Court,” he was quoted as saying. “Let them release my written statement also. Why are they keeping it? They have it.”

But there is now a direct contradiction over whether Kwarbo actually made those statements.

Family: “He Never Made Such A Statement”

On Thursday, Kwarbo’s wife, Bendu Kwarbo, issued a statement on behalf of the family distancing her husband from the allegations against Coleman.

The family said it “categorically dissociates” Kwarbo from reports attributing the allegations to him and said neither the family nor his lawyers knew about or authorized any statement accusing the police chief.

“Mr. Kwarbo himself firmly rejects and denies this allegation in its entirety and maintains that he has made no such statement,” the family said.

The family said Kwarbo’s lawyers had advised him to remain silent and allow the court process to determine the case.

It described the statement circulating in his name as “malicious” and urged media organizations and the public to verify information before publishing or repeating allegations.

The family also maintains that Kwarbo should not have been arrested and that the case against him is based on what it described as false and misleading allegations.

Coleman: “Sustained Disinformation Campaign”

Coleman, meanwhile, has rejected the allegation and characterized it as part of what he says has been a prolonged campaign to undermine his credibility.

“For the past four months, I have been the target of a sustained disinformation campaign intended to damage my character and silence my fight against the culture of impunity, including the ongoing drug investigation,” Coleman said.

The police chief said freedom of expression must be respected but warned against spreading what he described as false information concerning an active criminal investigation.

“The facts must be established through evidence and lawful process. Anyone found to have broken the law must be held accountable under that same process,” Coleman said. “I will remain focused on my duty. I will not be intimidated.”

The US$ 317 Million Drug Case

The dispute comes against the backdrop of Liberia’s largest cocaine trafficking investigation, involving a shipment authorities have valued at approximately US$317 million.

Kwarbo, a former Highway Patrol chief, was stripped of his duties and later arrested and charged alongside Anthony T. Blaye, who served as Chief of the Liberia National Police Financial Crime Division.

The two have been accused of using marked police vehicles to escort a large cocaine shipment.

According to findings attributed to a joint Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency and Liberia National Police investigation, the cocaine was transported from a coastal landing site to a stash house using two police vehicles in an escort formation, with one vehicle reportedly positioned ahead of the shipment and another behind it.

Coleman said investigators uncovered evidence indicating that state security personnel played a role in moving the narcotics from the landing site to a holding location.

The foreign nationals, a Serbian and a Colombian, are being accused of bringing the cocaine into Liberia through aircraft and shoreline landing operations.

Liberian authorities publicly destroyed the seized cocaine on July 30 in what officials described as the country’s largest-ever drug destruction exercise.

Kwarbo’s Bail Fight

Kwarbo has denied wrongdoing and, in August, filed a motion seeking bail before Criminal Assizes “C” at the Temple of Justice.

His lawyers, including Cllr. Sayma Syrenius Cephus, maintain that he is being detained largely on allegations that he provided an escort to principal defendants after the alleged crimes had already been committed.

Kwarbo’s lawyers argue that the prosecution has not presented objective evidence placing him at the scene before or during the commission of the alleged offenses.

The defense has also challenged allegations attributed to co-defendant Christian Nyantee, arguing that Nyantee may have a motive to shift responsibility and that uncorroborated accomplice testimony should not be sufficient to establish the legal standard required for continued detention.

Kwarbo’s lawyers further contend that he had no prior knowledge of the alleged drug operation and that providing security escorts can form part of routine security duties during major national-security operations.

The Questions That Remain

The latest dispute leaves several questions unanswered.

It remains unclear who spoke to Spoon FM on Kwarbo’s behalf, whether the statement attributed to him was actually made by him, and how the statement emerged from the prison.

It is also unclear whether the written statement Kwarbo was quoted as referring to exists, what it contains, and whether investigators have sought or obtained his telephone records through the court.

Analysts say those questions may be resolved through evidence presented in court rather than competing accounts outside the courtroom.

For now, the public has two sharply different versions: one attributed to Kwarbo naming Coleman as the officer who allegedly ordered the escort, and another from Kwarbo’s family saying he never made the statement.

Kwarbo remains in detention and, under Liberia’s Constitution, is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia: Bail Denied, The Former Vice President’s Lawyers Weigh A Trip To The Supreme Court And a Long Legal Fight
World.content:
MONROVIA – For three weeks, the most important document at Jewel Howard-Taylor’s home has been a visitors’ log.

By Willie N. Tokpa

Every person who passes her gate is written down. Police officers stand watch around the clock. She may step outside only when the court has approved a trip to the hospital in advance. The former vice president, once second in line to lead the country, now needs a judge’s permission to see her doctor.

On Thursday, her lawyers went to court hoping to change that. They left with the same restrictions in place and a stinging rebuke from the bench.

By evening, the defense team had gathered in Monrovia to decide what comes next. For lawyers who have shifted strategy more than once in five weeks, the choices are narrowing. The road now leads up Capitol Hill, to the Supreme Court.

“We believe that she is eligible”

Atty. Gbawu Kowou, one of her lawyers, said the defense would take its case to the Justice in Chambers.

“The court argued that the crime extended up to 2026 based on the allegation that she received US$15,000. We disagree,” he told FrontPageAfrica. “The defense believes the court did not properly apply Liberia’s law on bail and pretrial detention, and that is the reason we are filing a petition for certiorari before the Justice in Chambers. We believe that she is eligible for bail.”

The papers are ready, he said. The team hopes to file on Friday, September 25, or by Monday, September 28 at the latest. Cllr. Kabina Ja’neh and former Associate Justice Lavalah Supuwood will lead the fight.

And the woman at the center of it? “The Vice President has been briefed on the latest decision from the court,” Kowou said.

A judge’s rebuke

The defense’s argument was simple. The 2023 Controlled Drugs and Substances Act makes the charges against her grave and non-bailable. But her lawyers said the conduct she is accused of happened in 2021 and 2022, before the law existed. A law, they argued, cannot reach back in time.

Judge Ousman F. Feika of Criminal Court “C” turned to the defense’s own paperwork to answer them.

Attached to their motion was the Writ of Arrest. It alleges that she received US$15,000 from the cartel through Sheikh Bashiru Kante as recently as August 2026. If true, the judge reasoned, the alleged conduct did not stop in 2022. It ran well past the new law.

Then he went further. He accused the defense of ignoring a major part of its own exhibit and warned that such conduct runs against the lawyers’ code of ethics. It is rare for a judge to scold counsel this way in a pretrial ruling.

Her lawyers noted their exception and told the court they would “take advantage of the statute controlling.” In Liberian courtrooms, everyone knows what that means: we’ll see you upstairs.

The road upstairs

The tool they will likely use is a writ of certiorari. Just last month, on August 28, the Supreme Court ruled in the Capitol arson case that certiorari is the proper way to challenge a trial judge’s interlocutory ruling. Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay explained that it lets the high court review a lower court that has jurisdiction but is alleged to have acted irregularly or contrary to law.

Recent history offers the defense both hope and caution.

In March 2025, Justice in Chambers Ceanneh Clinton Johnson overturned a Criminal Court “C” decision revoking the bail of Peach Bility, son of Representative Musa Hassan Bility, and sent him home.

Six years earlier, it went the other way. Justice Joseph Nagbe granted the State’s petition and overturned a trial judge who had found grounds to admit murder suspect Oliver Dillon to bail. Dillon stayed behind bars.

A filing could also buy time. In a 2024 case, the State’s certiorari petition automatically halted scheduled Criminal Court “C” proceedings until a conference with the Justice in Chambers. A similar pause here would freeze action before Judge Feika while the high court looks at his ruling.

Whatever the outcome, the question reaches beyond one defendant. The Justices may have to decide whether a no-bail law passed in 2023 can apply to conduct that allegedly began before it. Judge Feika’s order leaned on the continuing nature of the alleged offense and did not squarely answer that argument. The defense is likely to press the gap.

Waiting on the grand jury

Other fights remain unresolved. Judge Feika still has to rule on defense motions to quash the arrest writ, a habeas corpus petition and a motion to suppress evidence.

The defense has already shown it is willing to change course. On September 17, it withdrew the preliminary examination before Magistrate L. Ben Barco, giving up an early chance to test the State’s evidence. That evidence includes WhatsApp messages and audio recordings investigators say came from Kante’s phone. No one has yet heard them played in court.

And over all of it hangs the grand jury. Judge Feika can decide whether she goes home or stays confined. He cannot put her on trial without an indictment, and more than a month after her arrest, there is none.

Her allies have noticed. Lenn Eugene Nagbe, chief of staff to former President George Weah, said the government’s failure to indict her raises questions about the strength of its case.

The August Term of Court is in its 39th day of jury sitting. The clock is running.

The bigger picture

Her case sits at the heart of Liberia’s widest drug investigation. It began with a cocaine seizure valued at about US$317 million and has reached into the police, the intelligence services and the prison system.

Her party, the Coalition for Democratic Change, calls it political persecution. The government says she is presumed innocent and will have her day in court.

She was released from Monrovia Central Prison on medical grounds on September 4. The court has warned she could be sent back if her health improves significantly.

So she waits. Behind her gate, under guard, with each visitor’s name written in a book, while her lawyers climb the hill to argue that the case against her belongs to 2021, and the State insists it runs right up to this summer.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Gives Police ‘Last Opportunity’ in Cybercrime Suspect’s Detention Case
World.content:
Court says it will make an ‘informed decision’ if the IG and the arresting officer miss Friday’s hearing

MONROVIA – Criminal Court “B” at the Temple of Justice has given the Liberia National Police (LNP) one last chance to appear and explain why it is holding Jerry Nyantee Wrato. Wrato is charged with several cybercrime offences, and his lawyers say the police arrested him illegally and have held him far beyond the 48 hours allowed by the Constitution.

By Rodney D Sieh

Assigned Circuit Judge Pape Suah postponed the habeas corpus hearing on Thursday, September 24, 2026. No police officer appeared in court for the second straight hearing. The judge moved the matter to Friday, September 25, at 11 a.m. and warned that if the police fail to appear again, the court “will make an informed decision and will use the appropriate legal authority.”

Wrato faces charges of misuse of device, cyberstalking, distributing data messages that incite damage to property or violence, and distributing intimate images without consent. He sat in the dock during Thursday’s proceedings.

Prosecution blames officials’ absence

Government lawyers Cllr. Isaac B. Williams, Sr. and Cllr. Irene N. D. Saie represented the Ministry of Justice. They asked for the postponement. According to the court minutes, they said the arresting officer, the Inspector General of Police, officers of Units 102, 103 and 106, the chief investigator and other senior officers were all out of Monrovia and out of the country.

The prosecutors told the court they had “belief and assurance” that the officers would be back in Montserrado County in time for Friday’s hearing.

Defence: ‘bad faith’ and ‘disrespect’

Wrato’s lawyer, Cllr. Garrison D. Yealue, told the court the request was “made in bad faith” and was “a complete disrespect” to the court. He said the police had “illegally arrested the Petitioner and illegally kept him for more than 120 hours.” He argued that the police were now refusing to answer to a key provision of the 1986 Constitution.

The defence also rejected the excuse that the officials were away. Counsel argued that the police is an institution. Even if the Inspector General is abroad, he said, more than 60 deputies and assistant directors remain in the country, and “they choose to disrespect this Honorable Court.”

Counsel asked Judge Suah to reject the prosecution’s request. He also asked the judge to issue contempt proceedings against the Inspector General and his senior officers for “intentionally, willfully and disrespectfully ignoring” the court’s order.

Judge questions government’s paperwork

In his ruling, Judge Suah said the court had halted the previous hearing because the police and the Ministry of Justice did not appear to show cause why the writ should or should not be granted.

The judge said the Ministry of Justice claimed the defendant was already before the court, but it had not provided “sufficient and convincing evidence” that the case was sent to court in keeping with law. He said the documents the state described as a return from the Magisterial Court did not show who made the return, when it was made, or when the case was received.

The court had ordered government lawyers to make sure the police authorities and the arresting officer came to Thursday’s hearing. Judge Suah said “not even a single police officer” appeared. He noted that under habeas corpus, whoever has a person in custody must come to court and show why that person should or should not be released.

The judge said that “to its greatest surprise,” the prosecution then asked for a continuance because the officers were outside the country. He described the police’s refusal to come to court as “a disrespect.” He said he would use all relevant legal authority under the 1986 Constitution and the habeas corpus statute to make sure the arresting officer appears.

Even so, Judge Suah granted the continuance as the respondents’ “last opportunity.” He ordered the Clerk of Court to serve notices of assignment on the Ministry of Justice and Attorney General, the Solicitor General, the Montserrado County Attorney’s office, and the Office of the Inspector General of Police.

The defence took exception to the ruling. The matter was then suspended until Friday.

World.title: Liberia: CMC Pulls Out of Weah-Led Opposition Coalition Talks
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Citizens Movement for Change (CMC) has withdrawn from the opposition coalition process convened by former President George Manneh Weah, less than three weeks after the party’s political leader, Rep. Musa Hassan Bility, sat at the table with other opposition leaders in Paynesville.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

In a statement issued Thursday, September 24, and signed by National Chairman James M. V. Yougie, the CMC said it has formally informed Weah and the other political leaders who attended the September 6 Opposition Political Leaders Forum that it will not endorse the current draft communiqué or remain in the process leading to the proposed coalition.

The party said the decision followed a review of the draft by its National Executive Committee, National Advisory Council and Diaspora Leadership, which concluded that the arrangement, in its current form, does not reflect the objectives for which the CMC was founded.

At the heart of the CMC’s objection is what it describes as the absence of a binding reform program. The party said any coalition seeking public confidence must first agree on changes to the country’s system of government, institutions, laws and political culture, including constitutional reform, institutional independence and transparent leadership.

“Liberians should not be asked to choose only between continuing the present order and returning to the immediate past,” Bility said in the statement. “Our country deserves a new option built around a new governing system and a serious program of national reform.”

The CMC said it will instead continue national consultations with citizens, civil society groups, community leaders and like-minded parties toward what it calls a “broad national third lane.”

The party stressed that its decision “does not close the door” to opposition cooperation. It said it remains willing to work with other opposition parties on electoral integrity, the rule of law and public accountability, and is open to future political cooperation in which every party is treated as an equal and decisions are reached through transparent consultation and consensus. The CMC also said its position should not be read as a personal criticism of Weah or any other participating leader.

A reluctant participant from the start

The withdrawal is not entirely a surprise. Before the forum, Bility had objected to how it was structured. In an August 28 letter to CDC Chairman Atty. Janga A. Kowo, he said the CMC appreciated the effort to promote dialogue among opposition parties but would not attend, arguing that opposition unity cannot begin with predetermined leadership and authority. He specifically questioned provisions designating a presiding leader and establishing a National Convening Secretariat under an already appointed coordinator.

Bility later reversed course and attended the meeting. At a press conference afterward, he welcomed the gathering, saying the focus should remain on ordinary Liberians and describing the goal as uniting to rescue them from the “so-called rescuers” — a reference to the Unity Party’s campaign slogan.

The September 6 forum

The forum was held at the Jamaica Resort in Thinker’s Village, Paynesville, four days after Weah returned to Liberia. Attendees included ANC Political Leader Alexander B. Cummings, Bility, MPC Political Leader Simeon Freeman and MOVEE Political Leader D. Maxwell Kemayah, along with senior CDC officials including former House Speakers J. Alex Tyler and Bhofal Chambers. Benoni Urey’s All Liberian Party was also represented.

Under the agreement reached there, each participating party was to nominate two representatives to a steering committee responsible for drafting a framework document defining the principles, structure and mechanisms of cooperation. Participants stressed that the initiative was not an electoral alliance or an agreement on a presidential ticket for 2029.

The push came amid sharp opposition criticism of the Boakai administration. The CDC had described President Boakai’s August 26 national address on the rule of law as “dishonest and nefarious.” On his return, Weah said the opposition has an obligation to speak collectively and argued the country is moving in the wrong direction under the Boakai administration.

The effort has also exposed divisions elsewhere. The National Patriotic Party suspended three senior partisans for allegedly using the party’s official letterhead to endorse the roundtable. Unity Party Secretary General Amos B. Tweh dismissed the gathering as posing no serious threat to the ruling party or to President Boakai’s reelection prospects.

The shadow of the CPP

The CMC’s exit revives memories of the last major opposition alliance. In February 2019, the Unity Party, ANC, ALP and Liberty Party formed the Collaborating Political Parties, which won six Senate seats in 2020 before a September 2021 dispute over its framework document triggered its collapse. The ALP walked out in December 2021, the Unity Party followed in February 2022, and a Liberty Party faction left the next month. The remaining Cummings-Brumskine ticket won 1.61 percent of the presidential vote in 2023, and the CPP formally dissolved in April 2024.

The CMC itself is a young party. Bility, who represents Nimba County District 7, founded it in March 2025 after resigning from the Liberty Party in September 2024.

World.title: Dignity at the Podium, Deportees at the Airport
World.content:
PRESIDENT JOSEPH NYUMA BOAKAI went to the United Nations on Thursday night and spoke powerfully about dignity. He demanded that Africa, a continent of 1.5 billion people, stop being discussed without a permanent voice on the Security Council. He said a global system “governed by so few” cannot keep deciding the fate of billions. He pledged that Liberia stands ready to “guarantee human dignity, and leave no one behind.”

FINE WORDS. BUT Liberians are entitled to ask how they square with what happened at Roberts International Airport just five weeks ago.

THE DEAL THE SPEECH LEFT OUT

IN AUGUST, LIBERIA agreed to accept up to 1,200 third-country deportees from the United States over the coming year, one of the largest such arrangements under the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The first 20 arrived at Roberts International Airport outside Monrovia. They are not Liberians. They include Africans as well as nationals from North America, South America and the Caribbean.

THE GOVERNMENT CALLS this humanitarian. Perhaps. But the facts warrant pause. According to Reuters, these deportees have in most cases won legal protection against repatriation after U.S. immigration judges found they risked torture or other abuses. In other words, Washington cannot legally send them home, so it sends them here.

IMMIGRATION LAWYERS SAY such deportations work as a loophole to push asylum seekers back to their home countries indirectly, and that many end up with little choice but to return to the very places they fled.

Is that what “leave no one behind” means?

NOT LIBERIA ALONE

LIBERIA IS NOT the only African country in this business. At least eight African governments now have confirmed agreements or arrivals, including Eswatini, South Sudan, Ghana, Rwanda, Uganda, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. The record elsewhere is troubling.

IN ESWATINI, DEPORTEES have been held at a maximum-security prison pending repatriation. Human Rights Watch has warned that transfers to Eswatini, Ghana, Rwanda and South Sudan exposed several hundred people to the risk of arbitrary detention, ill-treatment and refoulement. One regional outlet reports Ghana has repeatedly sent protected deportees home anyway, and that these deals have paid African governments more than $32 million.

SO HERE IS the contradiction. Africa goes to New York demanding to be treated as an equal partner in global decision-making. Yet at the same time, African governments, Liberia among them, are quietly agreeing to serve as holding grounds for people a powerful nation does not want and cannot lawfully return. That is not the posture of a continent seeking a permanent seat. It is the posture of a continent still taking instructions.

WHAT DID WE GET, AND WHAT DID WE GIVE?

LIBERIANS HAVE NOT seen the terms of this deal. The information minister said Liberia will receive U.S. support to manage the program and strengthen its migration system. What support? How much? Who decides who comes? Where will these people live, and who will protect them? What happens if one of them is later sent back to face torture after passing through Liberia’s hands?

A government that told the UN that trust is broken because principles are applied “inconsistently and selectively” cannot keep its own agreements hidden from its own people.

A SEAT MUST MEAN A SPINE

WE SUPPORT AFRICA’S demand for permanent seats on the Security Council. But visibility is not the same as influence, and a seat is worth little if it comes without the courage to say no. If Liberia wants a louder voice on the world stage, it must show that voice is its own and not borrowed from whoever holds the purse.

LIBERIA ALREADY SITS on the Security Council. It could use that seat to demand transparency and legal protections for every African nation being asked to host deportees. It could lead on the rights of migrants rather than quietly serve the policy that tramples them. That would be leadership worthy of a permanent seat.

THE PRESIDENT TOLD the world that Liberia is “living proof that dialogue can overcome division.” Let that dialogue begin at home. Publish the deal. Explain the benefits. And show Liberians that the dignity promised in New York applies at Roberts International Airport too.

World.title: Liberians Protest at UN Headquarters and Outside President Boakai’s Hotel Over Drugs and “Selective Justice”
World.content:
NEW YORK – Dozens of Liberians gathered in New York during the UN General Assembly to protest outside the hotel where President Joseph Boakai is staying, then at the United Nations Headquarters ahead of his address. Demonstrators said his government is not serious about fighting drug trafficking and is applying the law selectively.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

“Our children are dying every day. We say no to drugs. We need justice. Let the United Nations hear our cry,” the protesters chanted. “Our children are dying. Our women are dying. The youth are dying. Say no to drugs… No to drugs.” Other chants targeted specific officials: “Gregory Coleman should be expelled. He is a drug dealer. Gregory must go… The IG must go.” They also called for an end to police brutality. At the hotel, some chanted “No to selective justice” repeatedly, and a section of the crowd shouted slogans directed at the president himself, including “Boakai, no drugs” and “Boakai, cocaine king.” These are the protesters’ allegations. No evidence was presented, and the government has not been shown to have responded to them.

Speaking to onlookers, one organizer said the group came “to protest against a bad government in Liberia” and “to stop drug trafficking in Liberia.” The protesters pointed to the arrest of a former vice president, saying senior officials they accuse of ties to drug traffickers remain free. “Why are those people staying home? Why are they not being arrested?” the organizer asked.

Another participant said the president and his family had been accused online of involvement but were never brought in for questioning. “The president should bring his son for questioning,” the participant said. “Anyone that is accused of such things should be brought for questioning.”

The protesters said their plan was to wait for President Boakai outside the hotel, march behind his convoy to the UN General Assembly, and continue demonstrating there.

“We are here to tell the world that our president, Joseph Boakai, is not serious in fighting the drug crisis in Liberia,” one said. They said they wanted the president to act on the crisis after his speech and appealed to the United Nations to hear their concerns.

Demonstrators also contrasted the setting with protests back home. They said Liberian police often respond to citizens who assemble to petition the government with water trucks and heavy weapons, whereas in New York police simply ensured the protest stayed peaceful. “We want justice, we want freedom,” one said. “We want our people to express themselves without fear.”

The protest stayed peaceful, with the demonstrators saying they would continue to the UN after the president’s arrival. The Liberian government had not responded to the protesters’ claims at the time of writing.

World.title: Liberia Warns IMO Net-Zero Shipping Plan Could Burden Developing Economies
World.content:
Country pushes for equitable maritime decarbonization framework, citing risks to trade, food and energy security

NEW YORK — Liberia has renewed its call for a fair and equitable approach to decarbonizing international shipping, warning that the transition to net-zero emissions must not impose disproportionate economic costs on developing countries.

The call was made on September 23, 2026, during a high-level engagement with United Nations Member States in New York, where Liberia presented its proposed alternative approach to the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework.

According to a press release, Liberia’s proposal seeks to advance the objectives of the IMO’s 2023 Strategy on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Ships while ensuring that developing countries are not unfairly disadvantaged by the global transition to cleaner maritime transport.

Liberia, a major global flag State and a climate-vulnerable developing country with deep economic and historical ties to the sea, said ambitious climate action must go hand in hand with protecting developing economies.

The country maintains that maritime decarbonization should be pragmatic, affordable, scalable, performance-based and legally coherent within the IMO’s mandate.

“Net zero must not become a new burden on developing countries,” Liberia’s position emphasizes.

Concerns Over Trade, Food and Energy Security

Liberia cautioned that significantly higher maritime transportation costs could have consequences far beyond the shipping industry, potentially driving up the prices of essential commodities and undermining food security, energy security, trade competitiveness and sustainable development.

International shipping is central to the movement of food, fuel, medicines, machinery, construction materials and other essential goods, making the cost of maritime transport a critical concern for developing economies.

Liberia argued that the economic implications of maritime decarbonization must be considered alongside its environmental objectives, particularly for countries heavily dependent on maritime trade.

The country is also calling for economic impact assessments tailored to individual developing countries, noting that nations differ in their economic structures, trade profiles, technological capabilities, infrastructure and access to finance.

It said a comprehensive global assessment should be complemented by country-specific evaluations that adequately capture the vulnerabilities and circumstances of individual states.

Push for Practical and Affordable Transition

Liberia’s proposed alternative approach emphasizes commercially viable alternative fuels, operational and technological efficiencies, infrastructure development and capacity-building as practical pathways to reducing emissions from international shipping.

The country is also advocating predictable, transparent and equitable support mechanisms that respond to the needs of developing countries.

Liberia maintains that developing economies should not be required to absorb significant economic and trade costs upfront, with the expectation that subsequent financial support or redistribution will fully compensate for the impacts.

Instead, it argues that the framework should be designed from the outset to minimize disproportionate economic consequences.

The country further stressed the need for evidence-based decision-making before implementing measures with potentially significant economic implications.

Among the issues it wants considered are the affordability, technical credibility, legal coherence and administrative feasibility of proposed measures, as well as the availability and scalability of alternative fuels across different regions, ports and shipping routes.

Liberia Reaffirms Support for Climate Action

Despite its concerns, Liberia reaffirmed that its proposal is not intended to weaken global climate ambitions.

Rather, the country said it seeks a framework that allows environmental protection and sustainable development to advance together, while ensuring meaningful participation by all IMO Member States, regardless of their size, economic status or maritime interests.

Liberia said a fair transition could create opportunities for investment, innovation, technology transfer, infrastructure development and capacity-building, while protecting trade and economic security.

The country pledged to continue working with IMO Member States and other stakeholders toward a maritime decarbonization framework that balances climate objectives with economic realities.

Next Steps

The IMO and its Member States are expected to continue deliberations on the Net-Zero Framework at the next session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC), scheduled for November 2026.

Liberia said it would remain actively engaged in consultations leading up to and during the session, seeking an outcome that is environmentally ambitious, economically responsible and equitable for all Member State

World.title: Hichilema Calls for Fairer Global Health Systems at UN General Assembly
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has called for stronger and fairer global health systems, telling a high-level meeting on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly that poverty and geography must not decide who gets vaccines, medicines and other health technologies.

The speech was read on his behalf in New York on Thursday by Health Minister Professor Roma Chilengi, at a meeting held alongside the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. Mr Hichilema said countries should be able to protect their own populations, and that regions should have the capacity to respond together to health threats.

He said a strong public-health system must work at every link in the chain, from detecting an illness to laboratory testing, regional coordination and access to vaccines and treatment.

“Our shared task is to make those systems more dependable, in everyday care and in times of crisis. At the heart of that task are the people who need care and those who provide it,” he said.

The President then turned to how those systems are paid for. He said Zambia’s experience with debt restructuring had reinforced the need to create fiscal space for essential public services, particularly health. He called for timely and workable debt restructuring and, where necessary, debt relief, saying debt agreements should leave countries room to invest in essential services.

On emergency preparedness, Mr Hichilema called for health-security financing that does not worsen debt distress. He said grants should support cross-border preparedness, while concessional lending should remain consistent with debt sustainability.

He also raised concern over declining development assistance, citing preliminary figures from the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) showing a real-terms fall of more than 23 per cent in official development assistance in 2025. Zambia, he said, remained committed to working with health partners while increasing its own domestic investment in programmes addressing HIV, tuberculosis and malaria.

The Head of State asked for carefully planned aid transitions, so that patients do not lose access to essential services when donor support changes.

Climate change was the next point on his list. Mr Hichilema said heat, floods and drought threaten safe water, nutrition, disease control and the continuity of healthcare services. He pointed to Zambia’s 2023–2024 cholera epidemic and the severe drought of 2024 as proof of the close links between health, water, sanitation and food security.

He said no country could manage every cross-border health threat alone, which is why regional preparedness matters.

On access to health technologies, the President said the COVID-19 pandemic had exposed major inequalities in access to vaccines. He said the World Health Organisation (WHO) Pandemic Agreement offered a chance to build a fairer system, particularly through arrangements on pathogen access and benefit-sharing. Countries that share pathogen samples and genetic information, he said, should receive timely access to vaccines, diagnostics and treatments in return.

He also called for increased regional production, pooled procurement, technology sharing, predictable demand, effective regulation and investment in research and development.

“Africa must produce knowledge and solutions, not only receive products,” he said.

Mr Hichilema asked countries to create and use fiscal space for health by bringing finance and health authorities, creditors and development partners together around credible investment priorities, timely debt solutions and transparent delivery.

At home, he said, Zambia’s 2026 National Budget allocated K26.2 billion, equivalent to about US$1.1 billion, to health services, representing about 10.3 per cent of the national budget. He said the investment should translate into tangible improvements, including the recruitment of health workers, stronger health infrastructure, the availability of medicines and improved access to healthcare.

World.title: Haimbe Defends Cancellation of Six Passports as Mutambo’s Lawyers Give Government Seven Days
World.content:
Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe has defended the Government’s decision to cancel the passports of six Zambians living abroad, saying the move does not violate their rights, while lawyers for one of them, content creator Lillian Mutambo, have demanded her passport back within seven days or face court action.

Mr Haimbe spoke in an interview in New York, on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly. He said the cancellations took effect on 11 September because the holders violated the conditions under which the passports were issued, and stressed that withdrawing a passport does not equate to loss of citizenship.

“The cancellation of a passport does not amount to cancellation of citizenship; it does not amount to taking away the right of an individual other than the use of a passport to access foreign countries,” he said.

The six affected are former Ambassador to Ethiopia Emmanuel Mwamba, former Members of Parliament Binwell Mpundu and Emmanuel Banda, former presidential adviser Kaiser Zulu, academic Sishuwa Sishuwa and Ms Mutambo, whom the minister described as a social media commentator.

The minister singled out Mr Banda, the former Petauke MP, as the clearest case. He described him as a known felon who escaped lawful custody in Zambia while facing criminal charges, and alleged that he continued committing offences using platforms abroad.

“In those circumstances, every nation of this world is entitled to use legal means available to ensure that the individual comes and answers to the charges and criminal allegations before a court of competent jurisdiction,” Mr Haimbe said.

He said the Government exercised its discretion to withdraw Mr Banda’s passport, and then cancelled those of the other five because they also needed to answer questions within Zambia’s jurisdiction.

Mr Haimbe used the same interview to reject wider claims about the political climate. He dismissed assertions that arrests recorded after the general election were politically motivated, saying they were based on allegations of criminal conduct. Suspects, he said, had been granted access to lawyers and families in line with Zambia Correctional Service regulations, and every citizen remained innocent until proven guilty before a competent court.

On the election result, he said President Hakainde Hichilema secured more than three million votes against about 1.9 million for Brian Mundubile, and questioned how such a margin could be branded irregular. He said Zambia had been working on a national peace architecture since 2021 and was moving towards concluding an effective framework to ensure peace prevails at all times.

Ms Mutambo’s lawyers see the passport decision very differently. Aongola & Co, acting for the UK-based content creator, wrote on 21 September to the Chief Passports and Citizenship Officer, copying the Registrar General and the Attorney General. They said the passport was cancelled under Government Gazette Notice No. 1421 of 2026, dated 11 September, on unspecified “security reasons”.

“Our Client’s position is that the decision, and the manner in which it was made and communicated, is unlawful, ultra vires, procedurally improper and unconstitutional,” the firm said.

The lawyers said the power to cancel a passport is a statutory power that must be exercised strictly within the Passport Act No. 28 of 2016. They pointed to Section 12(1), which vests that power in the Chief Passports and Citizenship Officer, and noted that the Gazette Notice appears to attribute the cancellation to the Registrar General. They demanded that the Government identify any provision, delegation or instrument under which the Registrar General could exercise it.

They also said the Act sets out specific grounds for confiscation and cancellation, including wrongful possession, fraud or misrepresentation, deportation or repatriation at Government expense, and a warrant of arrest coupled with a risk of absconding. The decision-maker, they said, must name the ground relied on and the facts that bring Ms Mutambo within it. If national security is claimed as an independent ground, the lawyers asked the Government to cite the exact section, subsection and paragraph.

On reasons, the firm cited Section 12(2), which it said requires a passport holder to be informed of a cancellation and given reasons within 14 days.

“Our Client has not been furnished with adequate written reasons identifying the factual and statutory basis for the cancellation. A bare reference to ‘security reasons’ does not, in our Client’s estimation, satisfy the statutory and constitutional requirement for reasons,” the lawyers said.

The firm said the cancellation also interferes with Ms Mutambo’s freedom of movement under Article 22 of the Constitution, which protects the right of citizens to leave and return to Zambia. They acknowledged that the Constitution allows restrictions in the interests of defence, public safety and public order, but said any restriction must have a lawful statutory basis. They added that the decision can be challenged for illegality, procedural impropriety, failure to consider relevant matters and unreasonableness, and that Ms Mutambo was not given an adequate opportunity to make representations before it was taken.

Aongola & Co want the Government to withdraw the cancellation, restore and recognise the passport as valid, and confirm that she will face no adverse immigration, passport, border-control or other administrative consequences.

“We trust that you will treat this matter with the urgency warranted by the continuing infringement of our Client’s rights,” the lawyers said.

The seven days run from receipt of the letter, and the firm has said legal proceedings will follow without further notice if the passport is not restored.

World.title: DPP Defends Delay in Taking Mundubile and Makebi Treason Case to Court
World.content:
Director of Public Prosecutions Gilbert Phiri has defended the time it is taking to bring Tonse Alliance presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and other treason suspects before the courts, and has asked the public to give law enforcement agencies space to do their work.

The plea follows a call by the Law Association of Zambia for the release of Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and others who have been detained without being taken to court.

Mr Phiri said it is appalling that suspects in Zambia are expected to appear in court a day after arrest, whatever the complexity of the alleged offences. The state wants accused persons before a judge, he said, but due diligence has to come first so that each case is properly investigated and backed by sufficient evidence.

In complex matters, that work takes time. Investigators must obtain witness statements, medical reports and other evidence before a fully supported case can go to court.

To make the point, the DPP turned to earlier treason trials, citing that of Edward Jack Shamwana. The case, he said, took considerable time from arrest to trial and eventual conviction, and he insisted that agencies must be allowed adequate time to finish their investigations.

Mr Mundubile and his running mate are expected before the High Court in Solwezi today, Friday, in connection with a seditious practices charge.

World.title: Katele Kalumba Freed on Police Bond After Cyber Harassment Charge
World.content:
Former Cabinet minister Dr Katele Kalumba has been charged with cyber harassment over remarks against President Hakainde Hichilema and released on police bond, a day after soldiers and plain-clothes police officers picked him up at his home in Chienge, Luapula Province.

Police spokesperson Godfrey Chilabi confirmed the charge in an interview in Lusaka on Thursday evening. He said Dr Kalumba was arrested on Wednesday and taken to Kabwe in Central Province, where he was detained at Kabwe Central Police Station.

“Later today, he was officially charged and released on police bond awaiting court appearance. He was charged for a cyber harassment offence in relation to some remarks he made against the Republican President on September 10, 2026,” Mr Chilabi said.

Dr Kalumba, who served in the MMD government, was charged under the Cyber Crimes Act No. 4 of 2025. Police said the remarks were contained in a widely circulated social media post on 10 September, and that he is expected to appear before court in due course. The nature of the remarks was not disclosed.

The events in Chienge began in the early hours of Wednesday. His wife, Mrs Kalumba, said soldiers first went to Dr Kalumba’s lodge, which is next to the family home, around 04:00, but were denied access by the chief’s retainers.

A combined team of soldiers and plain-clothes police officers returned around midday. Mrs Kalumba said they picked up her husband at about 12:10, while he was with Headman Natende and Headman Semushi, and took him to Chienge Police Station. Officers were preparing to move him to Mansa, she said.

Her immediate worry was his health. Mrs Kalumba said the officers drove away without his heart medication, which she said he must take every day. “The medication they have left behind is important, it is non-negotiable for his health, he has to take it every day. This is sad,” she said.

She said Dr Kalumba is a known chronic patient with a heart condition and a spinal problem, and has a leg fracture that has only started healing and requires a special shoe. A journey by road would affect him, she said, because the family usually drives him to Mansa and flies him to Lusaka. His granddaughter was rushing to Mansa to take him his medicine.

Mrs Kalumba also raised concern over an incident involving her son, Akayombokwa Kalumba, who was attacked by an unknown person at a bar in Makeni Bonaventure in Lusaka using a carpenter’s saw. She said the attack followed a social media post claiming he had been shot dead, and that he sustained a cut and is undergoing treatment.

“I suspect it was a targeted attack. We suspect these are scare tactics and that these issues are related,” she said.

Separately, Dr Kalumba has been vocal about the country’s political tension. In a Facebook post, he urged President Hichilema to change direction following the arrest and detention of opposition presidential candidate Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 16 others on treason charges. It was not immediately clear whether that appeal is the post at the centre of the charge.

“Please, do not ignore this warning. The political climate is becoming dangerously tense. It does not have to remain so. You have the opportunity to change the direction of the national conversation,” he said.

He asked the President to consider releasing Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu, Xavier Franklin Chungu and others held for political or politically related matters, particularly those who have not yet been brought before the courts. He also called for a conciliatory national indaba to promote peace and unity.

“I’m therefore asking you now, as one Zambian speaking directly to another, where charges are weak or politically coloured, allow the appropriate legal mechanisms to resolve them and then concentrate on governing,” Dr Kalumba said.

He said the President should not use campaign and election disagreements to punish critics, and should not treat the opposition as an enemy. “Let the courts do their work where there are genuine criminal matters. Let political opponents breathe,” he said.

Government has rejected claims that the law is being used against political opponents. Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe said in an interview in New York that those in detention face individual criminal charges rather than political persecution, and that every citizen remains innocent until proven guilty before a competent court.

For now, Dr Kalumba is on police bond, and police say he will appear before court in due course.

World.title: State House, UPND Distance Hichilema From Third Term Calls
World.content:
State House and the ruling United Party for National Development (UPND) have moved to distance President Hakainde Hichilema from growing calls to remove presidential term limits, with State House describing the third term question as a peripheral issue and the party saying it has no position on it.

The calls have come from within the ruling party’s wider ranks, and the most direct came from Florence Chileshe Chama, a UPND nominated Member of Parliament. In a video shared widely online on 21 September, she said women want Mr Hichilema to remain in office beyond 2031. “As women in Zambia, we want development, we don’t want democracy,” she said.

Others followed a similar line. Chilufya Tayali, a UPND supporter, said removing the presidential term limit would strengthen democracy, while party official Michael Chuzu said on a television programme that the President was completing the late Anderson Mazoka’s term and would start his own in 2031.

State House answered on Thursday. Chief Communications Specialist Clayson Hamasaka said the people should not focus on the third term question but on the President’s development agenda. Speaking in Lusaka, he said national issues could not be resolved through press statements and social media commentary alone.

He then gave an assurance on how the country would be run. “One thing I can assure everyone is that President Hakainde Hichilema will not govern the country based on social media commentary,” Mr Hamasaka said.

He invited citizens with concrete ideas or proposals on matters affecting the country to take them to the relevant Government ministries or the State House desk. Mr Hamasaka added that the President would not stifle civil and legal discussion among citizens on issues of national interest.

UPND media director Mark Simuuwe took the same line and went further on what the President’s silence should be taken to mean. He said there had never been an official Government position, or a statement from Mr Hichilema, proposing a third term.

“The fact that the President has chosen not to comment should be respected. His silence should not be interpreted as either support or opposition to the various views being expressed,” Mr Simuuwe said.

He said the continued attempts by Socialist Party leader Fred M’membe to draw the Head of State into the conversation were unnecessary, and amounted to deliberately making him the subject of a conversation he had not started. It was contradictory, he said, to demand that the President speak while knowing that the same voices would accuse him of interference if he did.

Mr Simuuwe also reminded Mr M’membe of his own record, saying he had taken part in and promoted constitutional reform through his media platforms, including The Weekly Post. If Mr M’membe had a position on presidential term limits, he said, he should present his arguments and let Zambians agree or disagree.

On the question of change itself, Mr Simuuwe said constitutional provisions were open to democratic evolution. He pointed to the amendments to tenure limits for local government offices as proof that frameworks could be altered through proper legal procedures. “Let parliamentarians express their views. Let the constitutional process determine the outcome,” he said.

The party’s position was set out most plainly by secretary general Batuke Imenda, who said the UPND had not discussed the matter at all. “As a party, we have no position on this one, because it is not in our agenda. So, whether it’s for or against, we have not discussed it. In fact, our Grow Zambia Agenda is what is keeping us busy and not anything else,” he said.

Mr Imenda said the topic had never been tabled in party structures, so anyone speaking on it was doing so in a private capacity. He said the party could control its own members but not the general public, who were free to discuss whatever they wished under the expanded democratic space, and that the UPND would not be drawn into political speculation. He urged citizens to direct their energy to supporting the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The Constitution’s own words frame the question. Article 106(3) states that “a person who has twice held office as President is not eligible for election as President.” Mr Hichilema was sworn in for a second term on 1 September, and that term, which runs to 2031, is his last under current law.

Bill 7, signed into law on 18 December 2025, removed the two-term limit for mayors and council chairpersons and created 40 nominated seats for women, youth and persons with disabilities. Government says it does not remove presidential term limits. Attorney General Mulilo Kabesha has said upcoming constitutional reforms will follow due process, that Zambians will participate, and that political statements should not create fear.

Opposition voices see the matter differently. Saboi Imboela, president of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), said removing term limits would enable the creation of tyrants, because those who introduced the limits knew what removal would mean. “Those that created the term limits knew that if they removed them it would be the beginning of the creation of tyrants because people would now be untouchable,” she said.

Ms Imboela also questioned the UPND’s change of position. She said the late President Edgar Lungu was fought and taken to court, where it was agreed that he was not eligible to contest the 2026 election. “What is happening what has changed the UPND fought Lungu until they even went to court so why are they now pushing this narrative,” she asked.

She said the ruling party’s two-thirds majority in Parliament meant it could amend the Constitution if it wished, and that Mr Hichilema should groom a successor rather than cling to power at all costs. She urged Zambians to speak out because democracy was under threat.

For now, Mr Hichilema has not said he wants a third term, the UPND says the question is not on its agenda, and Article 106(3) remains in force.
