World.title: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? A visual investigation
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Satellite imagery shows Israel compacting and removing rubble and debris from Gaza, with possible human remains and potential evidence of war crimes still trapped under it, a CBC News visual investigation of several sites has found.

Multiple destroyed areas in formerly populated areas of Gaza are being cleared, according to CBC's analysis, to make way for new military outposts for Israeli Defence Forces (IDF).

Families in Gaza say this prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the ruins.

"Where are the bodies? Where are the houses? Where's the rubble?" said Dalal Faraj, a Palestinian whose home in Gaza City was bombed, after CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife showed her satellite footage of the now-cleared site.

UN officials have raised concerns in recent weeks that Israel is not properly handling rubble — and bodies that may still be under it — left by strikes in the almost three-year conflict sparked by the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023.

WATCH | Investigating the clearing of rubble in Gaza: Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? | Duration 4:10 CBC’s visual investigations team uncovers new satellite imagery that shows the IDF removing rubble from sites in Gaza that it bombed, which experts and human rights advocates warn risks destroying evidence of alleged war crimes. Families in Gaza interviewed by CBC say this activity prevents them from retrieving the bodies of loved ones trapped under the rubble.

In 2024, the International Criminal Court ordered Israel to take measures to preserve evidence of alleged violations of the UN Genocide Convention in Gaza.

"It is Israel's obligation under international law to do everything possible to ensure these remains are found, identified and buried with dignity," said Ajith Sunghay, head of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory.

In a statement to CBC News, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said it clears structures and dismantles infrastructure in Gaza "based on tactical necessity" and to "reduce the level of risk posed" to its troops. It says this activity is "carried out in accordance with operational necessity, the provisions of international law, and IDF directives."

The IDF denies any accusations it isn't preserving evidence and recovering remains, saying it "treats every body found in the area with respect and seriousness."

Families that CBC News spoke to say no one contacted them about the retrieval of the bodies before or after the IDF removed the rubble from their homes.

IDF military base built over neighbourhood

"Impossible … This is our area?" Dalal Faraj told CBC News, looking at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. "Where did the houses go? Where are my husband and son?"

Dalal Faraj, who lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza City, looks at satellite imagery of her former neighbourhood. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

In October 2023, as the war picked up pace, Faraj left her home in Shuja'iya, a neighbourhood in Gaza City. Her husband, Taha, 48, and son Nasr, 16, told her to take the five younger children and head to a safer location. Taha and Nasr told her they would catch up when they could.

On Oct. 8, 2023, a day after the war started, an Israeli strike hit her home. She hasn't heard from her husband or son since.

Nasr Faraj, left, and his father, Taha. (Submitted by Dalal Faraj)

The satellite images that CBC's visual investigations team was able to gather show the buildings that once stood in Faraj's neighbourhood are all gone.

As the area was cleared of rubble, a new Israeli military base was built on top of it.

This composite image shows satellite footage of the Faraj family neighbourhood and the location of their home in August 2023, left, two months before the start of the war, and in August 2026, with the Israeli military base at the centre. (Google Earth, Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

On March 10, 2026, a satellite captured a rubble-clearing operation in the Faraj family neighbourhood. CBC News identified 10 diggers and one truck in the area just north of their home.

A composite image of heavy land-clearing machinery the CBC News visual investigations team identified in a March 10, 2026, satellite image. The image shows a clearing operation near the Shuja’iya military base. The colour of the machinery suggests it’s not military, but probably civilian subcontractors. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

A month later, satellite imagery shows four diggers clearing terrain west of the Faraj family house.

In April 2026, excavators moved west of the military base, clearing rubble, as shown in this composite image. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Faraj, who now lives with her children in a displacement camp in Gaza, said she's been waiting for years to be able to return to her home to retrieve Taha and Nasr's remains and rebuild. Seeing the pictures broke the last of her hope, she said.

"This area used to be my home. We used to live in a safe place. We would go to school, go out and have fun. Suddenly, this happened," Faraj said.

CBC asked the IDF how many bodies found under the rubble in Gaza since last year's ceasefire have been returned to Palestinians. It did not answer the question.

Destruction of the 'Swedish Village'

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, 36, says 14 members of his family are still missing after the family home in southern Gaza was destroyed.

Abu Ouda lived in a settlement in the Rafah Governorate known as the "Swedish Village." Abu Ouda left the area in 2024, and Rafah was occupied by Israel in 2025.

Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda, left, speaks with family members about their neighbourhood in Rafah Governorate, which has been destroyed and cleared. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

"Warplanes started shooting at us, then came the F-16s, it shot at the house which we were in," Abu Ouda told CBC. "I left by a miracle."

Eight of the 14 members of the Abu Ouda family whose whereabouts are unknown after the IDF cleared rubble that may have contained their remains. (Submitted by Shaher Mohamed Abu Ouda)

"Until today, I think about what happened that day," he said. "I thought I would go back and see them, but after all these years, I won't even find a blouse."

Comparison shots of the location of Abu Ouda's home show the rubble was there until at least June 2026. By August, the rubble was gone, with heavy machinery tracks visible.

The three satellite images in this composite show the location of the Abu Ouda family home in Swedish Village in October 2023, May 2026 and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Footage from May 2026 shows a clearing operation, with six vehicles removing the rubble where the Swedish Village once stood.

CBC News identified vehicles clearing rubble in the satellite image taken on May 7, 2026, at the centre of what was Swedish Village, preparing the location for the military base. (Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

The latest satellite imagery from August 2026 shows the neighbourhood completely flattened, with a military base on top of it.

This composite image shows how the Swedish Village area looked in June 2024, left, and August 2026. (Google Earth/Pléiades Neo © Airbus DS 2026/CBC)

Abu Ouda is not surprised by the satellite images of his neighbourhood, because Rafah has been under Israeli control for years. But the images provided confirmation that he is unlikely to be able to retrieve his family's remains, he said.

"Fourteen people lost their lives and we still know nothing about them," he said. "Even the rubble is not there."

'A new type of destruction'

Júlia Nueno Guitart, a researcher at Forensic Architecture, an independent research group tracking developments in Gaza, confirmed CBC's findings. She said her group has collected more than 2,000 similar incidents and managed to confirm 43 cases "where people have remained under the rubble."

"We have been able to do so either by visual evidence, graffiti on the walls of some of the buildings where people remain or by reports from [Gaza's] Civil Defence, where they inform us of the impossibility of retrieving bodies under the rubble," Nueno Guitart told CBC News.

A graphic shows instances Forensic Architecture has identified in which civilians are reportedly under rubble. (Forensic Architecture)

According to Forensic Architecture's findings, the Israeli military is compacting and clearing rubble around newly established military bases even in areas where bodies are still under the rubble.

"What we are seeing after the ceasefire in Gaza is a new type of destruction, different to the one we have been documenting before the ceasefire," Nueno Guitart said.

According to Janina Dill, a professor at Oxford University in the U.K. and an expert on international law, removing rubble and flattening the bombed area is only compatible with international law if the war dead are collected, identified and buried, and if evidence required to prosecute potential war crimes or suppress violations of international law is preserved.

"If [the rubble removal] is done without taking care of these two considerations, then it is absolutely prohibited and incompatible with Israel's obligations under the Geneva Convention," Dill said.

World.title: AI 'slop' is dominating menus, as some restaurant owners turn to it to save time and money
World.content: The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. From cartoonish-looking sandwiches to doughnut-shaped shrimp , AI might be on the menu at your local fast-food restaurant. Diners have taken to the internet to share photos of sandwich boards and window displays bearing food they say looks rubbery, surreal and seems to be created with artificial intelligence tools — which have made it increasingly easy to generate visuals on the cheap. "This looks like what aliens would put in a presentation about what Earth food is," a Reddit user captioned in a post accompanied by a picture of a sandwich board with breaded shrimp and gyros with suspiciously geometric textures. Others described a CNE sandwich they assumed to be AI-generated as " uncanny and nauseating " and "slop." And for some Toronto customers, these kinds of images aren't just stomach-turning — they take them as a signal of the restaurant's values. "I feel like it's really inauthentic and it doesn't make me wanna go eat at your restaurant," said Cynthia Lem. For her, AI-generated imagery raises questions about what the actual food would look like once it arrives, making her wary of any establishments using the technology. The death of folk graphic design in favor of AI slop across our country's delis is leading to some incredibly Lovecraftian food horrors pic.twitter.com/snDyC675Ei —samfbiddle While some consumers say these images are ruining their appetites and raising worries about possible misrepresentations of menu items, those in the restaurant business say it's helped them reduce costs in a notoriously difficult industry. And marketing experts say use of the tech isn't necessarily bad if it's done thoughtfully. Not all AI use created equally Before taking a single bite, restaurant-goers rely heavily on imagery to dictate what they order, according to business consultant and Schulich School of Business marketing professor David Pullara. And that means businesses relying on heavy-handed AI imagery are taking a big risk. "Great food photography sells," said Pullara. "So if you're using AI to generate an image that's terrible, it's going to hurt your sales, it's going to hurt your brand." But while some consumers might object to the use of AI on principle, he thinks the risk of using it to enhance food photography is low if done well — especially if it can help small- and medium-sized businesses manage their costs. Restaurant businesses face thin margins, often making it difficult to turn a profit . According to Restaurants Canada's most recent survey of some of its members , 41 per cent said they were operating at a loss or just breaking even, with rising fuel costs only exacerbating issues. Pullara says hiring a professional photographer is expensive, and might be out of budget for a small restaurant business. For that reason, taking a high-resolution photo of food and using an AI application to make small tweaks could create an image worthy of putting on a menu, Pullara says. "I don't think it's the AI that makes the image unappealing. I think the problem is asking AI for a photo and just not using a common-sense filter about [whether] this actually looks good," Pullara said. That tweaking of real photos is how the marketing team at The Fancy Induced Burger uses AI. Fez Mian is a marketing manager manager for Canadian burger franchise The Fancy Induced Burger. He says staff at the company take pictures of food with their phones and enhance them using AI tools before using them on menu boards, in-store advertising and online. (Tina Mackenzie/CBC) A marketing manager for the Canadian franchise, Fez Mian, says he'll snap a picture of a burger as it comes out of the kitchen and run it through an AI application like ChatGPT, prompting it to enhance the texture and freshness of menu items. Those images are used across the business — on menus, in-store posters and online. The company doesn't rely on professional photographers or graphic designers as much these days as a result. That's saved them money and time, as Mian no longer needs to book a photographer, wait for the shoot date and then wait to receive the images before using them in marketing. "We're not, like, spending endless time planning and scheduling and whatnot," Mian said. "Within … five minutes, 10 minutes it's out the door." That speed is especially important on social media, Mian says, enabling them to create and post new content more frequently. Does AI cross the line into false advertising? For some consumers, the worry is about how the food item that shows up on their plate will compare to the enhanced image on the menu. WATCH | Some customers find AI food ads unappetizing : AI food pics on restaurant menus are killing customers' appetites | Duration closed caption 1:58 More small restaurants are turning to AI instead of professional photographers to generate food pictures for their menus, but the often unrealistic images are starting to turn some customers off. If AI imagery is vastly different from the actual product, Rotman School of Management marketing professor David Soberman says that could be a problem. "You wanna make your products look good, but you don't want your products to be misleading," Soberman said. If an AI-enhancement makes a steak look like it's an inch thick but the actual product is half the size, for example, that would be a problem. Burgers, fries and 'cheesy nuggets' enhanced with AI are pictured on the menu board at The Fancy Induced Burger. The marketing manager for the company says staff at the franchise take pictures of real food on their phones before tweaking them with AI and using them on menus boards, in marketing imagery and online. (Tina Mackenzie/CBC) But the same is true for food imagery enhanced using run-of-the-mill staging and image editing, Soberman says. Both Soberman and Pullara say they don't think AI imagery generally raises the likelihood of misleading consumers, especially since most have come to accept that images on menu boards will look better than the real deal. "I think people just kind of know that there's going to be some variance between what you're seeing on these professionally shot, produced photos and what you actually can have prepared in the back of the kitchen in two minutes," Pullara said. At The Fancy Induced Burger, Mian says there's always a human involved in checking the company's AI-enhanced images to make sure no extra ingredients were added in the process that might mislead customers. Still, Toronto-based food stylist Zoe Rousseau says they think the work they do is more authentic than AI-generated food imagery. Despite some common misconceptions based on industry standards from decades ago, Rousseau says food staging doesn't involve fake food most of the time. Instead, they take their time to pick the best-looking ingredients, make sure they're perfectly placed, and work with a team of photographers and prop stylists who help achieve a beautiful end product. Zoe Rousseau is a Toronto-based food stylist who has worked with major brands like Shake Shack and Boston Pizza as well as smaller companies. They say their work doesn't often involve inedible items; instead they take a lot of time to make the real ingredients look their absolute best. (Mark Bochsler/CBC) Rousseau says they understand why small businesses trying to cut down costs would try AI, but if the generated imagery simply "doesn't look like the food," it won't work to pull customers in. "I think that restaurateurs are better off taking pictures with their iPhone," Rousseau said. For that reason, they're not too worried about AI coming for their job. They hope that the backlash to AI menu items might even compel more businesses to invest in stylists and photographers, boosting their industry. "I can play with texture and I can play with angles," Rousseau said. "Just the freshness of it … the AI can't do that."

World.title: Feds disclose more details on Trump admin request to delay Gordie Howe bridge opening
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian government has disclosed a handful of fresh details around the delays in opening the Gordie Howe International Bridge, as well as some information related to the cost to build the sprawling span connecting Ontario and Michigan.

But the MP whose questions triggered the disclosure says he’s “not satisfied at all” with the responses, accusing Ottawa of still hiding key information about the $6.4-billion bridge that became mired in cross-border political controversy earlier this year.

"The truth is going to come out eventually, and the more you beat around the bush, the more suspicious people get," says Harb Gill, the Conservative MP for Windsor West.

In particular, federal authorities declined to provide details about some of the extra costs to get the bridge open.

Still, some of the responses shed additional light on a major infrastructure project that was swept up in broader cross-border tensions when U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to block the bridge’s opening in February.

That threat followed intense lobbying and hefty donations to Republicans from the owners of the nearby Ambassador Bridge.

In June, Prime Minister Mark Carney said the U.S. had requested to delay opening the new bridge, citing “technical aspects” that had been raised. He declined to explain those technical issues at the time, saying, “I don’t think it’s productive to work through those in public.”

Earlier this week, the federal government responded to Gill's questions from June, saying that the request from the U.S. came “on or about” June 10, and that those technical issues were “related to the governance and financial framework associated with the bridge."

The Gordie Howe International Bridge is seen from the air on July 27, 2026, its opening day. The event brought a second major bridge crossing to the Windsor-Detroit corridor. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

That same day, top government officials and ministerial staff from the infrastructure department, Privy Council Office, Prime Minister’s Office, and Global Affairs Canada “were collectively briefed” on the U.S. request to push back the opening, per the response from Housing, Infrastructure and Communities Canada.

The description of the issues appears to track with the provisions of the eventual deal between the two countries to open the bridge in late July. The agreement introduced a revenue-sharing arrangement with the U.S. and rules around toll rate changes, among other things.

PM needed to be more forthcoming: MP

Gill says Carney’s explanation of the issues in June was misleading, however, because the word “technical” implied “something that was technically wrong with the bridge” itself.

“Obviously, it was nothing technical,” Gill said this week. “It was the governance and financial framework. So if that's the case, then just say so. Why hide behind these other lines of ‘it's a technical issue’?”

Harb Gill, the Conservative MP for Windsor West, in Windsor, Ont., in July 2026. (Samantha Craggs/CBC)

Neither the Prime Minister’s Office nor the infrastructure department responded to questions before publication time. The White House also did not respond.

According to the responses to Gill's questions, though, a wide range of government entities were involved in “identifying, assessing, or addressing” the outstanding issues that led to the June delay: the infrastructure department; the Windsor Detroit Bridge Authority, the Crown corporation that runs the new bridge; Privy Council Office; Global Affairs Canada; Michigan’s Department of Transportation; and both countries’ border agencies and embassies.

That wasn’t the only delay in getting the bridge across the finish line, though. In separate responses to Gill's questions, the WDBA said its original contract with Bridging North America, the consortium of private firms tasked with designing and building the new span, "set out a substantial completion date of November 2024."

But in January of that year, the deal was amended to make September 2025 the deadline, "with the opening occurring in fall 2025."

The opening was pushed back again in October 2025, when the WDBA “stated that the bridge would open as soon as early 2026, and later to the targeted timeline of spring 2026.”

The bridge eventually opened on July 27, 2026.

"Factors contributing to delivery timelines included unprecedented disruptions as a result of the COVID-19 global pandemic, testing and commissioning as part of strong quality management, and some construction activities," the bridge authority wrote in response to Gill’s questions.

Calculating the costs

The opening delay requested by the U.S. in the spring did not increase the bridge’s price tag, the infrastructure department wrote.

The project costs had jumped from $5.7 billion in 2018 to $6.4 billion in 2024, however. Gill says he asked the government for the value of change orders to the construction contract in order to get a detailed accounting of the $700 million difference.

But the WDBA didn’t provide answers in their response to Gill.

“Windsor-Detroit Bridge Authority has concluded that producing and validating a comprehensive response to this question would require a manual collection of information that is not possible in the time allotted and could lead to the disclosure of incomplete and misleading information," the authority wrote .

Gill argues that if the price jump was due to the pandemic, “they should be able to tell us exactly where the $700 million went. That's not chump change.”

In a written statement Thursday, Heather Grondin, the WDBA's chief relations officer, said the authority "shares information transparently and in accordance with government requirements.

"The responses provided to MP Gill reflect available information and we will work directly with the MP to further understand his concerns."

Gill says he’ll keep pursuing more fulsome answers to his questions, both in the House of Commons and through his membership on the chamber’s industry committee.

World.title: Carney's comments over possibility of U.S. invasion reveal how contingency plans are always in place
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A senior U.S. military commander recently dismissed a journalist's hypothetical question about a feared American invasion of Canada as "absolutely and utterly preposterous."

The head of U.S. Indo-Pacific Command, Admiral Samuel Paparo, added: "Would you ask me please, also, what my attack plans are for the Martians?"

It seems, however, it hasn't been such a far-fetched notion for Prime Minister Mark Carney, nor his senior defence officials who have dusted off various long-established — in some cases decades old — contingency plans and worst case scenarios.

In an interview with the New York Times on Wednesday, Carney said he had prepared for the "extreme tail risk" that the Trump administration might order military action against Canada.

That's his way of saying there's a really, really low probability of this happening, but the risk is not zero.

The Times reported that the prime minister, after being pressed on whether he took U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to make Canada the 51st state seriously, "suggested that he had carefully examined the possibility of a U.S.-led military invasion," but declined to discuss in detail what that involved.

"All militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios," Defence Minister David McGuinty said Thursday. "Canadians should take it as described to the prime minister: a tail risk."

McGuinty also refused to discuss details of the contingency planning.

WATCH | Nothing unusual in military analyzing risk scenarios, defence minister says: Defence minister says preparations for possible U.S.-led military action are 'normal' | Duration closed caption 1:02 Asked by CBC News if the Canadian military is re-examining plans for potential U.S.-led military action, Defence Minister David McGuinty said 'all militaries in the world spend time analyzing risk scenarios.' The New York Times reported that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he has studied the possibility, which he called 'extreme tail risk.'

Vault full of contingency plans

While the default vision of the phrase "American military action" for many is one of heavily armoured tanks, jets and drones roaring across the Canadian border, an overwhelming number of experts agree such a scenario is unlikely given the vastness of Canada and the difficulty in securing the whole country.

It's generally agreed that in a conventional conflict the Canadian military would be quickly overwhelmed and resistance would take the form of a guerilla campaign.

There are, however, a number of other different scenarios. They range from the kind of rapid regime change that took place when former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro was captured by U.S. commandos, to the limited air campaign that's been fought over Iran.

As for contingency plans, the Department of National Defence, like militaries across the world, has a vault full of them — some dating back decades.

Retired Lt.-Gen. Andrew Leslie headed the section at the defence department that writes and updates the plans.

He said they are amended as world circumstances dictate, often when a new leader takes power in a country where Canada has an interest.

"You make judgment calls on what is likely to happen, what is unlikely to happen," Leslie said in an interview with CBC News.

"You consult with other departments, with other experts, and then you put it away again."

'Heightened focus' in light of Trump's threats

The planning, Leslie said, would have been updated after Trump's re-election in 2024 and would have been pulled out regularly, especially in light of the Trump administration's threats in January to seize Greenland by force.

"In the context of the threats that the White House has issued against Canada … those would have probably resulted in a heightened focus," Leslie said, citing talk of a 51st state and maps showing Canada as part of the U.S.

Over a year ago, Trump ruled out military action against Canada, saying he'd use economic coercion instead to force the country into the Union.

Given everything that's been said, it would have been natural for Carney to call for defence plans to be revised, Leslie said.

"What a lot of people sometimes forget is that a political leader's first remit at the national level is the safety, security of Canadians," said Leslie, who also served as commander of the Canadian Army.

"So it would be his duty to ensure that all due diligence and prudent steps have been taken to see what might have changed from the way that the old plans were written or updated. And it would be the duty of the Chief of the Defence Staff [Gen. Jennie Carignan] to advise them accordingly, which I'm absolutely sure she did."

WATCH | Invasion talk highlights state of U.S. relations, NDP's Don Davies says: Carney considering U.S. invasion of Canada shows 'profound change' in relations: NDP MP | Duration closed caption 0:47 Asked about reporting in the New York Times that Prime Minister Mark Carney said he studied the possibility of U.S. military action in Canada, NDP parliamentary leader Don Davies said the contemplation of such an 'outlandish possibility' shows everything we thought we knew about Canada-U.S. relations is 'up in the air.'

Impact of Trump's threats go unnoticed in U.S.

The notion of U.S. military action is a hot-button issue for many.

"I think every Canadian worries about it," New Democrat MP Gord Johns said going into the House of Commons on Thursday. Canadians are paying attention when Trump calls the country the 51st state or refers to Carney as the governor of Canada, Johns added.

There is, however, an increasingly puzzled reaction among some Americans who have grown accustomed to Trump's threats, taunts and trolling.

Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor at the University of New Haven in Connecticut and a former instructor at the U.S. Army War College, said many Americans, including himself, are unaware of how Trump's words affect people in other nations.

"I don't think I have a visceral sense of what Canadians are feeling about the United States," Schmidt said. "We really don't have a sense of the impact of what the president is saying has on other places."

He dismissed the notion of the U.S. military taking action against Canada, but said Carney has taken the prudent, responsible course of a leader and measured the risk.

Schmidt said he also wonders whether the prime minister's reference was intended as more of a political signal to not only the Canadian public, but Americans and others.

"When Mark Carney stands up and says that, it just highlights the absurdity of what the American president said. Right? It's a way to emphasize that absurdity," Schmidt said.

World.title: Mamdani's populist style is all over the Toronto election race
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Zohran Mamdani's 2025 mayoral campaign put a spotlight on cost of living issues and was characterized by colourful messaging, snappy social media videos and a where-there’s-a-will-there’s-a-way approach to making changes in New York — tactics many candidates in Toronto’s municipal election seem to be replicating. Last fall, the world watched as New York City elected a young, progressive candidate — a virtual unknown at the start — as mayor. Zohran Mamdani's campaign put a spotlight on cost of living issues and was characterized by colourful messaging, snappy social media videos and a where-there’s-a-will-there’s-a-way approach to making changes in New York. Since his victory, Mamdani has introduced city-run grocery stores, free public child care for two-year-olds and a mayoral office dedicated to protecting workers' rights. His approach to governance in New York became a sensation — and seems to be an inspiration for many candidates in Toronto’s municipal election, just a month away. Walk-and-talk, on-the-street social media videos have become a staple for mayoral candidates Chris Alexander, Brad Bradford and incumbent Olivia Chow as a way to explain their platforms. The style is also extremely popular among councillor candidates. Davenport incumbent Alejandra Bravo posted a video of her shooting hoops to promote more food and drink options in parks. Josh Matlow, the incumbent in Toronto–St. Paul's, made a video on the Eglinton LRT talking about transit policy. Some candidates have chosen to use colours close to Mamdani’s signature blue, orange and red in their marketing campaigns, while others are using a similar bubbly serif font on their campaign's social media. Saman Tabasinejad, executive director of third-party political organizing group Progress Toronto, which works to get progressive candidates, including Chow, elected, said Mamdani is a "generational talent" when it comes to communication. CBC Toronto's election podcast breaks down how candidates keep copying Mamdani: She said he is able to explain policy ideas in a way that helps voters see a clear path forward to a better city. She’s not surprised Toronto candidates are taking inspiration from Mamdani, but cautioned some candidates may be co-opting his style to promote otherwise clashing platforms. "If you want to be like Mamdani, that's great," she said. "But you’ve got to be like him in many other ways." Social media in place of traditional coverage Chiara Padovani, a progressive candidate in York–South Weston, said Mamdani’s social media videos were a clever workaround given his initial lack of traditional media coverage. Mamdani, a former state assembly member, was up against Andrew Cuomo, who was previously governor and comes from a political family. "[Mamdani] wasn't going to be getting mainstream media attention and he didn't let that stop him," Padovani said. It's something Padovani — who came within 94 votes of beating city council’s longest-standing incumbent, Frances Nunziata, in 2022 — says she can relate to. She says Mamdani's strategy can be applied to city councillor races at a hyperlocal level. "I think candidates who are challenging a mainstream candidate or a mainstream politician do need to find creative ways to get their message across," she said. In one of his social media videos, Uthish Ganesh, a history and English teacher and candidate in Scarborough Centre, promised to remove a bus lane along Kennedy Road, saying it creates gridlock for drivers and other commuters. Scarborough Centre candidate calls for bus lane removal on Kennedy Road: While the style of the video, right down to the campaign colours, is akin to Mamdani's, the New York mayor’s policies are very pro-transit. Ganesh told CBC that while some of his politics differ from Mamdani’s, he was inspired by the New York mayor's ability to mobilize voters face-to-face. "We knocked on doors for months before we posted anything worth watching," he said. "If you make videos first, you're guessing what people care about. If you knock first, you already know." Winning the ground game Mamdani had a team of nearly 100,000 volunteers and his success in on-the-street canvassing was a major lift in the campaign. In comparison, Progress Toronto currently has a team of around 3,000 volunteers, according to Tabasinejad. "He won because of a ground game. He was outspent by quite a bit," said Tabasinejad. Brian Evans, a politics and public administration professor at Toronto Metropolitan University, said that kind of mobilization is unlikely to happen in Toronto’s mayoral race, because there’s less political polarization here. Mamdani's campaign "drew the ire of Trump and it drew the ire of the uber, uber wealthy," Evans said. "It's going to be a totally different thing here." WATCH | Mamdani's campaign was met with pushback from president, financial elite: How Zohran Mamdani is reshaping New York’s mayoral race | Duration closed caption 2:01 Zohran Mamdani is shaking up New York’s mayoral race with a socialist platform that includes rent control and public transportation. The front-runner’s message is drawing both support and backlash from the city’s financial elite, including the U.S. president. Chloe Brown, a progressive who ran for mayor in 2022 and 2023 — finishing third and seventh, respectively — is now running for councillor in Etobicoke North. She is up against incumbent Coun. Vincent Crisanti and eight other candidates. Brown said left-wing voters in Toronto, particularly young ones, like to jump on the bandwagon of an exciting candidate, but fall short when it comes to volunteering in campaigns and even showing up at the polls. "So you get stuck wanting what New York [has], because you don't put in the effort of New York," she said. Brown also noted that Toronto already has a progressive mayor in Chow, although some councillors have opted not to adopt her policies in their wards. "It's not enough to want one Mamdani. You need to want 15 of them," said Brown. Toronto's progressive mayor This city copied some of Mamdani’s ideas even before the election races kicked off. Toronto council has greenlit a city-run grocery store pilot, approved a pitch to hire citizen snow shovellers and moved forward on banning surveillance pricing on groceries. All three were introduced in New York by Mamdani’s administration. Here in Toronto, it was Chow who pitched the snow shovellers and the surveillance pricing ban, while Anthony Perruzza, incumbent in Humber River–Black Creek, put forward the motion on grocery stores. Chow also raised taxes for homes over $3 million last year, in a move similar to Mamdani’s tax on luxury second homes . The Toronto and New York mayors also have similar politics on tenant protections and supporting city libraries. My day in New York continues with a mayors roundtable, and bilateral meetings with @NYCMayor and @jaumecollboni. Meetings with more mayors to follow this afternoon.

We’re exchanging ideas for improving service delivery and affordability for residents. pic.twitter.com/kcNHajUm4U —MayorOliviaChow Chow and Mamdani’s office have in fact had meetings since he took office, a source in Chow’s office told CBC Toronto. Chow was also in New York this week for a cities summit, co-chaired by Mamdani, and met with him one-on-one. One key distinction between the Toronto mayoral race and the last New York City vote is that the progressive has the incumbent advantage here, says Tabasinejad, which means Chow's campaign will have different challenges than Mamdani's did. In any case, the issues that defined the New York mayoral race — housing and affordability — are certainly at play in Toronto's election, Evans says. "But it will have nowhere near the drama."

World.title: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk is heading to the ISS next week
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's only been six months since Canada's Jeremy Hansen made history by flying around the moon. Now, it's Joshua Kutryk's turn to blast off into space.

But he'll be hanging around closer to home and will be in space for far longer, living and working on the International Space Station (ISS) for roughly six months.

"I never, ever, ever, ever … thought that I would have this opportunity to go out on behalf of Canada and do a mission like this," Kutryk said during a press call on Wednesday.

"I dreamt of it. I always dreamt of it and thought it would be the most wonderful experience, but I always viewed it as impossibly hard."

Kutryk, who was born in Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., is an engineer, fighter pilot and test pilot who has flown more than 4,000 hours on more than 40 different aircraft types.

He was chosen alongside Jenni Gibbons in 2017 by the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) in its recruitment program.

Kutryk was initially supposed to launch on Boeing's CST-100 Starliner. However, Boeing has suffered big setbacks, delaying its first crewed mission.

WATCH | Kutryk bound for the ISS: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk gets ready for ISS mission | Duration closed caption 2:02 Joshua Kutryk is set to be the next Canadian astronaut in space and the first to participate in a joint NASA-SpaceX mission. Kutryk is set to leave for the International Space Station on Sept. 12.

Instead, he'll be riding on SpaceX's Crew Dragon. Kutryk was initially supposed to launch on Sept. 12, but there was an issue with the spacecraft, so the launch was delayed to Oct. 1. He said he has faith that the vehicle is ready to fly.

While he's packing light, he'll still be bringing some items into space with him.

"I'm bringing many things from different Canadian organizations, universities, public service agencies that I'm affiliated with," Kutryk said. "I'm bringing a lot of Canadian flags. This idea of being Canadian is something that has always resonated with me."

But one thing of particular importance to him is an old pocket watch that travelled from Ukraine to Canada when his family immigrated here. The watch has actually beaten him to the ISS, however. It went up with an earlier supply launch.

Kutryk said the fact that the watch was likely built in the early 1900s, and is now in space, is something special.

"It's just this really important personal memento, but also a really neat metaphor for how much the world can change … because of how we explore," he said. "I plan to keep it pretty close during those six months."

'Can't wait to look out the window'

When asked what he's looking forward to the most, Kutryk said his answer may seem boring.

"The truth is, the answer to that is the simplest one, and that is: I just can't wait to look out the window," he said.

"The six-year-old kid and me, all the way up to the 44-year-old astronaut, husband, every version of a human I've been in between, the thing that I want to do the most is go to the biggest window I can find and just stare at Earth."

The Crew 13 launch, as it's called, will also include NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, Luke Delaney and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteriatnikov.

The four members of NASA's SpaceX Crew 13 mission display their mission plaque. From left are, Cmdr. Jessica Watkins and pilot Luke Delaney, both from NASA, Kutryk, and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos. (Morgan Gridley/NASA)

It will also be the first space mission for Delaney and Teteriatnikov.

The crew will join several astronauts who are already on station and will conduct several experiments , some of which are Canadian.

Kutryk says that, while there may be a lot of of unrest here on Earth, the mission illustrates how united the world can be.

"There's a lot of chaos. There's a lot of challenge, no doubt everywhere, and Canada's right in the middle of some of that," he said.

"For me, when I step into a suit, and I get to see what we're doing in space with all these countries — the United States, Canada, Russia and so many others in between — it separates me from all the bad headlines, and it shows me what we can do, what the future can be."

World.title: The 1990s boy band mall tour is back, and this time it's sponsored by Gap
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Remember when you could hit up your local suburban mall, catch a show from a pop star next to the food court and buy a new zip-up while you were at it? History is repeating itself.

On Tuesday, Gap announced it was launching a collaboration with emerging boy band Just Your Type (JYT) in the company's first project for its “fashiontainment platform.”

No, we're not really sure what that is either. According to Gap, the platform "leverages the power of its iconic brands to create content." It says it will co-produce a docuseries about the group’s formation and early journey, design a capsule clothing collection with the five members and create social media content to accompany the project.

Taking a page out of the pop playbook of the 1990s and 2000s, the collaboration will also feature a mall tour across the U.S.

CBC News reached out to Gap about whether the tour will come to Canada, but has not heard back.

The band behind the brand

JYT is a five-member boy band made up of performers Recker Eans, Toby Green, Caden Adamonis, Bryan Chan and Tyler George.

Haven’t heard of JYT? That’s not surprising — the group just released their debut single What U Want at the end of last year, and only have four songs out in total.

But music executives have been betting big on the group from the start.

In January, the group was officially signed by Republic Records in partnership with Grammy-nominated songwriter and producer Freddy Wexler, who developed them. Wexler has worked on hits for artists including Justin Bieber, Blackpink and Ariana Grande.

WATCH | Music video for No Pressure by JYT:

“From the moment these five kids stood in a room together, I knew we had something special. JYT isn’t a manufactured boy band; they chose each other,” Wexler told UDiscover Music , a Universal Music Group-backed site. “America hasn’t launched a global boy band in decades, and these kids are about to change that.”

With smooth harmonies and a knack for dancing in formation, it seems JYT are being positioned as spiritual successors to boy bands such as NSync and the Backstreet Boys — and potentially the American answer to the tightly choreographed, aesthetically and musically polished groups that have come out of South Korea, such as global K-pop sensation BTS.

Setting the tone

The group may be young, ranging from ages 15 to 17, but most have been working in entertainment for years; the band includes two former touring members of Kidz Bop, and some members have appeared as backup dancers in music videos and in guest roles on TV shows.

The collaboration suggests that Gap is doubling down on attempts to reach Gen Z and Gen Alpha. The company scored a viral ad campaign in 2025 featuring girl group Katseye, who performed a choreographed dance in Gap denim. This followed the hiring of designer Zac Posen to help boost its cultural capital in 2024.

“This campaign demonstrated the power of the playbook in action, featuring trend-right product, amplified by culturally relevant storytelling,” Richard Dickson, Gap CEO, said of the ad on a call with investors about the company's third-quarter results earlier this year. Comparable sales in that quarter rose five per cent, driven by the success of the ad, according to CNBC.

WATCH | Gap collaboration with KATSEYE:

Dickson called the collaboration a “true cultural takeover,” relying on a methodology Gap will continue to build on in the future.

The clothing giant's boy band gamble is a continuation of this, one marketing expert says.

"Inevitably, young people do set the tone in trends like this. So you're not doing this just so that you connect with teenagers and young adults," said Max Valiquette, a communications professional and trends expert. "You're doing this because if they say something is cool or interesting, it does tend to have an impact on older demographics and drive what they purchase, as well. "

Return of the mall tour

Groups like New Kids on the Block, the Backstreet Boys and even pop icons like Britney Spears famously performed in shopping centres when they were starting out, taking advantage of and driving foot traffic to these locations.

It "makes a ton of sense" that Gap would want to revive this tradition, Valiquette said.

"It's turning to a boy band to kind of test whether entertainment can fully move the needle on apparel sales, but not working with an established boy band. It is working with a boy band who are actually not established at all," Valiquette said.

"And it's building Gap while the band gets built. "

World.title: Belleville synagogue shooter had means to carry out 'mass casualty' event: police chief
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Belleville Police Service says the man who ambushed and seriously wounded an officer near a local synagogue Sunday had the means and motive to carry out a "mass casualty" event and was specifically targeting members of the city's Jewish community.

"The loss of life and irreversible damage that could have rippled through our community for generations cannot be overstated," Belleville Police Chief Murray Rodd said at a news conference Thursday, repeatedly emphasizing that the incident was "a hate-motivated crime."

Const. Jeff Smith confronted the gunman despite having been wounded in his vehicle, while another officer joined the fray and put his own life at risk, too, Rodd said.

"The only thing that stopped entry into the synagogue to execute the intent were the two officers," the police chief said in the most detailed account yet of Sunday's shocking shootout.

Just after 7 p.m., as a Yom Kippur service was getting underway inside Sons of Jacob Synagogue, located in a residential part of Belleville, shots erupted outside.

Rodd said Smith was parked outside the synagogue as part of his regularly assigned duties when he was ambushed by the gunman, and "that's when the shooting started."

Belleville Police played a short video clip showing part of the shootout. In it, Smith and the shooter are each crouched by vehicles as gunfire is heard.

WATCH | Shooter was armed with significant amount of ammunition, police say: Belleville, Ont., synagogue shooting a deliberate hate attack: police | Duration closed caption 2:37 WARNING: This story contains antisemitic language | Belleville, Ont., police say the recent shooting outside the Sons of Jacob synagogue that seriously injured a police officer was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack. Police also played a video of the shooting in which the suspect, Sean Ward, could be heard saying, 'You are going to die for the Jews.’

Someone can be heard shouting at one point, but it's difficult to make out what was said. According to the police service, the gunman was shouting, "You are going to die for the Jews."

Rodd said Smith was shot several times in the head and body and will need to undergo multiple surgeries related to serious head trauma.

"We are pleased to share that [he] continues to make positive progress in his recovery," the police chief said. "While he faces a long road ahead, his determination [and] resilience … continues to inspire all of us."

After Smith was wounded, Rodd said he was alone on the scene for nearly three minutes before a second Belleville police officer, Const. Michael McCurdy, arrived and "immediately moved toward the danger."

Belleville's police chief says that Const. Jeff Smith, who was shot during the shootout with the gunman on Sunday, 'continues to make positive progress in his recovery.' (Ashley Smith/Facebook)

The gunman was identified by investigators earlier this week as 29-year-old Sean Ward of the neighbouring city of Quinte West. They said he was wounded in the shootout and taken to hospital with life-threatening injuries.

On Tuesday, Ontario's Special Investigations Unit (SIU), the civilian agency that investigates police conduct during officer-involved shootings and other serious incidents, reported that Ward had died in hospital on Monday night.

WATCH | Expert shares warning signs of radicalization: ‘No one radicalizes in a vacuum’: Expert on synagogue shooter | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration closed caption 10:39 Belleville, Ont., police say Sunday’s shooting near the Sons of Jacob synagogue was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack targeting the Jewish community. An expert discusses the warning signs of radicalization and why he says people need to stay vigilant.

According to Rodd, the shooter used a shotgun but had "other resources" available, including "a significant amount of ammunition on his person and available to him."

Rodd noted that the shooter also had "combustible" materials in his vehicle.

One of the synagogue's street-facing windows was pierced by several bullets.

Bullet holes are seen in a window of the Sons of Jacob Synagogue after Sunday's shooting. (Michael Cole/CBC)

"It's … terrifying really how close we came to such a massacre," Doug Lobel, a Sons of Jacob member who was inside the synagogue during the shooting, told CBC News Network Thursday.

Members of Ontario's Jewish community on Thursday said they were appreciative that Belleville Police declared Sunday's incident a hate-motivated crime against Jews, but warned that it was only the latest in a series of such attacks — and that more needs to be done to prevent them.

"We need police services to be there, to be at our institutions, to be at our synagogues, and they have done really a great job to this point," said Steven Shulman, CEO of the Jewish Federations of Canada.

"But much more now is needed. It's very clear the threat that's there."

World.title: ACSN extends lockdown of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to Friday morning
World.content:
Santa Marta-based organized crime group ACSN said Wednesday that the lockdown it has imposed on parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast will be lifted on Friday morning.

In its first formal statement, the ACSN said that “the armed strike announced for 72 hours will end at 7:00AM on Friday 25 September 2026.”

The lockdown, which was initially called for 48 hours on Monday, has devastated the legal economy in the port city, particularly after ACSN assassins uploaded videos of them opening fire at stores that ignored the order to social media.

The online videos and half a dozen burnt buses and taxis all but cleared the streets of Santa Marta, which became a ghost town on Tuesday.

“We have never seen anything like this,” one Santa Marta resident told news program El Reporte Coronell.

President Abelardo de la Espriella announced the militarization of Santa Marta, but this was barely visible in the city’s downtown area and in the majority of Santa Marta’s neighborhoods.

“There are no police or soldiers in the streets, the people feel unprotected and are in panic,” said journalist Javier Manjarres on social media platform X.

“The current situation is a consequence of the behavior of the security forces and the decisions taken by the National Government in regards to our organization,” the organized crime group said in their statement.

The ACSN admitted that the clandestine lockdown was the result of the killing of Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” one of its commanders in the region around the Sierra Nevada mountain range just outside the city.

According to the group, security forces executed Cholo in front of his wife after his arrest.

An 18-year-old farmhand with no ties to the organization was also executed by the security, his family told media.

The lockdown has been imposed throughout the Magdalena and La Guajira provinces, a region where the group dominates organized crime and controls drug trafficking route to the Caribbean.

World.title: Colombia withdraws support for ICJ genocide case against Israel
World.content:
Colombia has withdrawn its participation in South Africa’s genocide case against Israel, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Tuesday.

In a statement, the court in The Hague said that Colombia’s government “decided to withdraw the Declaration of intervention that it had filed… on 5 April 2024 in the case concerning Application of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide in the Gaza Strip.”

The decision of the administration of President Abelardo De la Espriella is part of a wider attempt to restore ties with Israel and its main sponsor, the United States, and appease its Evangelical Christian support base.

In response to the ongoing genocide in Palestine, former President Gustavo Petro took a leading role in diplomatic efforts that sought to isolate Israel and seek justice for Israel’s victims through the world court.

In a response, the US Government put Petro on a blacklist and actively campaigned for the election of De la Espriella to prevent another leftist victory in elections earlier this year.

The new president, who took office in August, immediately restored diplomatic ties to Israel and lifted a ban on coal exports to the country in West Asia.

World.title: ACSN crime group shuts down parts of Colombia’s Caribbean coast
World.content:
Santa Marta-based crime group ACSN shut down parts of the city and the surrounding region after Colombia’s armed forces killed one of their commanders.

Jose Luis Perez, a.k.a. “Cholo,” and six of his comrades were killed during an offensive on Monday.

The son of Fredy Castillo, a.k.a. “Pinocho,” who is one of the alleged bosses of the crime group, was reportedly among those killed during the operation.

Shortly after, a pamphlet that was signed by the ACSN ordered an “armed strike” of 48 hours because of the “the fierce attacks that the government has been launching against our organization in the Sierra Nevada since this afternoon.”

Multiple buses were incinerated in the region around Santa Marta.

We hereby declare a 48-hour armed strike throughout the province of Magdalena, particularly along the Troncal del Caribe highway, in the city of Santa Marta, and in the banana-growing region. We do not want any businesses to remain open for a period of 48 hours. ACSN

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who traveled to the city, “they are trying to intimidate the public by promoting an armed strike.”

“I will not allow any criminal organization to subjugate citizens through threats and terror,” the president added.

Notwithstanding, multiple shop owners in Santa Marta and along the highway kept their shops closed on Tuesday, afraid to challenge the authority of the local crime bosses.

The district government closed public schools in neighborhoods where the ACSN is believed to have a strong presence. Public transport was suspended as videos of armed men opening fire on shops that failed to close voluntarily were posted on social media.

The ACSN control much of drug trafficking to the port of Santa Marta and to the coastline of the neighboring La Guajira province.

De la Espriella ended attempts to negotiate the group’s surrender and ordered a military approach after taking office in August.

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal warns ICC that De la Espriella supports “worst attack in history”
World.content:
Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP said that it would warn the United Nations and the International Criminal Court about plans of President Abelardo de la Espriella to cut its budget.

In a statement, JEP president Alejandro Ramelli raised the alarm warned about a pending proposal by far-right Senator Enrique Gomez (National Salvation) to reduce the tribunal’s budget by COP100 billion ($31.6 million), which received De la Espriella’s support.

A second proposal by another far-right party, the Democratic Center, sought to push all sentences against members of the security forces to military justice for revision.

According to Ramelli, the two bill proposals “prove the existence of a strategy to block the JEP’s functioning” and called on the international community to “put a stop to this effort to dismantle our financial system and calls for the essential resources needed for our operations to be guaranteed.”

These initiatives constitute a combined strategy of economic strangulation and the subjugation of the JEP to military criminal justice. It is the most serious attack we have ever faced against our independence and autonomy. JEP president Alejandro Ramelli

The president , who vowed to get rid of the JEP on campaign, said that the 2027 national budget “does not constitute any threat to any judge, it’s the Constitution at work.”

I do not have a policy of retaliation against the JEP. I have a duty to manage spending, demand results, and allocate the State’s limited resources to a justice system that serves everyone, not to a court that part of the country perceives—for reasons debated in Congress and in public opinion—as a system of privileges rather than an effective end to impunity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Since March of 2018, the JEP has played a key role in clarifying crimes committed during the armed conflict that erupted in response to the insurgency of the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC.

Among other things, the JEP found that the guerrillas recruited more than 18,000 children and that the security forces assassinated more than 7,800 civilians to inflate their combat kills.

Hundreds of former guerrillas and former members of the armed forces are taking part in a transitional justice system that seeks to solve as many as possible of the hundreds of thousands of crimes committed during the decades-long armed conflict.

World.title: Colombia pulls out of international LGBT coalition
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella pulled Colombia out of the international Equal Rights Coalition, which promotes the rights of sexual and gender minorities around the world.

The Foreign Ministry announced its departure from the coalition in a letter addressed to the organization of which Colombia was co-president until February next year.

According to Caribe Afirmativa, a gay rights NGO that was part of the international initiative, warned that the decision was “a serious setback in foreign policy and commitments to LGBTIQ+ rights.”

We also view this action as a snub to the international community, a break from the leadership role Colombia had established, and an unequivocal political signal regarding the place the current government is willing to grant to the rights of LGBTIQ+ people. Caribe Afirmativa

De la Espriella has appointed multiple prominent far-right figures in his government and has vowed to wage a “Culture War” against what it considers “gender ideology.”

On top of this, De la Espriella and multiple of his cabinet members oppose the right of gay couples to adopt children and reportedly sacked the newly appointed planning chief because he and his gay partner had adopted a child.

World.title: Court imposes strict conditions on Colombia’s military air strikes if minors are present
World.content:
A Bogota court imposed strict conditions on Colombia’s military authorities if they want to carry out air strikes on illegal armed groups in places where victims of forced recruitment are present.

The ruling of Bogota’s 34th Family Court lifted a suspension on the strikes that had been imposed earlier this month in response to a lawsuit.

The court imposed the following conditions on air strikes to evade violating International Humanitarian Law, which prioritizes the rights of child victims of forced recruitment over the success of military operations.

Don’t assume minors are legitimate targets because they form part of an illegal armed group

Intensify the verification and cross-checking of available information on the possible presence of minors at potential targets

Explicitly include this assessment to the legal and operational assessment of the attack

Assess the foreseeable risk of an attack on the lives and integrity of the minors

Examine the existence of less harmful means, methods, timing or operational alternatives that would allow the achievement of a comparable military advantage

Rigorously apply the principles of distinction, precaution, and proportionality before authorizing and executing the operation

The court additionally ordered family welfare institute ICBF to be integrated into military operations and strengthen the pathways for disengagement, restoration of rights, comprehensive care, and reintegration of children and adolescents who are victims of recruitment, with a differentiated and territorial approach.

The court asked the Ombudsman and the Inspector General’s Office to monitor compliance of the orders issued to maximize the protection of children’s rights.

The lawsuit had been filed in a successful attempt to protect children against the violence President Abelardo de la Espriella sought to unleash on illegal armed groups that refused to demobilize.

World.title: US maintains Colombia “failed demonstrably” in fighting drug trafficking
World.content:
The United States President Donald Trump maintained that Colombia “failed demonstrably during the previous 12 months to make substantial efforts to adhere to their obligations under international counternarcotics agreements.”

In an annual reviews, Trump stressed that the South American country maintains its an unwilling drug trafficking country “solely due to the incompetence and chaos produced by the previous far-left government.”

“If, as expected, Colombia makes progress on aggressive coca eradication and dismantling its narcoterrorist networks over the coming year, I will consider lifting the country’s ‘failed demonstrably’ status,” said the US president.

President Abelardo de la Espriella “has pledged to lead an aggressive campaign against coca cultivation and cocaine production, which reached record levels under the failed socialist policies of his predecessor,” Gustavo Petro, according to Trump.

Colombia is poised to resume its place as our foremost security partner in the hemisphere, and the country’s military, police, prosecutors, and courts now finally have a worthy champion in President de la Espriella. US President Donald Trump

De la Espriella, who took office in August, informally joined the US Government’s Shield of the Americas program in an attempt to increase cooperation between Trump’s conservative and far-right allies in the region.

As part of his counternarcotics efforts, the Colombian president tried to increase air strikes on so-called “narcoterrorist” groups, but was forced to stop this by a court to protect minor forced recruitment victims.

The National Police announced a pilot aerial fumigation program, but this was also suspended by a court because of health and environmental concerns.

The State Department vowed to seek $1 billion dollar in aid, but has yet to ask Congress for these funds while allegedly dealing with the world’s highest number of deaths caused by the consumption of illicit drugs.

World.title: Colombia’s statistics chief sacked for claiming Petro did not manipulate statistics
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked his statistics chief because he claimed he found no anomalies in labor statistics presented by the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.

In a press statement, De la Espriella’s press secretary said that DANE director Ricardo Valencia was sacked for claiming “that he had not found any anomalies in the DANE indicators for the month of July, figures compiled during the final month of the previous administration.”

Valencia made that claim “without any in-depth audits having been conducted beforehand,” according to the press secretary.

It is essential for the National Government to conduct a rigorous review of the information received and to ensure that the data on which strategic decisions for the country are based fully reflect the economic and social reality of Colombians. President’s Office

The former DANE director was sacked days after the President’s Office canceled another statistics press conference that are common because of the agency’s regular updates on the state of the Colombian economy

July’s labor statistics confirmed claims by the previous government that unemployment dropped to record lows after Petro raised the minimum wage.

De la Espriella has insisted that the country’s economy is in crisis contrary to evidence, which indicated Petro increased economic growth in his last half year in office.

World.title: Nine days from the vote, neither Brazilian front-runner comes close to 50%
World.content:
Nine days from the vote, neither Brazilian front-runner comes close to 50%

25th Friday, September 2026 - 00:10 UTC Full article

The survey was conducted on Tuesday 22 and Wednesday 23 among 2,002 voters in 125 municipalities, with a margin of error of two percentage points

Neither of Brazil's two leading presidential candidates is approaching the threshold needed to win outright on October 4, according to the latest Datafolha poll, which puts President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on 40% of voting intentions and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro on 36%.

The survey was conducted on Tuesday 22 and Wednesday 23 among 2,002 voters in 125 municipalities, with a margin of error of two percentage points. It was commissioned by the newspaper Folha de S.Paulo and TV Globo, and is registered with the electoral authorities under code BR-00304/2026. The field is completed by Augusto Cury on 5%, Ronaldo Caiado on 4%, Renan Santos on 3%, and Romeu Zema and Samara on 1% each. Blank or spoiled ballots account for 5% and undecided voters for 2%.

In a prospective October 25 runoff, Lula takes 47% and Bolsonaro 45%, a statistical tie. The previous week's readings were 39% and 36% in the first round, and 46% to 44% in the second, placing the shift within the margin. Folha stresses that this is a snapshot rather than a prediction.

The most significant finding is that Bolsonaro has interrupted a run that over four months had narrowed the gap from ten points to three; it is now back to four. In the unprompted question, without names presented, Lula records 36% and Bolsonaro 27%. Some 80% of voters say their choice is settled, and among those who identify with neither camp, 35% say they could still change their minds. Against the other candidates, Lula is also tied with Cury, 46% to 43%, and beats Caiado 46% to 42%, and both Zema and Renan Santos 48% to 39%.

By segment, Lula leads Bolsonaro among the poorest 50%, 46% to 32%, among the least educated 29%, 49% to 29%, and in the Northeast, the country's second largest electorate with 28% of voters, where he records 55% to 25%. Bolsonaro leads among evangelicals, 47% to 27%; among those earning two to five minimum wages, 40% to 34%; and in the South, 47% to 27%. In the Southeast, the most populous region with 42% of the sample, he holds a numerical advantage within a statistical tie, 37% to 35%. According to Folha, Lula's challenge is mobilising an electorate that tends to show higher abstention.

The poll also captured the week's political developments. The 15% increase in the Bolsa Família benefit, announced by Lula less than three weeks before the vote, did not shift the vote among recipients: the president moved from 52% to 53% and his rival from 28% to 27%. Bolsonaro accused him of trying to “buy the poor” with the measure.

The external factor returned to the centre of the campaign. The United States and fourteen countries announced in New York on Wednesday, after a meeting of the Americas Shield, their intention to take coordinated measures against 24 transnational criminal organisations, including the Brazilian factions First Capital Command and Comando Vermelho, involving asset freezes and immigration restrictions. Brazil is outside the mechanism. Washington designated both as terrorist organisations in May, a classification Lula's government rejects on the grounds that it could open the door to US military intervention on Brazilian territory, while Bolsonaro backed it after meeting Trump that same month. The senator accused the president of leniency towards organised crime; Lula had criticised foreign interference in electoral processes before the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, without naming Trump.

World.title: Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations before an assembly emptied by dozens of delegations
World.content:
Netanyahu rejects genocide allegations before an assembly emptied by dozens of delegations

25th Friday, September 2026 - 00:08 UTC Full article

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Thursday called genocide allegations against his country over the war in Gaza “the biggest lie of the century”, in an address to the United Nations General Assembly that dozens of delegations left before he began speaking.

“If there are any other moral cowards who haven't yet left this hall, please do so now,” he said as he opened his remarks. The walkout was led by representatives of Arab, Muslim and African countries. Figures differ by source: Foreign Policy counted more than a hundred delegates; Fox News, 77 delegations. The US delegation remained seated, and members of the Israeli party shouted “Am Yisrael Chai”.

Netanyahu argued that Israel acted to avoid becoming the victim of a genocide rather than to commit one, and linked the accusations to growing persecution of Jews. He described the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023 as “the darkest day in Israel's history” and “the largest massacre of Jews since the Holocaust”, comparing the roughly 1,200 victims to “40,000 innocent Americans slaughtered in less than 24 hours”, sixteen times the toll of the September 11, 2001 attacks.

On the legal position: the International Criminal Court is investigating Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity, not genocide. There is also a genocide case against Israel before the International Court of Justice, brought by South Africa and joined by other states, with no ruling on the merits. A growing number of specialists and the International Association of Genocide Scholars hold that Israel has committed that crime; Israel rejects this.

The prime minister defended the campaign against Iran, launched alongside the United States in February. Attacking that country “was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make”, he said, arguing that in defending itself Israel “is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall”, whose leaders, he said, thank him privately. He thanked Donald Trump for what he described as an act “to save civilisation”, and repeated: “We will continue to win because we have no other choice.” He noted that a country the size of New Jersey was fighting a war on seven fronts.

On settler violence in the West Bank, which has prompted sanctions from several Western countries led by the United Kingdom, he described those responsible as “a handful of juvenile delinquents”, around 150, accountable for “maybe two or three deaths” so far this year. These are his figures, disputed by UN monitoring bodies. He also attacked New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him “the antisemitic mayor of New York”.

Hours earlier, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas had addressed the assembly by video from Ramallah, after the United States denied him a visa for a second consecutive year. The assembly had voted 152 to 3 to allow him to speak remotely; the United States, Israel and Paraguay voted against. Abbas described Israel's campaign as a “genocidal war that has created an unprecedented humanitarian catastrophe” and denounced a policy of “racial discrimination, ethnic cleansing and terrorism” aimed at forcing Palestinians off their land. “Do not allow a new Nakba, do not allow more massacres,” he said, asking “how much longer some states will remain silent about Israel or continue supplying it with weapons”.

Netanyahu spoke a month before Israeli elections in which his continuity in government is at stake.

World.title: Punta Arenas/Falklands maritime links are based on history, economics and geography
World.content:
Punta Arenas/Falklands maritime links are based on history, economics and geography

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 23:47 UTC Full article

El Tratado de Límites de 1881 estableció un régimen excepcional para el paso marítimo bioceánico, que el Tratado de Paz y Amistad de 1984 reafirmó de manera específica

The announced maritime and trade link between Punta Arenas in Chile and the Falkland Islands has been strongly argued and supported by the main newspaper from the Chilean austral city on the Magellan Strait and capital of the Magallanes Region.

In its editorial La Prensa Austral argues that the recent transversal support from Chilean Senators during their trip to Punta Arenas transcends Argentine warnings in the event of the establishment of a trade link of the Chilean city with the Falklands/Malvinas.

“For Magallanes it is essential, given the freedom to develop its economic links from Chilean territory in accordance with Chilean and international law, no matter what third countries pretend or wish to condition activities of companies and/or individuals from the region”.

In the event of a resumption of a maritime exchange with the Islands, this must not be scrambled with the sovereignty dispute between Argentina and the UK over that territory.

“They are different issues, one is the position of a State regarding a conflict and the other very different, pretending that such a controversy should limit the capacity of established operators in Chile to develop licit commercial activities”.

The daily adds that Punta Arenas is not planning an artificial relation or lacking background. During most of its history Punta Arenas has had close trade and maritime contacts with the Islands, and as it has been repeatedly pointed out by businesses involved it is precisely to recover that relation which existed for over a century.

But the debate acquires a larger dimension when it is linked to the Magellan Strait.

The Boundaries treaty of 1881 established an exceptional ruling for the maritime bi-ocean passage and which the 1984 Treaty of Peace and Friendship reaffirmed specifically, ‘the Strait has been neutralized to perpetuity and its navigation ensured for the flags of all nations”. The 1984 treaty adds that Argentina must maintain “at any time and circumstances” the right for all ships to navigate expeditiously and without obstacles through its jurisdictional waters, from and towards the Strait.

This is a historic ruling that can’t be made relative in light of current controversies. It was conceived precisely to avoid that one of the strategic maritime corridors in the extreme continental austral could be subject to restrictions as a result of conflicts between States. Its fortress resides in the fact that the rules have been established before circumstantial differences.

That is why we also need to separate concepts. Strait treaties guarantee freedom of navigation and do not constitute a commercial authorization for each operation done from Punta Arenas. But this distinction does not weaken the fundamental argument. Chile exercises jurisdiction over its territory and ports, and companies operating legally from them develop their activities subject to Chilean legal system. The free crossing of the Strait also impedes converting the maritime passage in an indirect pressure mechanism on routes or destinations that may result politically uncomfortable for third parties.

This is why the Senators’ declaration is so relevant, precisely because it transfers discussions from rhetoric to the Treaties and permanent rules.

In a region whose history and development are indissolubly linked to the sea, these facts are particularly significant. Punta Arenas emerged and grew as an open port to the world, connected with diverse routes, markets and territories, this condition does not constitute any provocation at all, but simply are part of its own economic and geographic nature.
