World.title: UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”
World.content:
UK replies to Milei: “not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:59 UTC Full article

Photo: REUTERS/Kylie Cooper

The United Kingdom has asked for a written statement to be placed in the official record of the UN General Assembly in response to Argentine President Javier Milei's address, saying Buenos Aires' conduct over the Falklands “is wholly incompatible with the principles established in the United Nations Charter and is not the behaviour we expect of a democracy”.

The text, released by the British mission to the organisation, was submitted under agenda item eight of the 81st session, after Milei referred on Wednesday to sovereignty over the archipelago and over South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands. It is the same procedure London used in 2012 to reply to then president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.

The document states that the United Kingdom “has no doubt” about its sovereignty over both territories and their surrounding maritime areas, and that it remains steadfast in supporting the islanders' right of self-determination, set out in the UN Charter and Article 1 of the two international human rights covenants. It says Argentina “continues to deny that this fundamental human right applies” to those inhabitants and actively seeks opportunities in international fora to assert its sovereignty claim.

The United Kingdom has no doubt about its sovereignty over the Falkland Islands.



Our statement in response to the Argentine General Assembly Statement regarding the Falklands: pic.twitter.com/eWw8aS2MDI — UK at the UN (@UKUN_NewYork) September 23, 2026

The statement rebuts point by point the legal argument Milei set out. It says General Assembly Resolution 2065 “does not prohibit economic development or displace the Islanders' right of self-determination”, and that Resolution 31/49 “likewise does not limit or remove the rights of the Islanders to freely determine their political status and freely pursue their economic, social and cultural development”. It adds that calls for negotiations “do not modify or dilute the obligation of nations to respect the legally binding right of self-determination”. These are UK government positions, contested by Argentina.

On the ongoing dispute over oil companies, the text says efforts to obstruct and harass international companies involved in the archipelago's hydrocarbons, and other local industries, “are a wholly unacceptable attempt to exercise extra-territorial jurisdiction, and have no justification whatsoever in international law”, describing them as obstructive to global business and inconsistent with free trade. It further states that hydrocarbon development is a legitimate commercial venture regulated by the legislation of the archipelago's government in strict accordance with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, and that Argentine domestic law does not apply there.

The document includes a detail about the 2013 referendum that London does not usually highlight: alongside the 99.8% vote to maintain the current status, on a 92% turnout, the vote was supervised by independent observers from Canada, the United States, New Zealand and three South American countries: Uruguay, Chile and Brazil.

The statement closes a forty-eight-hour sequence. On Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham included the archipelago among the challenges to the rule of law in his address; that same night, Argentine Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno exercised the right of reply before the plenary and said “the illegal British occupation of the islands dates back to January 1833”, when the authorities and the established Argentine population were expelled. Milei spoke on Wednesday, and the British text followed hours later.

Argentina has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied and three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors. None of the allegations has been proven.

World.title: Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date
World.content:
Delcy Rodríguez tells the UN there will be elections in Venezuela, without setting a date

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 10:47 UTC Full article

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke

Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, announced on Wednesday before the United Nations General Assembly that her country will hold elections, without specifying when, and thanked US President Donald Trump for “his willingness to return to the path of diplomatic relations and cooperation”.

“Democracy is not measured by the existence of elections. Democracy is measured by the quality of the competition that precedes those elections. An election should be a solution, not a generator of irreconcilable conflicts,” she said before the announcement. She added: “I want to say it very clearly in this General Assembly: in Venezuela there will be elections and, in that direction, we have begun a political dialogue with sectors of the opposition,” under “equal conditions for all”. On timing, she said “the Venezuelan people, with their ancestral wisdom, will determine the right moment”.

Rodríguez said Venezuela has begun an “orderly, institutional and verifiable” transition to democracy, citing among its pillars a reform of the justice system and the “responsible exercise” of politics. She said the country had endured “two great and painful trials” this year: the “strangulation of its internal political life and the sharpened confrontation with the United States”, and the double earthquake of June 24, which left more than 6,500 dead. “Venezuela is being reborn,” she concluded, in a speech lasting under twenty minutes.

It was the first address by a Venezuelan head of state to the body's plenary since 2018, when Nicolás Maduro spoke. The tone contrasted with Rodríguez's own remarks in the same forum in 2019, when as vice president she said she came “in the name of the Venezuela that does not kneel before any imperial power”, conveyed Maduro's greetings and denounced Trump's “supremacist hatred” and “imperial claws”.

She did not mention Maduro at any point. Her predecessor remains in US custody alongside his wife Cilia Flores, awaiting trial on drug trafficking and related charges, which he rejects. Before her address, videos circulated in which Rodríguez declined to say whether she would visit Maduro at the Brooklyn detention centre where he is held.

The acting president also praised the agreement granting the United States access to more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, a share the US government puts at around a quarter of the country's total. Trump had referred to the deal the previous day, from the same podium, with the phrase “to the victor belong the spoils”.

According to Axios, citing White House sources, Trump pressed Rodríguez during Tuesday's meeting to call elections: “In the end, you're going to have to call elections,” he reportedly said. Neither participant confirmed that account. Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed it differently on Wednesday, saying the ultimate goal is “free and fair elections” but that an economic collapse must first be avoided. “If there is a social collapse or an economic crisis in Venezuela, not only are the elections in jeopardy, but also the survival of democracy in the country,” he said.

Rodríguez took office in an acting capacity on January 5, two days after Maduro's capture in a US military operation in Caracas, and faces questions over her legitimacy for not having been elected. Separately, the circle around opposition leader María Corina Machado said this week that three attempts to return to the country from Panama had been thwarted, bringing the total to seven in recent weeks.

World.title: Machado's team says three attempts to return to Venezuela failed in 24 hours
World.content:
Machado's team says three attempts to return to Venezuela failed in 24 hours

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 00:11 UTC Full article

Asked about the matter, Trump denied having told her not to return, saying he had said nothing to her about it

The circle around Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado said this week that three attempts to return to Venezuela from Panama, by sea and by air, were thwarted within roughly 24 hours. One was recorded in a flight manifest placing her among the passengers of an aircraft that never took off; the document does not establish why.

“In recent hours there have been three attempts, by sea and air, from Panama, without success. That makes seven attempts — yes, seven — in recent weeks. They will not let her return to her own country,” her international relations adviser, Pedro Urruchurtu, wrote on X. The reasons given for the cancellations come from the account of journalist Idania Chirinos, of NTN24, who is accompanying Machado in Panama: on Monday, a sea crossing was suspended when the vessel's owner cited mechanical faults that Chirinos called “strange”, even though Machado's passport had already been stamped by immigration; on Tuesday morning, a flight to Aruba did not take off; and in the afternoon the attempt via Curaçao fell through. “The Nobel Peace Prize winner is a prisoner in Panama,” Chirinos said. Her daughter, Ana Corina Sosa, confirmed to the same channel that she remains in that country.

The manifest for the third attempt, obtained by the outlet UHN Plus, details a flight scheduled for Tuesday, September 22, aboard a Beechcraft BE-90F, registration HP-4DMB, from Marcos A. Gelabert airport in Panama City to Hato airport in Curaçao. Alongside Machado it lists four others: Monique Herrera, Rafael Alfonzo, Esteban Fraga and Ferdelin Bonilla, whose name appears with different spellings depending on the source. According to El País, Alfonzo is the opposition leader's lobbyist in Washington and Bonilla an adviser to Panama's foreign minister and a director of a state electricity company; those details were not independently verified.

The document also records that Machado would travel on a Panamanian passport, serial PD2000017. The outlet that obtained the manifest describes it as diplomatic; El País says it would be a special travel document Panama grants on humanitarian grounds to foreigners with a documented public record, and that it does not entail acquiring a new nationality. Her Venezuelan passport expired years ago and the authorities have not renewed it. Panama's government has not commented.

There are two hypotheses about the source of the obstruction, and neither is established. El País attributes the blocking to Washington, citing Axios reporting that Deputy Secretary of State Chris Landau had approved an earlier trip while Assistant Secretary of State for Latin America Mike Kozak conveyed that US policy is not to facilitate Machado's return. Machado herself, however, said on June 29 that it was the Venezuelan government that had closed commercial airspace to prevent her from entering.

Leopoldo López's party, Voluntad Popular, recalled that Venezuela's constitution recognises citizens' right to enter national territory and called on the interim authorities to guarantee Machado's return and her political participation without restrictions.

Asked about the matter, Trump denied having told her not to return, saying he had said nothing to her about it. Secretary of State Marco Rubio had said days earlier that Machado can return to her country “whenever she wants”; asked this week about the failed attempts, he avoided a direct answer and noted he had spent the day at the UN.

Machado, founder of Vente Venezuela and the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize laureate, left Venezuela in early December that year to receive the award in Oslo, after more than a year and a half in hiding. The attempts coincided with the presence in New York of acting president Delcy Rodríguez, who is attending the General Assembly and met Trump on Tuesday.

World.title: The Shift from Display Ads to Affiliate Revenue in Sports Media
World.content:
The Shift from Display Ads to Affiliate Revenue in Sports Media

24th Thursday, September 2026 - 00:01 UTC Full article

For most of the 2010s, sports websites made money in the same way as everyone else online. They put banners on the page, sold ad space, and got paid when people saw the ads. If there was traffic, the bills got paid. What readers did after they got to the page didn't matter.

That model has been falling apart for some time.

Spending on sports media is going down. Readers scroll past banners without seeing them. Ad blockers stop many people from seeing the ads. More sports sites are competing for the same ad budgets, which pushes prices down even further.

At the same time, something else has been growing. Affiliate marketing, where sites earn money when readers sign up using a special link, is now a way for sports outlets of all sizes to make money. Fan blogs and big editorial rooms. The move is already underway.

The display ad problem

Adverts on the website did not suddenly stop working. The numbers just kept getting worse, year after year. Many publishers only reacted when things got really bad.

Banners only pay when they are viewed. If 1,000 people see the ad, the site owner gets a set fee. The rate depends on the niche, the traffic source, and how many other sites are selling the same space. In sports, that rate has been under pressure for years.

One reason is supply. More sports websites exist now than in 2018 or 2019. More sites mean more inventory. Having more inventory means advertisers can pay less.

It's partly because of a bad habit. People have learned to ignore banners. Researchers call this banner blindness. It's still here.

Then there are ad blockers. The exact number varies by survey, but around a quarter to a third of web users have one installed. The publisher doesn't get paid for that traffic.

Adverts on websites still make money. They are not useless. But because they're the main way the sports site makes money, they put publishers at greater risk every year.

Why affiliate revenue fits sports media

Affiliate marketing works differently. Advertisers pay for results, not for views. A reader clicks on a link, signs up at a sportsbook, and makes a deposit. This means the publisher gets a commission. If you don't take action, you won't get paid.

That fits well with sports content. A football site already brings people who care about the game together. Some of them bet. If the site mentions a sportsbook in a match preview or a betting guide, the link is inside the piece the reader came for. It doesn't feel like an interruption, like a banner would.

The money looks different too:

- A display ad costs the same whether the person reading it is a casual reader or a serious bettor.

- You don't earn money from an affiliate link until someone clicks on it. But one person signing up is worth more than thousands of banner views.

- With RevShare deals, the site keeps earning money while the player stays active. One good recommendation can pay for months.

This is a big reason why the change has got faster. A banner impression is one time only. A RevShare referral is a link between the content and the player that lasts forever.

But there is one condition. The audience has to trust the site.

A banner is a type of . Readers accept it the same way they accept adverts on TV. A review with a tracked link is different. People need to be able to trust that the recommendation is honest. If you promote brands that pay well, readers will notice. They stop clicking. Then they stop coming back.

Some publishers found this out the hard way. They joined every programme they could find, filled pages with links, and pushed books they had never tested. There was less traffic. There weren't enough sales. The company made less money than they thought they would.

The sites that do well choose partners carefully. They review casino affiliate programs that match their audience and test the product before recommending it. They say that a link is an affiliate link if it is clearly marked as such. People will keep visiting your website if you are honest.

What a working strategy looks like

The publishers that make the most money from affiliate sales tend to do the same few things.

The content answers a question the reader already has. Here are some match previews. Odds breakdowns. This is a guide to one feature on a sportsbook. The link makes sense because the article is already about that thing.

They don't try to run twenty programmes at the same time. Two or three that match the audience beat a dozen that don't.

They put the programmes through their paces to see how they measure up. If a book isn't popular, it can still make less money even if the price is higher.

Then they just watch what happens after they click. Sign up. Deposits. How long the player stays. The numbers are more important than the commission percentage.

They mix and match different types of deals. Pay the CPA for cash now. This is a long-term investment. Some programmes offer a mix of both, which works well for sites with steady traffic.

How the two models compare

Display ads Affiliate revenue What triggers payment Someone sees the ad Someone signs up, deposits, or bets How income looks Steady, but small Less predictable, higher ceiling What it depends on Traffic volume Audience quality and trust How it feels for the reader Banners can slow the page Links sit inside content they chose to read Where it is heading Rates down, blockers up More programmes, more brand spend Who decides The ad network The publisher

Where the shift is moving fastest

This is not only a UK or US story. Sports media in Latin America, Africa and parts of Asia has grown quickly. A lot of newer sites in those regions started with affiliate from day one. They skipped the banner years and went straight to pay-for-results.

Region Display ads Affiliate growth Notes UK High demand, crowded Mature, plenty of programmes Tight rules. Brand reputation matters US (legal states) Strong Growing as more states open Compliance changes state by state Latin America Lower CPMs Rising fast Local and global books both chasing affiliates Africa Limited advertiser interest Early, high potential Mobile-first. Fewer established programmes Asia Mixed by country Strong in several markets Language and local payments make or break it

Mobile has sped the change up. Most sports content is read on phones now. Banners on a small screen are even easier to skip than on a desktop. They also slow the page down, and readers leave before the article loads.

Affiliate links work the same on any screen. A text link in a match preview takes no extra space, loads at once, and sends the reader to a signup page built for mobile. For sports media, that audience is almost everyone.

What comes next

The direction is clear. Advertisers want to pay for results. Publishers who can send real players, not just page views, can earn more than display ads have offered in years.

But that doesn't mean every sports website should remove the banners tomorrow. The display can still be used. But publishers that rely only on banners are finding it harder to make a profit. The ones who earn audience trust through affiliate marketing—by being honest and giving decent recommendations—are the ones more likely to still be here in five years.

The change has already happened. The only question left is how quickly the rest of the industry will catch up.

World.title: Milei at the UN: “The Malvinas are a national cause for us”
World.content:
Milei at the UN: “The Malvinas are a national cause for us”

23rd Wednesday, September 2026 - 17:54 UTC Full article

It was his third speech as president to the body and the eighth of the day's speakers, running 19 minutes

Argentine President Javier Milei called on the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday to act over what he described as unilateral British actions in the Falklands, and accused the organisation of having “decided to look the other way” on the dispute. “The Malvinas are a national cause for us,” he said, repeating the phrase twice at the start of his address.

It was his third speech as president to the body and the eighth of the day's speakers, running 19 minutes. Foreign Minister Pablo Quirno, Economy Minister Luis Caputo and UN Ambassador Francisco Tropepi listened from the floor.

Milei focused his criticism on non-compliance with Resolution 31/49, adopted in December 1976, which urges Argentina and the United Kingdom to refrain from introducing unilateral modifications while the dispute continues. “Fifty years later the situation has not changed, but the unilateral modifications continue,” he said, adding: “What use is a resolution if for decades the other party can act against it and that resolution remains intact in the archives but powerless before reality? There is no shortage of words or resolutions; what is missing is that they carry consequences.”

On the archipelago's population, he argued that the principle of self-determination does not apply “since this is a population implanted by the occupying power on a territory whose sovereignty is in dispute”, and said the Assembly itself has determined as much in numerous resolutions. That is Argentina's reading of those texts. The United Kingdom holds the opposite position: in his address on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country would stand firm against those who “threaten the rights of British territories to remain British, such as the Falkland Islands”. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters in the archipelago chose to retain the status of a British overseas territory.

Milei listed the measures taken: “We presented warning notices, we turned to the available legal tools, we sanctioned the companies involved and their suppliers, and we sent Congress a National Sovereignty Defence Bill.” According to official figures released so far, the foreign ministry has 60 administrative proceedings open with no penalty applied, three criminal complaints covering ten companies and their directors, and around 180 warning notices sent to individuals and companies in 30 countries. None of the allegations has been proven. He repeated the call on London to “resume negotiations to find a peaceful solution” and to exchange views on the exploitation of natural resources.

“Malvinas”:

Por el reclamo de Javier Milei en la Asamblea General de la ONU pic.twitter.com/LX5iwTsBBB — ¿Por qué es tendencia? (@porquetendencia) September 23, 2026

Argentina had already responded to Burnham before the presidential address. Quirno exercised the right of reply before the plenary on Tuesday night, speaking for nearly three minutes alongside Tropepi: he reiterated Argentina's “full willingness” to resume bilateral negotiations and said the islands are “illegally occupied by the United Kingdom”. Asked whether the premier's remarks would require changes to Milei's speech, he said they would not, because “we already made the reply ourselves”. That same day, the foreign ministry delivered a formal protest note at the British embassy over the five-year extension of offshore oil licences, which it called an “unlawful act”.

Elsewhere in the speech, Milei described pandemic lockdown policies promoted by UN-affiliated bodies as “genocide”, saying they “cost the lives of millions of people who died alone”. It is an extreme and contested characterisation, made by the Argentine president.

On artificial intelligence, he announced that Argentina will not regulate pre-emptively and will offer “a cutting-edge legal framework”, with limited liability for companies and tax benefits, aligning with Donald Trump, who in Tuesday's address rejected any “globalist scheme” of regulation. Burnham, from the same podium on the same day, had called for the opposite: “a single set of global principles and standards”.

World.title: More than 7,000 ignore clouds to gather at Chichén Itzá for the equinox
World.content:
Thousands of people gathered in the esplanade in front of the great pyramid of Kukulcán in the Chichén Itzá archaeological site in the state of Yucatán on Monday and Tuesday to witness the famous descent of the serpent.

The spectacular light and shadow phenomenon takes place during the spring and autumn equinoxes each year when afternoon sunlight hits the pyramid at a particular angle. As a result, the silhouette of a serpent is projected on the wall of the north balustrade of the structure known as El Castillo.

The intricate design of El Castillo, also called the Temple of Kukulcán, allows for the projection of seven isosceles triangles of light which appear to the observer as a luminous and magical serpent moving down the pyramid toward the carved serpent head near its base.

This fascinating interplay of light and shadow — known as the hierophanies of the equinoxes — typically lasts from 10 to 30 minutes.

This year, the National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) implemented a special operation to receive tourists beginning on Sunday as the interplay of light and shadow was visible from Sunday through Tuesday.

El Castillo was built in a geometric pyramid shape with nine truncated levels, superimposed and progressively smaller with a small temple at the top.

Central staircases on each of the four sides, each with 91 steps. allowed access to the temple. In total, there are 364 steps, but including the platform on which the pyramid rests, the result is 365, precisely the length of the Maya civil year.

“It reminds us of the admirable precision with which the ancient Maya observed the movement of the sun and the cycles of the seasons,” the INAH said in a statement, adding that the calculations were fundamental to Maya agriculture.

INAH said the instant of the equinox this year occurred at 3:51 p.m. on Monday. In all, INAH recorded more than 7,000 visitors at Chichen Itza from Sunday through Tuesday.

Because autumn starts before the rainy season ends, there are often clouds at the equinox hiding the effect. This year was no exception, but there were enough breaks in the cloud cover for the visitors to get good looks at the phenomenon.

Last year, Chichen Itza surpassed Teotihuacán and Tulum as the most popular cultural tourism site in Mexico, according to the Tourism Ministry.

With reports from La Jornada Maya, National Geographic and Yucatán Magazine

World.title: Mayor of Juchitán, Oaxaca, arrested over alleged CJNG ties, triggering blockades and protests
World.content:
Federal and state security forces on Wednesday arrested the mayor of Juchitán, Oaxaca, and another man on charges of aggravated extortion and crimes against state security. The arrests triggered road blockades and protests in Juchitán, located on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec.

The federal Security Ministry (SSPC), Security Minister Omar García Harfuch and the Oaxaca Attorney General’s Office (FGEO) all announced the arrests of Miguel Sánchez Altamirano, a Morena party mayor, and Alberto de la Paz López, a man known as “La Parca” (or “La Parka).

En el marco de la política de Cero Impunidad instruida por la Presidenta @Claudiashein, durante un despliegue operativo en Oaxaca, elementos de @SEMAR_mx, @SSPCMexico, @Defensamx1, @FGRMexico y @GN_MEXICO_, en coordinación con la @FISCALIA_GobOax y @SSPC_GobOax, detuvieron a… pic.twitter.com/6xlOskXAh7 — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) September 23, 2026

The SSPC said in a statement that the arrests were carried out “within the framework of Operativo Enjambre” (Operation Swarm), a federal security strategy aimed at combating collusion between organized crime and municipal government officials.

“As part of an investigation into a criminal network linked to extortion, … small-scale drug dealing, human trafficking … and homicides — as well as protection schemes that allegedly facilitated the operations of members of criminal groups — agents pursued various lines of inquiry,” the Security Ministry said.

“As a result of these efforts, Miguel ‘N,’ the mayor of Juchitán de Zaragoza, and another person were identified. Both had active arrest warrants for … aggravated extortion and crimes against state security. Consequently, an inter-institutional operation was launched, during which both men were arrested,” the SSPC said.

The FGEO described the arrests as a “head-on strike against criminality.”

In a statement, the state Attorney General’s Office said that Sánchez, mayor of Juchitán since late 2022, is linked to a criminal group called Los Cromos. It said that the group — of which de la Paz is an alleged member — “functions as an operational arm” of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel.

The FGEO said that “intelligence work” determined that the mayor “participated in, promoted, and covered up criminal activities in the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, due to his close relationship and strategic ties with” Los Cromos.

Juchitán, a city of around 115,000 people, is located near the southern coast of the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, Mexico’s narrowest stretch of land between the Pacific Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico.

From Ciudad Ixtepec, also located on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, both Sánchez and de la Paz were transferred to Mexico City on a Mexican Navy plane. They are currently in prison pending initial court appearances.

UIF blocks accounts of people linked to Juchitán investigation

García Harfuch said in an X post that the Finance Ministry’s Financial Intelligence Unit froze assets and blocked bank accounts of people linked to the investigation that led to the arrest of Sánchez and de la Paz.

He subsequently thanked the government of Oaxaca and Governor Salomón Jara for their “ongoing collaboration and coordination” with federal authorities.

“Investigations and operational actions to completely break up this criminal structure and detain all those involved are continuing,” García Harfuch wrote, referring to Los Cromos.

“As new arrests are made, we will continue to report,” he wrote.

An angry response in Juchitán

The arrest of Sánchez and de la Paz on Wednesday morning sparked a hostile reaction in Juchitán.

The Reforma newspaper reported that main roads were blocked and protests were held in Juchitán. The newspaper wrote that moto-taxi drivers, Juchitán residents and even municipal police officers joined the protests.

At one point on Federal Highway 185, moto-taxi drivers and residents laid tires across the road and set them on fire to block traffic and “demand the release of Sánchez Altamirano,” Reforma reported.

La Jornada reported that Juchitán moto-taxi drivers were involved in a drug-dealing and extortion scheme allegedly led by de la Paz and allegedly protected by the city’s mayor.

🚨 Bloquean accesos a Juchitán de Zaragoza, Oaxaca, tras la detención del alcalde Miguel ‘Quetú’ Su detención forma parte de una investigación contra una estructura criminal a la que las autoridades relacionan con distintos delitos, entre ellos extorsión y cobro de piso a… pic.twitter.com/oRmJwl2RB0 — Milenio (@Milenio) September 23, 2026

Citing “sources close to the operation” and local media reports, Reforma reported that police officers “closed off the city’s entry and exit points following the arrest of their own mayor.”

If their goal was to prevent the transfer of Sánchez and de la Paz to Ciudad Ixtepec, where a military airport is located, they failed.

The Juchitán mayor is among more than 100 municipal officials who have been detained since Operación Enjambre began in late 2024. Among the other mayors who have been arrested are the mayor of Tequila, Jalisco, who was detained on extortion charges in February, and the mayor of Atlatlahucan, Morelos, who was taken into custody in May.

García Harfuch said earlier this year that the arrest of officials is part of the government’s commitment to “zero impunity.”

When there is proof that a current or former official has committed a crime, he or she will be “investigated and arrested” no matter what political party he or she belongs to, he said May 27. García Harfuch also said that officials detained during the current administration are from “all” of Mexico’s political parties.

With reports from La Jornada and Reforma

World.title: Senate bill would force Mexican pro soccer to bring back promotion and relegation
World.content:
The fight over the elimination of promotion and relegation in Mexican soccer has moved deeper into the Senate, where lawmakers this week published a bill that would require Liga MX to restore a path for second-division clubs to reach the top flight.

The proposal, introduced by Senator Clemente Castañeda, a member of the opposition Citizens’ Movement party from Jalisco, would amend Article 50 of the General Law of Physical Culture and Sport. It reportedly has support from 10 senators from several parties.

The bill would require promotion and relegation when two or more professional divisions operate within the same national competitive structure.

While its language could extend to other sports, the immediate target is Liga MX and the closed system separating the top division from the Liga de Expansión MX. Before 2020, that second-tier professional league was named Ascenso MX — “ascenso” meaning promotion.

“When they closed off the possibility of promotion, they didn’t just change a sporting rule,” Castañeda said. “They also restricted a path for players, staff and sports projects to grow in a country that needs to open up opportunities.”

The bill presented Wednesday must clear Senate committees and pass both houses of Congress before it can become law.

Liga MX owners suspended promotion and relegation in 2020 as part of a Mexican Football Federation (FMF) restructuring during the COVID-19 shutdown. Officials said a six-season promotion pause was needed to stabilize financially troubled lower-division clubs.

The system was expected to return after the 2025-26 season — with one second-division club getting promoted and one Liga MX club relegated each year.

Instead, Mexico’s soccer authorities removed it from league regulations, prompting protests by clubs, players and fans.

Still, the FMF insists that second-division teams are “eligible” for promotion if they meet certification standards, such as financial solvency and a formal organizational structure. One of the requirements is stadium capacity of 30,000 — a threshold that even some Liga MX clubs do not meet, critics say.

Five Liga de Expansión teams — Cancún FC, Atlético La Paz, Atlético Morelia, Leones Negros de la Universidad de Guadalajara and Mineros de Zacatecas — appealed to the Court of Arbitration for Sport after the policy change.

A 2025 ruling by the Lausanne, Switzerland-based body found that the FMF’s six-season suspension ran only through the 2025-26 season, clearing the way for promotion and relegation to return.

But the FMF and Liga MX instead removed the system from the regulations for the current 2026-27 season.

At Liga de Expansión opening matches last month, players from several teams spent the first minute standing still or passing without attacking to protest the policy. The disciplinary commission warned clubs that additional disruptions could result in fines.

The dispute has broadened beyond the Senate. Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission this month opened an investigation into possible monopolistic practices in pro soccer. The FMF could face fines of up to 10% of annual revenue if authorities find violations of competition law.

This week’s Senate proposal could also raise questions under FIFA statutes, which require member federations to manage their affairs independently and without undue third-party influence. FIFA’s council may temporarily suspend an association that seriously violates its obligations.

Mexico’s closed Liga MX structure contrasts with the major European leagues. The English Premier League, Spain’s La Liga, Italy’s Serie A, Germany’s Bundesliga and France’s Ligue 1 all promote clubs from and relegate clubs to their second divisions based on results.

But Liga MX is not alone. Major League Soccer in the U.S. and Canada and the A-League Men in Australia also operate without promotion and relegation.

With reports from ESPN, Associated Press and TUDN

World.title: Is internet satire under threat in Mexico? Why the ‘Anti-Meme Bill’ is controversial
World.content:
A Senate bill meant to strengthen intellectual property protection has sparked controversy over possible digital censorship in Mexico, particularly as it could apply to parodies or satires aimed at the government.

The bill, sent to the Senate by President Sheinbaum in May and due to be voted on soon, entails amendments to the Federal Penal Code and the Federal Law for the Protection of Industrial Property (LFPPI).

The initiative is part of a broader set of reforms that, according to the federal government, aim to strengthen the criminal framework regarding intellectual property and align it with international treaties such as the United States-Mexico and Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Critics, such as PAN Senator Ricardo Anaya (in the video), have dubbed the bill the “Anti-Meme Law,” arguing that its wording could affect journalists, cartoonists, and content creators who use official elements in satirical works.

That same “Anti-Meme Law” moniker has also been applied to a separate but similar reform — an amendment to the Federal Copyright Law regarding the liability of internet service providers — currently under debate in the Chamber of Deputies.

Regarding the LFPPI, the opposition parties say they are concerned about the addition of Article 403 Bis, which establishes an offense related to the misuse of government identity.

The original wording penalized the commercial use of logos, domain names, graphic identities, or official symbols of governments and public bodies — including via digital means — to deceive people, with sentences ranging from three to seven years in prison and fines of up to 1.17 million pesos (US $65,000).

Following public criticism, voting committees amended the proposal by reportedly reducing the prison time to one to five years. More importantly, it was clarified that the offense would only apply to those who use the government’s image for commercial, deceptive, or fraudulent purposes.

Under the amended terms, content that uses an official logo or colors for satire, parody, criticism, or memes — and is easily recognizable as unofficial — would not constitute an infringement.

In a statement, Morena Senator Javier Corral said that the interpretation of the bill had been blown out of proportion.

“I want to reject the idea that jail time is being proposed for memes or parodies, and to clarify that this provision has nothing to do with regulating freedom of expression. That is not the case,” he said.

“The wording we are now proposing not only eliminates any ambiguity but specifically seeks to establish that the act of misleading or deceiving one or more persons [through the use of government logos] must have the commission of an unlawful act as its purpose.”

It is anticipated the bill would be approved under the new terms.

With reports from El Universal, Eje Central, and El Financiero

World.title: MND Local Puerto Vallarta: Floating billboards, restaurant closures and a key resignation
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta is navigating a series of challenges as the city balances tourism, economic pressures and environmental concerns. A floating advertising screen has sparked debate over the bay’s visual and environmental impact, while a difficult low season has forced restaurants to cut staff and temporarily close. Meanwhile, the resignation of the city’s Environmental Guard director has added another layer to ongoing questions about how the municipality will manage growth and preservation.

Floating screen sparks controversy in Puerto Vallarta

A vessel featuring a large-format LED screen has begun sailing off the coast of Puerto Vallarta, displaying commercial s visible from various points along the tourist strip.

Residents, visitors and local representatives have warned that the screen could not only damage the natural landscape through light pollution but also the bay’s image as a tourist destination.

The screen has been linked to Oceanic Marketing, a company that offers maritime advertising via vessels displaying ads visible from the shore.

In response to the criticism, Municipal President Luis Ernesto Munguía González asked environmental federal authorities, as well as the navy ministry and port authority, to review the vessel’s operating conditions. The request includes verifying maritime and environmental permits, as well as safety standards regarding navigation and the use of maritime space.

The municipal government said that local regulations restrict large-scale billboards on land. However, authorities added there are currently no regulations pertaining to advertising installed at sea.

As such, authorities are now working to clarify which rules would apply



Puerto Vallarta restaurateurs affected by tourism decline

The sharp drop in visitor numbers during the low season has led Puerto Vallarta restaurants to implement staffing and operational adjustments to curb losses.

In the city center — particularly along the Malecón and its surrounding areas — some establishments have introduced staggered shifts, unpaid leave and early vacation scheduling, as a strategy to cut costs in the face of declining sales.

These measures primarily affect workers who rely on tips and commission, as lower foot traffic reduces both available working hours and daily earnings.

The situation has also led to temporary closures.

Martha Parra, head of the National Chamber of the Restaurant and Seasoned Food Industry (CANIRAC) in Puerto Vallarta, told news outlet Jafrico that at least 15 businesses have temporarily ceased operations and two have permanently closed.

Parra acknowledged that the combination of fewer tourists, high rent and overall economic downturn has made it hard for businesses with slim margins to stay afloat.

She noted that although the current off-season has been more challenging than previous years, it is not an isolated problem, as restaurants in other destinations have also reported declines between 20% and 30% compared to 2025.

Head of Puerto Vallarta’s Environmental Guard resigns

The restructuring of Puerto Vallarta’s city council saw a high-level departure this week, after Diego López Coronado resigned as director of the Environmental Guard.

The former official announced his departure on Wednesday via his official social media channels, describing his decision as “well-thought, deliberate and made with a strong sense of responsibility.”

In his letter to Municipal President Luis Ernesto Munguía González, López Coronado said his decision was based on personal and professional interests, adding that he had different views on certain municipal matters.

“Over time, however, I have found myself at odds with several of the decisions that have been made, and I reached a conclusion I cannot avoid; there are things that can no longer be defended,” López Coronado wrote.

López Coronado had previously served as director of social development before taking on the newly created environmental division, established through an administrative restructure approved by the city council a year ago.

López Coronado’s departure comes amidst an ongoing review of the organizational structure and assessment of the performance and tenure of municipal officials.

So far, the municipal government has not announced who will replace López Coronado, nor has it detailed whether further cabinet changes are forthcoming.

World.title: Hurricane Polo, having regained strength, drenches the Pacific coast and heads for Baja
World.content:
Listen to this article

The still extremely powerful Hurricane Polo continues to threaten Pacific coast states with flooding rain, high winds and high surf as it oscillates between Category 4 and Category 5 on the Saffir Simpson scale.

In an update issued at 9:15 a.m. Thursday, the National Meteorological Service (SMN) warned that “the likelihood of very heavy to locally intense rainfall in western and southern states” would continue to be a concern.

Strong winds and high waves were expected along the coasts, it said, specifically identifying the states of Colima, Jalisco, Michoacán and Guerrero. Intense rains and torrential downpours (150 to 250 mm) were forecast for coastal areas of Michoacán and Guerrero through early afternoon.

The U.S. National Hurricane Center (NHC) forecast tropical storm conditions across portions of the coast within the warning area from Tecpan de Galeana, Guerrero, north to Manzanillo, Colima.

Polo is expected to remain a major hurricane for the next few days and could strengthen yet again. In the meantime, it is currently sending hurricane-force winds outward up to 40 miles from its center and tropical storm-force winds some 125 miles out.

The NHC also projected that Polo — which was about 175 miles west-southwest of Zihuatanejo, Guerrero, and moving northwest at 9 mph — would move farther out to sea by Friday morning before approaching the Baja California Peninsula early next week. However, its core is expected to remain offshore rather than make landfall.

Polo is an unusual, record-setting hurricane

Polo was packing maximum sustained winds of 160 mph on Thursday, after wind speeds went from 85 mph to a peak of 180 mph (the second-strongest eastern Pacific hurricane on record) in just 22 hours earlier in the week.

Its transition from a “disorganized tropical depression” to a Category 5 hurricane was the fastest of any system on record in the Western Hemisphere.

Since then it has lost some strength, regained it, and then lost some of it again, moving back and forth between Categories 4 and 5. It could likely regain strength yet again.

Polo also tied Hurricane Rita (2005) as the warmest on record (determined by flight-level temperature readings inside a hurricane’s eye), surpassing some of the most intense Western Pacific super typhoons ever directly observed, according to Michael Lowry, a Miami-based hurricane specialist cited by USA Today.

With reports from USA Today, CBS News and N+

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: Mexico’s largest lakes
World.content:
Earlier this year, MND published “Mexico in Numbers” articles on “Mexico’s largest and most populous islands” and “Mexico’s biggest and smallest states.”

Today, we’re turning our focus to Mexico’s largest freshwater lakes by surface area.

Let’s jump in!

* The data in this article comes from the National Water Commission and the National Institute of Statistics and Geography.

1. Lake Chapala

Mainly located in Jalisco, but extending across the state border into Michoacán, Lake Chapala is Mexico’s largest freshwater lake.

The lake has a surface area of 1,116 km2 and a water storage capacity of 8.126 billion cubic meters.

Did you know that a VW Beetle crossed Lake Chapala on Sept. 8, 1968? Click here to read the incredible story.

2. Lake Cuitzeo

Situated mainly in Michoacán, but extending across the state border into Guanajuato, Lake Cuitzeo is Mexico’s second largest freshwater lake.

The lake has a surface area of 306 km2 and a water storage capacity of 920 million cubic meters. Based on the surface area measure, Lake Chapala is around 3.6 times larger than Lake Cuitzeo.

Lago de Cuitzeo, as the lake is called in Spanish, has lost a lot of its water in recent years due to drought. The situation was particularly dire in 2021.

3. Lake Pátzcuaro

Located in the municipality of Pátzcuaro, Michoacán, Lake Pátzcuaro is Mexico’s third largest freshwater lake.

The lake has a surface area of 97 km2 and a water storage capacity of 550 million cubic meters. Based on the surface area measure, Lake Chapala is around 11.5 times larger than Lake Pátzcuaro.

Lake Pátzcuaro is home to an endangered species of salamanders known as achoques. The island of Janitzio, a popular Day of the Dead destination, is located in the lake.

4. Lake Yuriria

Located in Guanajuato, Lake Yuriria is Mexico’s fourth largest freshwater lake.

This artificial lake, called Laguna de Yuriria in Spanish, has a surface area of 80 km2 and a water storage capacity of 188 million cubic meters. Based on the surface area measure, Lake Chapala is around 14 times larger than Lake Yuriria.

Lake Yuriria is located in the municipality of Yuriria in southern Guanajuato. The town of Yuriria is a pueblo mágico.

5. Laguna Catemaco

Located in the Gulf coast state of Veracruz, Laguna Catemaco (also known as Lake Catemaco) is Mexico’s fifth largest freshwater lake.

The lake has a surface area of 75 km2 and a water storage capacity of 454 million cubic meters. Based on the surface area measure, Lake Chapala is around 15 times larger than Laguna Catemaco.

The town of Catemaco is located on the northwestern shore of Laguna Catemaco. The town is famous for its sorcerers, or brujos.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Mexico pushes to raise regional content in electronics exports as US trade talks continue
World.content:
Mexico is working with the United States and Canada to develop a plan aimed at replacing manufacturing inputs from Asia and other parts of the world with regional content, a high-ranking Mexican official said Wednesday.

Speaking in Mexico City at the American Society of Mexico’s 5th Mexico–United States Binational Convention, Deputy Economy Minister for Foreign Trade Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez said that the goal is to increase regional value added in manufactured products, including electronic goods.

Mexico’s export revenue has increased significantly in 2026, in large part due to a sharp increase in the shipment to the United States of AI servers and other computer and electronic equipment. However, much of the content in such products is sourced from Asia, particularly Taiwan.

Gutiérrez said that Mexican value added in electronics sector exports to the United States is around 7% to 8% on average. That figure is well below the 44% of Mexican value added across all “Made in Mexico” exported products, per 2024 data.

According to a report by the news agency EFE, Gutiérrez said that the goal is to increase the Mexican — or at least regional — value added in electronic goods to “20, 30 or 40%, hand in hand with the United States and Canada.”

Gutiérrez said that Mexico, the United States and Canada are seeking to identify what additional inputs — for the electronics industry and other sectors — can viably be produced in North America.

“We’re working with the United States to develop a plan for a gradual transition,” he said.

According to EFE, Gutiérrez framed the initiative as part of Plan México, and said that the goal of reducing the reliance on imports from outside North America was being discussed in ongoing trade talks between Mexico and the United States.

Among the goals of Plan México, an ambitious economic development and industrial policy strategy unveiled by the federal government in early 2025, is to increase the use of domestically made content in products made by the Mexican automotive, aerospace, electronics, semiconductor, pharmaceuticals and chemicals industries.

As part of efforts to protect Mexican industry and ensure its ongoing viability, on Jan. 1 Mexico imposed new and higher tariffs on a wide range of goods from countries with which it doesn’t have free trade agreements. The tariffs apply to goods from China and Taiwan, among other countries, and have led to a reduction in imports across almost 1,500 product categories.

However, there are suspicions that some imports from Vietnam — which more than doubled in the first six months of 2026 — are in fact Chinese goods.

Gutiérrez: Fourth round of Mexico-US trade talks has been postponed

After the American Society of Mexico event on Wednesday, Gutiérrez told reporters that a fourth round of trade talks between Mexico and the United States won’t take place next week as planned. The talks could instead be held in October, he said.

Gutiérrez attributed the postponement to scheduling conflicts related to Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the United States and the upcoming G20 Summit, which will be held in Miami in December.

“We agreed with the United States that in the coming weeks we’ll announce when the fourth round [of talks] will be,” he said.

“… We’re working practically every day with the Office of the United States Trade Representative [and] with the Commerce Secretary [Howard Lutnick],” Gutiérrez added.

He said that Mexico is conducting the talks with the U.S. with a “cool head,” as advocated by President Claudia Sheinbaum.

“Our priority is ​reducing Section ​232 tariffs ⁠on steel, aluminum and automobiles,” Gutiérrez said.

The United States imposed duties on Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles last year. Nevertheless, a large majority of Mexico’s exports continue to enter the United States tariff-free under the USMCA free trade pact.

The ongoing trade-focused dialogue between Mexico and the United States is taking place after the Trump administration announced on July 1 that it had declined to renew the USMCA in its “current form.”

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said at the time that the United States would “continue to engage with Mexico and Canada to address the Agreement’s shortcomings and our trade deficits with these countries.”

Despite the U.S. government’s decision not to renew the USMCA for an additional 16 years, the trade pact remains in effect.

Reuters reported that the current Mexico-U.S. “negotiations are seeking an interim bilateral bargain ‌under ⁠which Mexico could win relief from some U.S. tariffs while addressing U.S. demands on areas including automotive content and Chinese investment.”

“… The negotiation agenda has expanded from 54 issues to nearly 90, which ⁠Gutiérrez ​described as the natural evolution ​of complex topics such as digital platform regulation,” the news agency reported.

With reports from EFE, Reuters and La Jornada

World.title: Mantiqueira Targets 6 Billion Brazilian Eggs a Year, Adds Paraná Capacity
World.content:
BRAZIL · AGRIBUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened On 24 September 2026 Mantiqueira gave new figures for its R$60 million (about US$11.6 million) Céu Azul project.

— The Paraná goal Capacity there rises from 1.8 million to 3.1 million hens, with about 120 small integrated farmers.

— The big plan About R$565 million (about US$109 million) nationwide to reach 6 billion eggs a year by 2028.

— Who owns it Meatpacker JBS holds 50% of the voting capital alongside the founding Pinto family.

— The catch The plan and its state amounts were public on 1–3 September; this week added job and flock figures.

— Jobs The Paraná project should create 80 jobs, and the Minas Gerais projects 330 by 2028.

Mantiqueira is spreading a nationwide expansion across five states, with new details this week for Paraná and Minas Gerais.

Eggs in a tray. Mantiqueira produces about 4 billion eggs a year in Brazil and aims for 6 billion by 2028. Photo: VIc Lic, CC BY 2.0, via Flickr.

Mantiqueira, South America’s largest egg producer, is putting R$60 million (about US$11.6 million) into western Paraná. The Céu Azul project, part of a nationwide expansion in Brazil, lifts capacity there by over 70%.

The flock at the site will grow from 1.8 million to 3.1 million hens.

New figures for the Paraná project came on 24 September. A day earlier, the company set out jobs and flock numbers for R$205 million (about US$39.6 million) of work in Minas Gerais.

What Mantiqueira Is Building in Paraná

In Céu Azul, the money pays for a modernised egg-grading area with new equipment and a larger network of integrated small farmers. The expansion adds capacity equal to 1.3 million hens.

About 120 integrated producers should benefit directly by the end of 2026, the company said. The project is expected to create 80 jobs, 50 of them direct.

Under the integration model, family farmers keep laying hens on their own properties, while the company runs the grading unit. About 90 farmers already take part in the region, Bem Paraná reported.

Mantiqueira also runs a unit in Francisco Beltrão, in south-western Paraná. The company says the Paraná work also advances higher-value categories and efficiency, two goals of the national plan.

The Nationwide Plan

Across Brazil, Mantiqueira plans to invest about R$565 million (about US$109 million) by 2028. It wants to raise annual output by 50%, from about 4 billion to 6 billion eggs.

The flock would grow by more than 7 million birds, from 17.9 million to 24.9 million, Diário do Comércio reported. The plan covers Minas Gerais, São Paulo, Paraná, Santa Catarina and Goiás.

It combines new farms, modernised sites and technology including automation, artificial intelligence and digital processes, Portal do Agronegócio reported.

Minas Gerais and São Paulo

In southern Minas Gerais, R$190 million (about US$36.7 million) will build a unit for 3 million hens. It is in São Sebastião do Rio Verde and is due in 2028, with about 120 direct and 100 indirect jobs.

The site will have 12 laying houses, six rearing houses and a sorting area, Diário do Comércio reported. With it, Mantiqueira will have eight units and support sites in the state.

Its existing Minas farms are in Itanhandu, Passa Quatro, Pouso Alto and Itamonte. It also processes liquid eggs in Uberlândia, runs logistics in Contagem and makes fertiliser in Campanha.

A further R$15 million (about US$2.9 million) expands the site in Pouso Alto by 700,000 birds, including quails, by June 2027.

In São Paulo, the company is enlarging its farm in Lorena, which it calls Latin America’s largest cage-free operation. The first stage lifts capacity to 1.5 million hens, and a second could reach 3 million by 2028.

Lorena has received four two-storey laying houses using German multilevel systems for cage-free hens. Its automated line can process up to 200,000 eggs an hour.

Lorena gets about R$200 million (about US$38.6 million), the largest single amount in the plan, Globo Rural reported. The 3-million-hen target there is for 2028, the company says.

Globo Rural reported R$50 million (about US$9.7 million) each for the Santa Catarina and Goiás units. The Santa Catarina money includes a new feed mill.

Who Is Behind Mantiqueira

Mantiqueira was founded in Minas Gerais by Leandro Pinto more than three decades ago. JBS, the meatpacker controlled by the Batista family, holds 50% of its voting capital.

The company operates 18 units in six Brazilian states and five in the United States. Its US arm, Mantiqueira USA, completed the purchase of Arizona’s Hickman’s Egg Ranch in November 2025.

The group aims to rank among the world’s four largest egg producers. By July it had about 6 million birds in the United States, a hard-currency market, O Diário do Paraná reported.

Pinto said the company is being built “for the long term”. He wants more scale, more higher-value products and greater efficiency, and a place among the sector’s largest companies worldwide.

The new cycle combines animal-welfare practices with productive efficiency, he said, so the company can keep growing steadily in the coming years.

Why It Matters

Speciality eggs, such as cage-free and organic, made up 32% of Mantiqueira’s Brazilian sales by July, up from 2% five years earlier.

For JBS, which entered the egg sector through its Mantiqueira stake in 2025, the plan grows a business it co-controls. In Paraná, about 120 small integrated farmers will host part of the new capacity, the company said.

Its brands include Happy Eggs for cage-free eggs, Fazenda da Toca for organic eggs and N.OVO protein drinks made from egg white. It also makes an organic fertiliser, Solobom.

The company exports to South America, Asia, Africa, the Middle East and South Korea, according to its own profile.

What Comes Next

The Paraná integration expansion is due by the end of 2026, and the Pouso Alto work by June 2027. The new Minas Gerais unit and the second Lorena stage run to 2028.

Watch for progress at São Sebastião do Rio Verde, the only brand-new unit in the plan.

The other growth front is the United States. There, Hickman’s lost about 95% of its flock to avian flu in 2025 and has been rebuilding since.

Sources: Bem Paraná, the Céu Azul investment, 24 September 2026; O Tempo, the nationwide plan, 23 September 2026; Diário do Comércio, Minas Gerais projects, 23 September 2026; Globo Rural, JBS stake and state amounts, 1 September 2026; Portal do Agronegócio, technology in the plan, 8 September 2026; JBS press release, the national plan, 3 September 2026; O Diário do Paraná, speciality eggs share, 15 July 2026. Exchange rate: Brazilian central bank PTAX rate of 24 September 2026, R$5.18 per US dollar.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is Mantiqueira investing in Paraná?

About R$60 million (about US$11.6 million) in Céu Azul, western Paraná. Capacity there will rise from 1.8 million to 3.1 million hens.

What is Mantiqueira’s national investment plan?

About R$565 million (about US$109 million) by 2028 across five states. The goal is to lift annual output from about 4 billion to 6 billion eggs.

Who owns Mantiqueira?

It was founded by Leandro Pinto, and JBS holds 50% of the voting capital. The group also operates five units in the United States.

How many jobs will the projects create?

The Paraná project should create 80 jobs, 50 of them direct. The Minas Gerais projects are expected to add 150 direct and 180 indirect jobs by 2028.

World.title: Cuba Tourism Falls 64.4% as August Brings Only 30,490 Visitors
World.content:
CUBA · TOURISM

Key Facts — What happened Cuba received 450,353 international visitors from January to August 2026, 64.4% fewer than a year earlier.

— August Only 30,490 visitors arrived, against about 136,000 in August 2025; only June was weaker this year.

— Biggest loss Arrivals from Canada, Cuba’s top market, fell 75.6% to 128,400.

— The hotels Seven foreign hotel groups managing 46% of rooms have left, the government acknowledged in July.

— The catch Power is failing too: the grid went down nationwide on 18 September, at least the seventh time this year.

— Havana’s answer New rules admit private travel agencies and let foreign firms operate directly in Cuban tourism.

New official figures show Cuba tourism shrinking further in August, as flights, hotels and electricity all fail at once.

Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana in a file photo from busier years; CiberCuba reported the square almost empty this week. Photo: Maxence, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Cuba tourism fell even further in August, according to official figures released on Thursday 24 September. The island received 450,353 international visitors from January to August 2026, 64.4% fewer than in the same months of 2025.

August alone brought just 30,490 visitors, the National Office of Statistics and Information (ONEI) said. Only June, with 28,100, was weaker.

The Cuba Tourism Numbers

The eight-month total is only 35.6% of last year’s level, or 813,979 fewer visitors, ONEI data show. In August 2025, about 136,000 visitors had arrived.

Counting all travellers, a broader ONEI category, arrivals reached 888,756, down 50.5%. The Rio Times reported the January–July figure of 419,863 earlier this month.

At that point the decline stood at 62.8%, and August pushed it to 64.4%. Month by month, arrivals have held between 28,100 and 35,561 since March, with July and August each about 77% below 2025.

The contrast with the boom years is stark. Cuba received about 4.7 million visitors in 2018 and 4.3 million in 2019, after the US–Cuba thaw.

Where the Visitors Went Missing

Canada, Cuba’s main market, sent 128,400 visitors, down 75.6%. That is 397,839 fewer Canadians than in the first eight months of 2025.

The Cuban community abroad supplied 103,481 visitors, down 35.6% from 160,751. Arrivals from the United States halved to 41,971.

Russia fell 73.3% to 21,563. Mexico sent 22,246 and Argentina 15,144, both down by more than 40%.

European markets shrank too. Spain fell 68.3% to 10,447 and Italy 61.2% to 8,669.

ONEI itself singled out Canada, Russia, the Cuban community abroad and the United States as the largest declines. Together those four markets account for more than 556,000 of the missing visitors.

Why Cuba Tourism Keeps Falling

According to the Spanish news agency EFE, US pressure since January paralysed flights and secondary sanctions drove out the main hotel groups. Tourism is one of Cuba’s three biggest sources of hard currency.

A shortage of jet fuel led Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Sunwing to suspend service, CiberCuba reported. Canada, the United States, Britain, Argentina and Ireland have issued travel advisories.

Air Transat has not flown passengers to Cuba since February, and no direct Canada–Cuba flights remain, The Rio Times reported this month.

In July the government acknowledged that seven international hotel groups had left under US pressure. They managed 46% of the country’s more than 80,000 rooms, including Spain’s Meliá, Iberostar and Barceló.

Canada’s Blue Diamond, Indonesia’s Archipelago International and Turkey’s ATG also left. CiberCuba puts the share of hotels closed at 73%, with occupancy around 21.5%.

CiberCuba links the hotel exits to US sanctions on GAESA, the military-run conglomerate that controls much of the hotel sector.

A Grid That Keeps Failing

On 18 September the national grid failed again, leaving millions without power. It was at least the seventh nationwide blackout this year: DW counted seven, CiberCuba at least eight.

“A total disconnection of the electrical system has occurred,” the Energy Ministry posted on X. At one point only 5% of Havana had electricity.

Blackouts of more than 30 hours have become common in Havana, and some provinces have gone past 60 hours. Cuba’s power plants depend on imported fuel, which US restrictions imposed in January have made scarce.

Havana blames US sanctions for the shortages. Washington says the outages reflect the failures of Cuba’s state-run economic model.

An independent study released last week estimated that 66% of Cubans now live in poverty, up from 45% in mid-2025, DW reported.

What Havana Is Doing

In June the government approved a package of 176 economic reforms, including new business models for private firms in tourism, EFE reported. These cover hotel management, car rental and passenger transport.

Private operators can also work as tour agents and guides. The government plans a 1% levy on these businesses to promote the sector’s sustainability and image.

Rules published in the official gazette on 3 September admitted private travel agencies and let foreign firms operate directly in the market. None of them handed management of state-owned hotels to private operators, The Rio Times found.

Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez said on 7 September that there were no negotiations with Washington at present.

Why It Matters If You Plan to Travel to Cuba

If you are thinking of a trip, check flights first. Direct links from Canada, once the backbone of Cuban tourism, have disappeared for now.

Confirm that your hotel is open and ask how it copes with power cuts. With most hotels closed, bookings made through third parties may not reflect the current situation.

Expect long power cuts that affect water, cooking gas, phones and transport, as well as hotels. Read your government’s travel advice before booking; Canada and Britain advise against non-essential travel.

For investors in the region, the figures show how fast a tourism economy can unravel. Flights, fuel and foreign hotel partners have all fallen away together.

What Comes Next

ONEI will publish September arrivals next month. Watch for any return of Canadian winter flights and for the first private agencies and foreign operators under the new rules.

Sources: EFE via ABC Color, ONEI figures for January–August, 24 September 2026; CiberCuba, market breakdown and hotels, 24 September 2026; Infobae, monthly arrivals and hotel exits, 24 September 2026; DW, nationwide blackout, 19 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many tourists visited Cuba in 2026?

Cuba received 450,353 international visitors from January to August 2026, according to ONEI. That is 64.4% fewer than in the same period of 2025.

Why has Cuba tourism fallen so far?

US pressure since January has disrupted flights and fuel, and sanctions drove out major hotel groups. Repeated nationwide blackouts have also hurt the tourist experience.

Are Canadian airlines still flying to Cuba?

No. Air Canada, WestJet, Air Transat and Sunwing have suspended Cuba service because of the jet-fuel shortage. Check with your airline for any change before booking.

Is it safe to travel to Cuba now?

Several governments have issued travel advisories, and Canada and Britain advise against non-essential travel. Long blackouts affect water, transport and communications, so plan carefully.

World.title: Essequibo: Guyana Urges Venezuela at 81st UN Assembly to Heed Coming ICJ Ruling
World.content:
GUYANA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela at the UN on Thursday 24 September 2026 to abide by the coming ICJ ruling.

— Venezuela’s line A day earlier, acting President Delcy Rodríguez asked Guyana to return to negotiations under the 1966 Geneva Agreement.

— The case Guyana wants the court to confirm the 1899 award that fixed the border; hearings ended in May 2026.

— The catch No judgment date has been set, and Venezuela still rejects the court’s jurisdiction.

— What is at stake Essequibo covers more than two-thirds of Guyana, and Venezuela’s sea claim reaches into the Stabroek oil block.

— What comes next Guyana expects a ruling between November 2026 and January 2027; the sea border needs separate talks.

On the UN stage, Guyana and Venezuela restated opposite paths for Essequibo while the world court prepares its judgment.

The ruined gateway of Kyk-Over-Al, a Dutch colonial fort on an island near the Essequibo River, in the region Venezuela claims. Photo: Dan Lundberg, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Guyana has used the UN General Assembly to press Venezuela over Essequibo, a vast region Caracas has long claimed. President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela on Thursday 24 September to abide by the International Court of Justice’s coming ruling.

“We urge Venezuela to abide by the forthcoming ruling in accordance with their obligation under the UN Charter, as Guyana will do,” Ali said in New York.

What Ali Said About Essequibo

Ali said Guyana went to the court only after decades of trying to settle the dispute bilaterally. That included a mixed commission and the good offices of the UN secretary-general.

He called the 1899 Arbitral Award “the full, perfect, and final settlement” of the border. Guyana had “endured long and repeated provocations and aggression”, he added.

It was his first address to the Assembly since the court finished hearing the case in May 2026. He said both countries had taken part in those hearings.

“We look forward to a new era of neighbourly relations,” he said. He tied that hope to the development of both countries and the stability and prosperity of the region.

Ali said Guyana has “always advanced the peaceful settlement” of the border controversy. It took part in the case in full respect for international law, he added, and encouraged Venezuela to do the same.

Venezuela’s Answer, a Day Earlier

Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, spoke from the same podium on Wednesday 23 September. She reaffirmed what she called Venezuela’s historic rights over Guyana-Essequibo.

“Here, I appeal to the Cooperative Republic of Guyana to resolve the issue and to return to negotiations,” she said. In Venezuela’s view, that is what the Geneva Agreement requires.

Agreements reached bilaterally last longer and work better than those imposed by outside bodies, she argued. She wore a brooch showing a map of Venezuela that included Essequibo.

Rodríguez took over after US forces removed Nicolás Maduro on 3 January 2026. She was previously responsible for Venezuela’s case at the court, AFP noted.

She said Venezuela wants to rebuild ties with its South American neighbours and the United States. Those ties must rest on respect and equality, she added.

She did not criticise the United States or ExxonMobil, Demerara Waves noted. Instead she thanked President Donald Trump and his government for their readiness to resume diplomatic relations and cooperation.

She called a recent US–Venezuela agreement “one of the most all-encompassing and significant ever signed”. It will help ensure the hemisphere’s energy balance, she said.

Where the ICJ Case Stands

The border dates from the colonial era. An arbitration tribunal in Paris fixed it in 1899.

The Geneva Agreement was signed in February 1966 by the United Kingdom, Venezuela and British Guiana, three months before Guyana’s independence.

Venezuela says the 1899 award is null and void. In its view the Geneva Agreement requires a practical settlement negotiated with Guyana.

Guyana filed the case in 2018 after the UN secretary-general referred the dispute to the court under the Geneva Agreement. It asks the judges to confirm that the 1899 award and its boundary are valid and binding.

The court ruled in 2020 that it had jurisdiction and rejected a further Venezuelan objection in 2023. It has also twice granted Guyana’s requests for provisional measures.

The latest, in 2025, ordered Venezuela not to hold, or prepare to hold, elections in the disputed territory.

Venezuela boycotted the court’s 2018–2020 jurisdiction phase but has taken part since then, while still rejecting the court’s authority.

No judgment date has been announced, and the court gives two weeks’ notice. Guyana’s government has estimated a ruling between November 2026 and January 2027.

Why Essequibo Matters

Guyana is a small English-speaking country just east of Venezuela. Essequibo makes up more than two-thirds of its territory of about 83,000 square miles.

Oil was discovered offshore in 2015. Venezuela’s maritime claim reaches into ExxonMobil’s Stabroek Block, Guyana’s main oil area.

That is why the dispute weighs on investors as well as diplomats.

The land boundary is what the court will rule on. The maritime boundary would need separate talks, because Venezuela has not signed the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The United States has said it is willing to help settle that maritime line after the ruling, Demerara Waves reported. ExxonMobil hopes to resume exploration in parts of the Stabroek Block nearer Venezuela afterwards.

Maduro’s repeated calls to annex the territory once raised fears of armed conflict. Ali and Maduro met in Argyle, St Vincent, in December 2023 and pledged not to threaten or use force.

Why It Matters If You Invest in Guyana

For oil companies, contractors and investors, a clear ruling could reduce a major political risk over Guyana’s offshore boom. That depends on Caracas accepting it, and the ruling would not settle the sea border.

Guyana is also a founding member of Trump’s Shield of the Americas, a US-led security coalition against drug cartels. Venezuela, under Rodríguez, is rebuilding relations with the US at the same time.

What Comes Next

The next milestone is the court’s announcement of a date to deliver its judgment. Both governments have now set out their positions before the full UN membership.

Watch too for any US move on the maritime boundary. Another question is how Rodríguez’s government would respond to an adverse ruling.

Sources: Department of Public Information, Guyana, Ali at the UN, 24 September 2026; Demerara Waves, Rodríguez at the UN, 23 September 2026; Department of Public Information, Guyana, on the judgment timeline, 5 June 2026; International Court of Justice, Guyana v. Venezuela case page; AFP via RTL Today, Guyana urges Venezuela, 24 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Essequibo dispute?

Venezuela claims the Essequibo region, which makes up more than two-thirds of Guyana. Guyana says the 1899 Arbitral Award settled the border for good and has asked the ICJ to confirm it.

What did Guyana say at the UN?

President Irfaan Ali urged Venezuela to abide by the ICJ’s forthcoming ruling, as Guyana will do. He said Guyana went to court only after decades of failed bilateral efforts.

When will the ICJ rule on Essequibo?

The court finished hearings in May 2026 but has not set a date. Guyana’s government has estimated November 2026 to January 2027.

What does Venezuela want?

Venezuela wants direct negotiations under the 1966 Geneva Agreement and rejects the court’s jurisdiction. It has nevertheless taken part in the proceedings since the jurisdiction phase.

World.title: Mexico South Korea Summit Ends With 17 Agreements but No Tariff Deal
World.content:
MEXICO · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts — What happened Claudia Sheinbaum and Lee Jae-myung signed 17 cooperation documents in Mexico City on Thursday 24 September 2026.

— The roadmap They adopted a Mexico–Korea Action Plan for 2026–2030 covering trade, AI, aerospace, defence and culture.

— The money The two export-import banks agreed to set up a credit line of up to US$100 million for companies.

— The catch Mexico’s tariffs of up to 50% on Korean cars stay, and any trade deal waits for the USMCA review.

— Investment treaty Lee said seven years of talks to revise the investment-protection treaty have been concluded.

— The numbers Bilateral trade reached US$27 billion in 2025, Sheinbaum said; Mexico’s foreign ministry has cited US$29.7 billion.

A Mexico South Korea summit, the first Korean state visit in 16 years, produced 17 accords but no tariff change.

Palacio Nacional on Mexico City’s Zócalo, seat of the presidency, where Sheinbaum received Lee for the first Korean state visit in 16 years. Photo: Daniel Case, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
