The Mexico South Korea summit ended with many agreements but left Mexico’s tariffs on Korean goods unchanged. Presidents Claudia Sheinbaum and Lee Jae-myung met at Palacio Nacional on Thursday 24 September.

Sheinbaum said their meeting lasted more than three hours. The Korean side timed the formal talks at 119 minutes, before a business meeting.

It was the first state visit by a South Korean president to Mexico in 16 years. The two countries mark 64 years of diplomatic relations this year.

Lee noted that Korea was celebrating Chuseok, its harvest festival and most important holiday, as the plan was adopted. He called it the start of a new stage in bilateral cooperation.

What Mexico and South Korea Signed

The two governments signed 17 cooperation documents, most of them memorandums of understanding, and adopted a Mexico–Korea Action Plan for 2026–2030. Sheinbaum called the plan the roadmap for the next four years.

They cover economic, financial and development cooperation, academic mobility, culture, tourism, science and technology, Sheinbaum said. Intellectual property, agriculture and security are also included.

Korean outlets listed a defence memorandum, an aerospace agreement and a declaration on artificial intelligence. There is also customs cooperation, including information on illicit goods, and electronic certificates for livestock imports.

The two sides also agreed to open a dialogue channel between ministries on crude oil and key resources, Korean media reported.

Money, Investment and Defence

Lee said the countries had concluded seven years of negotiations to revise their investment-protection treaty. The text still has to be signed and ratified.

The two export-import banks agreed to set up an on-lending credit line of up to US$100 million. It would help Mexican firms buy Korean goods and services and support Korean firms in Mexico.

On defence, Lee said the two would explore how Korea could help modernise Mexico’s armed forces through training, education and research. He wants Korean defence technology to lead to local production in Mexico.

He also asked for Sheinbaum’s support so both countries can enter third markets together. A Korea–Mexico Space Day in November will look for concrete aerospace projects.

The Tariff Question

Since 1 January 2026, Mexico has charged up to 50% on cars from countries without a trade deal with it. South Korea is one of them, along with China and India.

The decree, published on 29 December 2025, raised duties on 1,463 tariff lines. Its stated aim is to replace imports with Mexican production.

Lee raised Korean companies’ problems one by one, including tariff burdens and slow exemption and refund procedures, a presidential official told reporters.

Mexico did not accept everything but said it would look into some issues, the Asia Business Daily reported. Officials on both sides will continue the talks.

Seoul prefers a free-trade agreement, but Mexico is not ready during its USMCA review, the official said. Rules of origin are a key issue there, and the two agreed to explore a deal afterwards.

Until then, they will run a separate channel for trade, investment and industrial cooperation.

Why the Mexico South Korea Deal Matters for Business

Korea is one of Mexico’s five biggest trading partners, and Mexico is Korea’s top partner in Latin America, Sheinbaum said. She put bilateral trade at US$27 billion in 2025.

She put Korean investment since 2006 at more than US$11.5 billion, through more than 2,000 companies. Lee has cited a different figure, about US$13.3 billion from some 500 firms.

Sheinbaum also highlighted electric mobility, AI, digital technology, science and higher education as areas with great potential.

Sheinbaum wants Mexican small and medium-sized firms to join the supply chains of Korean companies in Mexico under her Plan México. Kia builds cars in Nuevo León, and Samsung and LG run plants in Querétaro, Tijuana and Reynosa.

Nine Korean business leaders joined a business meeting at the palace. They included SK Group chairman Choi Tae-won and LG Group chairman Koo Kwang-mo.

Before the summit, Lee told El Universal that Mexico is “a key strategic platform” for Korean firms. He named semiconductors, aerospace and electric vehicles as promising sectors.

Kia started building its EV3 electric model at Pesquería on 4 August 2026, the first EV3 line outside South Korea. The company plans to spend US$649 million at the plant between 2026 and 2028.

K-Pop Diplomacy

Sheinbaum spoke of the possibility of a K-pop culture centre in Mexico and a Mexican culture institute in Korea. She added that BTS is expected back in Mexico in 2027.

A working group will look at co-producing cultural content and training talent, Lee said. The K-pop group Stray Kids was due to play in Mexico on Friday.

Sheinbaum said young Mexicans’ enthusiasm for K-pop and Korean food shows the two peoples growing closer.

What Comes Next

Working-level officials will keep talking about Korean companies’ tariff complaints. The revised investment treaty still has to be signed and approved, including by South Korea’s National Assembly.

Looking further ahead, Korea chairs the G20 and Mexico hosts APEC in 2028, Sheinbaum noted.

Sources: EFE via Infobae, 17 agreements and the 2030 roadmap, 24 September 2026; El Universal, Sheinbaum and Lee statements, 24 September 2026; Quadratín, Sheinbaum on trade and investment, 24 September 2026; The Asia Business Daily, tariff issues raised at the summit, 25 September 2026; Seoul Economic Daily, the 17 agreements, 25 September 2026; El Universal, Lee interview, 23 September 2026; The Korea Times, joint action plan, 24 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mexico and South Korea sign?

They signed 17 cooperation documents, mostly memorandums of understanding, and adopted a 2026–2030 action plan. These cover trade, finance, AI, aerospace, defence, agriculture, security, education and culture.

Did Mexico lift its tariffs on Korean cars?

No. Lee raised the tariffs and customs delays, and Mexico said it would look into some issues, but no change has been announced.

Is there a Mexico–South Korea free-trade agreement?

No. Seoul wants one, and both sides agreed to explore it after Mexico’s USMCA review with the United States and Canada.

How big is trade between the two countries?

Bilateral trade reached US$27 billion in 2025, Sheinbaum said. Korea is among Mexico’s five largest trading partners.

World.title: Marcona Port: Peru Unblocks US$404.8 Million Chinese-Run Terminal
World.content:
PERU · INFRASTRUCTURE

Key Facts — What happened ProInversión and Shougang Hierro Perú signed a land agreement on Thursday 24 September 2026.

— What it unblocks A US$404.8 million port concession won by China’s Jinzhao group, suspended since 16 April.

— The deal Shougang will not exercise mining rights inside the port area, and the land stays with the transport ministry.

— Timing Construction should start in 2027, with the first stage taking about two years, the minister said.

— The catch Sources differ on the first stage’s cost, from US$127 million to more than US$271 million.

— Why it matters The terminal would mainly ship iron and copper concentrates from Jinzhao’s Pampa de Pongo project.

A land deal with Shougang frees the site for a new Marcona port on Peru’s southern coast, five months after it stalled.

Fishing boats in the harbour of San Juan de Marcona on Ica’s desert coast, where the new multipurpose terminal is planned. Photo: Marek Grzywa, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Peru has cleared the main obstacle to a new Marcona port on its southern coast. A land deal signed on Thursday 24 September clears the way for a US$404.8 million terminal run by China’s Jinzhao to resume.

The deal was struck between ProInversión, Peru’s investment promotion agency, and Shougang Hierro Perú. The Chinese-owned iron miner held mining rights over part of the site.

Shougang has mined iron at Marcona since 1992, when it bought the state company Hierro Perú. It ships its ore through its own port at San Nicolás.

Why the Marcona Port Was Stuck

The concession contract with San Juan Port S.A., part of the Jinzhao group, was signed on 31 March. It was suspended on 16 April because the project area could not be handed over.

Part of that land lay inside Shougang’s mining concessions. Under the new agreement, Shougang commits “expressly and bindingly” not to exercise or assert those rights within the port area.

The transport ministry, known as MTC, keeps title to the land. The deal allows the suspension to be lifted, the site to be delivered and engineering work to begin.

The standoff was physical as well as legal. During the handover on 16 April, Shougang staff blocked access to the site, the business weekly SEMANAeconómica reported.

ProInversión and the MTC argued the land had belonged to the state since 1948, before the Marcona mining concessions. Shougang said its surface rights from those concessions overlapped the port area.

A longer delay could have triggered a clause allowing the contract to be terminated, SEMANAeconómica warned in July. ProInversión called that risk low at the time.

What Will Be Built

The concession runs for 30 years. It covers the design, financing, construction, operation, maintenance and eventual transfer of a multipurpose terminal.

The full project includes two docks, three berths and equipment for bulk, general and container cargo, EFE reported. The first stage covers a pier with two berths, an access bridge, storage and loading systems, according to Gestión.

Estimates for that first stage differ. Gestión put it at more than US$271 million.

Reuters quoted Transport Minister José Tangherlini as saying US$200 million, while Canal N quoted him citing US$127 million.

Construction should begin next year and take roughly two years for the first stage, Tangherlini said. The terminal is expected to become Peru’s third-largest port, Reuters reported.

Jinzhao has already filed a third technical report with Senace, the environmental certification agency, Gestión reported in May. It proposes design changes worth about US$6 million.

These include two conveyor belts able to move 3,050 tonnes an hour.

The Mining Connection

The port will mainly ship iron and copper concentrates from the planned Pampa de Pongo mine, Gestión reported. It will also handle general cargo, containers and supplies for mining projects.

Pampa de Pongo is Jinzhao’s iron project in southern Peru, with a planned investment of US$1.781 billion. The port is part of the company’s wider plan for the area.

Reuters said Jinzhao would be the second Chinese company to build and run a port in Peru, after Cosco Shipping Ports. Cosco has operated the Chancay megaport north of Lima since late 2024.

Shougang’s San Nicolás dock is a private terminal for its own ore rather than a public port concession.

What Officials Said

Luis Del Carpio heads ProInversión. He said the deal “opens the way” for the investment to become “infrastructure, jobs and new opportunities for families in the south”.

Tangherlini said the terminal will serve 29 provinces and 280 districts in Ica, Ayacucho, Arequipa, Apurímac and Cusco. It will offer a new logistics option for the south’s productive activities and mining projects, he added.

The project also includes a social fund equal to 3% of gross revenue. It will pay for social activities in Marcona district and Nazca province, EFE reported.

The Doubts

Not everyone is convinced. When the contract was signed, La República questioned how much the port would do for the region beyond mineral exports.

The government has promised 1,500 direct and indirect jobs in the first five years. ProInversión estimates the 3% fund will raise more than 290 million soles (about US$85 million) over 25 years.

The newspaper said such funds often lack clear guarantees on how the money is spent. It also noted that the contract was ProInversión’s first as the granting authority, a new role for the agency.

Why It Matters If You Invest in Peru

For investors, the deal clears the way to unfreeze a concession that had been stuck for five months. It also deepens China’s role in Peru’s port network, after Chancay.

For southern regions such as Apurímac and Cusco, the terminal promises a new route to the sea for mineral and other cargo. Peru is one of the world’s biggest copper producers, Reuters noted.

The ministry calls the project a matter of public necessity and utility.

What Comes Next

Watch for the formal lifting of the contract suspension and the handover of the site to San Juan Port. Engineering studies and permits come next, with construction targeted for 2027.

Sources: Gestión, MTC on the Marcona port, 24 September 2026; EFE via Infobae, Shougang agreement, 24 September 2026; SEMANAeconómica, the land dispute behind the suspension, 19 July 2026; Canal N, Tangherlini on the first-stage investment, 24 September 2026; Gestión, Jinzhao design changes, 14 May 2026; La República, doubts over the port’s impact, 3 April 2026; Reuters via La Nación, Jinzhao construction timeline, 24 September 2026. Exchange rate: mid-market rate of 25 September 2026 (open.er-api.com), 3.40 soles per US dollar.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Marcona port project?

It is a new multipurpose terminal at San Juan de Marcona in Ica, southern Peru, with estimated investment of US$404.8 million. San Juan Port S.A., part of China’s Jinzhao group, holds a 30-year concession.

Why was the Marcona port suspended?

The concession, signed on 31 March 2026, was suspended on 16 April because the land could not be delivered. Part of it lay inside Shougang Hierro Perú’s mining concessions.

When will construction start?

Transport Minister José Tangherlini said construction should begin in 2027. The first stage should take about two years.

What will the port ship?

Mainly iron and copper concentrates from the Pampa de Pongo mine. It will also handle general cargo, containers and mining supplies.

World.title: World Bank Ecuador Program: Up to US$800 Million for Local Infrastructure
World.content:
ECUADOR · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened On 24 September 2026 the World Bank approved a ten-year Ecuador program worth up to US$800 million.

— Who runs it Ecuador’s state development bank, BDE, will lend the money to municipalities, provinces and public utilities.

— First phase Only this US$200 million World Bank loan is committed now, plus US$50 million from Spain’s AECID.

— What it funds Energy, transport, urban development, disaster risk management and affordable housing.

— The catch Loan terms, a disbursement timetable and specific projects have not been published yet.

— The goal More than three million beneficiaries and up to US$750 million in private capital over the decade.

A new World Bank Ecuador program will channel up to US$800 million to local governments over the next decade.

The municipal building in Cuenca, Ecuador’s third-largest city. Municipalities borrow from the state development bank BDE, which will run the new World Bank program. Photo: Micah & Erin, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

The World Bank Ecuador program approved on Thursday 24 September sets an envelope of up to US$800 million for local infrastructure. It starts with a US$200 million loan, and the money will flow over ten years to municipalities, provinces and public companies.

Ecuador’s state development bank, Banco de Desarrollo del Ecuador (BDE), will run it in three phases. Ecuador uses the US dollar, so the figures need no conversion.

What the World Bank Ecuador Program Pays For

The first phase includes US$200 million in World Bank financing, a quarter of the total envelope. Spain’s development agency, AECID, adds US$50 million in parallel co-financing.

That phase covers energy, transport and sustainable mobility, urban development, disaster risk management and affordable housing. It also pays for project preparation and training at BDE and in local governments.

Over the full decade, more than three million people are expected to benefit through better connectivity, energy access, urban infrastructure and housing. The program also aims to mobilise up to US$750 million in private capital.

The World Bank calls the structure a Multiphase Programmatic Approach. Later phases are prepared as separate operations, so the US$800 million is an overall envelope rather than a single payment.

The model is meant for long programs that build in stages, with each phase drawing on what the previous one achieved.

Who Can Borrow

BDE lends to Ecuador’s local governments, known by the Spanish acronym GAD, and to public companies. It will use the new funds for such loans, El Comercio reported.

El Comercio said the money will support urban works, roads and climate mitigation in towns across the country. Disbursement will be gradual over the decade.

Local projects will still need to be prepared and approved one by one. World Bank documents cite weak project preparation and target help at municipalities with low technical capacity.

Private developers in an affordable-housing pilot are also eligible, according to the World Bank’s project record.

What the Officials Said

“This financing represents a historic milestone for Banco de Desarrollo del Ecuador,” said its general manager, Carlos Rivera. It will help municipalities and provinces improve essential services and resilience to climate change, he said.

It will also speed up BDE’s transformation into a modern development bank able to tap new funding sources, Rivera added.

Ariel Yépez is the World Bank’s division director for Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Venezuela. He said the aim is to close infrastructure gaps, create jobs and promote sustainable growth at the local level.

The Fiscal Backdrop

The loan arrives as Quito spends more on local governments. Capital transfers to municipalities, provinces and parish boards rose to US$2.559 billion in January–August, up from US$2.008 billion a year earlier.

Total state spending grew 10% to US$18.848 billion in that period, the Fiscal Policy Observatory calculated. Revenue grew faster, by 17.7%, and the deficit fell to US$1.003 billion from US$1.974 billion.

Interest on public debt reached US$3.256 billion through August, US$432 million more than a year earlier. Spending under the annual public investment plan rose to US$626 million from US$396 million.

This month the Central Bank raised its 2026 growth forecast to 2.7% from 2.5%. It warned that a moderate El Niño could cut 2027 growth by 0.5 percentage points, and a strong one by 1.4 points.

Why It Matters If You Live or Invest in Ecuador

For residents, the program targets services people use every day: power, transport, housing and protection against natural disasters. The energy focus matters after the long power cuts of 2024, when drought drained hydroelectric reservoirs.

Power is again a concern. On 22 September the environment and energy ministry told 185 big industrial users to cut grid use one day a week.

Firms can cut load, run their own generators or shift production, and the ministry says households are not affected. The aim is to save water at the Mazar reservoir.

Mazar is the main reservoir of the Paute Integral complex, which has 1,757 MW of capacity. On 23 September it stood 22.2 metres above its critical operating level of 2,115 metres, Teleamazonas reported.

It has lost about ten metres since 1 September. September inflows averaged 55.2 cubic metres per second, against a historical average of about 75.

In October 2024, with Mazar at about 2,112 metres, scheduled power cuts rose from four to ten hours a day. By late that month they reached 14 hours.

Environment and Energy Minister Juan Carlos Blum wants Mazar to last until the December rains.

For investors, the US$750 million private-capital target points to co-financing and public–private deals at the local level. How that capital will be raised has not been published.

Foreign investment reached one of its highest levels in ten years in the first half, President Daniel Noboa said on 18 September. He expects more in oil and mining, and said firms are also interested in food, logistics, ports and power.

What Comes Next

BDE now has to turn the first US$200 million into loans for specific projects. Loan terms such as interest rate and maturity have not been made public.

Watch for the first municipal and provincial projects to be named. Also watch for detail on how the private-capital target will be met, and for the start of the second phase.

Sources: World Bank press release, 24 September 2026; El Comercio, municipalities and provinces, 24 September 2026; Primicias, the World Bank financing, 24 September 2026; Expreso, public spending January–August 2026, 7 September 2026; Expreso, the 2024 power cuts, 10 September 2026; Teleamazonas, Mazar reservoir level, 23 September 2026; El Comercio, 185 firms to cut grid use, 22 September 2026; teleSUR, the industrial power order and Mazar target, September 2026; Xinhua via The Peninsula, Noboa on investment and Central Bank forecast, 19 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the World Bank Ecuador program?

It is worth up to US$800 million over ten years, in three phases. Only the first phase is committed so far: US$200 million from the World Bank plus US$50 million from Spain’s AECID.

Who receives the money?

Banco de Desarrollo del Ecuador will lend it to municipalities, provincial governments and public service companies. It will fund projects in energy, transport, urban development, disaster risk management and housing.

Why are the figures only in US dollars?

Ecuador has used the US dollar as its official currency since 2000. Local amounts and the loan are therefore in the same currency.

When will projects start?

The World Bank has not announced when the first loans will reach projects. BDE will channel the first-phase funds into loans for eligible local projects.

World.title: Costa Rica Foreign Minister Fired After 139 Days Over Missed Trump Meeting
World.content:
COSTA RICA · POLITICS

Key Facts — What happened President Laura Fernández dismissed Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar on Thursday 24 September 2026.

— The reason The presidency says he attended a 22 September Shield of the Americas session with Trump without telling her.

— Her charge The presidency called it “negligence” that caused “great strategic damage” by keeping her out.

— The catch The meeting was public for days, and Fernández had said since July she would skip UN week.

— Who replaces him Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos becomes acting foreign minister once she is back from New York.

— A record At 139 days, Tovar is the shortest-serving foreign minister since 1948, La Nación calculated.

The Costa Rica foreign minister was fired while at the UN, blamed by the president for her absence from a Trump summit.

The Casa Amarilla in San José, home of Costa Rica’s foreign ministry. In his farewell, Tovar thanked Fernández for the chance to serve “from the trench of the Casa Amarilla”. Photo: Rodtico21, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Costa Rica foreign minister Manuel Tovar is out after only 139 days. President Laura Fernández fired him on Thursday 24 September while he was leading the country’s delegation at the UN General Assembly.

The presidency says Tovar went to a Shield of the Americas meeting with Donald Trump on 22 September without telling her. That, it says, kept Fernández from attending herself.

What the Costa Rica Foreign Minister Is Accused Of

“Tovar attended the session without giving prior notice or informing the President of the Republic of his participation,” the presidency said. It called this “negligence” that caused “great strategic damage”.

The statement said Tovar managed Costa Rica’s participation inadequately. Fernández considers the US-led coalition fundamental to the fight against drug trafficking and organised crime.

Later on Thursday, Fernández apologised in public to US Ambassador Melinda Hildebrand. The occasion was a US donation of security equipment in the south of the country.

“I regret my absence from the meeting called by the United States government,” she said. The error in passing on the invitation “was not overlooked”, she added.

“There are difficult decisions one must take as president, but there are mistakes that cannot be overlooked,” she said. She also restated her “firm commitment” to the Shield of the Americas.

What the Public Record Shows

The meeting was hardly a secret. On 17 September, Tovar told the Miami Herald that a high-level session was planned for the following week in New York.

Paraguay and the Dominican Republic announced their leaders’ attendance, the news site Delfino reported. The US State Department published its agenda, naming Secretary of State Marco Rubio as host, the night before.

Delfino found no public record showing when Trump’s own attendance was confirmed. When the session began, Rubio told the room that the president would join them soon.

Fernández had also said since July that she would skip the UN week to focus on security and investment at home. On 22 September she was in Barranquilla, Colombia, meeting President Abelardo de la Espriella.

It was her first official trip abroad. The two leaders agreed to share more intelligence, cooperate on air and maritime security and go after criminal finances.

Costa Rica has now gone five years without its president at the UN summit, La Nación noted. Fernández followed the example of her predecessor, Rodrigo Chaves.

How Tovar Responded

Tovar avoided a public fight and did not address the charge that he failed to inform her. He thanked Fernández for the chance to serve and wished her every success as president.

“I accept this moment with great peace,” he wrote on X. He also stressed the importance of the UN week for Rebeca Grynspan, the Costa Rican bidding to become UN secretary-general.

On the eve of the meeting, Tovar told business leaders in New York that Grynspan was the best choice for the UN. She has Costa Rica’s full support, he said.

How Congress and Diplomats Reacted

Opposition lawmakers voiced surprise. National Liberation leader Álvaro Ramírez cited foreign-policy errors and cabinet instability, with two ministers and three vice-ministers gone in under five months.

Abril Gordienko of the Social Christian Unity Party said it was hard to believe Tovar had not reported such a high-profile meeting. If so, she added, the decision was the president’s to make.

The governing bloc defended Fernández’s right to choose her ministers without further explanation.

Manuel González, foreign minister from 2014 to 2018, said he had never seen a minister removed mid-summit. Experts told La Nación the timing could weaken Grynspan’s bid.

What Happened at the Meeting

Trump launched the coalition on 7 March in Doral, Florida, and the New York session was its second meeting. It was held at UN headquarters.

The session brought together ten presidents, including Trump, Argentina’s Javier Milei and Chile’s José Antonio Kast. Costa Rica was represented by Tovar.

Other leaders present included Bolivia’s Rodrigo Paz, Ecuador’s Daniel Noboa, Paraguay’s Santiago Peña and Peru’s Keiko Fujimori. Colombia sent Vice-President José Manuel Restrepo.

Fifteen governments, Costa Rica among them, issued a joint declaration against 24 criminal groups they call narco-terrorist. They also plan to seek OAS consultations under the 1947 Rio Treaty.

The declaration covers the economy too. Members say they intend to explore investment screening and “trusted supplier” regulations for digital infrastructure.

In his remarks, Tovar highlighted Costa Rica’s security efforts despite having no army. He also asked partners to keep their attention on Cuba and Nicaragua.

Who Takes Over

The presidency announced the dismissal in a statement on Thursday morning, ending Tovar’s duties at once. It named a stand-in from inside the cabinet.

Indiana Trejos, foreign trade minister since May, becomes acting foreign minister once she returns from the UN mission. She has worked at the foreign trade ministry for 21 years.

She holds a master’s in political economy from the University of Essex and a degree from Tufts University. She also represented Costa Rica on the OECD’s trade committee.

She has worked on agreements with the United States and the European Union. Tovar himself ran that ministry under former president Rodrigo Chaves before moving to foreign affairs in May.

Why It Matters If You Live in Costa Rica

Nothing announced changes visas, residency or trade rules. But her public apology to the US ambassador signals how much weight Fernández places on ties with the Trump administration.

It also comes a week after Tovar told the Miami Herald that ties with Cuba amounted to a full break. Embassies had closed in March, and Havana says it was never formally notified.

What Comes Next

Watch whether Fernández names a permanent foreign minister, and who delivers Costa Rica’s address to the General Assembly on Monday 28 September. Tovar had been due to give that speech, La Nación reported.

Sources: Delfino, the meeting and the timeline, 24 September 2026; La Nación, Fernández on the dismissal, 24 September 2026; La Nación, Indiana Trejos profile, 24 September 2026; La Nación, shortest tenure since 1948, 24 September 2026; Infobae, Tovar’s response, 24 September 2026; La Nación, reactions in Congress, 24 September 2026; La Nación, former ministers on the Grynspan bid, 24 September 2026; CEAPI, Tovar on Grynspan in New York, 22 September 2026; EFE via ABC Color, Fernández apologises to the US ambassador, 24 September 2026.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why was the Costa Rica foreign minister fired?

President Laura Fernández says Manuel Tovar attended a Shield of the Americas meeting with Donald Trump on 22 September without telling her. The presidency says this kept her from attending and caused strategic damage.

Who is the new foreign minister?

Foreign Trade Minister Indiana Trejos is acting foreign minister. She takes over once she returns from the UN General Assembly in New York.

What is the Shield of the Americas?

It is a US-led coalition against organised crime that Trump launched in March 2026. Fifteen governments, including Costa Rica, issued its latest declaration on 22 September.

Does this affect foreigners in Costa Rica?

No changes to visas, residency or trade rules have been announced. The dispute concerns how the government handled a diplomatic invitation.

World.title: TV Azteca Bankruptcy Spreads to 5 Units in Mexico, Including Its Casino Arm
World.content:
MEXICO · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Five TV Azteca subsidiaries, including online-casino permit holder Ganador Azteca, sought concurso mercantil on 18 September 2026.

— Which court On 24 September a Mexico City judge passed the cases to the judge handling TV Azteca’s own case.

— Why it matters Mexico’s gaming rules extinguish a permit once its holder is formally declared in concurso mercantil.

— The catch Bet365 and Betano in Mexico have been suspended since November 2025, and the permit could now be extinguished.

— The numbers Ganador Azteca’s accumulated losses reached 1,020 million pesos (about US$58 million) by end-2024, above its share capital.

— The parent TV Azteca itself owes almost 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion) and is negotiating with creditors under court supervision.

TV Azteca’s court-supervised restructuring now reaches the company that holds the Bet365 and Betano gaming permit in Mexico.

An Elektra store. The retailer belongs to Ricardo Salinas Pliego’s Grupo Salinas, like TV Azteca, but is not part of the insolvency cases. Photo: Werther mx, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

TV Azteca’s financial troubles are spreading through its group in Mexico. Five subsidiaries of the broadcaster, including the company that holds its online-casino permit, have asked a court for protection from creditors.

They filed voluntary concurso mercantil petitions, Mexico’s court-supervised insolvency process, on 18 September. Agencia Reforma reported the filings on Thursday 24 September.

Which TV Azteca Companies Filed

The five are Ganador Azteca, Operadora Ganador TV Azteca, Servicios y Mantenimiento del Futuro en Televisión, Lasimex and Inmobiliaria Roca del Pedregal. All cited insolvency.

Judge Ruth Huerta of the Second Insolvency Court declared on 24 September that the cases were outside her jurisdiction. She sent them to Judge Tessy del Rocío Covarrubias, who declared TV Azteca itself in concurso mercantil in July.

Ganador Azteca holds the federal gaming permit, granted in 2018, under which bet365.mx and betano.mx operated. Operadora Ganador TV Azteca has been linked to Betano, according to El Imparcial.

Ganador Azteca is the first gaming-permit holder to seek concurso mercantil since at least 2010, Reforma noted. Back then, Entretenimiento de México went through an involuntary case and emerged with a restructuring in 2012.

What It Means for Bet365 and Betano Users

Both sites have been largely out of action since November 2025, when the Interior Ministry suspended the permit. They were still suspended in July, Los Reporteros reported.

The insolvency filings add a second risk. Mexico’s gaming regulations extinguish a permit once its holder is declared in concurso mercantil.

That would happen only when Judge Covarrubias rules on Ganador Azteca’s insolvency. No such ruling had been reported by Friday 25 September.

Customer money is part of the picture. At the end of 2024, Ganador Azteca owed players 245 million pesos (about US$13.9 million) in deposits, Reforma reported.

Reforma described these as balances that can only be withdrawn once players reach certain minimum betting amounts. The item grew 42% between 2023 and 2024.

If you hold a balance on either platform, keep records of your account and transactions. In a concurso mercantil the court ranks creditors’ claims, so paperwork matters.

A Casino Arm That Was Already Losing Money

Reforma’s review of financial statements shows that Ganador Azteca, which has no physical casinos, relied on loans from a sister company. Servicios y Mantenimiento del Futuro en Televisión lent it 1,004 million pesos (about US$57 million) in 2023.

It lent a further 1,591 million pesos (about US$90 million) in 2024. By the end of that year, Ganador Azteca still owed it 779 million pesos (about US$44 million).

Accumulated losses reached 1,020 million pesos (about US$58 million), more than its share capital. The auditor Grant Thornton warned of “a material uncertainty” about its ability to continue as a going concern.

Sales rose 68% in 2024 to 2,688 million pesos (about US$152 million), with a small net profit. But the company lost 269 million pesos (about US$15 million) in the first half of 2025.

At the start of 2025 it also owed royalties of 294.7 million pesos (about US$16.7 million). The creditor was Hillside, the British group that licenses the Bet365 brand.

The Dispute With the Government

In November 2025, the Interior Ministry suspended Ganador Azteca’s permits to run Bet365 and Betano over suspected money laundering. The company categorically rejected the allegations.

Two federal judges have since ruled the suspension unlawful. Those rulings still await confirmation by higher collegiate courts.

Where TV Azteca’s Own Case Stands

TV Azteca asked for concurso mercantil in March 2026 and was formally declared in the procedure in July. It faces debts of almost 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion).

The case is in a conciliation stage, in which the company negotiates with creditors. On 18 September TV Azteca said the conciliator had filed a provisional list of creditors and that its operations continue normally.

On Wednesday 16 September, it asked a New York bankruptcy court to recognise the Mexican case under Chapter 15. The aim is to stop creditors pursuing it separately in the United States.

According to Índice Político, the petition says TV Azteca needs protection from creditors trying to recover money outside the Mexican case. Judge Lisa Beckerman is handling it.

Creditors outside Grupo Salinas include Turkish producer Acun Medya, owed 556 million pesos (about US$31.5 million), Índice Político reported. Rival broadcaster Televisa is owed 185 million pesos (about US$10.5 million).

The biggest fight is with holders of US$400 million in notes issued in 2017, on which TV Azteca stopped paying in 2021. Mexican press reports put the claim, with interest, at about US$630 million.

In March, the court declined to extend TV Azteca’s protection to its subsidiaries, several of which guarantee those notes. Each would need its own filing to get that protection.

Why It Matters

The filings widen a restructuring that already touches one of Mexico’s two big national broadcasters. Bondholders argue some assets sit beyond their reach.

They point to broadcast concessions held by TV Azteca III, a unit that is not part of the case.

TV Azteca says its operations continue normally. For bettors and creditors, the key moment is any ruling on Ganador Azteca’s insolvency.

No public comment from TV Azteca on the five new filings had been reported by Friday.

What Comes Next

Judge Covarrubias must decide whether to declare the five subsidiaries in concurso mercantil. The New York court’s decision on Chapter 15 recognition is the other date to watch.

Sources: Reforma via Vanguardia, five subsidiaries file, 24 September 2026; El Imparcial, Ganador Azteca and its gaming permit, 24 September 2026; Proceso, TV Azteca’s Chapter 15 petition, 16 September 2026; Índice Político, TV Azteca’s New York petition and creditors, 17 September 2026; Los Reporteros, bet365.mx and betano.mx still suspended, 6 July 2026; El CEO, TV Azteca statement on its creditor list, 18 September 2026. Exchange rate: mid-market rate of 25 September 2026 (open.er-api.com), 17.67 pesos per US dollar.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a concurso mercantil?

It is Mexico’s court-supervised insolvency process, broadly similar to Chapter 11 in the United States. Once a judge declares it, a conciliation stage follows to reach a deal with creditors, and bankruptcy can follow if that fails.

Which TV Azteca subsidiaries filed?

Ganador Azteca, Operadora Ganador TV Azteca, Servicios y Mantenimiento del Futuro en Televisión, Lasimex and Inmobiliaria Roca del Pedregal. They filed on 18 September 2026.

Are Bet365 and Betano working in Mexico?

Both sites have been suspended since the Interior Ministry acted against Ganador Azteca’s permit in November 2025. Two court rulings against that move are under appeal, and a concurso declaration would extinguish the permit.

How much does TV Azteca owe?

The parent company faces debts of almost 24 billion pesos (about US$1.4 billion). Its biggest dispute is over US$400 million in notes issued in 2017, on which it stopped paying in 2021.
