World.title: Costa Rica Court Freezes Access to Playa Blanca Marine Wetland
World.content:
A Costa Rican court has temporarily suspended visitor and vehicle access to the Playa Blanca Marine Wetland in Garabito. The tribunal said public use cannot continue unchecked in a protected area that still has no management plan 32 years after it was created. The Contentious-Administrative Tribunal issued the precautionary order on Wednesday, Sept. 23. It covers the areas of direct and indirect access to the wetland, which lies southwest of the Punta Leona tourist complex on the Central Pacific coast.

The suspension will remain in place until the Ministry of Environment and Energy (MINAE) and the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) complete a scientific carrying-capacity study for the ecosystem. That study must set the conditions, limits and forms of visitation compatible with conservation. The measure can also end if a final judgment is issued in the underlying case.

Judge Víctor Orozco Solano signed the resolution. He was responding to an early precautionary request filed by environmental lawyer Wálter Brenes Soto in a lawsuit against the State, represented by the Attorney General’s Office, and SINAC. The order is provisional and does not decide the merits of the case. The court gave the State and SINAC three days to respond in writing and submit evidence.

In granting the measure, the tribunal found that the request met the standard of necessity and extreme urgency. It pointed to the risk of harm to the constitutional right to a healthy and ecologically balanced environment. It also cited the preventive and precautionary principles, along with in dubio pro natura, the legal doctrine that scientific uncertainty should be resolved in favor of nature.

In his filing, Brenes argued that the missing management plan threatens the wetland’s survival. He said no study establishes how many people and vehicles can enter the protected area, directly or indirectly. Brenes has said he went to court after noticing a sharp rise in visitors once access to Playa Blanca opened. He alleged that some visitors were drinking alcohol, playing music, lighting bonfires, camping and staying overnight. He also noted that the area has no public restrooms and no system for handling visitors’ waste.

SINAC has previously described a different situation. In an earlier constitutional case, the agency reported that a July 22 inspection found no significant tourist visitation inside the wetland. It added that urban development lies outside the wetland’s official boundaries. SINAC acknowledged, however, that a management plan would help it assess and reduce indirect impacts from the surrounding area.

The new order builds on a ruling by the Constitutional Chamber, known as Sala IV. In resolution 2026-033118, dated Aug. 27, the magistrates upheld an amparo appeal also filed by Brenes. They ordered MINAE and SINAC to issue a General Management Plan for the wetland within 12 months of being notified.

That plan is still neither approved nor in force. That gap led Brenes to seek the new precautionary measure. The suspension comes less than four months after the Municipality of Garabito removed the barrier that controlled vehicle entry through Punta Leona. The municipality cited a court ruling that recognized the access road as public. Since then, anyone has been able to reach the beach without being a guest or member of the resort and without paying to use the road.

Punta Leona maintains that the road crosses private land and that Playa Blanca has always had a separate official public access. The dispute over access at Punta Leona remains before the courts. The wetland was declared a protected wildlife area on April 7, 1994 and SINAC administers it through the Central Pacific Conservation Area (ACOPAC).

It covers about 5.5 square kilometers (2.1 square miles) from the shoreline, including marine waters up to six meters (20 feet) deep at low tide. It is the only marine wetland on Costa Rica’s Central Pacific coast. It is known for its coral and rocky reefs and as a nesting site for olive ridley sea turtles. It is also home to parrotfish, whose feeding helps produce the white sand that gives the beach its name.

As of this writing, authorities had not publicly explained how the order will be enforced on the ground. They also had not said whether it applies equally to people arriving on foot, or which agency will be responsible for controlling access while the State and SINAC prepare their response.

World.title: Atlantic Reaches Late September Without a Hurricane for the First Time Since 1914
World.content:
The Atlantic Ocean has reached late September without producing a single hurricane, something that has not happened in 112 years. As of this morning, the U.S. National Hurricane Center was tracking Tropical Storm Fay southwest of the Azores and a disturbance south of the Cabo Verde Islands. Neither had reached hurricane strength, and no hurricane has formed in the Atlantic this season.

The last season to go this deep into September without a hurricane was 1914, and that season never produced one at all. In records dating to 1851, only 1907 and 1914 finished without a hurricane. Both predate satellite tracking, so some storms from that era may have gone undetected.

The 2026 season has produced six named storms, Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard and Fay. None reached hurricane strength, which requires sustained winds of 119 km/h (74 mph). That is far below a typical year as the first Atlantic hurricane usually forms by Aug. 11, and by this point the basin would normally have produced about 10 named storms, four hurricanes and two major hurricanes, based on 1991–2020 averages.

The storms that did form were weak and short-lived. Accumulated cyclone energy, a measure that combines the strength and duration of every storm in a season, stood at 6.2 on Sept. 22, about 93% below normal for the date, according to the hurricane center. The main reason is El Niño. The warming of the equatorial Pacific strengthens upper-level winds over the Atlantic and Caribbean, and that wind shear tears developing storms apart before they can organize and intensify.

Forecasters expected a quiet year. In its August update, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration gave a 75% chance of a below-normal season, with seven to 13 named storms and two to six hurricanes. The season is not over. It officially runs until Nov. 30, and late September and October have historically produced dangerous storms, especially in the Gulf and along the U.S. East Coast.

Here in Costa Rica, the same El Niño is having a very different effect. The National Meteorological Institute has declared a meteorological drought across the Pacific slope and Central Valley, where rainfall is running up to 37% below normal and community water systems in 74 communities are rationing water.

Costa Rica rarely takes a direct hit from Atlantic hurricanes. Storms passing through the Caribbean have more often affected the country indirectly by pulling heavy rain across it, as Tropical Storm Nate did in 2017. The eastern Pacific has been far more active. Hurricane Polo regained Category 5 strength off Mexico’s Pacific coast with sustained winds of 260 km/h (162 mph), and the hurricane center was also issuing advisories today on Hurricane Odaly but neither storm is expected to affect Costa Rica.

If the Atlantic stays quiet through the end of November, 2026 would become only the third season on record without a hurricane.

World.title: Costa Rica Hotel Is the Only New Three-Key Michelin Stay in the Americas
World.content:
A luxury resort on Guanacaste’s Papagayo Peninsula has received the Michelin Guide’s highest hotel distinction, making it the only property in the Americas to reach the top tier this year. Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, was promoted from two to three Michelin Keys in the guide’s 2026 hotel selection, announced last week.

Only 18 hotels worldwide earned the top distinction for the first time, and Nekajui was the lone new addition from anywhere in the Americas. The promotion gives Costa Rica two Three-Key hotels. Nayara Springs in La Fortuna de San Carlos already holds the top rating, according to the guide’s listings.

Michelin singled out Costa Rica as a highlight of its 2026 selection for North and Central America and the Caribbean. Beyond Nekajui’s promotion, the country added four new One-Key hotels and three new Two-Key hotels. Costa Rica now has 23 Key hotels, according to the guide, compared with five each in Belize and Guatemala, four in Panama, two in Honduras and one in Nicaragua. That puts the country ahead of the rest of Central America combined.

Nekajui sits within Peninsula Papagayo, an area of about 567 hectares (1,400 acres) of tropical forest and beaches. Michelin’s inspectors describe a central lodge surrounded by rooms, suites and villas, some of them reached by a wooden suspension bridge that spans a ravine. The peninsula already had Michelin recognition before this year’s promotion. The Four Seasons Resort Costa Rica at Peninsula Papagayo holds two Keys, and the Andaz Peninsula Papagayo holds one, according to the guide.

The Michelin Keys were introduced in 2024 as the hotel counterpart to the Michelin Stars awarded to restaurants, and properties are assessed through anonymous inspections. The Keys recognize what the guide considers the most outstanding hotels within its broader selection of more than 9,000 properties.

This year’s edition added 470 hotels across 79 destinations, bringing the worldwide total to 2,832 Key hotels. Of those, 155 hold three Keys, 657 hold two and 2,020 hold one. Costa Rica’s Two-Key hotels are spread across very different landscapes. They include Pacuare Lodge on the Pacuare River, El Silencio Lodge & Spa in Bajos del Toro, Rancho Pacifico in Uvita, Casa Chameleon at Las Catalinas and Rio Perdido in Guanacaste, along with Nayara Gardens and Nayara Tented Camp in La Fortuna.

The One-Key list stretches from the southern Caribbean to the Osa Peninsula. It includes Hotel Aguas Claras in Puerto Viejo, Lapa Rios in Puerto Jiménez, Kura Boutique Hotel in Uvita, Origins Luxury Lodge and Rio Celeste Hideaway Hotel in Bijagua, and The Retreat Costa Rica in Atenas.

The Nicoya Peninsula stands out in the lower tiers. Nosara accounts for four One-Key hotels, Silvestre Nosara, Tierra Magnifica, Sendero Hotel and Esh Hotel & Spa, while Santa Teresa has two, Hotel Fermata and Hacienda AltaGracia. Michelin updates the selection every year, meaning distinctions can change with each edition. This year, 84 hotels worldwide moved up from one Key to two or from two Keys to three.

World.title: Honduras Adopts El Salvador-Style Prison Measures Against Gangs
World.content:
Yesterday, Honduras adopted measures that tighten prison conditions, similar to those imposed by the government of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, as part of a strategy against gangs and drug trafficking. Gangs such as Barrio 18 and its archrival Mara Salvatrucha operate in Honduras and have been linked to drug trafficking and the country’s high homicide rate of 24 per 100,000 inhabitants, four times the global average.

The prison restrictions approved by Congress, at the request of the right-wing government of President Nasry Asfura, follow last Friday’s designation of several criminal groups, including gangs, as terrorist organizations. The measures are aimed at isolating high-risk prisoners and eliminating alternatives to imprisonment for alleged members of those criminal organizations.

The package amends the Criminal Procedure Code and establishes that suspected members of those groups will be sent to maximum-security prisons following their arrest. It also stipulates that prisoners belonging to those criminal groups will be allowed only one hour of sunlight and outdoor time, either individually or in small groups of no more than two people.

The measures also call for the creation of specialized courts dedicated exclusively to cases involving members of those groups. The provisions were approved on the same day that Shield of the Americas, the Washington-led regional anti-drug alliance, announced an agreement to combat around 20 criminal organizations across the region.

Bukele’s anti-gang campaign, which has reduced homicides to historic lows, has been carried out under a state of exception that has led to the imprisonment of about 92,000 people without judicial warrants since 2022. Asfura, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, took office in January with reducing crime as one of his main objectives.

World.title: Teen found by police with gunshot wound in inner thigh and gun lying next to him brought to court in wheelchair for ‘Dusty-Eight’
World.content:
Teen found by police with gunshot wound in inner thigh and gun lying next to him brought to court in wheelchair for ‘Dusty-Eight’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: An 18-year-old Dangriga fisherman who was found suffering from a gunshot wound last week has now been remanded to prison after police alleged that a loaded .38 revolver discovered near where he was lying belonged to him. It also remains unclear, however, whether or not the injured gunshot victim shot himself or was shot by someone else and left there.

Jorge Bustillo, a resident of the Monument Site area of Dangriga, appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court late Wednesday and was charged with keeping a firearm without a gun licence and keeping ammunition without a gun licence.

He pleaded not guilty to both charges and was remanded to the Belize Central Prison until November 9, when he is expected to appear in the Dangriga Magistrate’s Court.

According to police allegations, shortly after midnight on Thursday, September 17, officers responded to reports of a shooting in the #2 New Site area of Dangriga.

Police said they found Bustillo lying face down in low bushes and suffering from an apparent gunshot wound to the inner thigh of his left leg. He was reportedly bleeding profusely and complaining of severe pain.

Approximately seven feet away, officers allegedly discovered a rusty .38-calibre revolver bearing serial number X013848.

Police said Scenes of Crime personnel processed the area and found the revolver contained five live .38 rounds and one expended shell.

No other person was reportedly found in the immediate area.

Bustillo was taken to the Dangriga hospital before being transferred to the Karl Heusner Memorial Hospital in Belize City for further treatment.

Following his discharge, police met Bustillo at the Queen Street Police Station on September 22 and informed him about the firearm recovered near the location where he had been found wounded.

Police said Bustillo indicated that he did not possess a gun licence, after which he was charged.

When he appeared in court, Bustillo was reportedly unable to walk without assistance and was taken into the courtroom in a wheelchair.

The circumstances surrounding the shooting itself, including who fired the shot that injured Bustillo, remain unclear from the information presented in court.

The firearm and ammunition charges against Bustillo remain allegations, and he is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in court

World.title: ‘Tanga’ murder trial stalled as only witness can’t be located as Marybeth refuses to testify
World.content:
‘Tanga’ murder trial stalled as only witness can’t be located as Marybeth refuses to testify

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The long-awaited murder trial of two men accused of killing well-known street figure Winston Joseph James, better known as “Tanga,” has been delayed after prosecutors told the High Court that a key Crown witness cannot be located.

Azzane Domingo, 23, and Eustace Lewis, 36, are jointly indicted for the murder of James, who was shot and killed in Belize City on January 21, 2022.

The trial before Justice Candace Nanton had been scheduled to begin this week, but on Thursday Crown counsel sought another adjournment, explaining that a male witness considered important to the prosecution’s case has still not been found.

The court was told that police, including officers attached to the GI3, have been attempting to locate the witness. Prosecutors said additional officers are expected to assist with the search over the weekend.

Attorneys Leeroy Banner, representing Domingo, and Senior Counsel Ellis Arnold, representing Lewis, expressed concern over the continued delay but did not object to one final adjournment.

Arnold indicated that if the prosecution is still unable to proceed at the next hearing, he may pursue another course of action on behalf of his client. Banner expressed similar concerns given the length of time the matter has remained before the courts.

Justice Nanton granted what was described as a final adjournment until Tuesday, September 29, 2026.

James was shot multiple times while driving a Nissan Pathfinder near the West Canal area of Belize City on January 21, 2022. His then-partner, Marybeth Wade, was travelling with him and was also shot but survived. James lost control of the vehicle following the shooting and crashed.

Domingo was charged with James’s murder on September 23, 2024, more than two and a half years after the killing. He was also charged in connection with the shooting of Wade. Lewis was subsequently arraigned on September 25, 2024, initially on a charge of abetment to murder.

Following their preliminary inquiry in August 2025, the men were committed to stand trial in the High Court. They have since been jointly indicted for murder.

The prosecution’s witness situation has previously attracted public attention. Wade, who had been described in court reporting as a key Crown witness because she was inside the vehicle when the shooting occurred, publicly stated in August 2025 that she did not intend to testify against the accused men.

The male witness prosecutors are presently trying to locate has not been publicly identified in the current proceedings.

Domingo and Lewis have not been convicted of the charge against them, and the allegations are to be determined at trial.

World.title: Arthur ‘Turo’ Hill gets life in prison for stabbing brother-in-law to death; Parole after 29 years
World.content:
Arthur ‘Turo’ Hill gets life in prison for stabbing brother-in-law to death; Parole after 29 years

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Arthur Hill, also known as “Turo,” has been sentenced to life imprisonment for the 2024 stabbing murder of his 19-year-old brother-in-law, Levan Christopher Aldana, and will not be eligible for parole until he has served 29 years.

Justice Candace Nanton handed down the sentence in the High Court on Thursday, just over two months after finding Hill guilty of murder following a judge-alone trial.

Hill’s sentence was backdated to February 1, 2024, giving him credit for the time he has already spent on remand.

The murder occurred on January 31, 2024, in Biscayne Village after Hill and Aldana had been socializing and drinking together. Reports said police were told the two men had previously gotten into altercations while drinking.

At trial, the Crown’s case rested heavily on circumstantial evidence and Aldana’s dying declaration identifying Hill as the person who stabbed him. A police officer testified that the mortally wounded Aldana said words to the effect of, “Dah Arthur Hill do it.” Justice Nanton found that evidence credible and, when considered alongside the other evidence, was satisfied of Hill’s guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

Evidence showed that Aldana and Hill were seen together shortly before the stabbing. Another witness testified that Hill later appeared at his home shirtless, barefoot and sweating, asked to use a telephone and requested a change of clothes. Police subsequently observed what appeared to be blood on Hill’s elbow.

A doctor testified that Aldana suffered three stab wounds — two to the neck and one to the abdomen. The abdominal wound proved fatal, causing extensive internal bleeding and damage to vital organs.

In determining Hill’s minimum period before parole eligibility, Justice Nanton began at 30 years. The court increased that by one year after considering aggravating factors, including the use of a knife, the relationship between Hill and the victim and the suffering caused to Aldana.

Two years were then deducted after the court considered mitigating factors, resulting in a minimum term of 29 years before Hill can become eligible for parole.

Aldana’s mother, Tracey Meighan, was present in court for the sentencing. During an earlier victim-impact hearing, she described Aldana as her first-born son and told the court that watching him suffering after the stabbing left her feeling helpless.

“A part of me died too,” she told the court.

Hill, who was represented by attorney Norman Rodriguez, had maintained his innocence during his trial. He was convicted on July 16, 2026.

World.title: Benque mechanic fined $500 after stealing Smart manager’s laptop left behind at restaurant; Manager didn’t realize his laptop was missing until 3 days later
World.content:
Benque mechanic fined $500 after stealing Smart manager’s laptop left behind at restaurant; Manager didn’t realize his laptop was missing until 3 days later

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 46-year-old Benque Viejo mechanic who admitted stealing a laptop bag containing more than $7,000 worth of electronics belonging to a Smart manager has escaped jail time after pleading guilty to theft.

Enrique Moralez appeared unrepresented in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Thursday, where he pleaded guilty to stealing the property of a manager at Smart.

The theft occurred on August 28 at Benny’s Restaurant on the Philip Goldson Highway, where the manager reportedly left behind a black laptop bag after purchasing food.

The bag, valued at $400, contained a laptop valued at $6,072, along with a $200 charger, a $50 USB adapter, a $75 USB-C adapter and a $300 USB DVD device. The items had a combined reported value of approximately $7,097.

According to the facts presented in court, the owner did not realize the laptop was missing until August 31, when he was preparing to go to work. He returned to Benny’s and inquiries led to a review of surveillance footage.

The footage reportedly showed Moralez, who had been sitting near Balan, picking up the bag after Balan left and walking out of the restaurant with it.

Police later identified Moralez and circulated a wanted notice for him. His wife subsequently turned over the laptop to police in Benque Viejo before Moralez surrendered himself on September 23.

In court, Moralez admitted taking the bag and its contents, telling the magistrate he had been drinking alcohol at the time and simply saw the bag and took it.

He told the court that what he had done remained on his mind, prompting him to return the property and turn himself in.

“I never knew I meh wah get into trouble,” Moralez reportedly told the court.

In mitigation, Moralez said he was a first-time offender, had recently buried his father and was responsible for caring for his sick mother.

Taking into consideration his early guilty plea, lack of previous convictions, recovery of the stolen property and his expression of remorse, the magistrate imposed a non-custodial sentence.

Moralez was fined $500 plus $5 cost of court, which he must pay by November 30, 2026, or serve two months in prison.

World.title: Shyne backs Darrell Bradley for UDP leader and says Panton cannot unify party
World.content:
Shyne backs Darrell Bradley for UDP leader and says Panton cannot unify party

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Former United Democratic Party leader Moses “Shyne” Barrow has thrown his support behind former Belize City Mayor Darrell Bradley as a potential future leader of the UDP, while launching a sharp attack on the leadership of Tracy Taegar Panton.

In a strongly worded Facebook post on Thursday, Barrow declared: “READ THE ROOM! DARRELL BRADLEY FOR UDP LEADER!”

Barrow claimed Panton has failed to unify the UDP and pointed to resignations and internal dissatisfaction as evidence of continuing problems within the party. Those assertions represent Barrow’s assessment of the current state of the UDP.

The former party leader said he is prepared to support Bradley to become UDP leader and eventually seek the office of Prime Minister.

The intervention comes as Bradley himself has publicly signalled that he is open to leading the UDP if the position becomes vacant. In a recent interview, Bradley said he considers himself an option for the party, while stressing that he is not currently campaigning against Panton and remains in communication with both Panton and Barrow.

Barrow also called for changes to the UDP Constitution that would allow Bradley to seek the leadership.

Bradley previously served two terms as Belize City Mayor and later as President of the Senate.

Barrow’s latest intervention adds another public voice to the ongoing debate over the UDP’s direction and leadership.

World.title: NTUCB rejects Briceño’s response to 11 demands; ‘Actions will increase until will of the people achieved’
World.content:
NTUCB rejects Briceño’s response to 11 demands; ‘Actions will increase until will of the people achieved’

By Breaking Belize News Staff: The National Trade Union Congress of Belize (NTUCB) has formally rejected Prime Minister John Briceño’s response to its 11 demands, saying none of the demands were met as submitted and announcing that it is preparing “activities and actions” in the coming days.

“These will increase in effectiveness and resolve until all 11 demands and the will of the people are achieved”, the Union cryptically said.

In a letter dated September 24, NTUCB General Secretary Timothy Dami said the Prime Minister’s September 15 response came 18 days after the union’s deadline and failed to address several matters, including the Vocational-Technical salary scale, two back-pay matters affecting Belize National Teachers’ Union members, and a timeline for filling the vacant Ombudsman post.

The union umbrella body also challenged Briceño’s assertion that unions have representation on the Belize Telemedia Limited (BTL) board through the Social Security Board. NTUCB argued that the seat is not specifically designated for a union or worker representative and maintained that Government could establish tripartite representation at BTL through its own appointments without requiring legislative changes.

Briceño had earlier rejected several of NTUCB’s major proposals, including its demand for the removal of BTL Chairman Markhelm Lizarraga and three other directors, restructuring of the Public Utilities Commission, and halting the Revenue Authority Bill. Government instead pointed to BTL’s record profits, the statutory independence of the PUC and the importance it attaches to the revenue-authority reform. Government also indicated that whistleblower legislation had been shared with social partners, campaign-finance proposals were being developed, and work was underway toward filling the Ombudsman vacancy.

NTUCB’s original August submission called for, among other things, tripartite representation at BTL, changes to the PUC, whistleblower and campaign-finance legislation, enforcement of civil-asset-recovery legislation, filling the Ombudsman vacancy and support for the Public Service Union’s position on the Revenue Authority Bill. It also contained specific salary, back-pay and education-related demands from member unions.

In Thursday’s letter, NTUCB said the Belize Chamber of Commerce and Industry and Belize Network of NGOs share its concerns on several of the core governance issues, including BTL representation, the PUC, whistleblower protection, campaign-finance reform, civil-asset recovery, the Ombudsman’s Office and the Revenue Authority Bill. The groups have previously acted collectively as part of Belize’s social partners on governance concerns surrounding BTL.

“None of our 11 demands were met as submitted,” NTUCB stated, adding that it had not even received a date and time for a meeting to work through the outstanding issues. The Congress said its council has met to consider Government’s response and has also met with the Joint Social Partners.

NTUCB said the actions now being prepared will increase “in effectiveness and resolve” until its 11 demands are addressed.

World.title: International News: U.S. issues security alert over armed shutdown in Colombia
World.content:
International News: U.S. issues security alert over armed shutdown in Colombia

By Zoila Palma: The United States has issued a security alert for Santa Marta and surrounding areas in Colombia’s Magdalena and La Guajira departments following a 72-hour transportation blockade, curfew and shutdown of civilian activities imposed by an illegal armed group.

The U.S. Embassy in Colombia said the restrictions were imposed by the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada (ACSN), also known as Los Pachencas, following a Colombian security operation against the organization. Authorities have deployed additional Army and police forces across the region.

The embassy reported numerous incidents, including vehicle burnings, intimidation of businesses, shootings and disruptions to public transportation and civilian movement. The group reportedly imposed the shutdown after Colombian security forces killed 13 of its members, including one of its top commanders, during a military operation earlier this week.

The U.S. Embassy advised American citizens to avoid demonstrations and areas with increased security activity, monitor local media and follow instructions from Colombian authorities.

World.title: Corozal schools receive 100 refurbished computers, ITVET gets VR welding systems
World.content:
Corozal schools receive 100 refurbished computers, ITVET gets VR welding systems

By Zoila Palma: Students at 5 primary schools in the Corozal District are benefiting from 100 refurbished desktop computers donated through a partnership between the Ministry of Investment and Transparent BPO.

St. Paul’s Anglican, Church of Christ, Christiline Gill, Assemblies of God, and Corozal Nazarene Primary Schools each received 20 desktop computers. The equipment is transforming classrooms into digital learning spaces and providing students with greater opportunities to develop essential computer skills.

In addition to the computer donation, the Investment Policy and Compliance Unit within the Ministry has equipped Corozal ITVET with four MIG Welding Virtual Reality Training Systems.

The advanced systems will allow students to train in a simulated environment, giving them practical opportunities to sharpen their welding skills using modern technology.

World.title: Court walkout looms
World.content:
Defence attorneys staging a ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston on Wednesday demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

Defence attorneys have been placed on alert to pull their services from the island’s courts for an entire week, starting next Monday, a move that will deal a significant blow to the Michaelmas term which began just over a week ago.

The lawyers arrived at the decision after a meeting on Thursday with Justice Minister Delroy Chuck which they say failed to produce any meaningful plans to reform the 2022 Firearms Act.

The emergency meeting was called following Wednesday’s ‘silent protest’ outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston, where members of the Jamaican Bar Association, the Advocates Association in collaboration with Bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

Some hours later, Chuck indicated that he would be meeting with representatives of the bodies to hear their concerns.

However, following those discussions, defence attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee, who was a key figure behind the protest, told the Jamaica Observer that the meeting amounted to little less than an exercise in futility.

“The minister could not give a timeline as to when anything would be taken to the legislature, and he has asked for the discussion to be placed in writing but before [the Act was passed] the Bar Association… made a submission to Parliament. We are not asking for anything different, so it’s not like our argument is new,” Harris stated.

“The meeting, in my mind, was an opportunity for us to say the same things we have already said, but we have not gotten any response from the minister to, for example, say when he will go to Parliament [with proposed amendments]. I know everything takes time, but I did not get any idea of a plan to put in action. So the minister didn’t confirm that he was going to put a plan in action, so there is no resolution,” Harris declared.

As such, she said attorneys will be moving to action the next stage of their protest.

“He was very courteous and he listened. He expressed that he understood our concerns, but he did not go any further to say exactly if they were going to be dealt with and when, so there is nothing. I am aware he has already been presented with similar arguments by the director of public prosecutions and even the chief justice. I am going to ask my members to withdraw our services,” Harris told the Observer.

“We are going to use the opportunity, perhaps, to do quick education. The public needs to be aware that we are not saying legislation must be weak on persons who use firearms to terrorise our Jamaican citizens, we are not saying the legislation needs to be weak; we are saying that the legislation is to be fair and cognisant that not every case is the same,” Harris said.

The protests come just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the Annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck said, while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “The security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” Chuck said.

The comments triggered furious commentary from several quarters.

A week later members of Jamaica’s legal profession met on Saturday, September 19 to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Act, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Act, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for specified violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons. It establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities, and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their September 19 meeting “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, the judiciary and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments”, the attorneys said in that statement.

World.title: Christiana clampdown
World.content:
Vendors on Wildman Street in Christiana on Thursday (Photos: Kasey Williams)

CHRISTIANA, Manchester — Mandeville Mayor Donovan Mitchell says, effective today, there will be a clampdown on unapproved buildings and illegal vending, as part of enforcement activities in the south-central town of Christiana.

“Yesterday (Wednesday) I came into Christiana and as the chairman of the local Board of Health I spent about five hours walking the streets of Christiana. I visited the abattoir. I visited the market. I visited the transportation centre. I looked at some businesses [and] buildings going up. I know at the council meeting early this month I made a statement and some people are up in arms and all of that… What is happening in the parish will not continue,” he said on Thursday while addressing the launch of Sam Fo Meats mobile application on Wildman Street in Christiana.

“I said it yesterday (Wednesday) to my team that Wildman Street, please be prepared, because I am going to be changing the entire look of Wildman Street. There will absolutely be no selling on the street. I am warning the businesses that are putting their sewage and grey water into our water channels to stop and stop before tomorrow [Friday] morning, because a team from the public health service will be coming out and we are going to make sure it cannot continue,” added Mitchell.

He pointed to the public safety concerns and hazards of waste water flowing on the busy commercial street.

“You cannot be walking on the street and all you are seeing is grey water. Businesses can’t build their buildings and put their grey water on the street. What about our children, the elderly? You are walking and miss your step in soap water and you break your leg and the first thing is they call the parish council,” said Mitchell, who chairs the Manchester Municipal Corporation.

“I am warning people who are building houses without plans from the Manchester Municipal Corporation. I am not holding bar; you have to do better. When a building collapses because you have not done the correct thing, who is the first person you blame? Government. Where was the Government when you were building? Not around, because you put zinc all around your place and you do what you have to do and when you are finished you open up the zinc and you see a building there that has not gone through the proper channel,” added Mitchell.

Pertaining to the Christiana abattoir, Mitchell said he is contemplating closing it for renovations.

“We are having some problems and I will tell you that maybe, based on the letters I am getting from the health services, I may have to close it even temporarily to make sure that things go right. I am warning, since I am in Christiana, that things are not going to be the same in Christiana. There has to be some changes,” declared Mitchell.

World.title: Skippa in int’l spotlight
World.content:
Dancehall artiste Skippa was named as one to watch by Jamaica Observer at the start of 2026 .

When the Jamaica Observer named Skippa one of its artistes to watch at the start of 2026, the prediction came with the expectation that the young dancehall artiste’s momentum was worth keeping an eye on. What has followed, however, stretches well beyond even his own expectations.

There was the touring, the growing audiences, the songs steadily finding new listeners, and, perhaps most significantly, recognition from one of the music industry’s most established brands — Billboard.

Still, as the artiste himself revealed, 2026 has so far surpassed his wildest imagination.

“We had goals around touring and growing the music, but everything kind of surpassed what we had in mind. The amount of shows, the places we’ve been received, the people connecting with the music in places we didn’t necessarily expect, and then Billboard on top of that — it’s been crazy,” he shared. “We’re grateful for all of it, because you can set goals, but sometimes the reality goes way beyond what you planned for.”

Speaking to the Splash, the entertainer said that, although he has been putting in the work, he was taken aback when he was named by Billboard as a Caribbean Rising Star. He admitted that the honour caught him completely off guard and that he had to resist getting swept up in the whirlwind that the moment ushered in.

“Honestly, I was taken aback. I’m not really the type to overreact, so I was just there trying to take in the moment,” he said. “Billboard recognising me as a Caribbean Rising Star, in a room with so many people who have been doing this at the highest level, that’s crazy. I’m grateful, for real, and it’s something I’ll always remember.”

For an artiste whose career has accelerated considerably in recent years, the recognition represents another marker in a journey that appears to be moving faster than he anticipated. Billboard may have just caught up to Skippa’s burgeoning career, but the proverbial writing was on the wall since the latter part of last year.

By December 2025, YouTube year-end statistics showed that the entertainer had already emerged as Jamaica’s third-most-viewed artiste on the platform, behind Chronic Law and Vybz Kartel, with approximately 79.9 million views. His numbers remained consistent in 2026, with the artiste repeatedly placing multiple songs among Jamaica’s most-streamed records.

Still, he remains humble, crediting his chart success to his loyal fan base rather than to a secret creative formula.

“I wouldn’t say I figured out some formula, because I think what really sets my work apart is that people just relate to me. I’m being myself and making music from my own experience and perspective, and people see themselves in that,” he said.

That connection, he believes, matters more than the numbers themselves — or any ‘trending list’ he may or may not find himself on.

“I don’t chase whatever trend is happening just because it’s working for somebody else. I just try to make good music and stay authentic, and the people decide what they want to run with,” he said.

It is a philosophy that has become increasingly important as the numbers have grown.

For Skippa, there is a difference between having a hit song and building something that can last.

“Consistency, for sure. I think that’s one of the biggest things,” he said. “You can have one song that catches fire, but building a career is different. You have to keep showing up, keep making music, keep performing, keep connecting with the people, and keep growing.”

With that mindset, the entertainer shared that he is looking at his recent success as motivation to go even further, rather than being tricked into believing he has somehow arrived.

“To come into this space and, in such a short time, see my name alongside artistes who have been doing this for years, that’s a big thing. It’s definitely something I’m grateful for and amazed by,” he said. “But I don’t look at it like I’ve arrived and that’s it. It just makes me appreciate the journey even more and motivates me to keep working.”

The entertainer sought to acknowledge the machinery working for his good behind the scenes. Naming his manager, Cristina; engineer, producer and DJ Travis; Chargie Records; Solitary Muzic; and Bankroller, among others, as people who have contributed to his progress, Skippa expressed that, “Everybody played their part, so when I’m on that stage accepting something like Billboard Rising Star, I know it’s not just about me.”

The prediction made by the Observer at the beginning of the year has taken on a life of its own. Having lived up to the ‘one to watch’ status, Skippa is now ready to take things to the next level as he cements his place among dancehall’s best.

World.title: Hyundai Jamaica goes elite
World.content:
Hyundai Jamaica’s launched its Palisade Elite Club programme on September 11. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Magna Motors, local dealers for the Hyundai line of vehicles, launched its Palisade Elite Club on Friday, September 11, at the official residence of the Mexican Ambassador to Jamaica Roberto Canseco Martínez in Cherry Garden, St Andrew.

“The Palisade Elite Club is something really special, and it’s a nice package for our customers who are interested in the 2026 Palisade. There are so many benefits, as we want to take care of our customers beyond buying a vehicle,” Carla Hollingsworth, marketing manager, Magna Motors, told the

Jamaica Observer’s weekly Auto magazine.

Purchasers of a 2026 Hyundai Palisade, the brand’s flagship model, will be immediately enrolled in this programme that boasts a large number of free benefits. Beyond the initial welcome package, Palisade Elite Club members receive a loaner vehicle during servicing with a dedicated service manager, premium detailing, airport concierge service that includes complimentary transfers twice a year, vehicle buy-back at a guaranteed value, and five years of service coverage. Non-vehicle related extras include airport lounge access.

The three-row premium SUV that is the Palisade is available in two trims, diesel and hybrid; both have all-wheel drive as standard.

“The Palisade Elite Club just makes sense for Hyundai Jamaica as we are a value-added brand globally. This is our way of stepping up that bar for our Hyundai Elite customers,” said Hollingsworth.

World.title: ‘I did not trip’: Dr Gabrielle Henry speaks on terrifying fall in new interview
World.content:
Miss Universe Jamaica 2025 Dr Gabrielle Henry .

Former Miss Universe Jamaica Dr Gabrielle Henry says moments before her serious and traumatic fall during the Miss Universe 2025 competition, she had simply been following instructions given to her by organisers.

“I stopped when I was told to stop, I looked at the cameras and then when I was instructed to go I turned to the left, which I was instructed to do,” she told Good Morning America (GMA), recalling the November 19, 2025 incident publicly for the first time, almost a year later.

At home, the video of her tumble generated shock and concern for the pageant queen, with Jamaicans offering prayers and well wishes.

The fall upended Henry’s life, shattering her dreams of representing Jamaica, she explained.

Henry’s disappointment was shared by her countrymen and was compounded by a series of prior shocks, including the Reggae Boyz’ failure to qualify for the World Cup and the passage of Hurricane Melissa.

“The devil may try to sabotage, but God’s purpose prevails! Get well soon, Gabby! We’re rooting for you to come back stronger and conquer the finals,” one user had posted under the Miss Universe Jamaica statement on Instagram.

Henry told GMA that after the fall, she was completely confused and disoriented, repeatedly blacking out for days.

“I have no recollection of the fall; I just know that the bottom of that hole was a concrete base, the first memory I have is that of waking up to my mother who was looking down on me. It was the first time I have ever seen my mother look so concerned, as soon as I saw my mom I blacked out again.” she shared.

When she regained consciousness fully, she was told she had received an intracranial haemorrhage and facial and back injuries.

“[A] brain injury is one of the most traumatising things; I would not wish it on my worst enemy. There is almost an out-of-body experience… it took me so long to get back to that place where I said, ‘This is MY body,’” Henry said in the report.

The doctor described the road to recovery as long and challenging, marked by sleepless nights and severe pain.

When asked who was to blame for the accident, she emphasised that she had not tripped and the fall could absolutely have been avoided.

“Proper measures should have and could have been put in place, it was the responsibility of those who had organised the stage who had put in the lighting to ensure that the protective mechanisms were also there,” she stressed.

Her comments align with allegations in a lawsuit she has filed against Miss Universe Organisation alleging that she was following rehearsed choreography when she fell into the unmarked hole.

READ: Dr Gabrielle Henry sues Miss Universe organisation over 2025 fall

The organisation in the wake of the lawsuit, has said they covered all of Gabrielle’s medical expenses in Thailand and “stood by her”.

The doctor confirmed that the pageant organisers had indeed supported her in the initial stages, including in Thailand however: “Following my return to Jamaica, I have not had much feedback from them as it pertains to covering my medical expenses which are still ongoing.”

The doctor is hoping to get back to practising ophthalmology eventually but noted that she has a long recovery ahead of her.

World.title: MINING MESS
World.content:
Mining and quarrying operation in progress Stock photo

THREE mining companies owed the Government penalties to the tune of US$13.7 million (approximately $2.2 billion) at the end of 2025 after they failed to rehabilitate 264.14 hectares of mined-out land as required by law.

At the same time, the March 2026 Schedule of the Mines and Geology Division (MGD) of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries identified US$828,000 in royalty principal and US$2.58 million in interest and penalties outstanding from two operators.

These are among the key findings of a performance audit by the Auditor General’s Department (AGD) dated July 2026, of the licensing, monitoring and enforcement actions of the MGD.

The audit report was tabled in the House of Representatives on Tuesday.

Auditor General Pamela Monroe Ellis noted in her overview that the MGD is responsible for regulating the sector under the Mining Act of 1947 and the Quarries Control Act 1984, to ensure that mining and quarrying operations are properly authorised, monitored, and enforced in keeping with the law and the public interest.

The audit found that one lessee accounted for 169.68 hectares (64 per cent of the area not rehabilitated) and US$9.89 million (72 per cent of the total monetary exposure).

“The weaknesses in enforcement were linked to the absence of a single, auditable, rehabilitation register; non-use of the security deposit mechanism during the review period, and the absence of finalised rehabilitation guidelines for quarries.

“Consequently, MGD could not demonstrate that all lease renewals were supported by the required information, reducing assurance that operators had the financial capacity to meet their obligations, and that Government had adequate protection, through the security deposit, against future rehabilitation or restoration costs,” said Monroe Ellis.

She added, “The long-outstanding rehabilitation obligations remained unresolved, and MGD could not demonstrate that the polluter-pays principle embedded in Sections 53A–55 of the Mining Regulations was being effectively enforced.”

Monroe Ellis said the audit assessed whether MGD’s licensing, monitoring, and enforcement arrangements were effective in supporting orderly and compliant mining and quarrying operations for the period 2019-2020 to 2023-2024.

“In particular, the audit examined whether applications were properly assessed before approval, inspection activities were adequately planned and targeted, breaches were followed up in a timely and consistent manner, and whether MGD maintained reliable records to support regulatory decisions,” she explained.

Among the other key findings was that one operator continued mining for six years after its licence had expired, in breach of Sections 25 and 31 of the Mining Act and Section 8 of the Quarries Control Act.

Monroe Ellis also found that six quarry operators continued operations after their quarry licences had expired. Five of them submitted renewal applications between 30 and approximately 607 days after expiry, while one submitted no renewal application.

“MGD also did not consistently issue reminder notices before licences ended, or take timely enforcement action after expiry. Continued operation beyond the authorised licence period weakened the licensing regime; reduced the deterrent effect of enforcement; and increased risks related to revenue collection, environmental oversight, and public confidence in the regulatory system,” said Monroe Ellis.

She also pointed out that mining leases were renewed without key documents, and the resulting risk materialised in unenforced rehabilitation obligations.

The auditor general explained that the Mining Act, and the Mining Regulations, require that lease renewals be supported by current financial statements, evidence of public notice to allow objections, and security deposits or letters of guarantee sufficient to protect the Government against rehabilitation or restoration costs.

“The regulations also require mined-out lands to be rehabilitated within the prescribed time frame; with statutory tools such as security deposits, restoration bonds, and penalty assessments to be used to enforce rehabilitation obligations.”

According to the audit, of the eight active operators reviewed, only four submitted up to date financial statements, two submitted none, and two submitted outdated statements.

“Further, there was evidence of public notice being issued for only four of the eight leases. In addition, four of the operators that were non-bauxite entities did not provide the required security deposits.”

Monroe Ellis said MGD advised that the security deposit requirement had been relaxed to promote investment but did not provide documented approval for this concession.

The audit also found that quarry inspections were not guided by a documented risk-based approach.

Said Monroe Ellis: “Good practice for regulatory oversight requires that inspection activities be guided by a documented, risk-based methodology. MGD’s own operational plans and the Quarries Control Act envisage inspection frequency and priorities being determined by risk factors such as size of operation, environmental sensitivity, compliance history and complaints, with inspection targets assigned and monitored.”

Yet, MGD did not have a documented method for prioritising quarry inspections, and managed only 243 inspections in fiscal year 2022/23 against a target of 400.

According to the audit, royalty arrears and quarry tax obligations were not systematically tracked.

It said MGD did not maintain accurate records on the status of royalty payments and quarry taxes, and the records were not reconciled in a timely manner.

Alarmingly, the audit also found that enforcement records were incomplete, even while MGD’s standard operating procedures require the maintenance of complete and reliable records of enforcement action, including reported breaches, investigations, referrals, corrective action, and outcomes.

“We could not confirm that enforcement action was consistently pursued for 14 of the 15 illegal quarrying cases recorded in MGD’s complaints register,” said Monroe Ellis. She outlined that nine police reports were reviewed; however, only one matched an entry in the register and showed evidence of follow-up actions.

World.title: Chuck to meet with protesting lawyers over Firearms Act discontent
World.content:
Several members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island armed with placards outside the Supreme Court on King Street in downtown Kingston Wednesday morning demanding that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 be addressed through meaningful reforms. (Photo: Karl Mclarty)

JUSTICE Minister Delroy Chuck on Wednesday voiced disappointment with the protest action taken by members of the defence bar to show discontent with the 2022 Firearms Act, but said it is hoped that a meeting scheduled for 2:00 pm today will help stave off further plans by the attorneys to abandon the courts all of next week if their demands are not met.

“I am really disappointed that members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association have taken the action today by demonstrating around the Supreme Court. On Sunday, September 13 during the Assize service I indicated that the matter was under consideration and told the association that I was prepared to meet with them,” the justice minister said.

In referencing the pending meeting today, he said the “government is very concerned about the prevalence of gun crimes and the need to protect law-abiding citizens of this country but remains open to dialogue on the Firearms Act 2022”.

Wednesday, members of the Jamaican Bar Association and the Advocates’ Association in association with bar associations across the island, armed with placards, demanded that their concerns about the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022 and its impact on “justice, due process, and the rule of law” be taken on board for reform.

The protest came just over a week after the justice minister’s comments at the annual Assize Service of the judiciary. Chuck, in his statements which evoked inflamed commentary from several quarters, said while the mandatory minimum sentences contained in the provision were being reviewed because of widespread concerns, “the security forces and a number of my colleagues feel that the Act is working and it is bringing down murders and shootings”.

“It is under consideration, but firearms are a major problem in our country, and that is why we don’t want to send a signal that we are going to relent on the enforcement to condemn the possession and the use of firearms. But it is under consideration,” the justice minister said then.

A week later, Saturday, September 19, members of Jamaica’s legal profession met to consider what they described as “the operation and impact of the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, particularly its mandatory sentencing provisions and the restrictions placed on judicial discretion”.

In a statement issued following that meeting, the attorneys said, “The legal profession supports strong and effective laws to combat gun violence and punish those who use illegal firearms to murder, rob, terrorise and intimidate our citizens. Our concern is not with strong penalties. Our concern is with a sentencing regime that does not adequately allow judges to distinguish between offenders, offences, and individual circumstances.”

The Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, which prescribes a mandatory 15-year sentence for violations, took effect in November 2022 and, among other things, provides penalties ranging from 15 years to life imprisonment for possession of illegal weapons, and establishes a dual regime — distinguishing between prohibited weapons or unregulated firearms and connected activities and firearms that are duly authorised or registered.

According to the advocates, their meeting on Saturday “identified several areas of serious concern, including the restriction of judicial discretion; the proportionality of mandatory minimum sentences in individual cases; the diminished incentive for early guilty pleas; the resulting increase in matters proceeding to trial and pressure on an already burdened criminal justice system; the treatment of imitation firearms; and the consequences of certain provisions for licensed firearm holders”.

“The legal profession is calling for urgent amendments to the Act, including consideration of an ‘exceptional circumstances’ provision allowing judges appropriate discretion in deserving cases, meaningful sentencing incentives for early guilty pleas, reform of the certificate regime, and a review of the provisions governing imitation firearms and licensed firearm holders. The profession also calls for urgent, structured consultation with the Government, Opposition, Parliament, judiciary, and other relevant stakeholders on the proposed amendments,” the attorneys said in that statement.

Noting that the “concerns are not new” as members of the legal profession and civil society have “written, spoken publicly and proposed amendments”, the professionals said “the time has now come for action”.

They said following those extensive discussions, the meeting resolved to pursue collective action, including a silent protest outside the Supreme Court on Wednesday, September 23 followed by the withdrawal of legal services from criminal courts for one week commencing Monday, September 28.

Wednesday’s protest action was, however, not sanctioned by all segments of the defence bar, with some attorneys voicing discontent over the method employed.

One attorney, in a biting commentary on a social media platform, said while he understood the reason for the concern, professional associations are expected to maintain a high level of discourse without resorting to making public spectacles.

Yesterday, attorney Tamika Harris, a member of the Bar Council of the Jamaican Bar Association and chair of its Criminal Practice and Procedure Subcommittee who was a key figure behind the protest, said the meeting this afternoon will inform the posture of defence attorneys in the island’s courts next week.

World.title: ‘Do not sleep on Jamaican talent’
World.content:
Delroy Lindo.

For veteran actor Delroy Lindo, Jabari’s People is more than another film project. It is an opportunity to give back to the country of his parents and tell a Jamaican story that he believes deserves to be seen by the world.

The 73-year-old British-born American actor, who recently earned his first Academy Award nomination for his performance in Ryan Coogler’s Sinners, is currently in Jamaica wrapping production on Jabari’s People, his feature directorial début, in which he also stars.

Lindo, who was born in London to Jamaican parents, and whose family has roots in Ocho Rios, St Ann, said he has long searched for a meaningful way to contribute to the island.

The opportunity to contribute eventually came through film when the screenplay for Jabari’s People came his way more than a decade ago.

“This script came to me in 2015,” he said. “This is potentially an opportunity for me to substantively contribute to Jamaica, to make a creative gesture that I feel enhances and contributes to Jamaican culture and also to export Jamaica globally in terms of presenting a story about Jamaica that is an affirmation of the people, the spirituality and the culture.”

Jabari’s People follows a troubled New York teenager grappling with the death of his mother who is sent to Jamaica to live with his grandfather.

For Lindo, the film also presents an opportunity to show an image of Jamaica that he believes has too often been overlooked on-screen.

“It’s not about gangsters, it’s not about ganja, and there’s nothing wrong with ganja, but it is a very different presentation of Jamaica… It is wholesome and it is investigating who we are as Jamaicans,” he explained.

That approach, however, has presented challenges in attracting financing, with Lindo saying some potential Hollywood investors were hesitant to support a Jamaican film that did not lean into familiar stereotypes.

The production has instead received backing from private investors, including Sue Rockefeller, Regina K Scully, Melony Lewis, and Adam Lewis.

The project has also sought support through the Jamaica Screen Development Initiative, the Government’s financing programme aimed at strengthening the local screen industry.

Beyond telling a different Jamaican story, Lindo said one of his priorities from the outset was ensuring Jamaicans played a significant role in bringing it to life.

“From the beginning it was my objective to employ as many Jamaicans as we could, and that’s what we have done,” Lindo shared. “Do not sleep on the talent that is here. As far as the Jamaican Government is concerned, wealthy individuals, who have the capacity to support the growth of Jamaican film, please do so.”

He acknowledged that some of the talent on the island remains underdeveloped, but argued that greater investment and opportunities could change that.

“Some of that talent is raw, no question, but what it needs is the nurturing, the support, because in the final analysis the talent that is here can have global impact,” he charged.

Jamaican-Canadian costume designer Antoinette Messam, whose credits include The Harder They Fall, Creed, and The Book of Clarence, echoed Lindo’s call for greater investment in Jamaica’s film ecosystem.

Messam said building a sustainable industry requires productions to deliberately spend locally and, equally, requires Jamaican businesses to position themselves to supply the needs of those productions.

“We want to spend the money locally. We want to keep the money in Jamaica. It is nothing for me to have the buyer in Miami ship me clothes because it is actually easier. But, if we are going to fund, finance, and create with local actors, local talent, local hair and make-up… if I want to keep the money here, I need you as a vendor to support me,” she said.

Messam, who previously worked with Lindo on The Harder They Fall, said her connection to Jabari’s People was also deeply personal.

“I love the heart of the story. I recognise that story. That story we have heard many times during our lives — if not from our family, through someone else’s family.”

The production has also tapped the experience of Jamaican Canadian producer Lena Cordina, whose credits include television productions such as Reasonable Doubt, The Hot Zone, and Hemlock Grove.

Cordina said she was particularly interested in the project because it offered a Jamaican story outside of the portrayals that have frequently dominated international screens, while acknowledging that securing investment for films outside established commercial formula remains difficult.

For Cordina, the value of productions such as Jabari’s People extends beyond what eventually appears on screen. She pointed to the wider economic activity generated when an international-standard production operates locally and employs Jamaican workers and businesses.

“From the parking lots, to the hotels, to the waiters that get tips in the restaurant, it helps the whole economy,” she said.

For Lindo, however, the ambition remains both economic and cultural, to demonstrate that Jamaica possesses the people, stories, and creative capacity to produce work capable of reaching audiences far beyond its shores.

And, after decades of searching for the right way to give something back to the country that shaped his family, Jabari’s People appears to have provided him with that opportunity.

World.title: Von der Leyen ally slams EU Commission’s AI response
World.content:
The enforcement of the EU's 2024 AI Act, which mandates that companies take measures to avoid losing control of their models, "is not on the level [where] we would like to have it," he added.

The comments shine the spotlight on the European Commission's Artificial Intelligence Office, which was put in charge of enforcing the AI Act in August.

Voss also said the Commission's overall response to the fast pace of technological developments is lagging, singling out von der Leyen's State of the Union last week.

"The Commission ... also the State of the Union is not ambitious enough regarding digital developments," said Voss, who is a member of the German Christian Democratic CDU, to which von der Leyen belongs.

One area where Voss sees a need for further regulation is liability of AI companies when their technology does damage. "What has been wrong from the beginning of this mandate is not to think about liability of AI," he said. "This can have an effect on every company."

POLITICO reported Monday that other European Parliament members have floated a proposal to add product liability provisions to address gaps in the AI Act.

World.title: Pope’s artificial intelligence guru admits he doesn’t use AI
World.content:
Pressed on whether he had any principled objection to the technology, he declared, “I’m quite willing and happy to learn,” he added. “I feel it’s my moral duty also to use it so that I have personal experience, and I hope it helps me with my work.”

Speaking on the fringes of Axel Springer’s WELT AI Summit in Berlin, Czerny called on European politicians and bishops to respond more clearly to warnings about the risks of frontier AI models forfeiting human control and oversight.

“There should be a dialogue between the bishops and the European governments to express the concern of the population to handle this with openness and with creativity … Otherwise, we will say five months or five years from now, ‘Oh, I felt there was a disaster coming, but there was nothing I could do.’”

The Roman Catholic Church is stepping up involvement in recent discussions over the future of AI. Paolo Benanti, the Vatican’s adviser on AI, attended a meeting of tech executives convened by King Charles III in Scotland last week to discuss the opportunities and risks surrounding the technology.

World.title: Deutschland und Spanien zetteln Papierkrieg zu „Made in Europe“-Auslegung an
World.content:
In der EU geht es um Aufträge, die einen erheblichen Teil der Wirtschaftsleistung ausmachen. Von Windparks bis hin zu Stahl und Zement für den Bau von Autobahnen und U-Bahnen.

Deutschland, das Exportkraftzentrum der Union, dringt auf eine breiter angelegte „Made with Europe“-Definition. Dies entspricht auch weitgehend dem ursprünglichen Vorschlag der Kommission. Er sieht die Aufnahme von Partnern vor, die Freihandels- oder Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben oder einer Zollunion mit der Union angehören. Der Kreis könnte bis zu 80 Länder umfassen.

„Deutschland lehnt Protektionismus und Diskriminierung ab“, heißt es in dem deutschen Papier. „Die EU muss ein verlässlicher Partner für ihre Freihandelspartner bleiben und ihren rechtlichen Verpflichtungen nachkommen.“ Außerdem wird darin eine „Opt-in“-Möglichkeit gefordert, um Staaten einzubeziehen, die EU-Firmen eine entsprechende Behandlung gewähren.

Dem deutschen Papier haben sich bisher keine anderen EU-Länder angeschlossen. Frankreich, die zweitgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Union, dringt wie Spanien in die entgegengesetzte Richtung und plädiert für einen restriktiveren Ansatz.

Der französische Industrieminister Sébastien Martin bestritt zwar nicht, dass Europa gegenüber Handelspartnern offen bleiben müsse, betonte jedoch, dass öffentliches Geld in die Produktion in Europa fließen müsse.

„Auch in Zukunft wird es möglich sein, Produkte zu haben, bei denen ein Teil der Wertschöpfung aus anderen Ländern stammt, aber die Produktion muss in Europa stattfinden, damit sie für öffentliche Fördermittel infrage kommen“, sagte Martin bei seiner Ankunft zur Sitzung am Donnerstag in Brüssel.

World.title: 2027 : LE BAROMÈTRE DU REJET
World.content:
Tondelier et Mélenchon en tête

A ce stade de la campagne, c’est… Marine Tondelier qui remporte la palme du rejet, talonnée par Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Pas moins de 81% des sondés situent en effet entre 0 et 3 les chances qu’ils votent un jour pour la candidate Ecologiste. Ils sont 73% à en dire de même pour l’Insoumis, et même 98% à 100% chez les catégories de la population “réfractaires”, “autoritaires”, “anti-assistanat”, “traditionnalistes”, ou encore “libéraux”, selon la classification de Cluster 17.

Une différence majeure, toutefois, entre les deux principaux épouvantails de notre classement : là où seuls 9% de personnes interrogées jugent qu’il y a une probabilité forte ou très forte (entre 7 et 10) qu’ils glissent “un jour” un bulletin dans l’urne pour Tondelier, ils sont 19% à se voir probablement ou très probablement voter pour l’Insoumis en chef — soit l’équivalent des intentions de vote en sa faveur pour le premier tour de la présidentielle, à ce stade de la campagne et telles que mesurées par Cluster 17. Le socle de ceux qui adhèrent positivement aux propositions du candidat Mélenchon est donc nettement plus important. Et c’est particulièrement notable chez les jeunes : 42% des 18-34 ans jugent probables ou très probables (entre 7 et 10) les chances qu’ils votent pour l’Insoumis.

A noter : le fort rejet suscité dans une partie de la population par Marine Tondelier, notamment “dans tout l’espace conservateur”, a beaucoup à voir, selon Jean-Yves Dormagen, avec le “problème d’image” de son parti : “Les Verts sont très clivants sur les questions culturelles et sociétales, et l’écologie est devenue clivante aussi. Ils sont perçus comme très radicaux, promigrations, et ultraprogressistes”, note-t-il, soulignant que cette structure d’image est comparable à celle des Insoumis.

Le Pen et Philippe : même rejet

Autres enseignements majeurs de notre baromètre pour la présidentielle : les candidats les plus centraux ne sont pas en reste quand il s’agit de rejet. Les Français sont respectivement 68%, 72% et 66% à juger faible ou nulle la probabilité qu’ils votent pour Edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal et Raphaël Glucksmann dans les temps à venir, et 69% pour le candidat des Républicains Bruno Retailleau. Et c’est bien Marine Le Pen qui est la moins rejetée : ils ne sont “que” 62% à déclarer que la probabilité qu’ils votent pour elle est faible ou nulle, contre 30% à l’envisager sérieusement (probabilité forte ou très forte, estimée entre 7 et 10).

Encore un peu plus dans le détail : 56% des personnes sondées jugent strictement impossible de voter pour Marine Le Pen (soit une note de 0 sur 10 ou une déclaration explicite de l’exclure), à touche-touche avec Edouard Philippe (55%), et à peine pire que Raphaël Glucksmann (53%). Ils sont en revanche respectivement 68% et 66% à l’exclure tout aussi catégoriquement quand il s’agit de Marine Tondelier et Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

La peur ou le rejet de l’Insoumis s’explique en partie dans le détail des traits d’image des candidats : Mélenchon est ainsi celui qui se voit le plus reprocher “un risque de dérive autoritaire” — le risque est estimé à 6,7 sur 10 en moyenne — devant Marine Le Pen, pour qui ce sujet est toutefois aussi un point faible (risque estimé à 5,6 sur 10 en moyenne).

World.title: Switzerland’s neutrality vote puts Russia sanctions on the line
World.content:
“It’s not a vote against neutrality — neutrality is very supported — it’s about what neutrality means,” said Fabio Wasserfallen, a professor of European politics at the University of Bern and a pollster at LeeWas.

But the referendum reaches beyond the Alpine nation. It raises the question of how neutral a country can remain in the current European security landscape — where Russia is waging war against Ukraine and the continent's traditional reliance on U.S. security guarantees is under threat.

Other neutral nations such as Austria and Ireland are looking to increase defense spending and build closer ties with NATO.

Under the current system, Switzerland's permanent neutrality is recognized in international law, but Bern retains discretion over how it applies its broader neutrality policy — and ultimately has the sovereign right to alter or abandon that status.

While it is barred from taking part in wars between states or providing military support, the government can decide whether to impose economic sanctions or cooperate with military alliances without joining them.

“Currently, the government has a bit of room to maneuver and uses it. The question of that referendum is whether people think that’s good or whether there should be stricter boundaries toward neutrality,” Wasserfallen said.

World.title: The Pope is fretting about frontier AI — what’s the EU’s answer?
World.content:
European lawmakers this week called for the EU’s artificial intelligence regulations to hold American tech companies liable for the risks their most advanced models pose to humanity. But how much sway does Europe have in an arms race dominated by the U.S. and China?

Host Anne McElvoy has been in Berlin attending WELT’s AI Summit, which brings together the AI and tech business leaders from across Europe with other interested parties. They include Cardinal Michael Czerny, who Pope Leo recently appointed to chair the Vatican’s Commission on AI. He tells Anne that European politicians need to heed warnings over the development of frontier AI models and enter a dialogue with the Catholic Church.

She also explores the wider questions of AI regulation with Axel Voss, who sits on the European Parliament’s Committee on Legal Affairs, and Pieter Haeck, senior technology reporter at POLITICO.
