World.title: Boredom, ranting and clowns: Welcome to the UN’s big bash
World.content:
However, the best-ever political doodler is surely South Korean lawmaker Yoo Young-ha, who was caught sketching a gorilla on his laptop during a parliamentary audit session in 2025. To be clear, there wasn’t a gorilla in the parliament for a life-drawing session (and, at the time of writing, my suggestion to release large primates into European Parliament plenary sessions is still being considered by the Conference of Presidents).

The excitement at this year’s big U.N. bash didn’t stop at, er, man loses interest and starts looking at social media. Oh, no. There was also the choice of music before Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio took the stage to talk about Greenland — “Send in the Clowns.”

Denmark said it had nothing to do with the choice of tune. A spokesperson for the European Clown Association said they couldn’t comment until their father returned from sick leave. They clearly had big shoes to fill.

But there have been far more explosive moments at the U.N. General Assembly over the years. In 2009, Libya’s Moammar Gadhafi ignored his 15-minute speaking limit and launched into a 96-minute rant, during which he ripped a page of the U.N. Charter in half (and he was introduced as “the king of kings,” which is also my work nickname).

And in 2015, Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe defended his anti-LGBTQ+ stance by yelling “we are not gays” into the microphone (OK mate, we get it, you don’t like gay people).

Most incendiary of all, last year the U.N. appeared to be suffering from the cost-of-living crisis just as much as the rest of us, resorting to using Ikea furniture. What looked suspiciously like a LACK side table — available in black, brown and white, and yours for just €9.99 — was placed between Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Trump during a meeting.

World.title: European bond yields ease after sell-off as US mortgage rates hit a high in Trump’s term
World.content:
The relief in European bonds on Friday morning is small and follows one of the sharpest bond routs in years.

 

The yield on France’s 10-year OAT was trading around 4.67% on Friday morning, down from around 4.7% earlier, while the yield on Germany’s 10-year Bund was around 3.59%, down from 3.61%.

The gap between French and German 10-year borrowing costs, the clearest gauge of the risk premium investors attach to Paris, blew past 110 basis points this week, its widest since the 2012 eurozone debt crisis.

The move reflects investors’ concerns about France’s debt and election risks, which were further amplified by ratings agency Scope’s downgrade of France. Investors are also weighing the risk of a 2027 presidential run-off between the far right and the far left. The cost of insuring French debt against default has also climbed to its highest in nearly a decade.

However, the bigger story was in the US.

The 30-year Treasury yield climbed to its highest level since 2004 this week, touching around 5.5%, as a fresh jump in oil prices compounded worries over persistent inflation and swelling government debt.

The 10-year Treasury yield, which anchors US mortgage rates, reached levels last seen in 2007.

US homebuyers are feeling the wider rise in borrowing costs: the average 30-year mortgage rate hit 7% this week, roughly a percentage point above where it stood before the Iran war began, and reached its highest level since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025.

Why bonds and stocks fall together

The unusual part is that bonds have stopped acting as a safe haven precisely when stocks have wobbled.

"Bonds and stocks are falling due to inflation," said Nick Saunders, CEO of online investment platform Webull UK.

Energy shocks and war have pushed prices higher while growth has slowed, and normally falling stocks would send investors into bonds. This time, with interest rates not falling, "the traditional safe haven" is less appealing.

Saunders pointed to the early 1970s, when a similar combination of energy shocks and wage pressure sent UK gilt yields soaring while stocks fell 73%, though he noted that today's economies are far less oil-intensive and labour markets have more slack to absorb creeping inflation.

Inflation-linked bonds, gold and other assets decoupled from stocks offer some shelter, Saunders said, though "it would be wrong to abandon bonds entirely."

Oxford Economics takes a calmer view of the broader move.

"We see the interest rate spike as mostly temporary, largely reflecting a repricing of monetary policy responses to surging energy prices," said lead economists Ricardo Amaro and Daniel Kral. They added that most government budgets can absorb higher rates given the long average maturity of their debt.

However, France and, to a lesser extent, Italy are exceptions. In a severe scenario, both would "need to tighten fiscal policy by over one percentage point of GDP to offset sustained rises in interest costs," the economists said. Spain, Greece and Portugal are better placed to withstand the pressure.

World.title: Could the EU AI Act deter 'housefishing' in European real estate?
World.content:
When scrolling online for a place to live, you might come across a bright-colored house for sale listed online with fall foliage and folksy furniture.

 

But then you notice that a few things look off: deformed electrical outlets or furniture that looks too big for the room. A floor lamp is coming out of a table in one picture and does not appear in the next, or the same piece of artwork is found in every room.

Real estate images like this are, most likely, made with AI. Listers are increasingly using digital platforms to spruce up living spaces for sale. Several online forums have called out AI real estate photos for being misleading and untrustworthy.

A user on an Irish housing subreddit posted side-by-side photos of a house with furniture, plants, and decorations and the real-life empty house. But in the AI version, the couch is blocking the stairs and the living room wall is bigger.

“AI now being used by estate agents to sell houses. Is this even legal?” the user wrote on 22 September.

Real estate agents have long used staging to help their clients visualize the potential of a space. Adding a sofa or bright flowers can make an empty apartment seem more appealing and livable.

But staging a place takes a lot of time and money. AI can speed up the process and cost much less — or almost nothing at all.

Some argue that virtually staging with AI is similar to normal staging — it just uses a new technology, says Steven Lee from the Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents.

“Agents already use home staging to make a place look nicer when you visit it,” Lee said. “So this is basically easier and cheaper to do, of course, on a computer.”

Yet changing the appearance of a home or apartment with AI could possibly trick some into believing a room is much bigger or a kitchen has more modern appliances. This is a particular concern for those relocating to a new city who may not be able to see a listing in person.

Sometimes it is hard to tell when an image is real or altered. The elderly are especially susceptible to AI deception, and some do not know what a deepfake is.

Claudio Teixeira is the head of digital policy at the European Consumer Organization. He said AI deceit in online marketplaces, such as the housing industry, are not talked about enough.

“Not everyone has the capability to see at first glance that this is indeed not real,” Teixeira said. “So this content needs to have a clear warning that it is AI generated.”

New EU regulation might help

New EU AI transparency rules may prevent the practice known as “housefishing.”

Article 50 of the EU AI Act, which became applicable in early August, requires AI-generated or modified content to be labeled.

The EU classifies an image of an apartment that is “furnished using AI” as partially AI-modified and requires the photos to have an AI transparency icon.

“Article 50 is more or less an expression of this protection of fundamental rights,” said CMS senior law associate David Rappenglück, who monitors applications of the act. “The message is basically quite easy: if you, as a customer or a bidder, are confronted with a picture which might be AI generated or manipulated, you should be informed about it.”

The providers of AI content, a company that develops AI systems such as Open AI or Anthropic, must label images in a machine-readable format. A deployer, someone who uses an AI system to create or enhance an image, must also include a visible label on the image.

But if a deployer does not label an image, it can be difficult for a regular person to check if AI has been involved at the provider level.

In order to check, they must plug the machine-readable code into another website which verifies it, said Akvilė Šikšniūtė, who works on the digital policy team in the European Consumer Organization. The extra step is often not very clear.

“I think we're still quite far away to the point where the consumers feel that they have places to turn to if they feel like they're misled or the content that they're seeing is not accurate,” said Šikšniūtė.

At what point should AI be labeled?

Using AI to add minor details such as changing the lighting or color of a wall is very different from expanding a room or creating an entirely new image. But the AI Act does not distinguish between partial manipulation or full generation, according to Rappenglück.

People may not know if an image is just slightly modified or entirely changed. So how do we determine what should be labeled? The details remain uncertain.

“It isn't clear because, for example, very subtle changes like changing a background wall could be considered as a minor change that AI was used to change that. Therefore, it perhaps would not even be marked,” said Šikšniūtė.

“I feel like this is where perhaps the misconception comes from for consumers slightly, because we expect now from all the communications we see that all the content will be labeled, and that's not the case,” she said.

Practical enforcement remains unclear

The punishment for not labeling content is steep. Those who do not follow the act could be fined up to €15 million or 3% of their worldwide turnover.

“We as lawyers would really recommend taking this quite seriously,” Rappenglück said.

“There's quite a hard enforcement mechanism and it's also enforced by the national authorities.”

Because the act only came into force last month, there are still a lot of unknowns about how it will work, and enforcement remains difficult in practice.

According to Rappenglück, images can be screenshotted and reported to the national government.

But because real estate moves so quickly, listings may only be up for a few days. That makes it harder for individual cases to be monitored.

“How do you actually ensure accountability of this sector to make sure that these practices do not gain hold? Right now, the apparatus is clear that this is not happening,” Teixeira said.

The industry itself is trying to enforce AI transparency. The Professional Institute of Real Estate Agents in Belgium is currently updating their code of ethics to align with the rules of Article 50.

A real estate agent remains responsible for what they publish. They can use AI but only if they disclose it, said Lee.

“They have to follow the code of ethics to be able to exercise their activities. And if they don't, I'm afraid they can get into quite a bit of trouble,” Lee said.

It is case-by-case, but that trouble could include suspension or revocation of their license.

Next steps

AI deception is happening beyond housing, in many different sectors. Teixeira hopes that AI enforcement becomes stronger and that consumers are not held to blame for falling for fraud.

“It must be a whole system at work, in order not just to ensure the consumers have more information to make our decisions, but also if everything fails, to ensure that rogue actors who are going on a rampage to make content more engaging by changing it willfully into something which they know is not true,” Teixeira said.

World.title: Finland and Sweden scramble Quick Reaction Alert jets to intercept Russian aircraft
World.content:
Finland's air force said on Friday that Swedish and Finnish fighter jets had been scrambled to identify Russian fighter jets flying over the Gulf of Finland.

 

The air force said that the two Nordic countries' Quick Reaction Alert (QRA) jets had been scrambled on Thursday.

They had identified a Russian detachment consisting of a Tu-134 transport aircraft, MiG-31 fighter jets and Su-30 fighter jets "in international airspace over the Gulf of Finland."

According to the military it was the first joint operational "identification mission" for the two air forces.

Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson commented on the operation on X, saying that "the Baltic Sea has never been as vulnerable as it is now - but it has also never been better protected than it is right now."

Tensions over the Baltic Sea have risen sharply in recent years and Nordic jets are regularly scrambled to intercept Russian aircraft.

In the wake of Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Sweden and Finland both dropped decades of military non-alignment and joined NATO.

A MiG-31 fighter of the Russian air force takes off at an air base during military drills in Tver region, 14 February, 2022 AP Photo

The incident came on the same day that the Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said that the risk of Russian military action against NATO countries was growing and an outright invasion was "highly unlikely" but possible.

"There is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia," Thomas Ahrenkiel, the head of the DDIS, told a press conference at which he presented an updated assessment of the threat from Russia.

He said that the agency still considered it "highly unlikely that Russia would see any interest in invading a NATO country, but we cannot rule it out".

In the DDIS assessment, the agency said that Russia would likely carry out more so-called "hybrid attacks" against targets in the West.

It noted that in the past such attacks had "mainly been aimed at creating fear and weakening public support for aid to Ukraine".

But they had now started to include actions meant to stop support from reaching Ukraine, such as sabotage against defence companies or railway transports carrying military equipment, the agency said.

The DDIS said it thought Russia would intensify such attacks, which could also include "destructive cyber attacks that cripple critical societal functions."

Europe on alert

European countries have been on high alert for any Russian interference, with fears that Moscow could target Kyiv's Western backers as the Kremlin's invasion of Ukraine drags on into its fifth year.

In November, NATO military officials said a new US anti-drone system had been deployed to the alliance’s eastern flank.

And following a violation of Polish airspace, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the formation of the Eastern Sentry programme, which aims to deter further Russian incursions.

Some European officials described the incidents as Moscow testing NATO’s response, which raised questions about how prepared the alliance is against potential threats from Russia.

The Kremlin has dismissed allegations that Russia is behind some of the unidentified incursions in Europe as "unfounded."

World.title: Old video of Greek protests shared with claims country is 'paralysed'
World.content:
A video of a large crowd in the Greek city of Thessaloniki has been shared online alongside claims that protests have brought the country to a standstill.

 

"Greece is paralysed", several posts say, claiming that airports, ports, factories and trains have stopped operating. Others describe massive protests erupting across the country.

The footage shows a real demonstration, but it was filmed more than a year before the posts appeared.

The posts alleging that 'Greece is paralysed' Euronews

The same footage was posted online in February 2025, when large demonstrations across Greece marked the second anniversary of the Tempi rail disaster.

In February 2023, 57 people were killed when a passenger train and a freight train collided near Tempi in central Greece, with the disaster sparking anger and calls for enhanced railway safety in the country.

The anniversary protests were accompanied by a general strike on flights, train services and ferries. Hundreds of thousands demonstrated in more than 300 cities and towns in Greece and abroad, demanding justice for the 57 people killed in 2023.

This, however, occurred in 2025. The resurfaced videos do not indicate a new shutdown in September of this year.

The disaster remains a painful issue in Greece. A criminal trial began in Larissa in March and is currently ongoing, with 36 defendants, including a station master and railway officials, facing charges connected to the collision and subsequent deaths. Relatives of the victims continue to seek answers, some of whom are giving evidence.

There were indeed protests in Greece in September: thousands of people demonstrated in Thessaloniki on 5 September 2026.

These protests surrounded the cost of living crisis and called for action on wages and pensions, coinciding with Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis' annual speech on the economy in the city.

More than 25,000 protested in Thessaloniki, according to police estimates cited by AP. Unions and other groups called for higher incomes.

These demonstrations are, however, separate from the footage posted in 2025, which is not recent.

World.title: How AI and robots provide companionship for people with Alzheimer’s
World.content:
At Paris’ Broca Hospital, elderly patients are taking part in experiments involving several different robots.

 

The NAO robot uses questions and exercises to encourage conversation and cognitive stimulation. In one session, it asks patients to complete familiar proverbs.

“I’m going to give you the beginning of a proverb, and you can try to tell me how it ends,” the robot tells them.

Another device, Paro, is designed to provide therapeutic comfort. The robotic seal is equipped with sensors that allow it to respond to a patient's movements and sounds.

Then there is Miroki, a robot designed to interact with patients through conversation.

For 72-year-old Michele, the experience is unusual but not unsettling. “No, I’m not worried, but I prefer human contact,” she says.

Patients react differently

Researchers say there is no single response to the technology. “There are all sorts of reactions,” says Lea Vecchioni, a psychologist and research engineer at the Broca Living Lab.

“Some patients are almost amazed. They find it remarkable to see in real life the sort of things they've only seen on television.” But others, she says, “clearly reject the technology and the robots”.

The researchers are looking at whether the machines can help patients engage with different forms of therapy.

“The robot can act as a facilitator that helps engage patients in therapy sessions,” says Maribel Pino, a cognitive psychology researcher and research director at the Broca Living Lab.

The potential applications include cognitive stimulation, speech and language therapy, physiotherapy and psychomotor rehabilitation.

AI personalised for each resident

In southern France, another experiment is using AI in a care home setting. At La Septfontoise in Tarn-et-Garonne, staff are testing Livana, an AI system designed to support residents when they become agitated.

The technology works through a phone and can create personalised conversations. Before the experiment began, staff collected biographical information about residents with the consent and cooperation of their families. That can include details about their interests and life stories.

The information is then used to personalise the system's voice and the content of its interactions. “The voice can have elements that help soothe the resident, based on their interests and life story,” says psychologist Elodie Jammes.

The system is being explored as a non-drug approach for residents living with Alzheimer’s or other neurodegenerative conditions.

A tool for caregivers

For La Septfontoise director Ghislaine Verines, the technology could provide another form of support for both residents and staff.

“The aim of the trial is to explore non-drug approaches that can improve residents’ wellbeing, while also providing additional support for care staff,” she says.

The experiments are taking place as researchers look for new ways of supporting people with cognitive disorders.

But Pino says the role of robotics should remain clearly defined. “I don’t think robotics should be thought of as a replacement tool,” she says.

“They are still tools, however sophisticated their conversational abilities or presence may become.” And there is one thing, she says, that technology cannot provide. “They will never replace the essential human relationships people need.”

Technology, but not instead of people

The French experiments show the range of ways AI and robotics are being explored in dementia care. Some technologies aim to stimulate conversation.

Others focus on therapy, comfort or personalised support.

But the researchers emphasise that their purpose is not to replace caregivers. Instead, the trials are testing what technology can add to care while keeping human contact at its centre.

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

World.title: India news: Elections 'rigged,' allege Rahul Gandhi and Cockroach party
World.content:
09/25/2026 September 25, 2026 Rahul Gandhi accuses Modi, Shah of being behind election 'rigging'

Gandhi accused the Prime Minister and the Home Minister of bypassing his opinion to elevate Gyanesh Kumar as the Election Commission head [FILE: July 22, 2026] Image: Sajjad Hussain/AFP

Both the opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and the Cockroach Party political movement called India’s elections "rigged," as the uproar over the Election Commission of India's (ECI) handling of the voter-list revision shows no sign of abating.

On Thursday, Congress Party leader Gandhi alleged that elections in India were being "rigged," and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. It followed a report by Indian Express on objections raised by two election commissioners to decisions related to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voter lists.

The report said that Kumar's fellow Election Commissioners had raised at least 14 objections over 10 months to decisions on voter registrations and electoral data. In one instance, one of the complaints said the ECI acted against the written advice of two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."

The three commissioners are overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), which the ECI says aims to remove deceased, relocated and duplicate voters and prevent the inclusion of "foreign illegal immigrants." Critics say the exercise has gone beyond that remit and removed millions of eligible voters, which has benefitted the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

"If the vote has been destroyed, then our Constitution has been destroyed. It no longer has power," Gandhi said during a press conference.

Gandhi also alleged that Kumar was elevated to Election Commission head by Prime Minster Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah, despite his opposition to the appointment. He went on to accuse them of being "at the top of the conspiracy," and called for them to be investigated.

Meanwhile, BJP spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi defended the ECI, saying on Thursday that the SIR process was legally sound and that the commission’s decisions were based on majority consensus. He said the law empowers the ECI to conduct an SIR at its discretion.

World.title: Italy to ban burqa in schools, limit foreign pupils
World.content:
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government has passed new school rules capping the number of students who don't speak fluent Italian and banning face coverings.

Italy's conservative government on Thursday approved a new decree banning face-covering Islamic veils — including burqas and niqabs — in schools and putting a limit on the number of students with a poor command of the Italian language in each classroom.

Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, called her Cabinet's measures "tools of common sense that do not divide," adding that they will help integration by avoiding what the right-wing leader called "ghetto classes."

She went on to say the rules would lead to all students receiving the "same opportunities."

Opposition parties and other critics have denounced the move by Meloni's government, with some calling it a "witch hunt” and others accusing the government of turning immigration into more of a political issue ahead of next year's general election.

What do Italy's new school rules entail?

The measures take effect right away but still require parliamentary approval within 60 days. Meloni's coalition currently holds a majority in the country's legislature.

Here is what the decree includes:

A per-classroom cap of 30% for foreign students who lack sufficient proficiency in Italian

In primary schools, the limit applies to pupils without Italian citizenship who were not born in Italy or did not attend at least two years of preschool

In lower and upper secondary schools, the same limit applies to students without Italian citizenship who have not attended the country's school system for at least three years

Failure to comply with the decree is punishable by a fine of up to €1,000 euros ($1,140)

Face-coverings banned in schools

The decree bans burqas and niqabs in schools but will continue to allow hijabs.

Meloni said the burqa ban was "a matter of security."

"When a woman — or worse, a young girl — is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," Meloni was quoted as saying in a television interview.

Italian Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the decree would affect about 1,000 classrooms, which come up to 0.3% of the nationwide tally.

According to official data, pupils without Italian citizenship comprised 11.2% of Italy's school population from 2022 to 2023, while classes with over 30% foreign students stood at 7.6% of the total.

What do critics say?

Opponents of the decree are worried that the new measure could force students to attend schools far from the neighborhoods where they live.

Reports have also highlighted concerns among school authorities regarding how the rules would work in areas with large migrant populations.

Independent child rights organization Save the Children had on Wednesday called on the Italian government to weigh the measure "with the utmost political responsibility,” adding that it risked creating discriminatory effects.

"Such a criterion would create ‘first-class' and 'second-class' students," the organization said in its statement.

Meanwhile, opposition leader Elly Schlein railed against the decree, accusing Meloni's government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children."

Meloni is at the head of the most right-wing government that Italy has seen since World War II.

World.title: Ethiopia: Internet disrupted in Tigray amid conflict escalation
World.content:
A web monitor reported an internet disruption in northern Ethiopia amid renewed fighting between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government.

Access to the internet has been disrupted in northern Ethiopia's Tigray region, the web monitor NetBlocks reported on Friday.

The region has been the site of renewed hostilities this week that shattered a 2022 peace deal between Ethiopia and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) militia.

During the 2020-2022 Tigray war, the region was largely cut off from the outside world and hundreds of thousands of people were left in famine-like conditions.

"Confirmed: Network data indicate a subnational disruption in ⁠northern ⁠Ethiopia corresponding to reports of a telecoms blackout in Tigray," NetBlocks said.

The cause of the disruption was not immediately clear.

The Reuters news agency cited Tigray residents saying panic buying left shop shelves empty.

"There is deep fear that banks, telecom networks, electricity and basic goods could be cut off again," a local resident told the AFP news agency, adding that there was "panic in the community."

The new rebel alliance transforming the Tigray conflict To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

TPLF offensive sparks fear of return to war

The TPLF took control of regional airports in Tigray earlier this week and also clashed with government forces in the neighboring Afar and Amhara regions. The militia said it was now in "full-blown war" with Addis Ababa.

The group also formed an anti-government alliance with the Fano militia in Amhara and five other armed groups.

In the 2022-2023 war, Fano fought alongside the federal government against the Tigrayan rebels.

The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 and was later sidelined alongside the rise of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.

World.title: How renewed fighting in Tigray could spread across the Horn of Africa
World.content:
The fresh hostilities in Ethiopia's Tigray region come after months of growing animosity between rebel forces and the federal government. Horn of Africa expert Martin Plaut warns of possible regional spillover.

Fighting has erupted again in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region. Tigrayan forces launched a major offensive on September 23, with fighting also reported in the neighboring regions of Afar and Amhara.

The escalation threatens the fragile peace established by the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war between Ethiopia's federal government in Addis Ababa and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF).

But the central question is bigger than the return of war to Tigray: could the conflict connect with the wars and rivalries already destabilizing the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea?

Martin Plaut, a British journalist and Horn of Africa expert, argues the conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia's borders.

"If a conflict were to spill over, it is quite possible that a conflict involving Eritrea and Ethiopia could then involve Sudanese forces as well, which could drag the whole region into a war," he told DW in an exclusive interview.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Jalale Getachew Birru, a senior analyst for East Africa at the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), also stressed that the conflict cannot be viewed in isolation. ACLED is an independent conflict-monitoring and research organization that collects and analyzes data on political violence and armed conflict around the world.

“The Ethiopia[n] case is not [an] isolated case for the Horn of Africa. It involves the neighboring countries as well, and it's being displayed across the Horn of Africa countries," Birru told DW.

Her assessment points to a broader regional dynamic: Ethiopia's conflict is unfolding alongside shifting alliances and competing interests in neighboring Sudan and Somalia. ACLED's current analysis likewise places the renewed Tigray conflict within a wider pattern of instability across the Horn of Africa.

The risk is not based on a single regional alliance. It comes from the fact that several conflicts are already geographically and politically connected, Birru noted.

African Union urges restraint

The African Union (AU) has also expressed deep concern about the possibility of further destabilization.

In a statement on September 23, AU Commission Chairperson Mahmoud Ali Youssouf warned that new political and military alliances risk reversing the progress made since 2020.

The AU called for an immediate end to actions that could escalate tensions, renewed direct talks under the Pretoria agreement and restraint by Ethiopia's neighbors. It also tasked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's high representative for the Horn of Africa, with supporting diplomatic efforts.

The AU's intervention reflects concerns that the crisis could have wider regional implications, including the possibility that it could interact with conflicts beyond Ethiopia's borders.

Old enemies, new alliances

The TPLF recently joined six other Ethiopian armed groups in an alliance seeking to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government. Among them is the Amhara Fano movement, which fought against the TPLF during the previous war.

The alliance is not a unified military force, and its members have different political objectives and territorial interests. But its formation could leave the Ethiopian government facing several fronts at once.

The fighting in Afar, a northeastern Ethiopian region bordering Eritrea and Djibouti, is particularly significant. The region contains the main transport corridor linking landlocked Ethiopia to Djibouti, through which much of Ethiopia's international trade passes. Sustained fighting there could therefore threaten a vital economic lifeline.

And beyond Afar lies Eritrea.

Eritrea's potential role

During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF. Since then, relations between Addis Ababa and Asmara, Eritrea's capital, have deteriorated. Ethiopia's ambitions for access to the Red Sea have added to Eritrea's security concerns.

"The war could certainly escalate, and Eritrea could become involved," Plaut said.

Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups opposed to the government, while Asmara has denied such allegations. The extent of any direct Eritrean involvement remains difficult to establish independently.

Sudan: Where conflicts could collide

Sudan has been at war since 2023 between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has drawn in regional powers and created one of the world's largest humanitarian crises.

Plaut argues that Ethiopia and Eritrea are already indirectly involved on opposing sides.

"The Ethiopians are on the side of the RSF and Hemedti," he said, referring to its commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo. "There has been strong evidence that there is a base in western Ethiopia which is supplying and training RSF fighters," Plaut added. DW has not independently verified that claim.

Explainer: How did Ethiopia's Tigray war start? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The United Arab Emirates (UAE) has faced allegations of supporting the RSF, which it denies. Plaut identifies Eritrea, Egypt and Saudi Arabia as supporting the Sudanese Armed Forces.

"So both Eritrea and Ethiopia are already playing a role, indirectly, in the war," he said.

If Ethiopia and Eritrea were to enter direct hostilities, Sudan's rival forces could have incentives to exploit the new situation, Plaut said. Fighting could put additional pressure on Sudan's eastern frontier and alter supply routes and military calculations.

Plaut sees the danger of a chain reaction: "Because you have the UAE backing the RSF and you have the Saudis backing the Eritreans and the Sudanese Armed Forces, this could all multiply and you could get one conflict leading into another."

"So the whole thing becomes a generalized conflict in the region," he said.

Red Sea connection

The Bab el-Mandeb Strait, one of the world's most important shipping choke points, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

Eritrea and Djibouti lie on its western side, Yemen on the eastern side. The war in Yemen has already shown how insecurity around the Red Sea can disrupt international shipping and draw in outside powers.

Eritrea's location and its control of the port of Assab give it strategic importance far beyond Tigray. Any major deterioration in Ethiopia-Eritrea relations could therefore affect the wider security architecture of the Red Sea.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have also developed extensive political, economic and security interests across the Horn of Africa. Their interests overlap in some areas but diverge in others, particularly over Sudan.

Danger is escalation, not inevitability

None of this means that a regional war is inevitable. There is no evidence of a single military alliance stretching from Tigray to the Gulf. Ethiopia's armed groups have competing interests, Eritrea may avoid direct intervention, and Sudan's warring parties have their own priorities.

But conflicts do not need a common command structure to become interconnected.

Ethiopia's broken Tigray peace deal opens old wounds To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Tigray war killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. The Pretoria agreement stopped the large-scale fighting, but many of the political and territorial disputes underlying the conflict remained unresolved.

Today, Tigray is again at war while Ethiopia faces several armed movements, Eritrea is a potential military actor, and Sudan is already engulfed in civil war.

Plaut warns that the humanitarian consequences could again be severe.

"There's certainly a danger of this becoming an extremely bloody conflict," he told DW. "After all, 600,000 people died in the last one in Tigray."

But he does not predict that the previous death toll will necessarily be exceeded. "Let's hope that it doesn't go in that direction," he said.

World.title: Nepal's leader says his country is paying the price of climate change
World.content:
Nepalese Prime Minister Balendra Shah called the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods a "warning to the world" — and questioned if the world had "really heard that warning."

Four weeks after catastrophic flash floods ravaged Nepal, the small Himalayan country's prime minister stood at the podium of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) to warn leaders about the impact of a warming world.

"I wish I could stand here today simply to speak about development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation. Instead, I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions," Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in his UNGA address Thursday.

Nepal's leader calls for cooperation to protect the Himalayas

The Nepalese leader stressed that the perils of climate change transcend national borders as he made a case for greater international cooperation for protecting the Himalayas.

"The Himalayas are not peripheral to the planet. They are part of the planet's life-support system," Shah said, proposing the establishment of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism, which he said would be led by Nepal, India and China.

Shah elaborated that the mechanism would help countries share satellite data and expertise, as well as monitor glacial lakes that pose a threat. He also called for stronger joint early-warning systems and coordinated, cross-border assistance in the event of a disaster.

"Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international cooperation, rather than a frontier of fragmented information," the prime minister said.

Nepal's prime minister was the youngest head of government to address the UN General Assembly Image: Ryan Murphy/Getty Images/AFP

Nepal paying 'colossal' price for climate change

Shah noted that his country contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions.

"We did not create this crisis. Yet we are paying a colossal price for it," he said, adding that he was not blaming any individual nation or continent.

"We are not here to turn climate change into another geopolitical battlefield. We are here to ask everyone to recommit to shared responsibility and solidarity," Shah said.

Grants, not loans, necessary for flood recovery

The Nepalese prime minister emphasized the principles of responsibility, reparation and resilience as he called for grant-based support rather than loans.

Shah said vulnerable nations should not be forced to take on additional debt to recover from climate catastrophes.

"When a climate-driven disaster destroys the infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega loan or a patchwork of small grants. We need adequate grant-based support from the world," he said.

The 36-year-old Shah was the youngest head of government to speak at the 81st session of the UNGA.

Nepal-Tibet floods — the deadly 'Himalayan tsunami'

On August 26, a glacier collapsed near the border between Nepal and China's ​Tibet Autonomous Region, unleashing landslides and a flash flood that ripped through downstream valleys.

In the days after the disaster, the world watched powerful images of the widespread destruction emerge from Nepal.

Entire villages were flattened. In other visuals, people trapped in hydropower tunnels deep within the Himalayas were seen crawling away a thick sludge of mud to reach rescuers.

Over 6,000 people are still reported to be missing, with search and recovery efforts still ongoing.

World.title: Jürgen Klopp starts Germany job with shaky Netherlands draw
World.content:
A late Netherlands goal denied Jürgen Klopp a win in his first match as Germany coach. The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund boss has big ambitions, but the game showed he's going to need more time to achieve them.

It looked, until the final moments, as though Germany would somehow hold on and grant Jürgen Klopp a victory in his first game as Germany coach.

"It felt mostly good," Klopp told German broadcaster RTL after the match, with his voice strained after a typically energetic display on the sidelines. "That was really exhausting for both teams today." He added that he naturally wanted a win but that he can "live with the point, too."

In the end, an injury time Cody Gakpo goal meant Klopp and his team had to settle for a 1-1 draw in their Nations League opener against the Netherlands. While the timing of the equalizer will sting, Germany was second best for much of the contest, which turned a ill-tempered at times. Nevertheless, Klopp was upbeat.

"I was very, very, very satisfied with many of the individual performances," he said, before admitting that "we can play better football and create more chances — that's for sure."

Gakpo plays his club football for Liverpool, where Klopp coached for more than eight years. So too does Dutch captain Virgil van Dijk, who thought he'd opened the scoring for the hosts early on, only to see his headed goal ruled out. A close-range finish from Lukas Nmecha then gave Germany the lead but not control of the game.

New faces, new coach, not yet new Germany

While there were a few patches of attacking play that resembled the kind of high-intensity, exhilarating football that Klopp produced at Liverpool and, before that, at Borussia Dortmund, Germany looked shaky at the back and were thankful for some wasteful Dutch finishing.

It is, though, difficult to judge much at this early stage. Klopp replaced Julian Nagelsmann after another poor World Cup showing from Germany and, after naming two different squads for the four Nations Leagues games in an extended international period, is still assessing how to make the most of what he has. Three players — Younes Ebnoutalib, Yannik Engelhardt and Philipp Treu — made debuts on Thursday, and more are likely follow over the next three games.

"I won't promise anything [in terms of trophies]. What I can promise is that we will definitely give it a try," he told reporters ahead of the game. "There's an impression that we have less quality than other countries. When things aren't working, you take a closer look and try to bring about changes. That's what we're working on now."

After Germany lost Kai Havertz to injury in the first half, having already had to change to starting XI after Jamal Musiala pulled out of the match in the warmup, the team was left without much of their attacking experience and class.

Klopp's record should buy him time

But Klopp won't panic. His methods, both tactically and emotionally, will take time to bear fruit. At Liverpool, it took nearly five years to win a trophy; at Dortmund, it took three.

"When the system isn't yet in place and the processes aren't yet established, then something like this happens," he said about Wednesday's performance. "I was very pleased with the passion, the intensity, but we can definitely play better."

Usually, waiting for success would not be acceptable for German national team fans. But after repeated recent failures, and with Klopp a popular figure, he has more credit in that bank than his predecessor, Julian Nagelsmann. The last coach to win a World Cup for Germany, Joachim Löw, said he will need it.

Jürgen Klopp has combined experienced internationals and newcomers in his first squads Image: Christian Schulze/nordphoto/picture alliance

"It is crucial now to give him the necessary time and space to implement his ideas," he told the Münchner Merkur/tz newspaper. "Jürgen stands for energy, intensity and a strong bond between the team and the fans. But even for him, not everything will work from one day to the next. After a disappointing World Cup, it takes trust, patience and a team that once again plays for Germany with great conviction."

Klopp calls for German unity, seeks Greece win

Klopp has already tried to unite the country behind the team. On the touchline in Amsterdam, he ran through his familiar repertoire of fist bumps, beaming smiles and growls at officials in a cap emblazoned with the words "one of 83 million" on it.

The headgear has already become a familiar sight. It's a reference to Germany's population and the 59-year-old has also referenced the importance of his team, and their flag, as a symbol of nationhood at a time when the far-right AfD (Alternative for Germany) are making substantial electoral gains.

"I'd like to reclaim the flag for myself — or for us," Klopp said. "I want us to always wave it in a way that makes no one think: 'What's wrong with you?' But, rather, that people simply get the feeling that you're happy and understand how lucky you are to have been born, raised or moved to this wonderful country."

While Klopp's charisma makes such a lofty ambition seem somewhat feasible, he's also pragmatic enough to know that for the German national team to be universally loved, it needs to win. Augsburg on Saturday, against Greece in the Nations League, would be a good place to start.
