World.title: TIMELINE: Mary Jane Veloso’s case and road to freedom
World.content:
The pardon granted to Mary Jane Veloso marks the end of a nearly two-decade ordeal that has spanned three presidents and years on death row

Former overseas Filipino worker (OFW) Mary Jane Veloso left the Philippines for a job in Malaysia in 2010. She instead found herself in Indonesia — behind bars and on death row — after being accused of smuggling drugs.

Sixteen years later, she will soon walk free. This is after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. confirmed on Friday, September 25, that he had granted her absolute pardon for the drug trafficking conviction decided upon by an Indonesian court in 2010.

Her pardon marks the end of a nearly two-decade ordeal spanning three presidents and years on death row.

Here’s a look back on how her case unfolded:

December 31, 2009

Veloso returns to the Philippines after prematurely ending her two-year contract as a domestic worker in Dubai. She says it is because she was nearly raped. For the next three months, she attempts to apply for jobs in other countries through her agency, but to no avail.

April 18, 2010

Maria Cristina Sergio, Veloso’s neighbor in Talavera, Nueva Ecija, offers her a job as a domestic worker in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia.

April 21, 2010

Veloso and Sergio arrive in Malaysia, only to find that the job she was promised is no longer available. Both stay in Malaysia for three days, during which Sergio and her boyfriend give Veloso a brand-new suitcase to use plus $500.

She later says that the suitcase seemed heavy, but its compartments were empty. She packs her belongings in the suitcase and leaves for Indonesia.

April 25, 2010

Veloso arrives at the Adisucipto International Airport in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, where authorities find 2.6 kilograms of heroin wrapped in aluminum foil hidden inside the lining of her suitcase. The drugs are later estimated to have a street value of $500,000.

She is arrested for drug trafficking and taken into custody.

May 12, 2010

Veloso’s parents find out that she has been jailed, weeks after Sergio had assured them that Mary Jane arrived safely in Malaysia. The family confronts Sergio, who tells them to “keep silent, don’t tell anyone, and don’t approach the media” if they want to keep Mary Jane and the rest of their family out of grave danger.

August 2010

Veloso’s family decides to report her case to the Department of Foreign Affairs and media outlets. They repeatedly request for updates and ask for help from other authorities like the National Bureau of Investigation, Philippine National Police, Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency, Office of the Vice President, and Malacañang.

October 4, 2010

The trial for Veloso’s case begins in the District Court of Justice of Sleman in Yogyakarta with Indonesian public prosecutor Sri Anggraeni recommending life imprisonment. Veloso is represented by a court-appointed pro bono lawyer apparently recommended by the Indonesian police themselves. (READ: What you should know about the case of Mary Jane Veloso)

October 11, 2010

The Sleman District Court convicts Veloso of drug trafficking and sentences her to death by firing squad.

October 22, 2010

The Philippine embassy in Jakarta reportedly files an appeal for Veloso with Yogyakarta’s Appeals Court.

October 2011

The late former president Benigno “Noynoy” Aquino III makes his first attempt to appeal for clemency on behalf of Veloso to then-Indonesian president Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.

At the time, Indonesia had a moratorium on executions, so the request was not acted upon.

October 20, 2014

A new Indonesian president, Joko “Jokowi” Widodo, assumes office. Shortly after, he announces that he will start rejecting all clemency requests from drug convicts on death row, citing Indonesia’s illegal drug situation being in a state of emergency.

January 2015

Jokowi rejects a batch of clemency appeals, including Aquino’s second attempt to appeal for Veloso by seeking a judicial review of her case. The Indonesian Supreme Court rejects this, and Jokowi would later urge the Philippines to respect his country’s laws.

February 9, 2015

Jokowi goes on his first state visit to the Philippines, during which Aquino raises Veloso’s case. Later that same month, her family visits her in jail in Yogyakarta.

March 3 to 4, 2015

The Sleman District Court holds a two-day trial, where lawyers argue that Veloso deserves a case review because she wasn’t given a capable translator.

March 25, 2015

The Indonesian Supreme Court rejects the case review request.

April 23, 2015

The Philippine government attempts to file a second petition for judicial review. Four days later, the Indonesian Supreme Court denies the application.

The DFA later announces that charges have been filed against Veloso’s alleged recruiter Sergio, her boyfriend who allegedly handed Veloso the suitcase where the drugs were found, and an African accomplice.

April 25, 2015

Veloso’s execution date is set for April 29, 2015. At the same time, global campaigns to stop her execution are mounted. (READ: #SaveMaryJane: A cause worth fighting for during the glorious days of social media)

April 28, 2015

Sergio voluntarily surrenders to the Nueva Ecija Provincial Police.

Aquino makes a last-minute phone call to then-Indonesian foreign minister Retno Marsudi, asking Indonesia to turn Veloso into a state witness who can help pin down a drug trafficking syndicate, which allegedly includes her recruiters.

April 29, 2015

Indonesia grants Veloso last-minute reprieve from her death sentence, just 11 hours before she is scheduled to be shot by firing squad. This would allow her to testify against her recruiters, although she would remain in detention.

September 12, 2016

A few months after then-Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte assumed office, Jokowi reveals to reporters that Duterte told him to “go ahead” if Veloso were to be executed.

Then-presidential spokesperson Ernesto Abella later clarifies Duterte’s statements, saying that he had said, “Follow your own laws, I will not interfere.” (READ: Duterte said he will not interfere with Indonesian laws – Palace)

January 30, 2022

Veloso’s recruiters are found guilty of illegal recruitment and life imprisonment. This is separate from the trafficking case pending in Indonesia.

November 20, 2024

After more than 14 years in detention, Veloso is allowed to return to the Philippines, as Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto agrees to transfer her case back home.

Indonesia also gives President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. the discretion to grant Veloso clemency. While this means she is spared from death row — since the Philippines has no such penalty — she could not walk free just yet. (READ: Once Mary Jane Veloso returns, no release yet, but safe from death penalty)

December 18, 2024

Veloso arrives in Manila after 14 years away from home, but is then detained at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City. Despite pleas for her freedom from advocates and supporters, Marcos says he would leave the decision on clemency requests to legal experts.

The embattled OFW would remain behind bars for nearly two more years.

September 25, 2026

Marcos confirms that he granted Veloso absolute pardon the day before. It is a form of executive clemency granted after conviction and extinguishes the person’s criminal liability from the case. The Parole and Probation Administration says this type of pardon also restores a person’s civil and political rights and cancels the penalty for conviction. – Rappler.com

World.title: Meet the new cornerstone investors lining up for GCash’s record IPO
World.content:
From the world's biggest asset manager to the World Bank's private sector investment arm, GCash has already secured about P36.5 billion in cornerstone commitments ahead of its October 6-12 IPO offer period

MANILA, Philippines – More than 20 global and local institutions have already lined up to buy into GCash even before its record-setting initial public offering (IPO) opens to ordinary investors.

Mynt, the parent company of GCash, said its cornerstone investors include some of the biggest names in global asset management. Among the most notable global investors are:

BlackRock

Capital Research and Management Company

T. Rowe Price

International Finance Corporation (IFC)

Schroders

Lazard Asset Management

FIL Investment Management

HSBC Global Asset Management

Together, the cornerstone investors have committed around P36.5 billion, according to Mynt’s preliminary prospectus. Mynt said the commitments would cover approximately the entire institutional tranche, subject to any reallocation.

Cornerstone investors are large institutions that agree in advance to buy shares in an IPO, giving an issuer a ready pool of demand before the public offer begins.

The biggest name on the list by sheer scale is BlackRock. The New York-listed investment giant had $15.3 trillion (P959.85 trillion) in assets under management as of end-June 2026, making it the world’s largest asset manager. Note though that the expected buyers are certain funds and separately managed accounts run by BlackRock subsidiaries, rather than BlackRock itself.

GCash is also not BlackRock’s first time coming into a company at the IPO stage. BlackRock-managed funds and accounts were named as a cornerstone investor in trading platform eToro’s 2025 listing, indicating interest in buying up to $100 million (P6.27 billion) of shares at the IPO price.

Another heavyweight is Capital Research and Management Company, part of Capital Group, which manages more than $3.6 trillion (P225.85 trillion). A Capital Group investment division was also among the cornerstone investors in US electric vehicle maker Rivian’s blockbuster 2021 IPO. Rivian’s cornerstone group, which also included Amazon and T. Rowe Price, indicated interest in buying as much as $5 billion (P313.68 billion) of stock at the IPO price. Rivian ultimately raised nearly $12 billion and its shares jumped about 29% on their first trading day.

T. Rowe Price, which managed around $1.9 trillion (P119.20 trillion) as of end-August, has played the same role in an even more recognizable listing. It committed up to €750 million (P53.48 billion) as a cornerstone investor in German luxury sports car manufacturer Porsche’s 2022 IPO. Porsche later described the listing as the largest IPO ever carried out in Europe, with a market capitalization of around €78 billion (P5.56 trillion) at its opening price.

Perhaps the most interesting incoming investor from a Philippine fintech perspective is the International Finance Corporation, the private sector arm of the World Bank Group.

GCash is not IFC’s first exposure to the local digital finance race. In 2022, IFC and two IFC-managed funds invested up to $18.5 million (P1.16 billion) in Voyager Innovations, the company behind rival Maya, as part of a funding round meant to support its expansion into digital banking. That means IFC is entering GCash as a cornerstone investor after already backing one of its closest competitors in the Philippine fintech market.

On the domestic side, Mynt named ATRAM Trust, BPI Asset Management and Trust, China Bank Capital, Metrobank’s Trust Banking Group, Philequity Management, and RCBC Capital.

The new investors are arriving just as several of GCash’s early private equity backers prepare to sell down their stakes through the IPO. Bow Wave Capital, Warburg Pincus, Insight Partners, and LGVP are among the existing shareholders using the listing as a partial exit.

Mynt is expected to set the final offer price on October 1, ahead of the October 6 to 12 offer period and its targeted October 20 debut on the Philippine Stock Exchange under the ticker GCASH. – Rappler.com

$1 = P62.6190, €1 = P71.3043 based on the September 24, 2026 reference exchange rates of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

World.title: Here’s PhilHealth timeline for expected benefit expansion until 2028
World.content:
PHILHEALTH. Philippine Health Insurance Corporation members process transactions at the PhilHealth National Capital Region Central Branch in Quezon City on September 26, 2023.

PhilHealth is seeking from lawmakers an additional P170 billion for 2027 to fully implement its benefit expansion, as well as cover projected insurance claims of indirect contributors

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) has a plan to expand various benefit packages until 2028, Bataan 2nd District Representative Albert Garcia said on Thursday, September 24.

Garcia laid out the “roadmap,” which seeks to lower out-of-pocket healthcare expenses, as he was the sponsor of the Department of Health and PhilHealth during the House plenary deliberations on their proposed 2027 budget.

The rollout of enhanced benefits is based on health conditions with the highest disease burden and financial risk for Filipino patients, according to Garcia.

The announcement of the planned schedule came even as the state health insurer continued to flag its budget shortfall for next year.

Under the 2027 National Expenditure Program, the government will be giving P74.4 billion to PhilHealth. It is lower than the P129.78-billion allocation in the 2026 General Appropriations Act.

Health officials are seeking from lawmakers an additional P170 billion in funding to fully implement the benefit expansion, as well as cover projected insurance claims of indirect contributors, or those whose premiums are subsidized by the government.

PhilHealth broadened its coverage for maternity benefits and for moderate to severe leptospirosis during the second quarter of this year.

Current benefits are listed on PhilHealth’s website.

World.title: Carlos Yulo redeems self, vaults to another Asian Games gold
World.content:
SHUSH. The Philippines's Carlos Edriel Yulo reacts during the men's vault final in the 2026 Asian Games.

After barely qualifying for the finals, Carlos Yulo captures a second artistic gymnastics gold medal for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games as he rules the men’s vault

MANILA, Philippines – Carlos Yulo simply delivers when the stakes are at their highest.

After barely qualifying for the finals, Yulo captured a second artistic gymnastics gold medal for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games as he ruled the men’s vault at the Nagoya General Gymnasium in Japan on Friday, September 25.

The reigning Olympic and world champion in the apparatus, Yulo delivered a breathtaking performance when it mattered most, brushing aside his seventh-place finish in the qualification as nothing more than a minor bump in the road.

Yulo scored 14.733 on his first vault and 14.466 on his second for an average of 14.599, enough to edge Iran’s Mahdi Olfati for the top prize and secure back-to-back victories after his floor exercise triumph the day prior.

Competing after Yulo, Olfati threatened to snatch the win from the Filipino after opening with an impressive 15.1 points, but a minor misstep on his second vault proved costly as the Iranian managed just 13.966 points for a 15.533 average.

Hong Kong’s Ng Ka Ki, who topped the qualifications, completed the podium with 14.116 for the bronze.

It was a masterclass in redemption for Yulo, who overcame an underwhelming qualification — where he netted just a 13.649 average after landing on his backside on his first vault — to emerge with the gold medal.

With this victory, Yulo has now won gold medals in both the floor exercise and vault at the Olympics, World Championships, World Cups, Asian Games, Asian Championships, and Southeast Asian Games.

Another Filipino saw action in the final, with Juancho Miguel Besana placing fifth with 13.783 points.

Yulo can score a hat trick of gold medals as he competes in the parallel bars final later on Friday. – Rappler.com

World.title: Barangay, SK elections postponed to November 2028
World.content:
PHILIPPINE LEADER. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr signs the law setting a five-year term for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials on September 24, 2026.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signs Republic Act No. 12326, which sets the term of barangay and SK officials to five years

MANILA, Philippines – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has signed Republic Act No. 12326, fixing the term of barangay officials and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) members to five years, Malacañang announced on Friday, September 25.

RA 12326, signed on Thursday, September 24, postpones the barangay and SK elections slated in November to the second Monday of November 2028, and every five years thereafter.

Under RA 12326, barangay officials are limited to two consecutive terms while SK officials are limited to a single term.

“Considering the extension of their terms by two years, incumbent elective barangay officials shall be regarded as having completed one term in their respective positions. Incumbent officials serving their last term in the same position in accordance with Section 1 hereof shall be ineligible to run for the same position in the November 2028 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections,” the law states.

The last BSKE was held in November 2023, and was supposed to be held in November 2025 but Marcos enacted a law moving the date to November 2026.

The House of Representatives and the Senate passed their versions of the bill setting a five-year term for barangay and SK officials earlier in September. – Rappler.com

World.title: #SaveMaryJane: A cause worth fighting for during the glorious days of social media
World.content:
#SaveMaryJane. Former death row inmate Mary Jane Veloso waves after arriving at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City, on December 18, 2024.

(1st UPDATE) In 2015, citizens all over the world campaigned to stop the execution of Mary Jane Veloso — a time when social media was a force for social good

MANILA, Philippines – She’s now going to be free, more than a decade after a global action to #SaveMaryJane kicked off online and became the fastest growing petition on Change.org, mobilizing hundreds of thousands of people from all over the world.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced on Friday, September 25, that he has pardoned Mary Jane Veloso, the overseas Filipino worker who was sentenced to death in Indonesia in October 2010 over charges she carried packs of heroin in her suitcase when she arrived at a Yogyakarta airport from Kuala Lumpur in April that year. Marcos said he signed the grant of absolute pardon on Thursday, September 24.

Despite repeated appeals by the Benigno Aquino III administration at the time, an Indonesian court scheduled her execution by firing squad on April 29, 2015, or five years after she was meted the death penalty.

The Rappler newsroom, barely three years old then, was enraged.

MovePH, our citizen engagement arm, made a quick decision to connect with partners and launch an online campaign to #SaveMaryJane. Leading the newsroom effort was Move’s organizer at the time, Voltaire Tupaz, who tapped Move’s local networks, coordinated with groups that had already been campaigning for Veloso’s freedom, identified advocates in Indonesia, and crafted a content-and-community plan with partners.

On April 1, 2015, Move amplified ways to help save Mary Jane from death row. Voltaire sat down with Mary Jane’s mother on April 22 for a Rappler Talk interview.

The global action to #SaveMaryJane on Change.org kicked off on April 26, mobilizing citizens from 127 countries to sign the petition — in what was described as a “huge and rare” outcome from a Philippine initiative.

In this story, Voltaire wrote how the petition reached the Indonesian president during that period, Jokowi Widodo — a time when social media was seen as a potent force for change and citizens were sharing the same sets of facts and truths.

The phone call

Intense public focus on the campaign enabled then-president “Noynoy” Aquino to once again make a final plea through a phone call on April 28 to then-Indonesian foreign minister Retno Masurdi. Aquino asked the Indonesian government to turn Mary Jane into a state witness against her recruiters who were allegedly part of a drug trafficking syndicate.

Here’s a photo of when the late Aquino made the call.

Things moved fast. Mary Jane’s recruiters surrendered to the Philippine police.

At 2:20 am on April 29, or 11 hours before she was to be shot by firing squad, then-foreign secretary Albert Del Rosario, through his spokesman, told reporters that Indonesia confirmed that Mary Jane’s execution had been put on hold.

#MaryJaneLives trended online.

After Rodrigo Duterte was elected president in 2016, he visited Indonesia and assured Jokowi that he would not stop Veloso’s execution. Duterte’s presidency was marked by a brutal war on drugs.

Both countries elected new presidents, however: Marcos in 2022 and Prabowo Subianto in 2024. Fresh from a huge victory in 2024, the Indonesian leader said his government was going to allow Veloso to be transferred to a Philippine jail.

A week before Christmas in December that year, Veloso arrived in the Philippines. She has been detained at the Correctional Institution for Women in Mandaluyong City since then, and in June testified against her recruiters.

This Christmas will be different for her and her family — and for those who believe that there are causes worth fighting for. And women worth saving. – Rappler.com

World.title: China ‘hinders’ PH resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal
World.content:
The PCG says a Chinese naval warship issued a radio challenge, warning it would take 'compulsory measures' to prevent the mission, while Chinese coast guard and maritime militia vessels were in the vicinity of Ayungin Shoal

MANILA, Philippines — For the first time since Manila and Beijing signed a “provisional understanding,” the Philippines has publicly confirmed that Chinese maritime forces “hindered” a rotation and resupply (RORE) mission to the BRP Sierra Madre at Ayungin (Second Thomas) Shoal.

In a statement on Friday, September 25, the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea (NTF-WPS) said both the China Coast Guard (CCG) and the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLA Navy) interfered in a RORE to Ayungin on September 24.

Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, said the RORE mission was called off at 11:08 pm on Thursday “for the safety of our personnel.” The PCG’s BRP Malabrigo was deployed to “provide security assistance” during the Navy mission.

A PLAN warship, said Tarriela, issued a radio challenge, warning that it would take “compulsory measures” to prevent the mission. Some 9 CCG and five Chinese maritime militia vessels were in the vicinity of Ayungin during the mission, based on reports from Philippine authorities.

CCG ships followed the M/V Lapu-Lapu, a civilian supply ship that the Navy uses for the RORE, with at least one of them carrying out “dangerous maneuvers” or sailing from 1,000 yards “creating a serious risk of collision.”

“In doing so, they put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation,” said the NTF-WPS, an inter-agency task force. No injuries were reported by the Philippines.

“The NTF-WPS calls on the China Coast Guard and the PLA Navy immediately cease interfering with lawful Philippine Roe missions. The Philippines will continue to conduct lawful operations in the West Philippine Sea and exercise its sovereign rights and jurisdiction in accordance with international law,” said the task force.

BRP Sierra Madre is a World War II warship that was purposefully run aground on Ayungin Shoal in 1999, after it became clear that a Chinese-made structure on Panganiban (Mischief) Reef was going to be used for military purposes.

The rusting Sierra Madre has since served as an outpost for a small group of Filipino soldiers, who are rotated and resupplied through RORE missions. These missions happen like clockwork, barring bad weather or occasional problems with military assets.

It’s a flashpoint for tensions between the Philippines and China because Beijing claims almost all of the South China Sea, including parts that are within Manila’s exclusive economic zone (EEZ). China’s claim has meant, for Filipino maritime frontliners, harassment from the CCG, PLAN, or the auxiliary Chinese Maritime Militia.

RORE missions to Ayungin are often where those tensions are most pronounced — CCG and maritime militia ships would also routinely try to stop the hauling of supplies and personnel to the Sierra Madre.

A “provisional understanding” — the full details of which are not public — was made in 2024, in the aftermath of a June 17 incident when CCG personnel harassed Filipino soldiers already moored close to the BRP Sierra Madre. A soldier’s thumb was cut off as the CCG rammed their boats into the Philippine Navy’s rubber boats.

In July 2026, CCG personnel entered the shoal and sailed close to the Sierra Madre, leading to a confrontation with Filipino soldiers. One soldier sustained a head injury.

The details of the understanding — sometimes called an agreement or arrangement — are confidential, although parts of it have been made public, typically through clarifications and denials by Philippine authorities.

The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), which negotiated the arrangement, has said the Philippines does not seek China’s permission to undertake RORE missions, nor is Manila barred from bringing construction materials to repair the rusting warship. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: No basis to claim that Villar siblings, Padilla face arrest to force VP Sara’s ouster
World.content:
Graft complaints against the Villars exist, but these are related to a water utility deal, not to Duterte's impeachment. Padilla, meanwhile, faces an obstruction of justice complaint over Dela Rosa’s escape.

Claim: Senators Mark Villar, Camille Villar, and Robin Padilla will be jailed as part of an effort to remove Vice President Sara Duterte from office.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A YouTube video posted on September 21 by the channel “News Update Files,” credited to “Banat By,” makes the claim.

Its thumbnail shows images of the three senators along with the text, “3 senador makukulong na? Ikulong para mapatalsik si VP Sara?” (3 senators about to be jailed? Jail them to oust VP Sara?) and “Minority bloc, bawas na naman ulit” (Minority bloc, reduced yet again.)

The video’s title reads, “Pwersahan na! Magkapatid na Villar at Sen Padilla makukulong na? Ikukulong kahit walang kaso?”

(By force now! Villar siblings and Senator Padilla about to be jailed? Jailed even without a case?)

The video appears to imply that the three senators are set to be arrested to further reduce the number of senator-judges voting in Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial. As of writing, the video has now garnered nearly 6,000 views and over 400 likes.

The facts: There are no arrest orders against the Villars. Although the Villars face graft complaints, these have not yet reached the courts. These complaints concern PrimeWater Infrastructure Corporation’s agreements with local water districts and have no connection to Duterte’s impeachment trial.

On September 18, the Office of the Ombudsman filed criminal and administrative complaints against Senators Mark and Camille Villar, former senators Manny and Cynthia Villar, and businessman Paolo Villar. Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said the complaints concern allegations that PrimeWater failed to meet its obligations to some water districts.

The complaints are currently under preliminary investigation, meaning no charges have been filed in court and no one has been arrested or detained as prosecutors have yet to determine if there’s enough evidence against the respondents.

Padilla is not among the respondents in the Ombudsman complaints. His connection to the misleading video’s narrative appears to come from a separate announcement that he does not intend to seek reelection in 2028.

He does, however, face a separate obstruction of justice complaint over his alleged role in helping Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa evade authorities. The Department of Justice has subpoenaed Padilla to appear before prosecutors on September 25 and October 9. Padilla has denied helping Dela Rosa escape and said he would attend the proceedings.

The video offers no evidence linking the Villar graft complaints or Padilla’s obstruction of justice complaint to Duterte’s impeachment trial, or showing that either was filed to influence how senators vote.

VP trial: The three senators are among the senator-judges in Duterte’s impeachment trial. The Senate recently voted to lower the voting threshold for convicting the Vice President. Senators Camille Villar and Robin Padilla did not participate in the voting, while Senator Mark Villar voted yes to lowering the threshold. (READ: A Villar split: Why is Mark Villar breaking ranks with sister Camille?)

Duterte faces four articles of impeachment covering allegations including misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Kazakhstan Launches Direct Flights From Almaty to Chongqing
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s low-cost airline FlyArystan has launched regular flights on a new route connecting Almaty with Chongqing, expanding Kazakhstan’s air connectivity with China.

The new service began on Sept. 23 and will operate twice a week, on Wednesdays and Saturdays, using Airbus A320neo aircraft, according to the Civil Aviation Committee of the Ministry of Transport.

The new service will become FlyArystan’s fifth destination in China, complementing its existing routes to Urumqi, Yining (Kulja) and Xi’an. The launch of the new route is expected to strengthen air connectivity between Kazakhstan and China and contribute to the development of trade, business, investment, tourism and cultural ties between the two countries.

The Civil Aviation Committee continues to work on expanding Kazakhstan’s international flight network and increasing the number of international routes.

World.title: News Digest: Foreign Media on Kazakhstan’s Political Reform, AI Push and Investment Potential
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest covers constitutional reform, the country’s drive to become a regional AI hub, nuclear energy cooperation, investment opportunities and Astana’s new airport project.

Kazakhstan’s new political era: Constitutional reform

EU Reporter published an article examining Kazakhstan’s post-referendum political reforms, focusing on the new Constitution, the newly elected 145-member Kurultai, the creation of the vice-presidency and People’s Council, and how these institutional changes are being linked to broader economic, technological and EU cooperation.

“Constitutional reform is not only about institutions. Its significance lies in how effectively they serve citizens, strengthen governance and contribute to the country’s development,” reads the article.

Inside Kazakhstan’s push to become a regional AI centre

Al Jazeera published an article on Sept. 21 about Kazakhstan’s rapid push to become a regional AI hub, covering its government-backed digitalisation drive, development of local AI technologies and talent, and the environmental and human-rights concerns accompanying that expansion.

One of the article’s notable examples is how Kazakhstan’s AI sector is opening new career opportunities for women. Valeria Tio, managing director of Astana Hub, said a woman who had worked as a barista at the hub found a job as a developer after one year of studying through its Tomorrow School programme, calling it “a real social elevator.” The program has trained 500 people in 18 months, while new cohorts are now being opened across 12 regions of Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan, UK discuss cooperation in peaceful use of nuclear energy

Kazakhstan and the UK discussed prospects for cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy during a meeting between the Agency of Kazakhstan for Atomic Energy, Deputy Chairman Timur Zhantikin and Lord John Alderdice, the UK Prime Minister’s Trade Envoy for Central Asia, reported Trend on Sept. 22.

“The meeting discussed current issues and prospects for developing Kazakhstan-UK cooperation in the peaceful use of nuclear energy,” the agency said.

Kazakhstan: A nation set to capitalise from its vast natural resources and investor appeal

Credendo released an article on Sept. 24 about Kazakhstan’s economic and investment outlook, highlighting its abundant natural resources, strong macroeconomic fundamentals and strategic position, as well as efforts to diversify through the Middle Corridor, critical minerals, infrastructure, digitalisation and AI.

“Kazakhstan is endowed with substantial commodity wealth, including oil, gas, uranium and critical minerals, leading to strong trade and investment commitments in transport and digital infrastructure, logistics, energy and critical minerals. Moreover, Astana is trading its resources against access to technologies,” reads the article.

Changi Airports to participate in construction of new airport in Kazakhstan’s Astana

Singapore’s Changi Airports International (CAI), a subsidiary of Changi Airport Group, will be involved in the construction of a new airport in Astana, according to the Astana akimat, reported Trend on Sept. 23.

The Astana akimat, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Transport and CAI have signed a Framework Cooperation Agreement aimed at developing a long-term strategic partnership in the field of airport infrastructure in the capital.

Under the agreement, the parties reached formal arrangements in two main areas: cooperation on the construction of a new airport in Astana and the development of the existing Astana International Airport.

World.title: India, Kazakhstan Seek to Turn Strategic Partnership Into Deeper Trade and Investment Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – India and Kazakhstan should translate their strong political partnership into deeper trade, investment, digital and energy cooperation, participants said at the India-Kazakhstan Strategic Dialogue on Sept. 24.

During the India-Kazakhstan: Anchoring Regional Stability and Economic Integration in a Multilateral World session, speakers highlighted the gap between close political ties and relatively modest bilateral trade.

Indian Ambassador to Kazakhstan Sailas Thangal said the countries need to address structural barriers limiting economic cooperation, including connectivity, logistics, customs procedures, payment mechanisms, market access and regulatory issues.

“Business delegations and exhibitions alone are not enough to enhance our bilateral trade and commerce,” he said, calling for concrete measures to turn existing potential into commercial partnerships.

“India and Kazakhstan have the trust, we have the complementarity, we have the political will. What we need now is to convert this essence into connectivity, governance and concrete partnership,” he said.

Trade remains below potential

Rakhim Oshakbayev, director of the TALAP Center for Applied Research, described the $923 million in bilateral trade in 2025 as a “long-standing anomaly.”

“Our political relationship is excellent. Many speakers talked about this. We are strategic partners,” he said.

However, he noted that logistical constraints continue to limit economic ties, describing the situation as “high politics, low logistics, big friendship, small trade.”

India accounted for around 0.64% of Kazakhstan’s total foreign trade in 2025. Oshakbayev attributed the limited trade partly to difficult transport routes.

“We are close in the sky and far on the ground,” he said, proposing greater focus on high-value goods and services that depend less on traditional transport links.

Uranium, pharmaceuticals and digital cooperation

Uranium was identified as one of the most promising areas for expanding economic ties. Oshakbayev referred to a long-term contract between Kazatomprom and India’s Department of Atomic Energy, saying press reports have valued it at more than $4 billion.

“Uranium is a perfect product for difficult geography, very high value, very small volume,” he said, proposing broader cooperation around the agreement, including training and the nuclear fuel cycle.

He also highlighted pharmaceutical production in Kazakhstan, which could serve both the domestic market and the wider Eurasian Economic Union market.

Participants identified artificial intelligence, fintech, cybersecurity, e-government and digital payments as other areas of potential cooperation, saying Indian technology companies could use Kazakhstan as a platform for accessing regional markets.

Strategic autonomy and regional cooperation

Former Indian Ambassador to Russia and former Deputy National Security Advisor Pankaj Saran said India and Kazakhstan could contribute to regional stability through diplomacy, economic development and diversified international partnerships.

“Both India and Kazakhstan maintain that independence of decision making. How can we both show to our people and to the region that we can be friends with everyone. We don’t have to choose one against the other,” he said.

Saran highlighted Kazakhstan’s balanced foreign policy and India’s strategic autonomy as areas of commonality, pointing to cooperation in regional stability, Afghanistan, peacekeeping and economic development.

He also cited growing energy requirements linked to the expansion of artificial intelligence and data centers as an area for potential cooperation.

Participants also called for stronger business, academic and people-to-people ties through joint research, healthcare, tourism and education, as well as practical cooperation in transport, energy, critical minerals, agriculture and technology.

The discussions highlighted opportunities to build on the strong political foundation of India-Kazakhstan relations by expanding trade, investment and practical economic cooperation.

World.title: Search Operation Ends After Bodies of Two Missing Service Officers Found In Caspian Sea
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s search-and-rescue operation in the Caspian Sea has officially ended after the bodies of two service officers who had been missing following a military exercise were found on Sept. 25, bringing the death toll from the incident to 14.

The bodies were found at around 9:15 a.m. on Sept. 25 during continuous search operations, according to the Defence Ministry. The incident occurred during a training and combat exercise when 17 servicemen were swept into the open sea amid a sudden and sharp deterioration in weather conditions and strong winds. Three service officers were rescued, while 14 died.

Sept. 25 was declared a national day of mourning in Kazakhstan by order of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev following the deaths.

Search operation concludes

The search-and-rescue operation was conducted around the clock under the direction of Defence Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kosanov. An operational headquarters brought together representatives of the Defence Ministry, the Border Service of the National Security Committee, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and local executive authorities of the Mangystau Region.

At its peak, the operation involved 252 personnel, 34 units of specialized ground equipment, 37 military divers, 14 vessels and boats, and more than 20 aircraft, including four helicopters. Search teams surveyed the sea, coastal areas and adjacent territory from the air.

The Defence Ministry expressed condolences to the families and relatives of those killed, saying they would receive comprehensive material and psychological assistance.

Criminal investigation continues

A government commission established on the instructions of President Tokayev and headed by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev continues to oversee the investigation into the circumstances of the incident.

At a government commission meeting on Sept. 24, Deputy Minister of Internal Affairs Sanzhar Adilov reported that criminal proceedings had been launched over negligent attitude toward service resulting in grave consequences and violations of navigation rules.

Investigators are conducting investigative and operational-search measures, while specialists have been involved and the necessary forensic examinations ordered. Bozumbayev instructed authorities to establish the full circumstances of the incident and take measures against those responsible.

“A special commission has been established to establish all the circumstances of the tragedy. Criminal cases have been opened. The investigation must be thorough, objective and prompt. Those whose actions or inaction led to this tragedy will be held accountable to the fullest extent of the law,” Bozumbayev said.

Families to receive assistance

Bozumbayev said the families of the deceased would receive substantial financial assistance in addition to payments provided for by law. Members of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi and representatives of major businesses have also expressed their intention to provide additional assistance to the families.

The Deputy Prime Minister instructed the Ministry of Labor and Social Protection and the Mangystau regional administration to ensure transparency and oversight in the distribution of funds allocated to the families, stressing that assistance should be provided directly and in full.

President Tokayev earlier expressed condolences to the families and relatives of the servicemen who died in the incident. The service officers rescued during the incident remain in stable condition and are receiving the necessary medical treatment, Deputy Health Minister Manas Ramazanov reported.

World.title: Tokayev Expresses Condolences Over Deaths of Service Members in Caspian Sea
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has expressed his condolences to the families and relatives of service members who died in a tragic incident during military exercises in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24.

Tokayev instructed the Government Commission to take all necessary measures to establish the circumstances of the incident and provide assistance to the families of those who died.

Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Defense reported that 19 service members were swept into the Caspian Sea during a naval exercise in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24 amid deteriorating weather conditions and strong winds. Three service members were rescued, including one who was hospitalized, while nine others died. Search operations continued.

World.title: ADB Forecasts Resilient Growth in Asia-Pacific, Kazakhstan’s Outlook Unchanged
World.content:
ASTANA — Economic growth across developing Asia and the Pacific is expected to moderate to 5% in 2026 from 5.5% in 2025 before rising slightly to 5.1% in 2027, according to the Asian Development Bank’s latest outlook.

The ADB’s September 2026 outlook revised its 2026 regional growth forecast upward by 0.1 percentage points compared with its July projection. Strong investment, government support and growing technology exports linked to global artificial intelligence investment are expected to continue supporting economic activity. At the same time, geopolitical tensions and climate-related risks are putting pressure on food and energy prices.

The bank lowered its regional inflation forecast for 2026 to 4.2%, from 4.3% in July, citing price stabilization measures. However, the forecast for 2027 was raised slightly to 3.5%, compared with 3.4% previously in July. Both projections remain above the 3% inflation rate recorded in 2025.

ADB identified escalating conflicts and a strong El Niño as the main risks to the regional outlook. A prolonged or broader conflict in the Middle East, as well as an intensifying war in Ukraine, could keep global energy prices high and volatile. Meanwhile, El Niño, the periodic warming of sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, is expected to continue through the first quarter of 2027, potentially increasing energy demand and reducing agricultural production.

Kazakhstan growth forecast remains unchanged

Kazakhstan’s economic outlook remains unchanged from the ADB’s July forecast. The bank expects the country’s economy to grow by 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027.

This projection is consistent with the ADB’s earlier assessment of Kazakhstan’s economic trajectory, which also forecast growth of 4.8% in 2026 and 4.5% in 2027 amid moderating oil production and continued government investment.

According to the report, growth will be supported by non-oil sectors and continued public investment. Manufacturing, construction and services are expected to contribute to economic activity despite disruptions in the oil sector. Off-budget financing and infrastructure spending are also projected to provide additional support.

The focus on non-oil sectors comes as Kazakhstan seeks to maintain economic momentum while reducing its reliance on hydrocarbons. Recent developments in construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and agriculture have also been highlighted as potential drivers of growth.

Inflation in Kazakhstan is forecast to gradually decline to 10.4% in 2026 and 9.5% in 2027, supported by earlier monetary tightening and prudential measures.

Across Central and West Asia, the ADB revised its growth forecasts downward by 0.1 percentage points for both 2026 and 2027, to 3.7% and 4.1%, respectively. The revision was attributed mainly to weaker-than-expected external demand, particularly in Türkiye.

Earlier ADB forecasts have likewise pointed to inflation and external economic conditions as key factors shaping Kazakhstan’s outlook. In July 2025, the bank raised its regional growth forecast while warning of increasing inflationary pressures in Kazakhstan and other Central Asian economies.

The ADB said developing Asia and the Pacific remain resilient despite growing economic and geopolitical risks. The bank emphasized the importance of measures to protect vulnerable populations from higher food and energy costs as governments navigate continued uncertainty.

World.title: Nine Servicemen Die in Incident During Caspian Sea Military Exercise
World.content:
ASTANA – Nine servicemen have died after 19 Kazakhstan Armed Forces personnel were swept into the Caspian Sea during a naval exercise in the Mangystau Region on Sept. 24 amid a sharp deterioration in weather conditions and strong winds, the Ministry of Defense reported.

Rescuers rescued three servicemen, including one who was hospitalized. Search operations for the remaining servicemen are underway.

The Government has established a commission to investigate the deaths, chaired by Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev. The commission includes the defense minister, Mangystau Region Akim Nurdaulet Kilybay and representatives of relevant ministries and agencies.

Units of the Naval Forces, the Ministry of Emergency Situations, aviation and other relevant services have been deployed to conduct search and rescue operations.

A commission from the Ministry of Defense, headed by Defense Minister Lieutenant General of Aviation Dauren Kossanov, has been urgently dispatched to establish the circumstances of the incident and coordinate the search and rescue efforts.

The Defense Ministry expressed its deep condolences to the families and relatives of the servicemen who died. The families will receive all necessary assistance and support.

The Prosecutor General’s Office has opened a criminal case into the deaths of the servicemen. An investigative team has been established, with officers from the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Ministry of Emergency Situations and the Prosecutor’s Office working at the site. Authorities have ordered necessary forensic examinations, and the investigation is under special control.

The Khazar Korgany-2026 exercise began on Sept. 22 in Kazakhstan’s sector of the Caspian Sea, involving more than 500 servicemen, Naval Forces vessels and boats, hydrographic vessels, Border Guard Service units and Air Defense Forces aviation.

World.title: Tokayev: Kazakhstan People’s Council to Strengthen State-Society Dialogue
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has called on the newly established Kazakhstan People’s Council to become a practical platform for dialogue between the state and society, saying its constitutional status opens new opportunities to address national and regional problems.

New platform for public dialogue

Speaking at the first session of the Kazakhstan People’s Council, Tokayev described its establishment as an important step in Kazakhstan’s ongoing political transformation. He said the new institution brings together representatives of different groups of society and is designed to strengthen public participation in state decision-making.

According to the President, the council is not an alternative to the Kurultai, Kazakhstan’s new legislative body, and must not interfere with its powers. Instead, the two institutions should maintain regular dialogue and coordinate their work, particularly when developing legislation that affects citizens’ interests, reported Akorda on Sept. 24.

The council includes representatives of ethnic and cultural associations, regional maslikhats and public councils, and civil society organizations. Tokayev said this composition would allow regional issues to be raised at the national level and establish a new system of interaction between the state and society.

He urged council members to avoid formalism and bureaucracy, maintain direct contact with citizens and address complex and pressing issues.

Economic and social progress

Tokayev highlighted Kazakhstan’s economic and social progress over the past seven years. GDP grew by 29% to $306 billion, while foreign exchange reserves and National Fund assets exceeded $138 billion. Kazakhstan attracted more than $162 billion in investment during this period, while small and medium-sized businesses accounted for more than 40% of the economy.

More than 20 million square meters of housing are built annually. Since 2019, 1,342 schools with capacity for more than one million students have been constructed. Life expectancy has reached 76 years, while more than 1,200 healthcare facilities have been opened.

More than 35,000 kilometers of roads have been built and repaired. Tokayev described these as record indicators in Kazakhstan’s history and said the country had entered the top 40 most competitive countries in the world.

Regional development and infrastructure

At the same time, Tokayev called for stronger public oversight of infrastructure projects and higher construction standards, citing concerns about the quality of some housing and roads.

He instructed the authorities to strengthen control over road construction, improve quality-assessment mechanisms and increase public oversight of infrastructure projects.

Tokayev also stressed the need to address Kazakhstan’s future workforce needs. By 2035, the country is expected to require 2.9 million specialists, including 1.8 million in skilled trades, notably in industry, construction, agriculture and IT.

Kazakhstan’s international role

Tokayev said Kazakhstan would continue to deepen international cooperation and attract investment, while promoting the country’s interests, history and culture internationally.

He said his goal was to position Kazakhstan on the global stage as a middle power and promote the country’s opportunities.

Concluding his address, Tokayev urged the People’s Council to remain closely connected with citizens and ensure that its work produces practical solutions to issues affecting the country and its people.

World.title: ‘No security guarantees’: Why Georgia’s Kamara festival was cancelled
World.content:
Kamara festival cancelled in Georgia

The Kamara music festival, scheduled to take place in the Georgian city of Gori on 26 September and close with a performance by opposition-minded musician Kordz, has been postponed indefinitely. The festival’s organiser, the Danish Cultural Institute, said it considered it unsafe to hold the event.

Kordz (Aleksandre Kordzaia) said he had faced attacks and threats from local authorities, members of the ruling Georgian Dream party and pro-government media.

The EU Delegation to Georgia responded to the festival’s cancellation by expressing regret. It said the Kamara festival was held as part of the EU-funded Creative Compass Georgia project and stressed that it “firmly believes in freedom of artistic expression”.

The delegation also noted that the EU had supported Georgia’s cultural sector for 30 years, including efforts to preserve the country’s cultural heritage, develop its creative industries and build links between Georgian artists and cultural organisations and their European counterparts.

Georgian parliament speaker Shalva Papuashvili responded critically to the EU Delegation’s statement. He said he had initially hoped the EU ambassador would realise that supporting “hatred and violence” in Georgia was unacceptable, but argued that the delegation’s statement suggested otherwise.

Papuashvili was particularly critical of the EU’s reference to the importance of freedom of artistic expression. He said the EU Delegation did not understand Georgia or Georgian society.

“This statement by the delegation is a direct incitement to hate speech, insults against mothers, labelling people as slaves, fascism and radicalism. The EU embassy is encouraging this,” Papuashvili told journalists.

The Georgian Musicians’ Union, in turn, responded to Papuashvili’s comments and the cancellation of Kordz’s performance by expressing solidarity with the musician. It said freedom of expression for artists was not a political privilege but a fundamental right.

The union said direct attacks by public officials on an artist over his civic stance went beyond debate and became a tool of censorship.

“It is unacceptable to use official power and rhetoric to intimidate musicians or disrupt concerts,” the union said.

It described Kordz as one of the prominent figures on Georgia’s music scene and warned that restricting artists’ ability to perform in their own country because of political pressure could have a serious impact on the cultural environment.

“Art cannot exist in an atmosphere of censorship and fear,” the statement said.

World.title: Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge with stones
World.content:
Russian tourists pelt Abkhaz Supreme Court judge

In Abkhazia, Russian tourists pelted a Supreme Court judge with stones. A criminal case was opened only several days later, and only after public pressure.

The incident took place in Sukhum on the evening of 20 September. According to official information, two Russian nationals, Yury Chudin and Sergey Bessonov, became involved in an altercation with a local woman in the street, threatened to kill her and then threw stones at her.

The woman was taken to hospital with a closed head injury, a laceration and bruising to her eyelid, and a haematoma.

The victim was later identified as a judge of the Supreme Court of Abkhazia, although neither investigators nor the media have named her. The cause of the altercation also remains unknown.

The incident was included in the official police report only after the Telegram channel Aiashara reported it a day later. The channel highlighted the fact that no criminal case had been opened, prompting a strong reaction on social media.

It was only after this that, on 23 September, the investigative department of the Sukhum police classified the attack on the judge as a criminal offence. Initially, the actions of the two Russian tourists had been treated as an administrative offence. Chudin and Bessonov refused to undergo medical tests for drug and psychotropic substance use, and a court subsequently sentenced them to 15 days in administrative detention.

The case has been transferred from the police to the Sukhum prosecutor’s office for further investigation. The ruling states that the decision was made in view of the public attention surrounding the case and the status of the victim.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Sovereignty, occupation, peace and economic ambitions: Georgian PM addresses UN
World.content:
Speaking at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze outlined the country’s international role, sovereignty, occupied territories, prospects for peace in the South Caucasus and economic ambitions.

His key messages brought together several themes: Georgia sees its future as based on sovereign choice, links cooperation with international partners to dialogue and mutual respect, and views itself as an important link in the Middle Corridor and the South Caucasus for regional stability and economic development.

Our own path’: sovereignty shaped by Georgia’s historical experience

From the UN podium, Irakli Kobakhidze linked Georgia’s historical experience to the issue of sovereignty. He said that for centuries Georgia had stood at the crossroads of civilisations, embracing different cultures and ideas while seeking to preserve its own identity.

“For centuries, we have stood at the crossroads of civilisations, opening our doors to different cultures, people and ideas, while firmly protecting our unique identity and distinctiveness,” the prime minister said.

He argued that Georgian statehood had repeatedly faced challenges, but that this experience had strengthened the country’s determination to chart its own course.

Kobakhidze placed particular emphasis on one of the key principles of the international order — the equal application of the same rules to all states.

“Historical experience has also taught us that we must always remember the price of sovereignty, that stability needs to be protected, and that the strength of the international order ultimately depends on the extent to which the same principles are applied equally to all states,” he said.

rakli Kobakhidze at the UN podium. Source: SOVA News

‘Long-term partnerships can only be achieved through dialogue’

Speaking about relations with international partners, the Georgian prime minister said Tbilisi was ready to continue cooperation with all countries that sought relations based on mutual respect and sovereign equality.

He said international cooperation was essential for Georgia but should be free from pressure and coercion.

“The progress we want to achieve in our own country is inconceivable without developing cooperation with other countries. Georgia once again expresses its readiness to continue relations with all international partners that are prepared to work with us on the basis of mutual respect and sovereign equality,” he said.

According to the prime minister, long-term partnerships are built through dialogue rather than coercion.

In the same context, he spoke about the role of the UN, saying that amid growing global uncertainty, the organisation remained an important international forum for dialogue and joint action.

Kobakhidze also voiced support for UN reform. He said the UN80 initiative offered an opportunity to improve the organisation’s effectiveness, transparency and accountability.

Occupation and appeal to Abkhaz and Ossetian communities

Georgia’s territorial conflicts featured prominently in the prime minister’s speech.

Kobakhidze said 20% of Georgia’s territory remained occupied by the Russian Federation and hundreds of thousands of people were still unable to return to their homes.

He then directly addressed the Abkhaz and Ossetian communities:

“Twenty per cent of our country’s territory remains occupied by the Russian Federation, while hundreds of thousands of our citizens remain internally displaced and are unable to return to their homes. One of the main themes of this year’s session is rebuilding trust, and it is against this backdrop that I would like to address our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers and sisters.

“For centuries, we shared one homeland and were bound by a common history. The dividing lines drawn today can neither erase that history nor determine the future of our children. We believe that the benefits brought by peace and Georgia’s economic development should not be limited by artificially drawn dividing lines. People living in our occupied historic regions should also be able to enjoy these benefits — those who have been and will always remain an integral part of our shared future.”

South Caucasus: opportunity for ‘fresh start’

Regional security also featured prominently in the Georgian prime minister’s speech.

Kobakhidze said the challenges facing Georgia could not be considered without taking into account the broader regional context.

He said Tbilisi sought to act as an honest broker in regional initiatives, promoting cooperation and helping to find peaceful solutions.

“Today, we see a real opportunity to make a fresh start in building a more peaceful and interconnected region,”Kobakhidze said.

He added that greater regional cooperation should not be limited to political stability, but should ultimately translate into tangible economic opportunities.

‘Peace cannot be achieved through force’

Against the backdrop of international conflicts, Kobakhidze also addressed the issue of peace, saying that lasting peace could not be achieved through the use of force.

“Lasting peace cannot be established through the use of force; it must be based on dialogue, mutual understanding and mutual respect,” the prime minister said.

He said that amid the challenges facing the world, preserving peace and strengthening international cooperation remained key priorities.

Kobakhidze also said that a coordinated response to global challenges, conflict prevention and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals required stronger international cooperation.

Economic growth: from figures to social outcomes

Another key part of the prime minister’s speech focused on Georgia’s economic performance and its goals for the coming years.

Kobakhidze said strong economic indicators should ultimately be reflected in people’s everyday lives — through higher per capita output and real wages, lower poverty, better jobs and greater economic resilience.

He said Georgia’s poverty rate had fallen from 21.3% in 2020 to 7.1%. The prime minister said one of the government’s main priorities over the next five years would be to reduce the urban-rural divide and expand opportunities in the regions.

“Ensuring that the benefits of economic growth are widely shared and that no one is left behind,” he said, describing one of the key priorities for the period.

Middle Corridor and Georgia as a link between Europe and Central Asia

In the economic part of his speech, Kobakhidze placed particular emphasis on Georgia’s geographical location. He said Georgia was an integral part of the South Caucasus and the Middle Corridor, giving the country an important role in connecting Central Asia with Europe.

The prime minister said direct access to the Black Sea offered advantages for trade and investment, while Georgia’s infrastructure could provide landlocked countries with access to global supply chains.

“Through our free trade agreements, we have created a network providing access to a market of approximately 2.3 billion consumers,” Kobakhidze said.

Georgia and UN: ‘The choices we make today’

Kobakhidze concluded his speech by addressing global responsibility. He said the decisions made by the international community today would shape the world in which future generations would live.

“The choices we make today will determine what kind of world we leave to future generations. Let us make sure we leave them a world that is more peaceful, secure and united than the one we have today,” the prime minister concluded.

World.title: ‘TRIPP project will move forward slowly’: US discusses regional connectivity agenda
World.content:
US discusses upcoming investments in the TRIPP project

Discussions in New York focused on the peace agenda between Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as regional connectivity. The US administration organised an event titled “Prosperity through Peace: Investing in the Trans-Caspian Trade Route and the TRIPP Initiative”.

The “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP) is a road that will connect Azerbaijan with its autonomous exclave of Nakhchivan through Armenian territory. For several years, Yerevan and Baku failed to reach an agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan demanded a road that it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia’s authorities said they were ready to unblock all roads but rejected the term “corridor”, which implies that the country would lose control over the territory and, therefore, its sovereign rights. The two sides reached an agreement only on 8 August in Washington. They agreed that the road would remain under Armenia’s sovereign control, while the US would join the unblocking process as a business partner. The project therefore took the name “Trump Route”, after the mediator. The road will be about 43km long. TRIPP also includes plans to build railway lines, energy infrastructure and digital communications networks. The US views TRIPP as a multimodal corridor designed to expand connectivity along the East-West axis, linking the South Caucasus, Central Asia and the West.

The speakers included the foreign ministers of Armenia and Azerbaijan, as well as Brendan Hanrahan, head of the US State Department’s Bureau of European and Eurasian Affairs. US special envoy for peace missions Steve Witkoff, representatives of Georgia and Central Asian countries also took part in the discussion.

According to Radio Azatutyun (Radio Liberty), Witkoff emphasised that, according to various estimates, the TRIPP route could cut delivery times for certain goods by 2.5 to three weeks:

“Witkoff’s key message was that the project’s potential benefits could extend beyond the two countries. It could create a new East-West transport artery, speed up the movement of goods, expand access to Central Asian markets and strengthen the role of American companies in this strategically important region — Eurasia.”

The Trump administration sees the project as a kind of test of whether the political momentum generated by the Armenia-Azerbaijan peace process can translate into tangible commercial infrastructure.

The official Yerevan statement on the event was brief. It said the speakers had discussed progress in the region since the Washington summit on 8 August 2025. They also discussed investment in the Trans-Caspian Enterprise Fund. The fund aims to attract private investment in projects along the wider Trans-Caspian trade route, also known as the “Middle Corridor”.

Armenian officials have repeatedly said that the fund has an “indirect and secondary” connection to the TRIPP initiative itself. The TRIPP Development Company will be specifically responsible for developing and implementing the project. Initially, the US will own 74% of the company’s shares, while Armenia will hold 26%. After the 49-year term expires, Armenia’s share will rise to 49% if the partners extend their agreement for another 50 years.

“The section running through Armenia is not yet ready for construction”

The event in New York focused on moving the TRIPP initiative towards practical implementation. The discussion covered issues such as financing, the creation of institutional mechanisms and infrastructure planning.

“Progress in the next phase will be measured not so much by diplomatic statements as by feasibility studies, investment commitments and, ultimately, construction itself,” US representatives said.

As part of engineering and feasibility studies, experts are currently examining the proposed railway route, taking technical, environmental and social factors into account.

The studies are expected to be completed in late 2026 or early 2027. The next steps will involve selecting companies to participate in the project and assessing investment opportunities.

According to US participants in the discussion, however, the territory through which the railway will run is not yet ready for construction. At the same time, they stressed that the United States takes the initiative seriously, pointing to the work already underway to advance TRIPP. They also warned that the project would not be completed overnight.

“TRIPP will move forward slowly, given the project’s technical complexity and geopolitical sensitivity,” said Andrew D’Anieri, deputy director of the Eurasia Center at the Atlantic Council.

He said the process would require engineering studies, regulatory decisions, funding and tenders. Only then would the “technically complex construction” phase begin. Preliminary estimates suggest that building the railway itself would also take considerable time — at least 18 months from the start of construction.

Pashinyan: “TRIPP will open a new era for our country and economy”

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan is also in the United States. In New York, he took part in a panel discussion at the Concordia Summit, held on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Speaking about the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan and the opportunities it has created, he stressed that efforts are now focused primarily on implementing TRIPP. The project, he said, would unlock the full potential of regional connectivity.

“It will open a new era for our country and economy,” the prime minister said.

Alongside TRIPP, the Armenian government also intends to implement its Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to fully reopen the country’s transport links.

The prime minister’s office said that Pashinyan had discussed the implementation of TRIPP and the reopening of regional transport links with the Turkish president during his visit to the United States the previous day.

World.title: Georgian judge challenges in Constitutional Court law criminalising insults against public officials
World.content:
Georgia: judge challenges officials’ insult law

A judge at Kutaisi City Court in Georgia, Tsitsino Kikvadze, has asked the Constitutional Court to review the constitutionality of Article 173¹⁶ of the Administrative Offences Code.

Kikvadze says the provision, which establishes special administrative liability for insulting state and political officials and public servants, may violate freedom of expression.

The judge notes that such conduct is already covered by Article 166 of the Administrative Offences Code. But Article 173¹⁶ ties liability to a person’s official status and therefore provides for harsher penalties.

Under the contested provision, verbal insults, swearing, offensive remarks or other insulting acts directed at a state or political official, public or civil servant while they are performing their duties or in connection with their work are subject to administrative liability.

Since June, Georgia’s Interior Ministry has had a new department tasked with combating hate speech, including monitoring what people write and say in public places. Lawyers criticised the initiative at the time as an attempt to legalise censorship. On social media, the department was dubbed the “scrolling agency”.

Since then, dozens of people have been fined. Also, TV host Vakho Sanaia was sentenced to 14 days of administrative detention and activist Giorgi Akhobadze to one month, both over Facebook posts.

What arguments did the judge make in her constitutional petition?

The constitutional petition stems from a specific administrative case.

On June 23, 2026, a unit of the Interior Ministry’s Human Rights Protection Department filed an administrative offence complaint with Kutaisi City Court against citizen Irakli Kezevadze.

According to the complaint, Kezevadze verbally insulted Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze in a Facebook post on June 3. At the court hearing, he confirmed this and said he had been drunk.

Kezevadze also described his difficult social and family circumstances. He said his wife had died three years ago, he had no children, was unemployed and was caring for his sick mother.

Asked whether he continued to make similar comments on social media, he said he no longer did so and was “not engaged in such activities at all”.

Duplication

Judge Kikvadze argues that such conduct is already covered by Article 166 of the Administrative Offences Code. The purpose of that provision is to protect public order and the peace of all citizens. Article 173¹⁶, by contrast, provides special protection to a particular category of people — public officials — and makes liability dependent on their official status.

The two articles provide for different penalties

Article 166 provides for a fine of 500 to 3,000 lari (about $190-$1,100) or up to 20 days of administrative detention.

Article 173¹⁶ provides for a fine of 1,500 to 4,000 lari (about $600-$1,500), while administrative detention can last up to 45 days.

Harsher penalties for insulting public officials than private citizens

The judge also considers it problematic that Article 173¹⁶ does not allow for exemption from liability.

Under Article 166, however, the court has the option to exempt a person from liability.

According to Kikvadze, this means that for essentially similar conduct, the court’s options differ solely because of the victim’s official status and the context of their work.

Politicians should tolerate more criticism than private citizens

Kikvadze’s petition places particular emphasis on freedom of expression.

She notes that Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution protects freedom of expression and that restrictions are permitted only in cases established by the Constitution.

In this context, Kikvadze cites the case law of Georgia’s Constitutional Court and the European Court of Human Rights, which holds that public officials, and particularly political officials, are expected to tolerate a greater degree of criticism than private individuals.

Her submission cites European Court of Human Rights cases including Lingens v. Austria and Handyside v. the United Kingdom.

Judge warns law could deter citizens from criticising authorities

One of the judge’s main concerns is the possible “chilling effect” of the provision.

The risk of a substantial fine or administrative detention for expressing an opinion in harsh or insulting terms about a state or political official could deter citizens not only from prohibited conduct, but also from criticism that is lawful.

Kikvadze points to a statement by Kezevadze that he no longer makes such comments and “doesn’t engage in such activities anymore”.

These words alone do not prove that the provision has a chilling effect on everyone, but they illustrate how sanctions can lead to self-censorship.

The judge’s petition also cites a 2021 ruling by the European Court of Human Rights in Vedat Şorli v. Turkey. The case concerned the use of a special criminal provision in Turkey for insulting the president.

The European Court found a violation of Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It held that imposing a special and more severe liability regime when the president is involved raises concerns regarding freedom of expression.

According to Kikvadze, the case does not directly concern the Georgian provision being challenged, but provides an important reference point when assessing whether public figures should receive greater legal protection and face different sanctions based on their status.

The state can protect officials — but is a stricter regime necessary?

The judge says the state has the right to protect public officials and political figures from unlawful interference while they are carrying out their duties.

But she stresses that the issue is not whether such protection is a legitimate aim, but whether the special and more severe regime under Article 173¹⁶ is necessary to achieve it.

The Constitutional Court should consider three questions when assessing the contested provision:

To what extent is a special, harsher penalty necessary to protect public officials;

Whether less restrictive means could achieve the same aim, including Article 166 of the Administrative Offences Code or civil-law remedies;

Whether the protection of public interests achieved through the stricter Article 173¹⁶ is proportionate to the harm that the restriction on freedom of expression may cause, including its potential “chilling effect”.

Kutaisi City Court is also asking the Constitutional Court to assess whether it is constitutional for Article 173¹⁶ to impose special administrative liability for verbal insults specifically against state and political officials, public and civil servants, while excluding the possibility of exempting the accused from liability.

Tsitsino Kikvadze has been a judge in Georgia’s common courts system since 2005. She has worked at Kutaisi City Court since 2013 and was appointed as a judge for life in 2016. In 2024, she was among the judges who signed a public statement protesting the government’s decision to suspend Georgia’s EU accession process.
