World.title: Armenia-Azerbaijan relations in crisis: domestic and external factors
World.content:
Crisis in Armenia-Azerbaijan relations

The process of normalising relations between Armenia and Azerbaijan is facing a crisis. Armenian analysts attribute it to instability driven by a combination of regional and global factors. In their view, the absence of official mediators in the negotiations does not prevent the US, Russia and Iran from influencing the positions of Yerevan and Baku. Against this backdrop, competing narratives are hardening, with new claims over borders and cultural heritage.

The general turmoil of recent weeks has also affected civil society. Dialogue under the “Bridge of Peace” initiative has stalled. The Azerbaijani side asked to postpone a meeting between experts from the two countries, which was due to take place in Yerevan in the coming days, “until tensions subside”. Boris Navassardian, a political analyst and the initiative’s Armenian co-founder, announced the decision.

“We want these meetings to go ahead, not be postponed. The Armenian side believed that, in this acute situation, the two sides needed to meet, try to reach a mutual understanding and agree on the kind of atmosphere they wanted to foster in the media and public sphere. However, our colleagues from Azerbaijan apparently do not consider contact at this stage appropriate,” he said.

The Azerbaijani publication Minval Politika explained the cancellation by citing an “information campaign” against Azerbaijan by Armenia and what it described as an attempt by the Armenian authorities to interfere in Azerbaijan’s sovereignty. However, the publication provided no evidence to support these claims. Tensions escalated after 150 diplomats from 58 countries, accredited inAzerbaijan, visited Karabakh. They toured the territory that the entire Armenian population left in 2023 and visited historical and cultural sites. Hikmet Hajiyev, an aide to Azerbaijan’s president, accompanied them. He showed the diplomats the Armenian monasteries of Gandzasar and Dadivank, claiming that they formed “an integral part of the ancient Caucasian Albanian Christian heritage”. The “Bridge of Peace” initiative uses a Track 1.5 dialogue format. It complements official negotiations rather than replacing them. As part of the process, experts, civil society representatives and media professionals held direct discussions and explored steps to prepare their societies for peace. The project has held four meetings so far: two in Armenia and two in Azerbaijan.

Commentary by political analyst Boris Navassardian

Radical narratives as a tool of pressure

“The current situation is not an isolated incident but the result of deep-rooted problems in the normalisation process. Mutual expectations may not be met, or the parties may be moving away from the principles agreed at the meeting held in Washington on 8 August 2025 under the mediation of the US president. The reasons may relate to the unblocking of transport links, delimitation and the issue of enclaves, or Baku’s desire to reassess its relations with the US, the EU and Russia.

Neither side has a shared vision of the endgame.

Two approaches dominate in Azerbaijan. The first holds that the outcome of the 44-day war in Karabakh has not yet been fully realised, and that Baku should secure further advantages: a favourable settlement on the enclaves and special rights to use Armenia’s transport links.

The second approach is more radical. Some members of the expert community claim that Azerbaijan has a right to all of Armenia’s territory except for 10,000 square kilometres. This refers to maps of the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic from 1918–1920, which a delegation led by parliamentary speaker Alimardan Topchubashov took to the Paris Peace Conference at the time.

These views cannot be described as Baku’s official position, but neither are they marginal: a significant part of Azerbaijani society takes them seriously.

They may serve as a tool to pressure Yerevan into making smaller concessions. But the narrative is taking root in society. Given who is voicing these claims, they are unlikely to run counter to the position of Azerbaijan’s leadership. Rather, they form part of a narrative struggle and the negotiating process, in which psychological pressure serves as an element of diplomacy.

This factor cannot be dismissed. It must be taken seriously and countered effectively. The best solutions in this case are mutual recognition of territorial integrity, the establishment of interstate relations as set out in the initialled peace agreement, and the delimitation of borders while taking local residents’ interests into account.

Even when the issue involves socio-economic difficulties or the forced relocation of just a few hundred people, it affects the overall atmosphere. A constructive approach requires these factors to be taken into account.

There are also people in Armenia who build their political platforms around the idea of returning Nagorno-Karabakh and making claims against Azerbaijan. The situation there is not entirely smooth either. But Baku objectively has greater resources and influence than Yerevan. The authorities there are not under direct pressure from society, but they take public sentiment into account. That is why constructive approaches need to gain wider acceptance in Azerbaijan as well, not just in Armenia. This could influence diplomacy.”

External factors

“It is unclear how constructive approaches will work in practice. Recent weeks have shown that hopes of building relations between Baku and Yerevan independently of the external environment have not been fully realised.

Turbulence within the US, the conflict between Russia and Ukraine coupled with Moscow’s changing ambitions, and the situation in Iran all affect the Armenian-Azerbaijani process. Any changes have an impact on the course of normalisation. Today, domestic and external factors have become intertwined, creating instability. External powers influence the parties’ positions even though, according to official statements from Yerevan and Baku, there are no mediators in the negotiations.

US initiatives to develop cooperation with Armenia have provided a key economic and technological foundation for constructive relations. These include the TRIPP project [a transit route through Armenian territory linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhchivan] and the development of data centres in Armenia. However, the situation in the US itself, particularly the midterm congressional elections, could lead to a change in this policy.

If Washington’s positive pressure weakens, the parties may shift their focus to other factors.

We can see clear attempts by Russia, on the one hand, to threaten Armenia and obstruct the implementation of agreements, including TRIPP, and, on the other, to make favourable offers to Azerbaijan to preserve its influence in the region. Iran is also pursuing its own interests and signalling its intention to prevent TRIPP from going ahead under the US framework.

All these factors influence the positions of the two capitals. Although, de jure, none of the three countries mentioned is a mediator or a direct participant in the negotiations.”

The battle of narratives

“When assessing statements coming out of Baku, from the rhetoric of officials to remarks by public figures, we need to distinguish clearly between different levels. On the one hand, some former officials and experts have made direct territorial claims against Armenia. Yerevan must categorically reject this position and refuse to discuss it altogether.

On the other hand, there is the issue of ‘Western Azerbaijan’. Formally, it is framed not as a territorial claim but as the right of Azerbaijanis to return to the places where they lived before the conflict began in 1988–1990. This issue is not currently part of the official negotiating agenda, although advocates actively promote it in the public sphere.

If Baku attempts to formally include this idea in the negotiations, it would mark a departure from the principles agreed in August 2025 and pose a serious threat to the peace process.

For now, however, it remains at the level of a public movement. It is possible to coexist with this movement while trying to influence the balance of narratives within Azerbaijani society.

Another issue concerns statements by presidential aide Hikmet Hajiyev in Gandzasar, Nagorno-Karabakh, about cultural and historical heritage. We are witnessing a relatively new phenomenon: Baku is seeking to portray Christian monuments on its territory exclusively as part of the heritage of the modern Azerbaijani state.

One possible explanation is that Azerbaijan is trying to reshape its relations with the EU. An analysis of the difficulties in its dialogue with Brussels may have led Baku to conclude that the European Union is a political bloc rooted in Christian traditions. To improve its image, Azerbaijan needs to show that Christian culture is not alien to it. This may explain why Baku is so persistently promoting the narrative that Christian heritage in this territory belongs exclusively to Azerbaijan, while Armenia, which enjoys particular favour in Europe, has no connection to it.”

Separating the past from the present and the future

“Armenia should respond to these developments in a differentiated manner. At the official level, Yerevan should state clearly and consistently that Azerbaijan’s attempts to reshape narratives and change the external environment surrounding the negotiations to gain advantages are hindering normalisation. Armenian diplomacy must actively oppose these efforts.

At the academic and expert level, there is a need to demonstrate with evidence that Baku’s attempts to revise established views of cultural and historical heritage lack scientific credibility and are unfounded. Above all, these issues must not be allowed to become entangled with politics.

In the field of civil diplomacy, the guiding principle should be that genuine differences over interpretations of the past must not stand in the way of contact. Dialogue should focus on the present and the future, where the development of ties remains the only basis for ensuring regional stability.”

A frozen “bridge”

“Parliamentary elections in Armenia temporarily suspended civil society dialogue as attention shifted to domestic politics. However, after the elections, the parties came up against difficult issues that they had initially postponed. It was clearly impossible to reach an immediate agreement on matters such as the basic content of textbooks. But experts were ready to discuss removing elements of mutual insults from educational materials. At the very least, they managed to move towards an agreement on this level.

However, the general situation in recent weeks has effectively frozen dialogue under the “Bridge of Peace” initiative. The parties had to postpone discussions of sensitive issues until the initiative’s prospects become clearer.

Meanwhile, cooperation continues in other formats. In particular, the Yerevan and Baku press clubs, which are preparing to mark 30 years of cooperation, continue to produce joint programmes.

Armenian-Azerbaijani relations require movement in both directions. Communication at the civil society and expert levels lays the groundwork for a constructive official process. Agreements in the fields of communication and economics also directly influence public sentiment.

Progress in both directions must be intensive. The “Bridge of Peace” initiative would benefit greatly from the practical launch of economic projects. Any progress in this area makes civil society dialogue more effective. In turn, public attitudes influence the parties’ willingness to compromise. All sides must make an effort. This is the only way to preserve the positive climate that has taken shape in recent months.”

Crisis in Armenia-Azerbaijan relations

World.title: Georgia joins joint statement in support of Ukraine at UN
World.content:
51 UN member states, including Georgia, have signed a joint statement in support of Ukraine, calling on Russia to agree to a full ceasefire and begin peace talks. EU High Representative Kaja Kallas read out the statement in New York during the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.

According to Ukrainian media, the United States did not join the statement.

The signatories expressed solidarity with Ukraine and reaffirmed their support for Kyiv’s efforts to achieve peace amid the ongoing war with Russia.

“Ukraine wants peace. We want peace. Russia must end its aggression, agree to a ceasefire and engage meaningfully in negotiations to achieve a comprehensive, just and lasting peace in accordance with international law,” the statement said.

The countries also called for freedom of navigation and commercial shipping in the Black Sea, the protection of critical infrastructure and the unimpeded export of Ukrainian grain. They said these measures were important for maintaining global food security.

The signatories also urged Russia to immediately return all Ukrainian civilians who had been unlawfully detained, forcibly transferred or deported, including children. The call also covered prisoners of war and internees.

Georgia’s Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili also took part in events on Ukraine held in New York. She attended the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform, titled “Unity under pressure, a call to action”, which took place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

Bochorishvili said Ukraine was particularly important to Georgia because the country itself was experiencing the consequences of violations of its territorial integrity.

“For Georgia, Ukraine is not just another item on the international agenda. We know very well what it means when a state’s sovereignty and territorial integrity are violated,” the minister said.

According to Bochorishvili, Russia’s occupation of two regions of Georgia continues and remains one of the country’s main security challenges.

“We know very well how devastating occupation can be for individuals, families and society. Based on this experience, Georgia attaches particular importance to solidarity, respect for international law and an unwavering commitment to the principles on which a peaceful and secure international order should be built,” Bochorishvili said.

She also discussed the role of the International Crimea Platform, describing it as an important mechanism for keeping international attention focused on Ukraine and turning political support into concrete action.

Bochorishvili said Georgia supported efforts to end the war and achieve a lasting peace based on the UN Charter and the principles of international law.

“Georgia stands firmly with the Ukrainian people and once again reaffirms its unwavering support for Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” she said.

The Crimea Platform is a high-level international forum held annually to provide political support for Ukraine.

UN adopts statement in support of Ukraine

World.title: “Four members of my family are fighting: my mother, two brothers and me” – story of Ukrainian Olha Bihari, known by call sign “Witch”
World.content:
Olha Bihari, Ukraine’s drone commander

Hromadske

Thirty-four-year-old Olha Bihari, who goes by the call sign “Witch,” heads the Unmanned Systems Directorate of Ukraine’s 20th Army Corps. Before joining the military, she studied neuroscience, later earned a law degree and worked in human rights advocacy.

After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Bihari went to the recruitment office with her mother and younger brother. Her other brother has been fighting since 2015. Today, four members of the family are at war.

In an interview with the Ukrainian publication Hromadske, Bihari spoke about her family, commanding troops, losses, unmanned systems and why a modern military must rely on technology and data analysis.

Based on a report by Hromadske

Kramatorsk, family and war

Olha was born in Kramatorsk. She says Ukrainian identity was an important part of her family history.

Her paternal grandfather was an engineer and a dissident from the Prykarpattia region of western Ukraine. His family had ties to the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN). He was monitored by the KGB, never joined the Communist Party and continued to speak Ukrainian.

In the 1990s, her grandfather joined the People’s Movement of Ukraine and campaigned for the country’s independence. He later became involved in public life in Kramatorsk.

Her maternal grandmother came from a Cossack family in the Poltava region. The family maintained Ukrainian traditions at home, sang folk songs and celebrated traditional holidays.

Olha wanted to become a scientist and studied neuroscience. But after the Maidan, she decided not to leave the country to pursue a scientific career abroad. She earned a law degree and, starting in 2019, worked in human rights advocacy.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, on Feb. 25, 2022, Olha, her mother and her younger brother went to a military recruitment office. By then, her other brother had already been fighting since 2015.

▇ “No one even considered not serving. How could we? You are either a victim or a defender.”

Before the war, Olha’s mother worked as a journalist. She later trained as a military psychologist and now serves in Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces.

Her younger brother was studying law and went to war at 18. Olha suggested that he finish his studies first.

“Olya, what’s the point of studying to defend people’s rights? If the Muscovites come for us, it won’t help,” he replied.

“We knew very well what occupation was like and, in general, what that whole romance of Russian unity among peoples smelled like,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

When the whole family is at the front

According to Bihari, serving together helps the family understand one another. They have a family group chat where they share photos and news every day.

Once, Olha ran into her younger brother in a village near the front. Knowing that his sister barely slept and sometimes did not have time to buy food, he came to cook her dinner and leave enough food for several days.

But when family members are in danger, professional composure cannot keep fear at bay.

During the fighting for Bakhmut, one of Bihari’s brothers found himself surrounded.

“I thought I was going to lose my mind. In those days, I lived on coffee. I had no right to show my emotions, because I could demoralize my troops.”

She did not call her brother. Instead, she called his commander, trying to find out what was happening and whether there was a way to evacuate him.

Bihari generally does not tell her family about her own dangerous missions. If a guided aerial bomb lands nearby or an FPV drone strikes her vehicle, she tells them about it only after she returns.

“When my brother was trapped in Bakhmut and couldn’t get out, I thought I was going to lose my mind,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.



From neuroscience and law to command

In the spring of 2022, Bihari began serving in the territorial defense infantry near Kyiv. She had no military experience.

According to her, much of what happened in those first weeks was driven by initiative. About 200 people joined the unit, most of them civilians. There was not even a complete personnel roster.

Bihari began gathering data, establishing communication with the command and learning how to navigate military documentation.

▇ “Whoever was willing to take responsibility did so.”

That was how she gradually found herself in a command role.

In 2023, Bihari went to Bakhmut as the acting commander of an infantry platoon. It was there, she said, that she fully understood the importance of planning.

“Casualties are not a matter of chance. They are the result of how well you planned the logistics, scheduled the time of deployment and organized the actions of your units.”

She later completed leadership courses at the Ukrainian Ground Forces Academy.

Bihari has served in infantry, artillery and unmanned systems. She considers organizing units and training personnel her greatest achievements.

“In civilian life, I was criticized for my blunt, tough personality. In the military, it is seen as normal,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

“Most casualties are the result of poor planning”

Bihari believes one of a commander’s main responsibilities is to understand each person’s capabilities.

She recalls a serviceman who was afraid to go out to positions. After talking to him, she realized the problem was not that he was unwilling to serve. In her view, he had simply been assigned to the wrong role.

Bihari transferred him to electronic intelligence, where he became a successful specialist.

“Everyone has their strengths. If a commander has problems with personnel, I always step in.”

She connects her approach to command with her scientific background: analysis, methodology and forecasting.

▇ “Most casualties in the military are either the result of emotions taking over and you acting reactively rather than proactively, or a failure in planning.”

“Most casualties in the military are either the result of emotions taking over or a failure in planning,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

“We can no longer fight a war in excel”

These days, Bihari’s day begins at around 5 a.m. with a briefing to her senior commander on the situation at the positions.

After that, she always sets aside 10 minutes for coffee and planning. From the many tasks before her, she chooses one priority that she intends to devote most of her resources to.

Bihari describes unmanned systems as a “delivery service.” Drones can carry out strikes, remotely mine areas, deliver ammunition, food, fuel and water, and robotic systems are also used to evacuate the wounded.

A significant part of her work involves data analysis.

Bihari says she digitized military management processes because it is impossible to handle such a volume of information manually.

▇ “We can no longer fight a war in Excel. We have to see earlier, understand faster and act ahead of events, because the enemy has the advantage in numbers, while we have to rely on intelligence and technology.”

She analyzes thousands of strike, logistical and other tasks, identifies weak points and then works with specific units.

She receives around 300 phone calls a day. The fewest she can remember having in a day is 128. On top of that come video conferences and meetings.

Bihari does not use artificial intelligence to analyze military data. She says much of the information is classified or intended for official use only, making it impossible to upload it to external systems.

Three hours of sleep, a son and a manicure

Bihari says she is not very emotional. When a problem arises, her principle is simple: find a solution first, reflect later.

During an especially difficult period, she slept an average of three hours and 40 minutes a day for three months.

“I went to the car, closed the doors, screamed it out, came back — and that was it. I was fine. I could keep working.”

She has no days off and has not taken a vacation in more than a year. She unwinds by reading books on military leadership and planning, and by driving and riding her motorcycle.

She barely sees her son now. When they do meet, they speak to each other in English.

At the same time, Bihari has kept a habit instilled by her grandmother in childhood — taking care of her nails. She does her own manicures, sometimes sacrificing two hours of sleep to do it.

“Nails are actually very useful. I’ve used them to fix a car and even to pull a fragment out of my leg.”

“I barely see my child these days,” Bihari said. Photo courtesy of Hromadske.

Injuries and attitudes toward sexism

Bihari has not officially reported her injuries. She says she feels uncomfortable going to a military hospital with a minor shrapnel wound when there are soldiers there who have undergone amputations.

She also says her hearing has deteriorated following concussions.

Asked about sexism in the military, Bihari says she tries to analyze not the comments themselves but the reasons behind a person’s behavior.

She responds to flirting and inappropriate compliments with a direct question.

“What do you want? Why did you say that? Are you trying to build some kind of relationship with me, or do you just want to chat?”

She says such conversations usually stop after that.

Bihari also uses her public profile to raise money. One charitable campaign raised six million hryvnias for winter uniforms for female service members.

She considers financial independence essential. She started working at the age of 12.

“If you want to see people around you rather than resources, you need to be able to stand on your own. And that is the principle I live by.”

Exchange

World.title: Alat FEZ highlights export-oriented manufacturing as key advantage
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Export-oriented manufacturing companies focused on producing high-value-added goods for markets outside Azerbaijan are our advantage, Chairman of the Board of the Alat Free Economic Zone (FEZ) Valeh Alasgarov said at the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum held in Baku today, Trend's correspondent reports from the event.

He noted that, to be successful, Azerbaijan should not simply replicate other free economic zones but should offer more distinctive advantages.

"The difference between the Alat Free Economic Zone and other free economic zones lies in the breadth of its competitive advantages.

The Alat Free Economic Zone is located at the intersection of the North-South and East-West transport corridors, near the Caspian Sea. This means that we offer our clients all types of transport and logistics services, including road, rail and sea transport," he said.

Alasgarov also added that one of the most important aspects of the Alat Free Economic Zone is its legislation.

"In other countries, zones are established under the standard laws of those countries. In our case, there is a specific Law of the Republic of Azerbaijan on the Alat Free Economic Zone. This is a very important factor for investors," he stressed.

The second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum is being held in Baku.

The two-day forum is organized by Azerbaijan's Ministry of Economy and the Azerbaijan Export and Investment Promotion Agency (AZPROMO), under the ministry, in strategic partnership with The European House – Ambrosetti.

The forum's plenary and panel sessions will address strategic topics including the Middle Corridor, energy and the green transition, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, infrastructure, industry and free economic zones, critical raw materials, agribusiness, financial cooperation, small and medium-sized business development, tourism, and investment in real estate and human capital.

World.title: Kazakhstan proposes annual investment dialogue with China
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. The Kazakhstan-China Investment Forum should become a permanent platform for direct interaction between the business communities of the two countries, Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said at the Kazakhstan-China Investment Forum in Almaty today, according to the presedential press service.

“I propose holding it annually in September under the name Almaty Investment Dialogue ‘Kazakhstan-China.’ A number of specific agreements have been reached today. I am confident that these agreements will benefit not only Kazakhstan and China, but also the sustainable development of the entire Eurasian continent,” the president said.

Tokayev noted that the implementation of joint initiatives requires an appropriate financial architecture. He told forum participants that the Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC) has been operating successfully in Kazakhstan for many years.

“We see great potential in developing cooperation between the AIFC and Hong Kong, one of the world’s leading financial centers. In early September this year, Samruk-Kazyna became the first issuer from Central Asia and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization countries to enter China’s interbank market, issuing panda bonds worth more than 3 billion yuan ($450 million). Kazakhstan intends to make the entire investment cycle as short, transparent and technology-driven as possible. The signing of the agreement to establish a Kazakh-Chinese investment fund under Kazakh Invest, the national investment promotion company, is another important step in this direction,” Tokayev said.

Tokayev added that Kazakhstan attaches particular importance to strengthening its enduring friendship with China.

“For our country, this is one of the most important goals of our foreign policy. If we look at our common history, the Chinese people have never caused any harm to our people. For many years, the two peoples have coexisted in genuine harmony, maintaining mutual respect and providing support to each other. In the current unstable and uncertain times, Kazakhstan and China, as reliable partners, should act together, side by side, to confront numerous challenges and threats,” he said.

World.title: Azerbaijan meat production growth to further stabilize prices — minister (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Increased meat production in Azerbaijan will help further stabilize prices, Minister of Agriculture Majnun Mammadov told Trend in an exclusive interview on Friday on the sidelines of the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku.

The minister noted that Azerbaijan has only recently begun implementing the State Program for the Development of Various Areas of Agriculture, with increasing production set to be one of the key objectives in the coming period.

"The state program was adopted recently, and its implementation has only just begun. As it is implemented, we will seek to increase agricultural production in the country, including meat production. As meat production increases, prices will become increasingly stable," Mammadov said.

The minister expressed confidence that the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum would have a positive impact on attracting investment to the country.

According to him, the forum supports the development of various sectors, including transport and logistics, agriculture and industry.

"I believe this event will have a positive effect on attracting investment to Azerbaijan. Various sectors, including transport, logistics, agriculture and industry, will benefit from this," the minister stressed.

Mammadov said investors are also showing interest in various areas of agriculture.

"Under the state program, the development of various agricultural sectors in Azerbaijan is currently envisaged. Most of the inquiries received by the Ministry of Agriculture over the past few months show that investors intend to invest in greenhouse farming, fruit growing and livestock," he said.

The minister added that the investment projects being implemented are expected to contribute to expanding agricultural production and, consequently, increasing the supply of products on the market.

"We hope these projects will have a positive effect," Mammadov said.

The second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum is currently being held in Baku.

The two-day event is organized by Azerbaijan's Ministry of Economy and its subordinate Azerbaijan Export and Investment Promotion Agency (AZPROMO), in strategic partnership with The European House – Ambrosetti.

This year's forum is dedicated to the theme "Restoring Trust in a Divided World: The South Caucasus as a Pillar of Global Interconnectedness and Investment Stability" and brings together leading global investors, government representatives, international financial institutions and business leaders.

World.title: Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan discuss further strengthening of bilateral relations
World.content:
Photo: Press Service of the Cabinet of Ministers of Kyrgyzstan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. State Secretary of Kyrgyzstan Arslan Koichiev held a meeting with Vice President of Kazakhstan Erlan Karin in Astana, during which the sides discussed further strengthening and development of bilateral relations.

According to the press service of the President of Kyrgyzstan, the sides highlighted the importance of the principles of mutual respect, accord, unity, mutual assistance and mutual understanding, which serve as the basis for strengthening friendly and good-neighborly relations between the two countries.

"The meeting focused on further strengthening and development of Kyrgyz-Kazakh relations," the statement said.

Particular attention was paid to preserving and further developing the historical, cultural and humanitarian ties that have existed between the Kyrgyz and Kazakh peoples for centuries.

The sides emphasized the importance of continuing mutual support and constructive dialogue, and exchanged views on further expanding public and humanitarian ties between Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan.

Meanwhile, Kyrgyzstan and Kazakhstan maintain close political, economic and humanitarian ties and regularly hold high-level meetings and consultations on bilateral cooperation.

The two countries are members of regional organizations and participate in various multilateral formats. Bilateral cooperation covers trade and investment, transport, energy, culture, education and other areas.

Historical and cultural ties between the Kyrgyz and Kazakh peoples also remain an important element of bilateral relations, with the countries regularly holding cultural, educational and humanitarian events.

World.title: Azerbaijan looks to public procurement to drive new businesses and local industry
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Azerbaijan’s public procurement system can help lay the foundation for new businesses and drive local industry, Elnur Bagirov, chairman of the State Service for Antimonopoly and Consumer Market Control, said at the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum today in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the even.

He noted that physical platforms need to be supported by a strong institutional framework for an investor to make a competitive and long-term decision when entering any market, including Azerbaijan.

“Within this framework, a competitive and transparent public procurement system can be one of the most effective tools for implementing new projects by providing initial demand and a reliable market route.

“Azerbaijan’s new law on public procurement is a clear example of such a modern institution. Adopted in July 2023 and entering into force in January 2024, the law brings the national system closer to international best practices by strengthening competition, transparency, equal treatment and efficiency.

“Most importantly, the law also completed the transition to electronic procurement. Through the unified e-Tender portal, procurement planning, notices and documents, bid submissions, communication, results and procurement records are managed within a single digital environment. For investors, this means greater visibility of market opportunities, fewer administrative barriers and a more transparent and predictable route to public procurement,” he added.

The second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum is being held in Baku.

The two-day forum is organized by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy and its subordinate Azerbaijan Export and Investment Promotion Agency (AZPROMO), in strategic partnership with European House – Ambrosetti.

Plenary and panel sessions at the event will address strategic issues including the Middle Corridor, energy and the green transition, artificial intelligence and digital transformation, infrastructure, industry and free economic zones, critical raw materials, agribusiness, financial cooperation, small and medium-sized business development, tourism, real estate and investment in human capital.

World.title: Syria seeks to expand energy, industrial ties with Azerbaijan — minister (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Syria is interested in expanding cooperation with Azerbaijan in trade, technology, energy, agriculture and industry, Syrian Minister of Economy and Industry Mohammad Nidal al-Shaar told Trend in an interview on Friday on the sidelines of the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku.

He made the remarks on Friday on the sidelines of the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku.

The minister said there are significant opportunities to expand cooperation between the two countries.

"There are many opportunities for Syria and Azerbaijan in trade, technology and, of course, energy. Energy is undoubtedly at the top of the list. We already have experience of cooperation with Azerbaijan in the gas sector, and we hope this cooperation will continue to cover other areas as well," al-Shaar said.

According to him, agriculture, agricultural products and various industrial sectors are also among the areas where cooperation between Azerbaijan and Syria can be developed.

"As with Azerbaijan and Syria, there are areas where both countries have good opportunities. Agriculture and industry are among them. I think cooperation in these areas could bring significant benefits to both countries," the minister said.

Al-Shaar also stressed the importance of today's announcement on the establishment of a Joint Business Council between Azerbaijan and Syria for developing business ties between the two countries.

"This platform will serve as a kind of gateway for interaction between Syria and Azerbaijan. Business representatives play a very important role in creating partnerships, exploring investment opportunities and attracting capital to both countries," he said.

According to the minister, the Joint Business Council will enable business communities in the two countries to explore mutual investment opportunities more closely.

"We want to allow business representatives to explore the opportunities available in both countries. This platform will be a means of advancing the interests of the governments in trade and investment," al-Shaar said.

The Syrian Minister of Economy and Industry also assessed the impact of Azerbaijan's natural gas exports to Syria on the country's energy supply.

"This has, of course, had a very positive impact and has enabled us to generate more electricity. We hope to continue such business ties with Azerbaijan," the minister added.

World.title: Azerbaijan targets further economic diversification through 2030
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Azerbaijan’s National Development Strategy through 2030 envisages further economic diversification with a focus on the private sector, Economy Minister Mikayil Jabbarov said Friday at the second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum in Baku, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

According to Jabbarov, priority areas under the strategy will include industrial production, services and investment in human capital.

“Further diversification of the economy should be led by the private sector, with a focus on areas such as industrial production and the development of services, while placing greater emphasis on investment in human capital and people so that they are prepared for the changes taking place,” Jabbarov said.

He noted that the energy transition and artificial intelligence will play an important role in implementing the strategy, including by increasing economic productivity and improving the delivery of public services.

According to the minister, ensuring access to long-term financing and developing capital markets will be among the key priorities through 2030.

“Regional partnerships are of paramount importance, as an important part of the strategy is export-oriented. We cannot afford to be limited by our domestic market,” he said.

Jabbarov also highlighted the importance of the Middle Corridor, stressing that its role extends beyond the transportation and transit of goods.

“The Middle Corridor is not only a means and route for transporting or transiting goods, but also involves joint processing, the creation of hubs, the development of a favorable environment, a financial center and regional financial resources, as well as joint investments,” he said.

According to Jabbarov, these areas are part of the objectives of Azerbaijan’s National Development Strategy through 2030.

The second Azerbaijan International Investment Forum is being held in Baku.

The two-day event is organized by Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Economy and its subordinate Azerbaijan Export and Investment Promotion Agency (AZPROMO), in strategic partnership with European House – Ambrosetti.

This year’s forum is dedicated to the theme “Restoring Trust in a Divided World: The South Caucasus as a Pillar of Global Interconnectedness and Investment Stability” and brings together leading global investors, government representatives, international financial institutions and business leaders.

World.title: Azerbaijan has become an important link and gateway between Asia and Europe - President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 25. Our country's global strategic partnerships and growing foreign investment in the non-oil sector are paving the way for deeper integration into global value chains in areas such as manufacturing, trade, energy, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, and advanced technologies, President Ilham Aliyev said in his address to the participants of the 2nd Azerbaijan International Investment Forum.

“These positive trends have also been recognized by international rating agencies. Fitch and Moody's have upgraded Azerbaijan's sovereign credit ratings to investment grade, with the outlook for the next period assessed as “stable” and “positive” respectively. Our financial resilience is further underscored by strategic currency reserves, which exceeded 110% of GDP at the end of 2025,” the head of state said in his address.

“Located at the intersection of the East-West and North-South corridors, Azerbaijan has become an important link and gateway between Asia and Europe. The Middle Corridor links Central Asia across the Caspian Sea with the South Caucasus, Türkiye and Europe, while the emerging Zangezur Corridor, also known as the TRIPP connectivity route, will further strengthen Azerbaijan's role as a regional hub, and create new opportunities for trade, investment and industrial cooperation across Eurasia,” the Azerbaijani leader added.

World.title: Man dies after fall at Hanging Rock summit
World.content:
The death of a man at tourism spot Hanging Rock on Friday afternoon has prompted the closure of the reserve over the long weekend.

Victoria Police said man was died after he fell while climbing onto a rock at the summit of the volcanic formation, which lies 75 kilometres north-west of Melbourne.

The man fell just before 1pm.

"Despite the efforts of several off-duty medical professionals at the scene, the man was unable to be revived and was declared deceased at the scene," a police spokesperson said.

Hanging Rock Reserve was closed on Friday and will remain so on Saturday September 26, according to the Macedon Ranges Shire Council.

The council cited a medical incident as the reason for the closure.

The Grand Final Eve public holiday on Friday made the AFL Grand Final weekend a three-day break for many Victorians.

Police will prepare a report for the coroner.

World.title: Police lay 115 additional charges on Sydney alleged childcare abuser
World.content:
The Australian Federal Police (AFP) has laid an additional 115 charges against a former Sydney childcare worker who allegedly abused more than 130 children.

Hamish Tait is now facing 444 charges related to the alleged abuse of children over a 16-year period.

The additional charges laid on Friday include 105 counts of producing child abuse material, one count of carrying out a sexual act with a child under 10, five counts of filming a person engaged in a private act in circumstances of aggravation, and four counts of possessing child abuse material.

The AFP said the charges related to the exploitation of children known to Mr Tait, and those who attended five early childhood education facilities in Sydney's north-west in which he worked at or attended.

The alleged offending is said to have occurred between 2009 and 2025.

The additional charges relate to previously identified alleged victims, with no further people identified, the AFP noted.

Mr Tait, 35, has been remanded in custody since he was arrested and first charged by the AFP in July.

The matter remains before the courts and is next scheduled to be heard at Parramatta Local Court on October 8.

Hamish Tait's alleged offending is said to have occurred between 2009 and 2025. (Supplied)

2.4 million electronic files reviewed

The investigation, dubbed Operation Moonbi, has involved the review and analysis of 2.4 million electronic files.

Police established a website under Operation Moonbi, which included a list of the more than 55 childcare centres where Mr Tait worked at or attended between 2009 and 2025, predominantly in Sydney's north-west.

Alleged abuse has been identified at five centres.

In July, the AFP released images of distinctive clothing in an attempt to identify alleged victims.

The images were found on electronic devices seized as part of the investigation under Operation Moonbi.

AFP Detective Acting Inspector Emmanuel Tsardoulias previously described victim identification work as "painstaking and detailed".

"Our victim ID team is tenacious, committed and will stop at nothing to identify children or victims of child exploitation," he said.

World.title: Live: Brazil fans descend on Townsville ahead of Socceroos clash
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Socceroos veteran Milos Degenek is bracing for world heavyweights Brazil to hand Australia's new generation a "reality check" when the two nations meet this week.

But the 57-cap defender isn't worried for Australian football, adamant the Socceroos can "do something special" at the 2027 Asian Cup after the heartbreak of their World Cup exit.

The Socceroos have only won the Asian Cup once, beating South Korea for the 2015 title.

"It's an exciting thing ... for all the new ones and the young faces that we have here," Degenek said. "For them, it's a reality check. "It's very important for the coaches to have a look at the new faces they have in here, to put them through a test, if I may say, where they have to experience 30,000, 40,000 people and play against Brazil. "For them [it's] to see if these boys are ready for the Asian Cup … but I'm really, really confident that we can do something special."

- AAP

World.title: Father rejects coroner's conclusion on newborn son's death
World.content:
The grieving father of a baby who died five days after birth has rejected the findings of a Queensland coronial inquest that found the death was not preventable.

Hugo McGregor was born by emergency caesarean section at Mackay Base Hospital in March 2023 and transferred to Townsville University Hospital, where he died.

An inquest into his death was held in Townsville last year after Jenna and Andre McGregor raised concerns about their son's care before his birth.

On Wednesday, Deputy State Coroner Stephanie Gallagher found there were no missed opportunities that may have changed the outcome.

"I accept that it is theoretically possible that had he been delivered earlier, he may have been born in better condition," she said in her findings.

"However, the expert evidence is clear that the care provided to both Jenna and Hugo was reasonable and appropriate, and there were no prospective reasons to warrant an earlier delivery or any additional intervention or escalation beyond what was done."

Jenna McGregor told the court she and her husband Andre would never forget Hugo. (ABC News: Hannah Walsh)

Father 'deeply disappointed'

In 2025 the inquest heard that the McGregors felt hospital staff should have been concerned at the lack of labour progress earlier and considered an earlier caesarean, and that the delay in receiving an epidural contributed to their son's death.

In a statement provided to the ABC on Friday, Mr McGregor said he would apply to the state coroner to have this week's findings set aside, saying there needed to be "greater transparency and safer maternity care in Queensland".

He said an earlier hospital and health service internal review found shortcomings in the care provided.

"My son died following a series of events in a Queensland public hospital. A Root Cause Analysis subsequently identified dozens of failures. Yet not one of these were mentioned during the inquest," Mr McGregor's statement said.

" As his father, I am entitled to ask why so many of those failures appear to have had so little impact on the ultimate findings. "

Mr McGregor said he was disappointed that his wife was not called as a witness.

In her findings, Magistrate Gallagher accepted that the hospital had made changes since Hugo's birth and was satisfied they were appropriate.

These included embedding obstetric ward rounds to allow for earlier patient review by the obstetrics team and improvements to staff culture.

Magistrate Gallagher said expert witnesses had not raised these issues as relevant to Hugo's death.

"There are no further recommendations this Court could make with respect to the maternity services at MBH or the management of labour pursuant to the relevant policies and guidelines more broadly," her findings said.

Cause of death

Ms Gallager listed the cause of Hugo's death as hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy caused by a sudden and profound onset of bradycardia (slow heart rate).

The inquest heard Hugo was born "pale, floppy and unresponsive" and after being resuscitated was transferred to Townsville University Hospital, where he died five days later.

An obstetrics expert Edward Weaver told the inquest Hugo developed metabolic acidosis — an accumulation of carbon dioxide and lack of oxygen — that caused a sudden "crash" in his heart rate.

An autopsy showed the placenta had signs of infection and inflammation, which likely impaired its function and increased metabolic demands on the baby, the inquest heard.

"These factors made it more likely that, once Hugo's capacity for physiological buffering was exhausted, he would develop a sudden bradycardia," the inquest findings said.

Magistrate Gallagher wrote in her findings that a family statement was read at the conclusion of the evidence, "which made clear that Hugo was loved and cherished by his parents from the moment of his conception, and by his grandparents and extended who had long hoped to meet him".

Uncomplicated pregnancy

The Inquest into newborn's hospital death heard Ms McGregor had an uncomplicated pregnancy and was transferred from Proserpine to Mackay because there were no anaesthetists on-call due to fatigue.

She arrived in Mackay at 6am on March 11, 2023, and by 9:10am had requested an epidural, which was not administered until two hours later, when an anaesthetist was available.

By 3pm she was given an infusion to strengthen labour contractions. This was stopped at 4:01pm, when Hugo's heart experienced a "sudden and profound drop" and she was taken to the operating theatre.

Jenna and Andre McGregor hold baby Hugo Alexander after his birth at Mackay Base Hospital in 2023. (Supplied, Jenna and Andre McGregor)

The inquest heard one midwife recall that staff could not find a heartbeat as they neared the operating theatre, a distance of 800-900 metres from the labour ward.

"By the time Jenna reached the operating theatre Hugo had been bradycardic for about 18 minutes," Magistrate Gallagher wrote.

The inquest heard there was a disagreement when a decision was made to try a spinal anaesthetic instead of a general anaesthetic as recommended by the midwives.

"None of the witnesses could recall precisely the time that elapsed between the failed attempt at a spinal anaesthetic and the administration of a general anaesthetic," the findings said.

"It was likely no more than a matter of minutes. The disagreement between the RMs (registered midwives) involved and the anaesthetic team was unfortunate and ideally should have been avoided.

"Any delay caused by the failed attempt was unlikely, however, to have had any material impact on Hugo's condition when born, or on his prognosis."

World.title: 'Evil' Catholic priest who sexually abused girls in foster care jailed
World.content:
A former Catholic priest and serial paedophile who sexually abused two young girls in foster care 36 years ago has been jailed for more than two years.

Robert James Hickman, 81, was previously imprisoned for sexual offences in New South Wales against multiple victims.

Hickman had pleaded guilty to sexual penetration of a child, and indecent dealing with a child in Perth in 1990.

WA District Court Judge Karen Shepherd described his actions as a "breach of trust" given his position, and too serious to justify a suspended term.

He was sentenced to two years and six months in jail, to be served immediately at Casuarina Prison.

Hickman's history of sexual offences against children began in the late 1970s, the court has heard. (ABC News: David Weber)

The court heard the Perth victims were aged 11 and 13 when Hickman flew over from Sydney on official business in 1990, and attended a dinner with other members of the Catholic Church at their foster home.

The man the girls knew as "Father Bob" then went into their bedroom to give "goodnight prayers" and read out a bible story.

He told one of the girls he was going to give her a "special blessing" before touching her indecently.

The Perth victims told the court the sexual abuse had deeply affected them. (ABC News)

The priest then groped the other girl in a similar manner before leaving the room, saying "goodnight girls, God bless, it was lovely to meet you".

The court heard the girls had then cried themselves to sleep.

One girl reported the incident to the foster mother, who initially dismissed her as a liar.

Nine years later, the foster mother reported the incident to the Catholic Church's WA Professional Standards Office, and received a letter of apology from Hickman.

The church offered money as part of a non-disclosure agreement.

'A very evil soul'

In a statement read out in court by prosecutor Rachael McCallum, one of the victims described the impact of the abuse as "immeasurable".

The woman said she had to carry the burden of having been sexually abused, and being told she was a liar, at a time when she was living in a new environment after her parents had died.

Prosecutor Rachael McCallum read the victim impact statements in court. (ABC News: David Weber)

She "had to keep everything inside", the statement said, going on to describe Hickman as "a very evil soul".

The other victim provided a statement in which she said the abuse had changed her life "forever", but she had decided to forgive Hickman for her own mental health.

"I choose not to give you any power from this day forward," she said in the statement.

Health issues

Hickman was investigated by the child abuse squad in 2015 and arrested and extradited to WA from NSW 10 years later.

His lawyer Simon Freitag said he had served five years of a ten year prison sentence in NSW, from 2015 to 2020, for sexual offences against multiple victims.

In 2001, he received a suspended sentence, and a community corrections order had been imposed for similar offending in 2024.

Mr Freitag said Hickman's offences occurred from the late 1970s to the early 1990s, but he had "not reoffended in decades... He is not presently a danger to children".

Hickman is recovering from cancer surgery and has several other health issues.

He will eligible for parole after serving 15 months in prison.

World.title: 'He will be finished': Toplace lawyer's promise to fugitive developer
World.content:
A Toplace employee warned fugitive property developer Jean Nassif that serious building defects could "f***" the company, as the corruption watchdog continues to examine efforts to target the former building commissioner.

The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) is examining whether donations linked to Mr Nassif were exchanged for political favours, including removing David Chandler as building commissioner and trying to stop him from investigating Mr Nassif's developments.

The warning came in a 2021 exchange between Mr Nassif and employee David Krepp, which was read to the inquiry by counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer SC.

Mr Krepp was discussing defects identified by Mr Chandler.

"That's going to f*** us Jean, the defects are huge," Mr Krepp said.

Mr Nassif responded by telling Mr Krepp to speak to Toplace lawyer Sharangan Maheswaran, who is a main target of the major inquiry.

"All right mate, talk to Sharangan, get Sharangan to release the personal lawsuit against Chandler," Mr Nassif replied.

Mr Maheswaran denied being part of a campaign designed to damage the commissioner's career or have him removed.

'He will be finished'

Jean Nassif fronted ICAC from Lebanon, where he fled to in 2023. (ABC News)

Mr Maheswaran also sent material concerning Mr Chandler to political contacts, including a video of Mr Chandler at a building site that he believed could damage the commissioner.

"I want to keep it highly secret. You will see in the next four weeks, he will be finished," he told Mr Nassif.

Mr Maheswaran rejected the suggestion that the actions amounted to a coordinated campaign against Mr Chandler.

He told the inquiry he believed the material was intended to draw attention to conduct he considered concerning.

Mr Chandler is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Mookhey refers claims to ICAC

Jean Nassif has blamed David Elliott (left) and David Chandler for the demise of Toplace. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow, Abubakr Sajid)

The inquiry also heard that NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey referred Mr Maheswaran's claims about the building commissioner to ICAC a day after a meeting with the Toplace lawyer in 2021.

In a statement, Mr Mookhey — who was an opposition MP at the time — said Mr Maheswaran described his client as a "prominent builder" whose projects had been affected by prohibition orders issued by Mr Chandler.

Mr Mookhey said Mr Maheswaran raised allegations that Mr Chandler had subjected his client to additional inspections, incorrectly issued defect notices, and made references during site visits that his client interpreted as an allusion to separate defamation proceedings.

Mr Maheswaran agreed that he asked Mr Mookhey to question the minister and building commissioner about these matters at a forthcoming budget estimates.

Dr Dwyer: Mr Mookhey told you that he had a duty to report your allegations to the ICAC, didn't he? Mr Maheswaran: Yes, that's correct. Dr Dwyer: And he said that he could not raise your allegations in any parliamentary forum … He told you instead that he would be referring it to ICAC and that you too might have the same obligation to refer to ICAC. Mr Maheswaran: I don't recall the second part, but he certainly said it should be referred to ICAC.

Avoiding parliamentary scrutiny

The hearing also turned to Mr Maheswaran's relationship with Robert Assaf, a prominent member of the right-wing Liberal group known as the NSW Reformers, which is at the centre of the inquiry.

Mr Maheswaran denied attempting to intimidate Mr Assaf or discourage him from giving evidence to a previous 2023 parliamentary inquiry.

The commission heard that Mr Maheswaran had fed Mr Assaf a false story involving another individual's drug use, allegedly to test whether Mr Assaf was leaking information.

Alleged $5m 'extortion attempt' labelled a 'lie' at NSW ICAC The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption heard fugitive property developer Jean Nassif claimed he was being extorted by former Toplace contractor Navid Ardestani, who was pursuing him for money he believed he was owed.

Mr Assaf was also referred to as "the rat", although Mr Maheswaran said he believed Mr Assaf gave himself the nickname.

The inquiry previously heard about attempts by several people to avoid being compelled to appear before the 2023 parliamentary inquiry.

Mr Maheswaran travelled to Cessnock shortly before he expected to be served with a summons, telling a friend he "fled Sydney in anticipation of the hearing".

"They can't find me to serve me," he told the friend.

The key figures in ICAC investigation Eight weeks of public hearings by the ICAC that could change the NSW Liberal Party forever begin on Monday.

He later returned after learning he had not been called to appear.

The inquiry previously heard that a private investigator was engaged to monitor lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood's home and alert him if anyone attempted to serve him with a summons.

Mr Maheswaran denied arranging the surveillance.

World.title: Eagles keep Dons winless, Dogs put Power on the brink
World.content:
Ella Roberts has celebrated her 50-game AFLW milestone in grand style, producing a typically brave effort as West Coast survived a frenetic Essendon comeback to post a 10-point win at Windy Hill.

The Eagles led by as much as 34 points during the third quarter of Friday's match and the margin was still 28 points at the final change, with Essendon scoring just two goals up until that moment.

But any thoughts of West Coast simply cruising to victory were extinguished as Essendon launched wave after wave of attack in the last quarter to put the Eagles under all sorts of pressure.

In the end, it was Essendon's missed chances that resulted in them falling just short, with the Bombers kicking 2.7 to 0.1 in the final quarter as West Coast clung on for the 6.9 (45) to 4.11 (35) win.

Roberts starred on her special day with 31 disposals, four clearances, one goal assist, nine tackles and 717m gained, while Jaide Britton kicked two goals and Amy Franklin kicked 1.3 and took six marks in a powerful display.

Maddy Prespakis (27 disposals, 466m gained) and Steph Wales (20 disposals, one goal) fought hard for the Bombers, who slumped to a 0–7 record.

West Coast started their season with four losses on the trot, but are now back in the finals mix at 3–4 following three consecutive wins.

Over at Whitten Oval, the Western Bulldogs improved to 5–2 with a 13-point win over lowly Port Adelaide (2–5).

Bulldogs forward Heidi Woodley was the star in the 10.2 (62) to 8.1 (49) win, kicking a career-high four goals from 18 disposals.

Ellie Hampson kicked three goals to go along with a goal assist in her Port debut, while Shineah Goody chipped in with two majors and Matilda Scholz had a huge day in the ruck with 22 disposals, 40 hit-outs and five clearances.

But the Bulldogs' deadly accurate return of 7.0 in the second half meant Port were never able to claw back the 13-point half-time deficit.

In the afternoon game at Princes Park, Carlton romped to a comfortable 11.10 (76) to 3.3 (21) win over Richmond.

AAP

World.title: The Lachie Neale case highlighted a flaw in AFL’s rules. Here’s my lawyer’s fix
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion The Lachie Neale case highlighted a flaw in AFL’s rules. Here’s my lawyer’s fix Darren Kane Sports Columnist September 25, 2026 — 7:23pm

September 25, 2026 — 7:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Usually, the AFL punishes on-field misconduct in the currency of matches, which it considers fungible.

But that premise is false; it produces a small number of cases where sanctions are grossly out of whack with the crime. On Thursday night the AFL Appeal Board overturned Lachie Neale’s one-match ban and instead fined him $10,000. Sensible outcome and good luck to him. But the route Neale took back to the MCG – wide open to him; bolted shut to almost everybody else – demonstrated that the defect lies in the rules, and that rescuing one man’s week fixes nothing. Lachie Neale is free to play in Saturday’s grand final. AFL Photos Late in the first quarter of last Saturday’s preliminary final, Neale slugged Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the guts, behind play and off the ball. The match review officer graded the conduct intentional, the impact medium and the contact to the body. That yielded a fixed sanction of one match. On Tuesday night, the tribunal found the blow forceful and intentional, delivered off the ball to an unsuspecting opponent; rejected the player’s account as inconsistent with the camera vision; and held that the case for exceptional and compelling circumstances didn’t outweigh the nature of the conduct.



On Thursday night, the Appeal Board saw it differently. The tribunal had erred in law, it held, by weighing the intentional nature of the strike against Neale when asking whether exceptional and compelling circumstances existed. Intention was an element of the charge, already proved, so counting it again was double-dipping. That left only the other side of the ledger, being Neale’s exemplary playing record: over 300 games, two Brownlow Medals, two premierships as captain and four All Australian selections. Thirteen seasons without a suspension. Loading The Appeals Board applied some creative mathematics and rounded one match down to $10,000. Is all of this necessary? We all know that nobody would bother with all the legal gymnastics if this was a round-seven match. Had it gone the other way, Neale would’ve been the first player since 2003 to miss a grand final over something done the week before. Sport, sometimes, can be a cruel mistress.



We should rightly accept the findings of fact. The place to quarrel is with the arithmetic that follows. The Appeals Board corrected an error of law. Excessiveness is not assessed just by looking at the number of matches, but also the particular effect of the sanction. On the face of the sanctioning table, a one-match suspension in round seven and a one-match suspension on the eve of the grand final are identical. Which is where the trouble starts. A home-and-away fixture is one of 23, and missing one is almost always recoverable – the coach usually picks you again the following week, and by October nobody really remembers. A grand final is one of one. Every other game of the season is, distilled down, a qualifying round for it. Brisbane Lions Lachie Neale and Ty Gallop at the grand final parade on Friday. Eddie Jim Forget Neale; he’s sorted. Think instead about the 20-year-old charged over the identical strike in the preliminary final that got his side there. Run Thursday’s legal reasoning for him (or her). The legal error gets corrected, and the Appeal Board turns to the other side of the ledger to find ... what, exactly? A handful of games. No Brownlows, no captaincy, no decade of clean football, because he hasn’t had a decade. He misses the only grand final he’ll ever play. The rule squashes him with the same disproportion, and not a skerrick of relief.



The only key that opens the door is a stellar CV, and a CV takes years to build. Relief flows to the bloke with two premiership medallions already in the cupboard; the kid who’s never played in one serves the full week. Upside down. It rewards longevity when the harm falls hardest on youth. The criminal law worked this out a long time ago. Two offenders can cop the same sentence and carry wildly different loads out the courtroom door. What’s written on the warrant is seldom the whole of the punishment. Sentencing courts have long accepted that consequences falling outside the sentence itself – extra-curial punishment – can properly be weighed in fixing it. Lachie Neale copped an initial one-game ban for this gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. Getty Images, Fox Footy Put differently, a judge asks what the penalty will actually do to the person in the dock, not merely what it’s labelled as. A few codes have fixed the problem. In UEFA Europa League regulations, accumulated yellow cards are wiped after the quarter-finals so that nobody sits out a final over a booking collected months earlier. Has discipline in the knockout rounds gone to hell in a handbasket? Not noticeably. UEFA simply wrote into its rulebook what every punter already knew; that a final isn’t just another match.



Back, then, to the AFL’s table. It measures offending from three angles – conduct, impact and contact – and the gravity of sanction not at all. Was it intentional? How hard? Where did it land? Those questions all get answered. What will the week off actually cost the bloke serving it? Never asked. The objections aren’t stupid, mind you. Treat the grand final differently, and two players who commit identical acts in the same preliminary final walk away with different outcomes, depending solely on whether their team won. The criminal law worked this out a long time ago. Two offenders can cop the same sentence and carry wildly different loads out the courtroom door. Go soft in grand final week and you blunt the deterrent at precisely the moment when stakes, fatigue and the odd festering grudge make misconduct most likely. Jack Ginnivan’s ribs didn’t hurt any less because it’s September. Discretion, left to its own devices, had an unfortunate habit of favouring the famous. Reopen it, and every finals series turns into a festival of pleading exceptionality. Besides, the AFL guidelines already permit a reduction for exceptional and compelling circumstances. Lachie Neale won that argument eventually. The system works, then, right?



Aristotle apprehended all this millennia before the Match Review Officer did. The bloke who taught us to treat like cases alike also recognised that a general law will inevitably misfire in the unusual case, precisely because it’s general. The correction, equity, is to decide the case as the lawmaker would have, had he foreseen it. There can’t be any amnesty or discounting. Alternate sanctions must be BIGGER for any player who elects it, and the price is published in advance. The deterrent gets sharper. And for completeness, a sporting sanction was never compensation to Jack Ginnivan; its job is to uphold the competition’s standards. The existing exceptional and compelling circumstances discretion is constructed around the player – his record, his character, his standing. The Tribunal weighed it one way; the Appeal Board, correcting the scales, the other. Fair enough, both ways. But the discretion is aimed at the wrong target. Everybody always knew what this appeal was about; nobody could say it. Had the same strike happened in May, Neale would’ve copped his week, and nobody would’ve bothered with a five-hour hearing on a Tuesday night, let alone a sequel on Thursday.



So what’s my lawyer fix? I’d give any player faced with a grand final ban for a rats ‘n’ mice misconduct charge the option of a sanction carrying over to the next season, by also paying a hefty fine. In lawyer-gibber, it reads like this: Where a player is found to have committed a reportable offence attracting a fixed sanction of one match, and the match to which that sanction would apply is the Grand Final, the player may elect to serve instead a suspension of four matches commencing with the first match for which he is otherwise selected in the following premiership season, together with a financial sanction double the maximum applicable to the classification. The election is available once in a player’s career. It is not available where the offence is graded severe impact or high contact, or is a second or subsequent offence in the same season. The election, once made, is irrevocable and follows the player to any club. It’s confined to the lowest rung of suspension, where the gap between offence and consequence is widest and the competition’s interest in keeping a player out of that particular match is weakest. It costs the player more. Four matches plus a double-maximum fine, for a medium-impact strike to the body, sits well above anything the table would dish out in any other week of the year.

World.title: Arcade games are making a comeback – but not in the way you’d think
World.content:
CultureArt & designVideo games Arcade games are making a comeback – but not in the way you’d think Nell Geraets September 25, 2026 — 7:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Brie Healy was a child, her father became obsessed with Space Invaders. He discovered the 8-bit arcade game during a family visit to a local cafe, becoming so hooked that he dropped the kids off at home and returned for hours to beat his high score. “[The 8-bit] style brings me back to that feeling of childhood,” the Hobart-based game developer and artist says. “When I see those types of games, it makes me think about those specific moments, like when I used to sit behind my brother while he played video games because he wouldn’t let me have a turn.” Craig Duturbure playing his new 8-bit game Quiver at ACMI’s Play On display. Pablo Barnes Most adults today probably share similar memories. For Ratmouse Games’ co-founder Anthony Doueihi, it’s of playing Time Crisis with friends in an arcade, and for his fellow co-creator Peak Distapan, it’s of chasing high scores in Point Blank on his PlayStation. Craig Duturbure, meanwhile, recalls getting lost in the 1983 scrolling shooter Xevious. These Australian developers are counting on this nostalgia to pull audiences into their new 8-bit arcade games, all of which are displayed at ACMI as part of the interactive showcase Play On. But there’s a twist: the games may look old-school, but they explore very modern-day anxieties.



Duturbure’s game Quiver, for example, flips typical video-game violence on its head. In his 2D radial shooter, instead of shooting weapons to incite violence, you shoot Cupid’s arrows to spread love. Inspired by the 1983 tube shooter Gyruss, the aim of Duturbure’s game is to spread as much goodwill as possible before the end of Valentine’s Day. Loading “Today, this style of game doesn’t always have to be about violence and shooting things to death. We’ve got enough bad news. Just make people happy,” the Melbourne-based developer says. “There’s a sort of elegance to 8-bit games because they’re so pure in a way that you can’t hide behind flashy stuff. You just have to boil it down to core mechanics and what could be fun. It makes sense to people.” Healy’s game QIP, meanwhile, places you inside a miniature toy world where you must locate different items to piece together your character’s identity. This was partially inspired by Healy’s desire to live inside a Polly Pocket house, but it was also created to encourage players to consider their own identities, something that has become increasingly difficult in the age of social media and constant visual stimulation. Who are we when we’re not simply a notch in the algorithm?



Retro arcade games are enjoying a comeback, but not exactly in the way you’d think. ACMI “I see video games as an in-depth way to spark those kinds of feelings and questions in people. And it’s more interactive, it’s guided, so you can disarm the player with a fun vibe or something they can relate to, and then get them to do some self-reflection.” Retro 8-bit styles have proven particularly effective in prompting such self-exploration, Healy says. The pixels make the visuals more abstract, meaning any player could see themselves in the “blurry characters”. And unlike more modern games, 8-bit games generally don’t require hundreds of hours of gameplay or major strategising, leaving more room for either introspection or simple fun. Anthony Doueihi, Peak Distapan, Jae Pietersen Scott, Craig Duturbure and Brie Healy (left to right) at ACMI’s Play On display. ACMI Ratmouse Games’ Pop-up Crashout leans more towards “simple fun”. With the help of a desktop assistant, players must fend off a deluge of pop-ups and malware while exploring the early internet. It harks back to a time when the internet was less stale and each website had its own charm, Doueihi says. However, Distapan says it also touches on the digital fatigue and online anxiety most of us currently feel thanks to relentless algorithms and constant cyberthreats.



“I grew up loving the internet, but I feel like a lot of that love is gone – for fair reasons. I want people to recapture that joy,” Distapan says. All of these games attempt just that: to recapture the joy retro games evoked. Since gaming is a relatively new form of pop culture, Doueihi says nostalgia around ’80s and ’90s arcade games has only really begun to kick in somewhat recently. Related Article Video games Fans have waited 13 years for this video game. It may already be spoiled That said, arcades never disappeared. Jae Pietersen Scott, who created the music for Pop-up Crashout, says arcade games have simply evolved into things like Dance Dance Revolution or MaiMai. What’s different now is the growing nostalgia for specific ’80s or ’90s games, and the simplicity and communal nature they fostered. In fact, ACMI is set to open a Community Games Library as part of Melbourne International Games Week, an initiative similar to street libraries where visitors bring their favourite childhood games to swap with someone else. “There’s a trend in media towards analogue technology, and that’s feeding into how we’re consuming and making art as well,” Scott says. “Arcade games, since the very beginning, have been something that’s brought people together. That never stopped.”



Play On, presented with Now or Never, will run at ACMI until January 31, 2027. The Community Games Library will feature at ACMI as part of Melbourne International Games Week between October 2 and 11. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.
