World.content:
The biggest inclusion in tonight’s game is Roosters No.7 Sam Walker, who returns from a syndesmosis injury in a huge boost to the visitors’ chances.

Sam’s father Ben Walker, a two-time premiership-winner with the Broncos of the late 1990s, says the Roosters halfback is not the off-the-cuff playmaker he may seem.

“The beauty of being able to talk to him after a game is asking what he saw in a moment before executing a pass or a kick,” Ben explains.

“And I know the way he plays looks a bit chaotic and off the cuff, but those explanations of, ‘I know this defender has a habit of turning in on this play’, or, ‘The fullback can drift too far across field late in a half’ – that’s where you learn he’s far more considered and more calculating than people would think.

World.title: Socceroos v Brazil LIVE updates: Brazil’s behaviour sparks debate back home; Tony Popovic’s side make first appearance since World Cup
World.content:
Having spent the preceding days training in Brisbane, where they will return for the second match of this series, both teams arrived in Townsville yesterday, and were received by local dignitaries and a couple of hundred fans who came for a brief meet-and-greet session.

Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti and representatives from Wulgurukaba Walkabouts, who performed a smoking ceremony to welcome the team to Townsville.

The Brazilians were welcomed to their hotel with a traditional smoking ceremony, which was led by Wulgurukaba Walkabouts, a group of local Aboriginal dancers and cultural performers. It took place without incident ... but the reaction of some players, who appeared to be laughing, sniggering or covering their faces during the ceremony, have triggered criticism and backlash back in Brazil.

A number of Brazilian outlets have picked up on the footage, and some of them accused the players of cultural insensitivity or disrespect. On social media, the reaction has been much harsher, with many Portuguese-speaking accounts talking of feeling ashamed or angry about the way they acted, and more embarrassing than Brazil’s infamous 7-1 defeat to Germany at the 2014 World Cup. The discussion has since been picked up by some conservative-leaning Australian accounts, dragging it into typical culture war areas.

I was there, and could definitely detect a sense of confusion and/or bemusement from the visitors, the vast majority of whom are in Australia for the first time, and would have had no idea what was in store. Footballers can be quite immature, and especially superstars of this calibre. Perhaps they should have been better briefed beforehand by the Brazilian federation on what they were about to see, how meaningful it is, and the importance of treating the moment appropriately.

World.title: The billionaire’s son with ties to Trump who is about to run Hollywood
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions The billionaire’s son with ties to Trump who is about to run Hollywood Brooks Barnes September 25, 2026 — 7:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The age of the Hollywood mogul was supposed to be over. Movies are dead, haven’t you heard? Even the grandest studio – Warner Bros. – had started to resemble a relic of a powerful past. Then came a “kid.” David Ellison, the son of Oracle’s billionaire co-founder Larry Ellison, was 23 when he arrived in the movie capital in 2006. Hollywood insiders laughed behind his back. He was dumb money to be fleeced, another starstruck rich guy with a chequebook. A 2015 GQ profile ran with the headline “The Kid Pays for the Picture”. David Ellison was already an unusual figure in modern Hollywood – a controlling owner who was also CEO and a hands-on movie and television producer. Adding Warner Bros. Discovery will expand his power to a scale without precedent. AP On Monday, after a remarkable, almost inconceivable run of dealmaking and brinkmanship, David Ellison – all of 43 years old – stood on the verge of adding Warner Bros. Discovery to his Paramount Skydance, giving him control of two businesses that helped invent the movie and television industries. A settlement with 12 states cleared the antitrust lawsuit that was the remaining obstacle to the $US111 billion ($158 billion) takeover.



Ellison was already an unusual figure in modern Hollywood – a controlling owner who was also CEO and a hands-on movie and television producer. Adding Warner Bros. Discovery will expand his power to a scale without precedent, spanning a wider range of media than the empires of classic moguls such as Jack Warner and Louis B. Mayer. Related Article Billionaires How Trump’s billionaire mate is reshaping America Even Bob Iger, for all his regal command as Disney’s CEO over the decades, never combined all those roles. “David’s about to become the Hollywood equivalent of Superman, Caesar and Midas combined,” Joseph M. Singer, a veteran film financier and former studio executive, said in an email. “He won’t just be sitting at the table. He’ll have extraordinary influence over who gets a seat.” Singer had publicly opposed the sale of Warner Bros. Discovery to Paramount Skydance, citing concerns about consolidation-related job losses and the roughly $US79 billion in net debt that the conglomerate would carry at closing, among other worries.



“I believe David’s intentions are good and his ambitions genuine,” Singer said. “But I remain concerned that this concentration of power is not in the interests of our business. I hope I am proved wrong.” Other critics were not so generous on Monday. A senior agent and two film producers privately likened Ellison to Michael Corleone in The Godfather, a Paramount film. The character began as an outsider and became the boss, consolidating power with startling effectiveness. Paramount Skydance’s deal to take over Warner Bros is getting closer to becoming a reality. Bloomberg The Ellison family’s ties to President Donald Trump – which included a dinner that David Ellison hosted in April “honouring the Trump White House” – have made many Democrats and a sizable contingent in Hollywood wary of his growing power. His empire will now span CNN and CBS News; HBO, MTV, BET, Comedy Central and TNT; the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services; and two of Hollywood’s oldest movie studios. Put another way, Ellison will soon have Batman, Harry Potter, Captain Kirk, Wonder Woman, Ethan Hunt, Maverick and SpongeBob SquarePants reporting to him.



“We vehemently oppose the agreement to allow David Ellison to take over Warner Bros. Discovery,” a campaign called Block the Merger said in a statement. “This is a bad deal for the future of film, entertainment, independent journalism and a strong democracy in this country.” Related Article Updated

Vale ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies The campaign was organised by the Future Film Coalition, a nonprofit that gathered thousands of signatures from film and television workers opposed to the merger. Ellison settled the antitrust lawsuits with California and 11 other states after months of legal and political combat. The lawsuits argued that the merger would reduce competition in movies and cable TV. The states relented after Ellison agreed to concessions, including a five-year commitment to release at least 30 movies annually, $US1.5 billion in additional domestic production spending, and the creation of an independent board to safeguard editorial independence at CNN and CBS News.



In an email to Paramount employees, Ellison said he expected the Warner Bros. Discovery takeover to close in about two weeks. He will exercise control of Paramount and Warner Bros. through his family’s 77.5 per cent stake in the company’s voting shares. “This is the first time since Walt Disney that you will have a family own and control a major Hollywood company with this level of hands-on management,” said Gerry Cardinale, a Paramount board member. Cardinale is the founder of RedBird Capital, the second-largest investor in Ellison’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery. “There’s a changing of the guard taking place,” Cardinale added, referring not only to Ellison’s ascension but also to an owner-operated model that Hollywood had largely abandoned. Donald Trump with Larry Ellison. The Ellison family’s ties to the president – which included a dinner that David Ellison hosted in April “honouring the Trump White House” – have made many Democrats and a sizable contingent in Hollywood wary of his growing power. Bloomberg Amassing all that power may prove easier than wielding it.



Along with the mountain of debt, Ellison’s new company will need to contend with a cable TV business that is shrinking as viewers continue to cut the cord. He must also integrate two enormous companies – he has promised $US6 billion in savings – while navigating internal turmoil and political and editorial pressures at CBS News and CNN. Despite owning two major streaming services, Ellison will still be competing against Netflix and YouTube. He also faces Hollywood’s most basic problem: how to make movies and TV shows that enough people want to watch. ‘David’s about to become the Hollywood equivalent of Superman, Caesar and Midas combined.’ Film financier and former studio executive Joseph M. Singer After a banner run last year, Warner Bros. has stumbled badly at the box office in 2026. It ranks sixth among the seven largest studios in domestic market share this year, according to data from Rentrak, which tracks ticket sales. Paramount is seventh. Each has about 5 per cent of the market, compared with 24 per cent for Universal, the leader, and 21 per cent for Disney. On Monday, however, Hollywood focused less on Ellison’s challenges than it did on his remarkable rise.



It was only 13 months ago that he completed an $US8 billion deal to buy Paramount, home to CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon and its namesake movie studio. Four months later, Ellison launched a hostile bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, which had already agreed to sell itself to Netflix. By February, he had outmanoeuvred Netflix and had a deal in place. Related Article Opinion

Rupert Murdoch Have the Murdochs lost faith in Donald Trump? Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Twelve Democratic state attorneys general then sued to block the Warner takeover. Thousands of film and television workers publicly opposed the combination. The Writers Guild of America mounted its own legal challenge. None of it stopped him. A man who spent years struggling to be taken seriously had become impossible to underestimate.



In the email to employees, Ellison positioned the closing not as a culmination but as a beginning. “Closing is really just the starting line,” he said, adding: “I’m confident we’re going to build something special together in the years ahead. “Let’s go!” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Once Emily realised what chemicals were in her beauty products, she couldn’t turn back
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessWellness Once Emily realised what chemicals were in her beauty products, she couldn’t turn back Sarah Berry September 25, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Emily Fletcher lists the products she uses on a typical day. There’s body wash and face cleanser, shampoo and conditioner, toothpaste, vitamin C serum, facial moisturiser, body lotion and sunscreen, foundation, concealer, blush, mascara, lip liner, lip gloss, deodorant, hand soap and a natural fragrance. At 18 different items, it’s only slightly more than the average person, who uses about 14.5 personal care products a day, from soap and toothpaste to cosmetics, fragrances and hairstyling products. But a paper published in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology says these 14.5 products expose a person to an estimated 100 or more unique ingredients each day, “many of which are known or suspected allergens, carcinogens, endocrine disruptors or neurotoxicants”. Emily Fletcher uses 18 personal care products most days. Sam Mooy Teenagers who are exposed to beauty and skincare content on social media use more products than their peers and the average adult, the research found. This is a “critical window of susceptibility”, alongside pregnancy, says Yousuf Mohammed, an associate professor in the school of pharmacy and pharmaceutical sciences at the University of Queensland.



Most of us use personal care products on the assumption that they will help us or, at the very least, not harm us. But this may not be the case. “Inactive ingredients found in personal care products act as the vehicle, preservative or texture enhancer for a formula,” Mohammed says. “While they do not directly treat a specific skin condition – a job reserved for active ingredients – their impact on your body and health can be profound.” He cites new research that found 98 per cent of tested personal care items contained undisclosed chemicals, many carrying hidden health hazards. ‘I wouldn’t put this in someone’s eye’ When Fletcher, 41, gave birth to her first child 11 years ago, she began thinking about the products she was buying for her newborn daughter.



Women in her mum’s group recommended this cream or that wipe. But, when the optometrist looked more closely at them, she found ingredients they wouldn’t use in eye drops because they can cause allergic reactions. “I wouldn’t put this in someone’s eye, so why am I wiping it over a large surface area of a baby’s skin,” she wondered. Related Article Cardiovascular health This popular sweetener is linked to higher heart attack and stroke risk Fletcher didn’t think it was fair that someone should need a science degree to identify the products that don’t contain harmful ingredients. So, she began blogging. As her blog gained traction, it evolved into a directory and annual Clean + Conscious Awards to “highlight those brands who are actually doing the right thing”. Today, the global beauty and personal care market – worth $US698.38 billion ($992 billion) is home to tens of thousands of brands and hundreds of thousands of products.



What we apply can be absorbed by the skins, says Dr Jacinta Martin, a reproductive and developmental biologist at the University of Newcastle. “But also potentially through mucosal surfaces, such as the lips and mouth, inside the nose, around the eyes or through genital and vaginal tissues, depending on the product being used – important when we consider period products,” she says. “There is also the potential for inadvertent ingestion, particularly with products applied to or around the lips and mouth.” Such exposure is relatively new. Emily Fletcher first become concerned about product ingredient lists when shopping for her baby. Getty Images What impact are these ingredients having on us?



Until the middle of the 19th century, many people stayed stinky all day. The bubonic plague outbreak sparked widespread fear of washing with water; soap was primarily for clothes, not bodies; and commercial toothpaste, deodorant and shampoo came to market only between 1873 and 1903. Few people used cosmetics, which were associated with immoral behaviours, and in 1916, only one in five Americans used toiletries at all. Now, as Martin says: “We are potentially applying many different products, containing many different chemicals, to our skin, hair and lips every day, and doing that repeatedly over many years – including during important periods of growth and development.” Editor's pick Alcohol Elizabeth was the life of the party. As a new mum, alcohol helped her feel like herself again People who use more products tend to have higher levels of chemicals such as phthalates, phenols and parabens circulating in their bodies, said lead author of the new study, Emily Barrett, a professor in the Department of Biostatistics and Epidemiology at Rutgers School of Public Health.



Those chemicals have been linked to a wide range of outcomes, including preterm birth, asthma and reproductive issues, Barrett says by email. “Complementary studies in animals also show that those chemicals can interfere with important biological processes that can then contribute to disease.” Yet direct causation between personal care products themselves and these health issues has not been established. “I think concern is warranted, but not panic,” Martin says. “I don’t think we know enough yet.” Specifically, there are questions about the concentrations and combinations of different chemicals, how much actually enters the body, how frequently we’re exposed, when in our lives that exposure occurs, and what happens when exposures occur repeatedly or in combination over long periods of time. So, what action should we take?



It’s not just down to the consumer, experts say. Brands need to be more transparent about ingredients, and governments need to tighten regulation around the chemicals used. But you can still reduce your exposure. In Barrett’s study, a three-day health product intervention where participants’ standard products were replaced with “cleaner” products (selected to be free of phthalates, parabens, triclosan and benzophenone-3), urinary concentrations of many (but not all) of the chemicals declined by up to 45 per cent. Here’s how to overhaul your routine. Go fragrance-free: Phthalates are used in fragrances to make the scent last longer. So the first step is to use fragrance-free products or only those scented with essential oils. “Avoid ‘unscented’, as these often use masking chemicals to hide smells,” Mohammed says. Additionally, he says, because blends are legally protected as proprietary trade secrets, a single listing of the word “fragrance” or “parfum” can mean dozens of undisclosed chemicals, including petrochemical derivatives and neurotoxins.

So the first step is to use fragrance-free products or only those scented with essential oils. “Avoid ‘unscented’, as these often use masking chemicals to hide smells,” Mohammed says. Additionally, he says, because blends are legally protected as proprietary trade secrets, a single listing of the word “fragrance” or “parfum” can mean dozens of undisclosed chemicals, including petrochemical derivatives and neurotoxins. Simplify your routine: Consider how many products you need to use. “Fewer products generally means fewer opportunities for exposure to unnecessary chemicals,” Martin says. “I wouldn’t tell people to throw out everything in their bathroom cabinet. My advice would be to take a sensible approach to reducing unnecessary exposure.”

My advice would be to take a sensible approach to reducing unnecessary exposure.” Swap sunscreens: Particularly during vulnerable periods such as childhood and pregnancy, Mohammed suggests switching from chemical filters to physical mineral sunscreens utilising zinc oxide or titanium dioxide, which sit safely on top of the skin rather than potentially absorbing into the bloodstream.

Avoid forever chemicals: PFAS is widely used in personal care products to make them longer-lasting or waterproof. To reduce PFAS exposure, avoid products with ingredients such as PTFE or the terms “perfluoro-” or “polyfluoro-” .

Get advice: It can be difficult to navigate ingredient lists, Barrett says: “But, luckily, there are a lot of great user-friendly (and free) apps and websites such as Skindeep, Clearya, Yuka and more that can help you choose safer products.”

It can be difficult to navigate ingredient lists, Barrett says: “But, luckily, there are a lot of great user-friendly (and free) apps and websites such as Skindeep, Clearya, Yuka and more that can help you choose safer products.” Reconsider your hair care: Hair care products often contain hormone-disruptors and carcinogens, says Barrett. “I’d recommend doing your homework when shopping for hair oils, crèmes, relaxers and chemical straighteners (or skip them altogether).”

Hair care products often contain hormone-disruptors and carcinogens, says Barrett. “I’d recommend doing your homework when shopping for hair oils, crèmes, relaxers and chemical straighteners (or skip them altogether).” Control what you can and relax about the rest: “You have to keep balance,” Fletcher says. “Ultimately, stress could be more damaging than anything. So what I do is I tend to just control what I can at home and then, anything that’s an external exposure, I don’t worry about.” Make the most of your health, relationships, fitness and nutrition with our Live Well newsletter. World.title: Five of the best homes in Melbourne with more than four bedrooms
World.content:
PropertyNewsVictoria residential property Five of the best homes in Melbourne with more than four bedrooms Shona Hendley September 25, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

While the typical Australian home has approximately three-to-four bedrooms, larger families, intergenerational families, or those who want to host guests or have space for hobbies can benefit from extra bedrooms. Beyond functionality, properties with more bedrooms can command a higher market price and broaden the buyer pool when you sell. Whatever your reason, there are plenty of options on the market: here are five of the best homes in Melbourne with more than four bedrooms. 12 South Terrace, Clifton Hill VIC With a marble gas fireplace, veranda access, a fitted timber walk-in robe, and a luxurious dual-vanity ensuite featuring a private steam sauna, a double shower, an automatic toilet, and a heated towel rail, this Clifton Hill home has a main bedroom suite you may never want to leave.



The single-level home features two additional bedrooms with built-in robes, plus two other potential bedrooms that can also be used as a library or study, depending on your needs. The period details of the home are also impressive; the circa 1986 Victorian heritage is showcased through high ceilings, an ornate stained-glass entry and an extra-wide arched hallway. 18 Kerferd Street, Malvern East VIC This Gascoigne Edwardian has five bedrooms across its two levels.



The guest bedroom and master suite are on the ground level, with the latter including a walk-in robe and an ensuite. The three bedrooms upstairs all include built-in robes, with two also featuring window seats. With a retreat and bathroom servicing the level, this makes an ideal self-contained children’s/teen or guest retreat. Outdoors, the property features an in-ground trampoline, a nine-metre heated pool, bore water, irrigation, a gas barbecue, and a pergola. 43 Kinane Street, Brighton VIC



This double-storey Brighton property offers exclusive, luxurious living through its high-end materials, fixtures and fittings, and meticulous attention to detail. All five bedrooms are on the first floor, with three bedrooms featuring built-in robes and a master suite with both walk-in and built-in robes, an ensuite with spa, and access to a balcony. Other features include double-glazed, thermal-break aluminium windows and sensor-activated remote-control windows; outdoors, a floodlit north-south tennis court; a large, gas-heated swimming pool with an automated cover; a north-facing, paved entertaining area with an open fireplace; perimeter garden beds; an outdoor bathroom; and established trees. 4 Maxwell Court, Toorak VIC



Only moments from Toorak Village, this six-bedroom, three-level Toorak home offers space and privacy. World.title: The Lachie Neale case highlighted a flaw in AFL’s rules. Here’s my lawyer’s fix
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion The Lachie Neale case highlighted a flaw in AFL’s rules. Here’s my lawyer’s fix Darren Kane Sports Columnist September 25, 2026 — 7:23pm

September 25, 2026 — 7:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Usually, the AFL punishes on-field misconduct in the currency of matches, which it considers fungible.

But that premise is false; it produces a small number of cases where sanctions are grossly out of whack with the crime. On Thursday night the AFL Appeal Board overturned Lachie Neale’s one-match ban and instead fined him $10,000. Sensible outcome and good luck to him. But the route Neale took back to the MCG – wide open to him; bolted shut to almost everybody else – demonstrated that the defect lies in the rules, and that rescuing one man’s week fixes nothing. Lachie Neale is free to play in Saturday’s grand final. AFL Photos Late in the first quarter of last Saturday’s preliminary final, Neale slugged Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the guts, behind play and off the ball. The match review officer graded the conduct intentional, the impact medium and the contact to the body. That yielded a fixed sanction of one match. On Tuesday night, the tribunal found the blow forceful and intentional, delivered off the ball to an unsuspecting opponent; rejected the player’s account as inconsistent with the camera vision; and held that the case for exceptional and compelling circumstances didn’t outweigh the nature of the conduct.



On Thursday night, the Appeal Board saw it differently. The tribunal had erred in law, it held, by weighing the intentional nature of the strike against Neale when asking whether exceptional and compelling circumstances existed. Intention was an element of the charge, already proved, so counting it again was double-dipping. That left only the other side of the ledger, being Neale’s exemplary playing record: over 300 games, two Brownlow Medals, two premierships as captain and four All Australian selections. Thirteen seasons without a suspension. Loading The Appeals Board applied some creative mathematics and rounded one match down to $10,000. Is all of this necessary? We all know that nobody would bother with all the legal gymnastics if this was a round-seven match. Had it gone the other way, Neale would’ve been the first player since 2003 to miss a grand final over something done the week before. Sport, sometimes, can be a cruel mistress.



We should rightly accept the findings of fact. The place to quarrel is with the arithmetic that follows. The Appeals Board corrected an error of law. Excessiveness is not assessed just by looking at the number of matches, but also the particular effect of the sanction. On the face of the sanctioning table, a one-match suspension in round seven and a one-match suspension on the eve of the grand final are identical. Which is where the trouble starts. A home-and-away fixture is one of 23, and missing one is almost always recoverable – the coach usually picks you again the following week, and by October nobody really remembers. A grand final is one of one. Every other game of the season is, distilled down, a qualifying round for it. Brisbane Lions Lachie Neale and Ty Gallop at the grand final parade on Friday. Eddie Jim Forget Neale; he’s sorted. Think instead about the 20-year-old charged over the identical strike in the preliminary final that got his side there. Run Thursday’s legal reasoning for him (or her). The legal error gets corrected, and the Appeal Board turns to the other side of the ledger to find ... what, exactly? A handful of games. No Brownlows, no captaincy, no decade of clean football, because he hasn’t had a decade. He misses the only grand final he’ll ever play. The rule squashes him with the same disproportion, and not a skerrick of relief.



The only key that opens the door is a stellar CV, and a CV takes years to build. Relief flows to the bloke with two premiership medallions already in the cupboard; the kid who’s never played in one serves the full week. Upside down. It rewards longevity when the harm falls hardest on youth. The criminal law worked this out a long time ago. Two offenders can cop the same sentence and carry wildly different loads out the courtroom door. What’s written on the warrant is seldom the whole of the punishment. Sentencing courts have long accepted that consequences falling outside the sentence itself – extra-curial punishment – can properly be weighed in fixing it. Lachie Neale copped an initial one-game ban for this gut punch on Jack Ginnivan. Getty Images, Fox Footy Put differently, a judge asks what the penalty will actually do to the person in the dock, not merely what it’s labelled as. A few codes have fixed the problem. In UEFA Europa League regulations, accumulated yellow cards are wiped after the quarter-finals so that nobody sits out a final over a booking collected months earlier. Has discipline in the knockout rounds gone to hell in a handbasket? Not noticeably. UEFA simply wrote into its rulebook what every punter already knew; that a final isn’t just another match.



Back, then, to the AFL’s table. It measures offending from three angles – conduct, impact and contact – and the gravity of sanction not at all. Was it intentional? How hard? Where did it land? Those questions all get answered. What will the week off actually cost the bloke serving it? Never asked. The objections aren’t stupid, mind you. Treat the grand final differently, and two players who commit identical acts in the same preliminary final walk away with different outcomes, depending solely on whether their team won. The criminal law worked this out a long time ago. Two offenders can cop the same sentence and carry wildly different loads out the courtroom door. Go soft in grand final week and you blunt the deterrent at precisely the moment when stakes, fatigue and the odd festering grudge make misconduct most likely. Jack Ginnivan’s ribs didn’t hurt any less because it’s September. Discretion, left to its own devices, had an unfortunate habit of favouring the famous. Reopen it, and every finals series turns into a festival of pleading exceptionality. Besides, the AFL guidelines already permit a reduction for exceptional and compelling circumstances. Lachie Neale won that argument eventually. The system works, then, right?



Aristotle apprehended all this millennia before the Match Review Officer did. The bloke who taught us to treat like cases alike also recognised that a general law will inevitably misfire in the unusual case, precisely because it’s general. The correction, equity, is to decide the case as the lawmaker would have, had he foreseen it. There can’t be any amnesty or discounting. Alternate sanctions must be BIGGER for any player who elects it, and the price is published in advance. The deterrent gets sharper. And for completeness, a sporting sanction was never compensation to Jack Ginnivan; its job is to uphold the competition’s standards. The existing exceptional and compelling circumstances discretion is constructed around the player – his record, his character, his standing. The Tribunal weighed it one way; the Appeal Board, correcting the scales, the other. Fair enough, both ways. But the discretion is aimed at the wrong target. Everybody always knew what this appeal was about; nobody could say it. Had the same strike happened in May, Neale would’ve copped his week, and nobody would’ve bothered with a five-hour hearing on a Tuesday night, let alone a sequel on Thursday.



So what’s my lawyer fix? I’d give any player faced with a grand final ban for a rats ‘n’ mice misconduct charge the option of a sanction carrying over to the next season, by also paying a hefty fine. In lawyer-gibber, it reads like this: Where a player is found to have committed a reportable offence attracting a fixed sanction of one match, and the match to which that sanction would apply is the Grand Final, the player may elect to serve instead a suspension of four matches commencing with the first match for which he is otherwise selected in the following premiership season, together with a financial sanction double the maximum applicable to the classification. The election is available once in a player’s career. It is not available where the offence is graded severe impact or high contact, or is a second or subsequent offence in the same season. The election, once made, is irrevocable and follows the player to any club. It’s confined to the lowest rung of suspension, where the gap between offence and consequence is widest and the competition’s interest in keeping a player out of that particular match is weakest. It costs the player more. Four matches plus a double-maximum fine, for a medium-impact strike to the body, sits well above anything the table would dish out in any other week of the year.

World.title: Arcade games are making a comeback – but not in the way you’d think
World.content:
CultureArt & designVideo games Arcade games are making a comeback – but not in the way you’d think Nell Geraets September 25, 2026 — 7:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Brie Healy was a child, her father became obsessed with Space Invaders. He discovered the 8-bit arcade game during a family visit to a local cafe, becoming so hooked that he dropped the kids off at home and returned for hours to beat his high score. “[The 8-bit] style brings me back to that feeling of childhood,” the Hobart-based game developer and artist says. “When I see those types of games, it makes me think about those specific moments, like when I used to sit behind my brother while he played video games because he wouldn’t let me have a turn.” Craig Duturbure playing his new 8-bit game Quiver at ACMI’s Play On display. Pablo Barnes Most adults today probably share similar memories. For Ratmouse Games’ co-founder Anthony Doueihi, it’s of playing Time Crisis with friends in an arcade, and for his fellow co-creator Peak Distapan, it’s of chasing high scores in Point Blank on his PlayStation. Craig Duturbure, meanwhile, recalls getting lost in the 1983 scrolling shooter Xevious. These Australian developers are counting on this nostalgia to pull audiences into their new 8-bit arcade games, all of which are displayed at ACMI as part of the interactive showcase Play On. But there’s a twist: the games may look old-school, but they explore very modern-day anxieties.



Duturbure’s game Quiver, for example, flips typical video-game violence on its head. In his 2D radial shooter, instead of shooting weapons to incite violence, you shoot Cupid’s arrows to spread love. Inspired by the 1983 tube shooter Gyruss, the aim of Duturbure’s game is to spread as much goodwill as possible before the end of Valentine’s Day. Loading “Today, this style of game doesn’t always have to be about violence and shooting things to death. We’ve got enough bad news. Just make people happy,” the Melbourne-based developer says. “There’s a sort of elegance to 8-bit games because they’re so pure in a way that you can’t hide behind flashy stuff. You just have to boil it down to core mechanics and what could be fun. It makes sense to people.” Healy’s game QIP, meanwhile, places you inside a miniature toy world where you must locate different items to piece together your character’s identity. This was partially inspired by Healy’s desire to live inside a Polly Pocket house, but it was also created to encourage players to consider their own identities, something that has become increasingly difficult in the age of social media and constant visual stimulation. Who are we when we’re not simply a notch in the algorithm?



Retro arcade games are enjoying a comeback, but not exactly in the way you’d think. ACMI “I see video games as an in-depth way to spark those kinds of feelings and questions in people. And it’s more interactive, it’s guided, so you can disarm the player with a fun vibe or something they can relate to, and then get them to do some self-reflection.” Retro 8-bit styles have proven particularly effective in prompting such self-exploration, Healy says. The pixels make the visuals more abstract, meaning any player could see themselves in the “blurry characters”. And unlike more modern games, 8-bit games generally don’t require hundreds of hours of gameplay or major strategising, leaving more room for either introspection or simple fun. Anthony Doueihi, Peak Distapan, Jae Pietersen Scott, Craig Duturbure and Brie Healy (left to right) at ACMI’s Play On display. ACMI Ratmouse Games’ Pop-up Crashout leans more towards “simple fun”. With the help of a desktop assistant, players must fend off a deluge of pop-ups and malware while exploring the early internet. It harks back to a time when the internet was less stale and each website had its own charm, Doueihi says. However, Distapan says it also touches on the digital fatigue and online anxiety most of us currently feel thanks to relentless algorithms and constant cyberthreats.



“I grew up loving the internet, but I feel like a lot of that love is gone – for fair reasons. I want people to recapture that joy,” Distapan says. All of these games attempt just that: to recapture the joy retro games evoked. Since gaming is a relatively new form of pop culture, Doueihi says nostalgia around ’80s and ’90s arcade games has only really begun to kick in somewhat recently. Related Article Video games Fans have waited 13 years for this video game. It may already be spoiled That said, arcades never disappeared. Jae Pietersen Scott, who created the music for Pop-up Crashout, says arcade games have simply evolved into things like Dance Dance Revolution or MaiMai. What’s different now is the growing nostalgia for specific ’80s or ’90s games, and the simplicity and communal nature they fostered. In fact, ACMI is set to open a Community Games Library as part of Melbourne International Games Week, an initiative similar to street libraries where visitors bring their favourite childhood games to swap with someone else. “There’s a trend in media towards analogue technology, and that’s feeding into how we’re consuming and making art as well,” Scott says. “Arcade games, since the very beginning, have been something that’s brought people together. That never stopped.”



Play On, presented with Now or Never, will run at ACMI until January 31, 2027. The Community Games Library will feature at ACMI as part of Melbourne International Games Week between October 2 and 11. Must-see movies, interviews and all the latest from the world of film delivered to your inbox.

World.title: Socceroos v Brazil LIVE updates: Brazil’s behaviour sparks debate back home; Tony Popovic’s side make first appearance since World Cup
World.content:
Having spent the preceding days training in Brisbane, where they will return for the second match of this series, both teams arrived in Townsville yesterday, and were received by local dignitaries and a couple of hundred fans who came for a brief meet-and-greet session.

Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti and representatives from Wulgurukaba Walkabouts, who performed a smoking ceremony to welcome the team to Townsville.

The Brazilians were welcomed to their hotel with a traditional smoking ceremony, which was led by Wulgurukaba Walkabouts, a group of local Aboriginal dancers and cultural performers. It took place without incident ... but the reaction of some players, who appeared to be laughing, sniggering or covering their faces during the ceremony, have triggered criticism and backlash back in Brazil.

A number of Brazilian outlets have picked up on the footage, and some of them accused the players of cultural insensitivity or disrespect. On social media, the reaction has been much harsher, with many Portuguese-speaking accounts talking of feeling ashamed or angry about the way they acted, and more embarrassing than Brazil’s infamous 7-1 defeat to Germany at the 2014 World Cup. The discussion has since been picked up by some conservative-leaning Australian accounts, dragging it into typical culture war areas.

I was there, and could definitely detect a sense of confusion and/or bemusement from the visitors, the vast majority of whom are in Australia for the first time, and would have had no idea what was in store. Footballers can be quite immature, and especially superstars of this calibre. Perhaps they should have been better briefed beforehand by the Brazilian federation on what they were about to see, how meaningful it is, and the importance of treating the moment appropriately.

World.title: The billionaire’s son with ties to Trump who is about to run Hollywood
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions The billionaire’s son with ties to Trump who is about to run Hollywood Brooks Barnes September 25, 2026 — 7:15pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The age of the Hollywood mogul was supposed to be over. Movies are dead, haven’t you heard? Even the grandest studio – Warner Bros. – had started to resemble a relic of a powerful past. Then came a “kid.” David Ellison, the son of Oracle’s billionaire co-founder Larry Ellison, was 23 when he arrived in the movie capital in 2006. Hollywood insiders laughed behind his back. He was dumb money to be fleeced, another starstruck rich guy with a chequebook. A 2015 GQ profile ran with the headline “The Kid Pays for the Picture”. David Ellison was already an unusual figure in modern Hollywood – a controlling owner who was also CEO and a hands-on movie and television producer. Adding Warner Bros. Discovery will expand his power to a scale without precedent. AP On Monday, after a remarkable, almost inconceivable run of dealmaking and brinkmanship, David Ellison – all of 43 years old – stood on the verge of adding Warner Bros. Discovery to his Paramount Skydance, giving him control of two businesses that helped invent the movie and television industries. A settlement with 12 states cleared the antitrust lawsuit that was the remaining obstacle to the $US111 billion ($158 billion) takeover.



Ellison was already an unusual figure in modern Hollywood – a controlling owner who was also CEO and a hands-on movie and television producer. Adding Warner Bros. Discovery will expand his power to a scale without precedent, spanning a wider range of media than the empires of classic moguls such as Jack Warner and Louis B. Mayer. Related Article Billionaires How Trump’s billionaire mate is reshaping America Even Bob Iger, for all his regal command as Disney’s CEO over the decades, never combined all those roles. “David’s about to become the Hollywood equivalent of Superman, Caesar and Midas combined,” Joseph M. Singer, a veteran film financier and former studio executive, said in an email. “He won’t just be sitting at the table. He’ll have extraordinary influence over who gets a seat.” Singer had publicly opposed the sale of Warner Bros. Discovery to Paramount Skydance, citing concerns about consolidation-related job losses and the roughly $US79 billion in net debt that the conglomerate would carry at closing, among other worries.



“I believe David’s intentions are good and his ambitions genuine,” Singer said. “But I remain concerned that this concentration of power is not in the interests of our business. I hope I am proved wrong.” Other critics were not so generous on Monday. A senior agent and two film producers privately likened Ellison to Michael Corleone in The Godfather, a Paramount film. The character began as an outsider and became the boss, consolidating power with startling effectiveness. Paramount Skydance’s deal to take over Warner Bros is getting closer to becoming a reality. Bloomberg The Ellison family’s ties to President Donald Trump – which included a dinner that David Ellison hosted in April “honouring the Trump White House” – have made many Democrats and a sizable contingent in Hollywood wary of his growing power. His empire will now span CNN and CBS News; HBO, MTV, BET, Comedy Central and TNT; the Paramount+ and HBO Max streaming services; and two of Hollywood’s oldest movie studios. Put another way, Ellison will soon have Batman, Harry Potter, Captain Kirk, Wonder Woman, Ethan Hunt, Maverick and SpongeBob SquarePants reporting to him.



“We vehemently oppose the agreement to allow David Ellison to take over Warner Bros. Discovery,” a campaign called Block the Merger said in a statement. “This is a bad deal for the future of film, entertainment, independent journalism and a strong democracy in this country.” Related Article Updated

Vale ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies The campaign was organised by the Future Film Coalition, a nonprofit that gathered thousands of signatures from film and television workers opposed to the merger. Ellison settled the antitrust lawsuits with California and 11 other states after months of legal and political combat. The lawsuits argued that the merger would reduce competition in movies and cable TV. The states relented after Ellison agreed to concessions, including a five-year commitment to release at least 30 movies annually, $US1.5 billion in additional domestic production spending, and the creation of an independent board to safeguard editorial independence at CNN and CBS News.



In an email to Paramount employees, Ellison said he expected the Warner Bros. Discovery takeover to close in about two weeks. He will exercise control of Paramount and Warner Bros. through his family’s 77.5 per cent stake in the company’s voting shares. “This is the first time since Walt Disney that you will have a family own and control a major Hollywood company with this level of hands-on management,” said Gerry Cardinale, a Paramount board member. Cardinale is the founder of RedBird Capital, the second-largest investor in Ellison’s deal for Warner Bros. Discovery. “There’s a changing of the guard taking place,” Cardinale added, referring not only to Ellison’s ascension but also to an owner-operated model that Hollywood had largely abandoned. Donald Trump with Larry Ellison. The Ellison family’s ties to the president – which included a dinner that David Ellison hosted in April “honouring the Trump White House” – have made many Democrats and a sizable contingent in Hollywood wary of his growing power. Bloomberg Amassing all that power may prove easier than wielding it.



Along with the mountain of debt, Ellison’s new company will need to contend with a cable TV business that is shrinking as viewers continue to cut the cord. He must also integrate two enormous companies – he has promised $US6 billion in savings – while navigating internal turmoil and political and editorial pressures at CBS News and CNN. Despite owning two major streaming services, Ellison will still be competing against Netflix and YouTube. He also faces Hollywood’s most basic problem: how to make movies and TV shows that enough people want to watch. ‘David’s about to become the Hollywood equivalent of Superman, Caesar and Midas combined.’ Film financier and former studio executive Joseph M. Singer After a banner run last year, Warner Bros. has stumbled badly at the box office in 2026. It ranks sixth among the seven largest studios in domestic market share this year, according to data from Rentrak, which tracks ticket sales. Paramount is seventh. Each has about 5 per cent of the market, compared with 24 per cent for Universal, the leader, and 21 per cent for Disney. On Monday, however, Hollywood focused less on Ellison’s challenges than it did on his remarkable rise.



It was only 13 months ago that he completed an $US8 billion deal to buy Paramount, home to CBS, MTV, Nickelodeon and its namesake movie studio. Four months later, Ellison launched a hostile bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, which had already agreed to sell itself to Netflix. By February, he had outmanoeuvred Netflix and had a deal in place. Related Article Opinion

Rupert Murdoch Have the Murdochs lost faith in Donald Trump? Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Twelve Democratic state attorneys general then sued to block the Warner takeover. Thousands of film and television workers publicly opposed the combination. The Writers Guild of America mounted its own legal challenge. None of it stopped him. A man who spent years struggling to be taken seriously had become impossible to underestimate.



In the email to employees, Ellison positioned the closing not as a culmination but as a beginning. “Closing is really just the starting line,” he said, adding: “I’m confident we’re going to build something special together in the years ahead. “Let’s go!” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: Once Emily realised what chemicals were in her beauty products, she couldn’t turn back
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessWellness Once Emily realised what chemicals were in her beauty products, she couldn’t turn back Sarah Berry September 25, 2026 — 7:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Emily Fletcher lists the products she uses on a typical day. There’s body wash and face cleanser, shampoo and conditioner, toothpaste, vitamin C serum, facial moisturiser, body lotion and sunscreen, foundation, concealer, blush, mascara, lip liner, lip gloss, deodorant, hand soap and a natural fragrance. At 18 different items, it’s only slightly more than the average person, who uses about 14.5 personal care products a day, from soap and toothpaste to cosmetics, fragrances and hairstyling products. But a paper published in the Journal of Exposure Science & Environmental Epidemiology says these 14.5 products expose a person to an estimated 100 or more unique ingredients each day, “many of which are known or suspected allergens, carcinogens, endocrine disruptors or neurotoxicants”. Emily Fletcher uses 18 personal care products most days. Sam Mooy Teenagers who are exposed to beauty and skincare content on social media use more products than their peers and the average adult, the research found. This is a “critical window of susceptibility”, alongside pregnancy, says Yousuf Mohammed, an associate professor in the school of pharmacy and pharmaceutical sciences at the University of Queensland.



Most of us use personal care products on the assumption that they will help us or, at the very least, not harm us. But this may not be the case. “Inactive ingredients found in personal care products act as the vehicle, preservative or texture enhancer for a formula,” Mohammed says. “While they do not directly treat a specific skin condition – a job reserved for active ingredients – their impact on your body and health can be profound.” He cites new research that found 98 per cent of tested personal care items contained undisclosed chemicals, many carrying hidden health hazards. ‘I wouldn’t put this in someone’s eye’ When Fletcher, 41, gave birth to her first child 11 years ago, she began thinking about the products she was buying for her newborn daughter.



Women in her mum’s group recommended this cream or that wipe. But, when the optometrist looked more closely at them, she found ingredients they wouldn’t use in eye drops because they can cause allergic reactions. “I wouldn’t put this in someone’s eye, so why am I wiping it over a large surface area of a baby’s skin,” she wondered. Related Article Cardiovascular health This popular sweetener is linked to higher heart attack and stroke risk Fletcher didn’t think it was fair that someone should need a science degree to identify the products that don’t contain harmful ingredients. So, she began blogging. As her blog gained traction, it evolved into a directory and annual Clean + Conscious Awards to “highlight those brands who are actually doing the right thing”. Today, the global beauty and personal care market – worth $US698.38 billion ($992 billion) is home to tens of thousands of brands and hundreds of thousands of products.



What we apply can be absorbed by the skins, says Dr Jacinta Martin, a reproductive and developmental biologist at the University of Newcastle. “But also potentially through mucosal surfaces, such as the lips and mouth, inside the nose, around the eyes or through genital and vaginal tissues, depending on the product being used – important when we consider period products,” she says. “There is also the potential for inadvertent ingestion, particularly with products applied to or around the lips and mouth.” Such exposure is relatively new. Emily Fletcher first become concerned about product ingredient lists when shopping for her baby. Getty Images What impact are these ingredients having on us?



Until the middle of the 19th century, many people stayed stinky all day. The bubonic plague outbreak sparked widespread fear of washing with water; soap was primarily for clothes, not bodies; and commercial toothpaste, deodorant and shampoo came to market only between 1873 and 1903. Few people used cosmetics, which were associated with immoral behaviours, and in 1916, only one in five Americans used toiletries at all. Now, as Martin says: “We are potentially applying many different products, containing many different chemicals, to our skin, hair and lips every day, and doing that repeatedly over many years – including during important periods of growth and development.” Editor's pick Alcohol Elizabeth was the life of the party. As a new mum, alcohol helped her feel like herself again People who use more products tend to have higher levels of chemicals such as phthalates, phenols and parabens circulating in their bodies, said lead author of the new study, Emily Barrett, a professor in the Department of Biostatistics and Epidemiology at Rutgers School of Public Health.



Those chemicals have been linked to a wide range of outcomes, including preterm birth, asthma and reproductive issues, Barrett says by email. “Complementary studies in animals also show that those chemicals can interfere with important biological processes that can then contribute to disease.” Yet direct causation between personal care products themselves and these health issues has not been established. “I think concern is warranted, but not panic,” Martin says. “I don’t think we know enough yet.” Specifically, there are questions about the concentrations and combinations of different chemicals, how much actually enters the body, how frequently we’re exposed, when in our lives that exposure occurs, and what happens when exposures occur repeatedly or in combination over long periods of time. So, what action should we take?



It’s not just down to the consumer, experts say. Brands need to be more transparent about ingredients, and governments need to tighten regulation around the chemicals used. But you can still reduce your exposure. In Barrett’s study, a three-day health product intervention where participants’ standard products were replaced with “cleaner” products (selected to be free of phthalates, parabens, triclosan and benzophenone-3), urinary concentrations of many (but not all) of the chemicals declined by up to 45 per cent. Here’s how to overhaul your routine. Go fragrance-free: Phthalates are used in fragrances to make the scent last longer. So the first step is to use fragrance-free products or only those scented with essential oils. “Avoid ‘unscented’, as these often use masking chemicals to hide smells,” Mohammed says. Additionally, he says, because blends are legally protected as proprietary trade secrets, a single listing of the word “fragrance” or “parfum” can mean dozens of undisclosed chemicals, including petrochemical derivatives and neurotoxins.

While the typical Australian home has approximately three-to-four bedrooms, larger families, intergenerational families, or those who want to host guests or have space for hobbies can benefit from extra bedrooms. Beyond functionality, properties with more bedrooms can command a higher market price and broaden the buyer pool when you sell. Whatever your reason, there are plenty of options on the market: here are five of the best homes in Melbourne with more than four bedrooms. 12 South Terrace, Clifton Hill VIC With a marble gas fireplace, veranda access, a fitted timber walk-in robe, and a luxurious dual-vanity ensuite featuring a private steam sauna, a double shower, an automatic toilet, and a heated towel rail, this Clifton Hill home has a main bedroom suite you may never want to leave.



The single-level home features two additional bedrooms with built-in robes, plus two other potential bedrooms that can also be used as a library or study, depending on your needs. The period details of the home are also impressive; the circa 1986 Victorian heritage is showcased through high ceilings, an ornate stained-glass entry and an extra-wide arched hallway. 18 Kerferd Street, Malvern East VIC This Gascoigne Edwardian has five bedrooms across its two levels.



The guest bedroom and master suite are on the ground level, with the latter including a walk-in robe and an ensuite. The three bedrooms upstairs all include built-in robes, with two also featuring window seats. With a retreat and bathroom servicing the level, this makes an ideal self-contained children’s/teen or guest retreat. Outdoors, the property features an in-ground trampoline, a nine-metre heated pool, bore water, irrigation, a gas barbecue, and a pergola. 43 Kinane Street, Brighton VIC



This double-storey Brighton property offers exclusive, luxurious living through its high-end materials, fixtures and fittings, and meticulous attention to detail. All five bedrooms are on the first floor, with three bedrooms featuring built-in robes and a master suite with both walk-in and built-in robes, an ensuite with spa, and access to a balcony. Other features include double-glazed, thermal-break aluminium windows and sensor-activated remote-control windows; outdoors, a floodlit north-south tennis court; a large, gas-heated swimming pool with an automated cover; a north-facing, paved entertaining area with an open fireplace; perimeter garden beds; an outdoor bathroom; and established trees. 4 Maxwell Court, Toorak VIC



Only moments from Toorak Village, this six-bedroom, three-level Toorak home offers space and privacy. World.title: Victim of Te Awamutu train incident was a young person
World.content:
A young person was the victim of a "tragic" train incident over the weekend, the Waipā District Council revealed.

The person died after the incident at Te Awamutu train stop on Sunday night.

Emergency services had rushed to the Waikato railway station around 6.20pm and said the person had "died at the scene".

The Waipā District Council said in a Facebook post it was young person that had a "tragic and untimely passing".

It also shared the details of a vigil to be held at Anchor Park in Te Awamutu on Sunday 11:30am.

"Everyone is welcome to attend and take a moment to remember, reflect and stand together.

"Our thoughts are with the whānau and all those affected at this difficult time."

Embedded content removed for printing https://www.facebook.com/WaipaDistrictCouncil/posts/pfbid02V7NAPEamf2r2yqUWjrcfqoUz8bZQiBxbQwmxPdZWbwoN9huy1tbvcYy9m6eFGn58l

A passenger, who RNZ agreed not to name, had said at the time it was something she would never forget.

"We weren't told what happened, but looking at the trauma of the bystanders... the trauma of staff, something I'll never forget."

She said she heard people yelling "stop" as the train left the station before it came to a halt.

The staff were extraordinary, she said, keeping passengers hydrated and informed as much as possible.

Senior Sergeant John McCarthy had previously said police were "providing support to whānau and those who acted immediately to try to help.

"Chief investigator of accidents Louise Cook said following the incident it had appointed a team of investigators who were now gathering evidence.

"Our investigators will focus initially on establishing what happened and identifying any evidence that could assist the inquiry. Our first priority is to gather evidence while it is available.

World.title: Marmite smears, live locusts to celebrate Orana Wildlife Park's 50th birthday
World.content:
Gibbons at Christchurch's Orana Wildlife Park have been treated to smears of Marmite and peanut butter on poles, and gift-wrapped boxes of cooked corn and live locusts, as part of the zoo's 50th birthday celebrations.

Festivities marking five decades since the park's opening on 25 September, 1976 came days after the cash-strapped park received a $1.2 million lifeline from ratepayers, with neighbouring councils also urged to chip in to secure its future.

Orana Wildlife Park chief executive Rachel Haydon said the zoo's drive-through safari, which ran from 1976-95, was still a big talking point.

"I do love people's stories of claw marks on the Cortina hood and things like that," she said. "Let's say, in our vision for our future, we are aiming to bring back a different version of a drive-through, so that still speaks to that nostalgia, but thinks about safety through a modern lens as well."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405604917112

Haydon said that different version of the drive-through would be part of a masterplan design, due be released in coming months, as the park grapples with financial difficulties.

An independent analysis by consultants BDO estimated a funding shortfall of $4.1 million for 2026/27 would increase to approximately $4.6-5.6 million each year for the following five years.

Earlier in September, park managers warned that the zoo might have to close without a cash injection.

On Wednesday Christchurch City Council agreed to contribute $1.2 million, as long as Orana approached other organisations for contributions, including neighbouring councils.

Haydon said Orana was grateful to the city council and had employed a fundraising and partnership manager.

"We have begun engagement with Selwyn and Waimakariri [District Councils]. No hard-and-fast plans yet, but we are organising times to hope to present and see what is possible."

Haydon said she understood councils faced tough funding decisions, but feedback showed that Orana park was valued by visitors.

Orana Wildlife Park celebrates its 50th anniversary. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

"I'm blown away by the emails and words people have sent through to me and the team about what the park means to them," she said.

On Friday, London holidaymakers Ryan and Liz Simes paid a visit to Orana Wildlife Park, with three-year-old son Reuben.

Ryan Simes grew up in Christchurch and said it was a nostalgic trip back to the park, which he hoped can climb out of a financial hole.

"I'm sure there are plenty of billionaires in the country who could reduce their lifestyle by 0.001 percent and it would cover it for years to come," he said. "The government could probably take their hands out as well, instead of reducing everything for everyone."

A historic image of lions in the carpark of Orana Wildlife Park as it celebrates 50 years. ORANA WILDLIFE PARK / SUPPLIED

On a visit from Sheffield in the Selwyn district, Jess Herring was celebrating son Archie's third birthday. She was not opposed to other councils financially backing Orana Wildlife Park.

"We all learn a lot about conservation coming here and a lot of children don't get the opportunity see these animals otherwise," she said. "I've been coming since I was a little child.

"It's such an integral part of Christchurch and such a big attraction, it would be a shame to see it go."

World.title: Shane Jones backs NZ First's controversial New Plymouth candidate selection
World.content:
New Zealand First deputy leader Shane Jones is backing the party's controversial candidate selection for the New Plymouth electorate.

Murray Chong has served 13 years on the district council and is one of three rotating deputy mayors.

He's no stranger to the headlines.

Chong was kicked out of the chamber last year, after describing council's procurement policy as "racist", because it had a goal to improve partnerships with iwi, hapū and Māori businesses.

A vocal critic of Māori wards, he abstained in 2024, when council voted to retain its Māori ward, citing safety concerns.

Chong had previously defended the flying of a Confederate flag, widely regarded as a symbol associated with slavery and racial oppression in the United States, at an American car rally.

Jones was in New Plymouth on Friday, speaking to a campaign rally attended by about 300 supporters.

He said Chong was a long-term supporter of New Zealand First and the core policies it represented.

"We all know that he's got strong opinions, but hey, Shane Jones and Winston Peters have got strong opinions. Lined up against us, he's in the third form in terms of being opinionated, if opinionated is a bad thing.

"He's a very valuable member, very loyal to to the core elements that make up our party's identity and how we want to take our country back."

He said Chong's job would be to go out win votes based on the party's record and policies.

"I don't think people are going to totally make their decision on the basis of one or three colourful lapses.

"They're going to ask themselves how is this party going to contribute to a more cohesive nation, a better set of responses for cost of living and getting industry charged up again, and I can't think of a better person to be pro-industry in Taranaki than our candidate."

Chong said many of the controversies were a long time ago.

"I've learned a lot and I'm a very well respected councillor, which I've proved.

Murray Chong was named NZ First's candidate for New Plymouth. RNZ/Robin Martin

"I had twice as many votes as any of the other candidates last election, and I've been the highest-polling councillor for the last two elections, so I mustn't be that bad."

Chong stood for New Zealand First in 2017, before heading over to New Conservative in 2020.

He was excited to be back.

"Oh, it's good," he said. "I mean, at the end of the day, they hold true to my values and I've always stood for the same values based on their policies, compared to any other party."

Earlier, Jones apologised to the party's supporters for New Zealand First's role in the oil and gas exploration ban, which he said had "destroyed" the Taranaki economy.

"Bugger the climate, lets go for jobs," he said to loud applause.

Jones explained New Zealand First's position on a proposed LNG terminal was that during the heat of an election campaign was no time to sign up to such as deal.

His preference was the "re-emergence of indigenous gas", repeating his "drill, baby, drill" catchphrase, when pointing to recent government investment in exploration projects.

Jones promised to cut "red and green tape" and not let any "frog, lizard or hitherto unknown bat" get in the way of legitimate projects.

He wanted action on State Highway 3 at Awakino Gorge - which had been closed several times over the past year, due to weather events - indicating a complete new road similar to the Manawatū solution could be in order, but its expense would need to be kept in check.

Immigration settings needed a rejink, where the focus was on migrants New Zealand needed, rather than those that needed New Zealand, Jones said.

He labelled the India Free Trade deal as the "Indian free travel deal".

The New Zealand First deputy steered away from the controversy over the failed bid to mine vanadium on the seabed off the South Taranaki coast during his speech.

"Winston has told me not to upset the good people of Taranaki."

Following the meeting, Jones said mining the seafloor was still on its radar.

"I was disappointed that the panel seemed to take great glee in turning it down. The applicants obviously were unable to meet the threshold, but the party remains committed to the extraction and utilisation of seabed minerals as a policy plank of our party."

People leaving the meeting enjoyed what they heard. Jay liked the commitment to try and reboot local industry.

"Oh look, I definitely agree with the oil and gas. That's pretty pivotal for our community."

Stuart was impressed.

"I found it very inspiring and uplifting, mostly the getting rid of the woke nonsense that we've been subject to for the last several years."

Jones' approached resonated with Chris.

"Just getting us all back on track. The common sense and pragmatism and, yeah, getting back to the values that we grew up with."

Partner Roger also echoed her thoughts.

"The common sense, really. I mean, getting behind making some money, instead of all this bullshit that's going on.

World.title: Santana Minerals mining company offers $10m to protect lizards in Central Otago
World.content:
An Australian mining company is offering an additional $10 million to protect lizards in a bid to help get its Central Otago gold mine project approved.

Santana Minerals is seeking fast-track approval to build an open-cast mine in the Dunstan Mountains to target a $4.4 billion gold deposit.

The company initially proposed 81 hectare sanctuaries, but its evidence suggested the conservative lizard population growth in those areas would equate to about 13 percent of the number of killed or displaced lizards.

Legal submissions for the conservation director general this month said an estimated 590,000 protected lizards would be killed, as mine development proceeded under the company's revised proposal to manage lizard impacts.

The fast-track expert panel asked the company to consider creating a "substantially larger, better-sized exclusion fenced sanctuary".

In response, Santana offered to use the $10 million funding to build a 140-150 hectare pest exclusion fence, eradicate introduced pest mammals in the fenced area and maintain zero densities of targeted pests over 30 years for the benefit of Central Otago lizards.

It also proposed to increase the number of southern grass skink that could be salvaged and relocated from approximately 800 to 1800, and establish a dedicated relocation site or sites for them.

A few days earlier, on 21 September, the Department of Conservation provided legal submissions agreeing that killing hundreds of thousands of lizards was foreseeable, but challenged the idea that the scale of mortality was "not directly intended" or was "unavoidable".

"The applicant's own evidence confirms that the deaths of many thousands of lizards could be avoided and that the mortality envisaged is directly intended as a consequence of the [Bendigo-Ophir Gold Project] proceeding," the submission said.

The expert panel heard closing legal arguments, with Kā Rūnaka saying the company's evidence indicated the environmental and cultural impacts could not be adequately mitigated or avoided.

A Santana Minerals spokesperson said detailed responses to the submissions would be filed in due course.

The application has already been paused twice.

World.title: Search continues for Queenstown woman Erika Rodrigues Coelho
World.content:
The search continues in Queenstown for a 47-year-old Brazilian woman, who has not been seen or heard from since Friday, 18 September.

Erika Rodrigues Coelho's rental car was found at Skippers Saddle, near Coronet Peak, on Monday.

Police say search and rescue volunteers have carried out an extensive search of the surrounding area, with support from coastguard, drones and a helicopter.

Senior Sergeant John Fookes said the car - a white Toyota RAV4, with a black roof and registration RKM122 - was apparently parked at Skippers Saddle sometime during the afternoon or evening last Friday.

"Land Search and Rescue volunteers have spent hundreds of hours searching the Shotover, Devil's Creek and other nearby catchments, as well as points of interest and routes that could have been taken by Erika from where the vehicle was left," he said.

"Coastguard Queenstown's underwater drone has been used by one of their volunteers to search a mountain tarn [pond] near Skippers Saddle."

Police are asking the public to report any sightings of Erika since 18 September via 105 - or any information that could help find her.

Any sightings of Erika should be reported via 111, police said.

"We want to stress that even the smallest amount of information can make a huge difference to our investigation and finding Erika," a police spokesperson said.

World.title: Ministry investigating 'serious concerns' about Horowhenua College's leadership
World.content:
The Ministry of Education is investigating concerns raised at Horowhenua College in the lower North Island.

Stuff is reporting more than a dozen staff and community members have sent a letter to the ministry and Teaching Council raising "serious concerns" about leadership and governance at the college.

In July, teacher Asaria Saili - previously the language dean - was dismissed after an investigation upheld concerns regarding his conduct towards a student.

Horowhenua College presiding board member, Juliana Mansvelt declined an interview with RNZ, but in a statement said the school had not received any formal complaints directly.

Do you know more? Email mary.argue@rnz.co.nz

"We are aware that concerns have been raised with the Ministry of Education and are working with the Ministry while these matters are being looked into."

She said it would not be appropriate to comment further, but said the board took its responsibility to provide "a safe and healthy workplace, and to govern and oversee the school effectively, very seriously".

Mansvelt said the board regularly sought independent governance advice and if concerns were raised with the school, they would be managed through the complaints process.

She encouraged anyone with feedback or concerns to get in touch.

Teaching Council chair, Patrick Walsh confirmed it received a letter raising concerns on September 16, and that it was being considered through the council's statutory process.

"Where concerns are raised with us that fall outside our mandate, including concerns about school culture, leadership and governance, we pass those concerns on to the relevant agency, such as the Ministry of Education, to investigate.

"We will not be commenting on the contents of the letter, or on the detail or progress of any matter that may be before the Council, including allegations about individuals," he said.

In response to questions from RNZ, the ministry's acting director of education for Greater Wellington, Te Rangipai Renata, said ministry staff met with the college principal and the presiding member of the board on Wednesday.

"We are assessing the information provided and working through our usual processes.

"When concerns are raised, it is important that we establish the facts and give those involved an opportunity to respond before reaching any conclusions."

World.title: 'Cynical' Freo coach bemoans how long AFL took with Neale reprieve
World.content:
Brisbane coach Chris Fagan doubted Lachie Neale would be cleared for the AFL grand final, as his "cynical" Fremantle counterpart Justin Longmuir took umbrage with the lengthy process.

But both coaches are happy with the end outcome, with Fagan declaring Neale's availability "good for footy".

The dual Brownlow Medal winner will feature in the premiership decider against Fremantle — his former club — at the MCG on Saturday after having a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan downgraded in a drama-filled hearing on Thursday.

Neale was instead fined $10,000 as the appeals board gave the four-time All Australian midfielder the ultimate reprieve due to having never previously been suspended in his decorated 320-game AFL career.

"I didn't think he would (get off)," Fagan told reporters on Friday.

"It was a bit like last year, I didn't think he was going to play last year until the day before the game when he got through a fitness test.

"So it's sort of history repeating itself, just in a different way. Good for footy I reckon but we were pretty much ready for him not to be playing, I must admit."

Brisbane swayed the appeals board that the tribunal had made an error of law in not considering the exceptional and compelling circumstances of Neale's past record.

Longmuir expected Neale to be cleared all along, although thought the decision would have come earlier in the week.

"I'm a bit cynical with these things. Sometimes I feel like that's the outcome that gets reached a little bit later than what I thought it would get reached," the Dockers coach said.

"We prepared for Brisbane's best and he's clearly in their best team. Even if he didn't play, we felt like someone else would have had to step up and they've got a lot of those 'someone else's' that are probably searching for midfield time."

Longmuir later added: "If players who have great records, who have contributed so much to our game, get a bit of leeway at certain times, I don't think that's a bad thing for the game".

Defender Noah Answerth, injured in Brisbane's qualifying final loss three weeks ago, was available and would have returned had Neale been suspended, but misses out.

"Coaches aren't supposed to have favourite players but he's (Answerth) one of mine," Fagan said.

The AFL's gut feel to Neale's gut punch leaves fans dazed and confused It was the AFL's Folarin Balogun moment, and the decision to let Lachie Neale play in the grand final has left many seeing red.

"If Lachie hadn't have played, Noah would have come into the team and Jaspa Fletcher would have pushed up onto a wing."

For the second year in a row, Neale has been the headline story of grand final week.

Last year, the 33-year-old famously overcame a calf injury that appeared season-ending to play a second-half super-sub role in the Lions' stunning demolition of Geelong.

Neale's fourth-straight grand final will almost certainly be his last for Brisbane, with a move to Collingwood looming in the off-season.

"Who says it's my last?" Neale replied to a question about his future.

With rain expected on Saturday, Neale will figure prominently as one of the Lions' best wet-weather players.

Brisbane take an unchanged team into the grand final as they attempt to become just the third side in the last 69 years to complete an AFL premiership three-peat.

And should they win, it would be the second three-peat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.
