World.title: Fagan's future undecided as Lions focus on making grand final history
World.content:
Chris Fagan will again wait until after the grand final to confirm his future as he stands poised to join one of AFL coaching's most select clubs.

There has been speculation over the last few days about whether Saturday could be it for the two-time Brisbane premiership coach.

While Fagan said nothing had changed from the last couple of years — he will speak with Lions hierarchy once the season is over — the 65-year-old acknowledged on Friday that he had been in the role for a decade.

If Brisbane beats Fremantle on Saturday at the MCG, Fagan will become only the seventh VFL/AFL coach to mastermind a premiership three-peat.

"I'm only worried about the game tomorrow," Fagan said at the pre-game media conference.

"Every year, for the last two or three years, I've had a chat with our CEO and president about when's the right time for me to finish up.

"This is my 10th year, so I've been going for a while. I will get through this game and probably have the usual chat I've had every other year."

Chris Fagan has led the Lions to four straight grand finals. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Fagan's long-time confidant Leigh Matthews, who coached the Lions to their 2001-03 three-peat, and former Brisbane captain Jonathan Brown discussed Fagan's future earlier this week.

Brown suspected Fagan would want to try for four in a row if the Lions won. While Matthews said coaching was a lifestyle and Fagan might decide at some point he did not want to do it anymore.

"It's fair enough to speculate about it, but I honestly don't know right at this point in time whether I will keep going or not," Fagan said.

"I was like that last year and the year before, so we just have to work out the right time to go.

"It's not the big issue; we have to play a big game tomorrow."

Justin Longmuir says he is hoping to emulate Chris Fagan's long-term success. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

As Fagan and the Lions try to win another premiership, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir and his team are looking to win the club's first flag.

Sitting next to Fagan, Longmuir said the goal was to make sure that whatever happened on Saturday, it was only the start of a successful Dockers era.

"I've thought about this moment for a number of years," Longmuir said about the prospect of Fremantle winning the premiership.

"It would fill me with great pride to be able to do that. But win or lose tomorrow, it's not the end of the journey.

"We want to create something that 'Fages' has created, where you're contending for a number of years."

AAP

World.title: Front-running Freo ready to claim first flag
World.content:
Football fans unite in glory, but the bonds of fandom are often forged in failure.

It is fair to say that Fremantle fans have suffered more than most since their club's entry to the AFL. It's also fair to say that, as a result, Dockers fans are some of the most passionate and dedicated in the league. It's why something like Wharfie Time is endearing instead of cheesy. The Purple Army is something to believe in.

The Fremantle experience has often been one of struggle. Struggling against the bigger brother in blue and yellow. Struggling against the tyranny of distance in a league based on the other side of the continent. Struggling against the weight of its own history.

The anchor is sometimes less a motif of their moniker and instead a weight tethering their expectations.

But this year everything seems different. This year Fremantle has led from the front, often without looking back.

Even as the pack came for the Dockers, they didn't fold under the pressure. Instead, they buckled down and somehow got better.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained last week.

"So we all know what's on the line, but we've just got to make sure that we give our best at each moment, and the next moment's the most important one."

The Dockers showed a resilience often only attached to the best of teams. It's also one baked into the identity of their side.

Fremantle aren't just stocked with high-draft picks. The Dockers are also filled with players overlooked and discarded by others. Almost half of the side that will run out on Saturday fits into those categories, with a few rookies to boot. If these players had given up at the first rejection, they wouldn't be in the league.

More pertinently, Fremantle wouldn't be in the big dance without many of these names.

If Fremantle's fandom and side are somewhat unconventional, its success on the field is anything but. Like many successful teams of years' past, they have been built on a solid defensive base, with enough star power to shine through when needed. Like many great teams, they are more than the sum of their parts.

Like many great teams, they play their best footy when it matters most. Last week, Fremantle put together arguably the best quarter of its season to make the grand final.

"We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us … I'm just so proud of everyone," captain Alex Pearce said in the immediate wake of last week's victory.

Thirteen years after their first grand final, the Dockers finally seem primed to break their premiership drought. In their way stands a side featuring the only remaining Fremantle player from that 2013 loss: Lachie Neale.

Strength in defence

Alex Pearce (right) is the lynchpin of a formidable defensive unit for Fremantle. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Often the leaders of a side dictate the identity and style of a side.

Led ably by captain and All-Australian Alex Pearce, Fremantle's backline may not be as star-studded as other defensive units around the league, but it is as sturdy as any. They scramble, hustle and fight through all four quarters. Regularly through the year teams fell away as the Dockers held strong.

The Dockers have had the league's most consistently good defence across all facets of the game. Some backlines drop their heads when the tide starts to turn — not Fremantle.

Fremantle excels at defending before danger begins. Its midfield works hard to prevent clean exits from stoppages and contests around the ground. Although the Dockers don't have the best clearance differential or ability to win ground balls in the mid-arc, they are exceptional at preventing opposition teams from scoring from these sources.

When they lose possession in their front half, the Dockers stay eager to get the ball in their hands. They are the best side in the league at winning the ball back in the middle third of the ground.

If the ball does end up inside their defensive 50, no side is better at repelling opposition forwards. Miserly is an understatement about how Fremantle defends. It is the biggest reason that the Dockers are still alive in season 2026.

When they win the ball back, they can turn on the jets and blow opposition sides away.

The cherry on top

Players such as Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton (right) ensure Fremantle can beat teams offensively as well as defensively. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Few fans turn up to the footy for stout defence. It's the action at the other end that hypnotises.

Despite their defensive DNA, Freo are not lacking for weapons of their own. They turn defence into attack at the drop of a hat thanks to a plethora of creative players.

Fremantle can put on a show like few others when everything is firing, possessing the ability to pile goal after goal on the scoreboard. While their defence is often understated, their attack is anything but.

Few players generate more highlights than Shai Bolton, with the former Mark of the Year winner routinely getting Purple fans off the edge of their seats. Bolton isn't alone however.

The Dockers side is stocked with players that use the ball well.

Murphy Reid has quickly cemented himself as an attacking line breaker, while Caleb Serong, Jordan Clark and Corey Wagner gain ground with ease.

Luke Jackson also proves a challenge for any opponent as the most capable ruck at ground level in the league. Jackson has the most score involvements of any ruck this year.

The Dockers often attack in straight lines, and use the tallest timber in the league to their advantage.

But when sides like Sydney take those avenues away, Fremantle doesn't shy away from changing angles of attack and look laterally as well.

That ability to win aerial contests has another benefit. It tends to encourage opposition players to fly more often than they should, leaving Fremantle with an outnumber at ground level. That allows even more room for the ground gang to work in.

Up forward, the Dockers can beat you in any number of ways. The likes of Hye Amiss, Patrick Voss and Josh Treacy can take clunks and convert them into sure scores. At ground level, Michael Frederick, Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton regularly hit the scoreboard and strike fear into the hearts of opposition small defenders.

Their big men love a bomb from the top of the arc, but Freo don't tend to score a lot from out wide. That makes Hayden Young's preliminary final heroics all the more notable.

Perhaps Fremantle's biggest strength is their evenness across the board. Against Hawthorn it wasn't just the stars like Bolton and Luke Jackson that stood up late, but also players like Judd McVee and Frederick. It is clear that there's belief in this team, and dedication to a united cause.

The Final Challenge

Lachie Neale (centre) and the Brisbane Lions are standing between Fremantle and its maiden premiership. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Although Fremantle has been the best side across the year, it isn't coming into the grand final at the peak of its mid-season powers. The Dockers have won just three quarters in their three finals so far — a feat no other team has achieved before.

The Dockers have struggled late in the year when the ball has hit the deck against good sides, and some of the best midfields have overwhelmed their attacking midfield unit. These may sound like minor issues, but to win a grand final against the two-time defending champions, everything has to be on point.

But the Lions are a side that the Dockers have vanquished through the year. In round 12, the Dockers eased to a 25-point win in one of their most impressive wins of the year. The Dockers absorbed the Lions' clearance dominance while preventing them from getting the upper hand in the marking battle. Fremantle worked out a way to penetrate the Lions' whole ground defence, scoring a massive 52 points from their defensive half.

But it was also a Brisbane side that Longmuir acknowledged wasn't at their best coming into the game.

Fremantle got the better of Brisbane in the only meeting between the two sides during the home-and-away season this year. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"We felt like there were some opportunities there. You know, Fages [Lions coach Chris Fagan] would come in here and say they're not in the greatest form," he said.

"I just don't want to be disrespectful with that because they've been in the last three grand finals."

Longmuir and Fagan both know that premierships aren't won in May. The early season Lions are vastly different to the side that Fremantle has to beat in the grand final.

But there's hope in the West that the result will be the same and that the Dockers three-decade drought will be over.

World.title: Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
World.content:
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.

Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.

But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.

He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.

Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.

"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group," Woolf said.

"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.

"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.

"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."

Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.

Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew have never met a rugby league problem they couldn't solve by running over it and now the two wrecking balls will go head-to-head with an NRL grand final berth on the line.

"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.

"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."

Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.

"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.

"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."

Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has tried his very best to convince Stone to play on next season.

"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.

"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."

The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.

"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.

"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."

The Dolphins have won 16 of their last 18 matches coming into Friday night's NRL preliminary final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.

"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.

"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."

Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.

"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.

"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.

"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."

AAP

World.title: Brazil’s big-name squad meets mega hype from soccer fanatics
World.content:
As some of the world's most famous football players arrive in a city known for its love of another football code, soccer fans hope the hype might change people's minds.

The Brazilian soccer team landed in Townsville yesterday ahead of their friendly clash with the Socceroos tonight at North Queensland Stadium.

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti brought a squad of big names, including Vinícius Júnior and captain Marquinhos, whose combined yearly salaries are estimated at more than $55 million.

Brazilian superstar Vinícius Júnior met with fans in Townsville to sign autographs. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

For the city's small and vibrant Brazilian community, their arrival has been a cause for celebration.

Enthusiastic fans wore jerseys and held signs, screaming out to the star-studded team, after they touched down in Townsville.

"We love to party, we love dancing, and we like to cheer for our soccer team," Tatiane Pinheiro said.

"Very loud, very excited, everyone is going to be so excited to watch the game."

Football fanatics came from far and wide to welcome both the Brazil and Socceroos teams. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

The friendly match is one of two games in the series, with the other scheduled for Brisbane on September 29.

It will be the 12th time the Socceroos and Brazil have met since their first match-up in 1988.

Australia has beaten the five-time World Cup champions just once, in 2001.

But a lopsided head-to-head has not tainted the excitement in Townsville, which has been decked out in green and gold in anticipation of the international game.

Brazilian community fires up

Ms Pinheiro, a Townsville resident and Brazilian national, said she was excited to welcome crowds of Brazilians from around the country to her city.

Tatiane Pinheiro expects to meet Brazilian fans who have flown in from around the country. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Everyone that we know from other cities is coming to watch the big game," she said.

Organisers said more than half of the sell-out crowd of 25,000 were visitors from outside of Townsville.

Louise Monteiro (right) came with friends and family to greet the Brazilian team in her new hometown of Townsville. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Louise Monteiro and her family recently moved to Townsville, and she is originally from Brazil.

She said it was difficult for her to decide which team to support.

"I think I'll always support Brazil first," she said.

"If Socceroos play against another team, I'll be supporting Socceroos."

Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know Everything you need to know as the youthful Socceroos take on a Brazil team on the rebuild under legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti in Queensland, with international friendlies in Townsville and Brisbane.

Townsville Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the occasion trumped every event she'd ever seen in Townsville.

She said the hype among her community had been building since the announcement, including gathering for pre-game events.

"The supporter part of Brazilian football is such a big thing," she said.

"All the Brazilians are so excited to go and support the team and just to be there."

Brazilian community leader Ronie Reed said the local community has been very excited about the game. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Ms Reed has lived in Townsville for 14 years and organises many local events for the South American community, which is often made up of the many backpackers who visit North Queensland.

"We want to show our presence; we want to show the impact that we have," she said.

"We want everyone to know how good it is to have this community here."

The Brazilian team lined up for a photo in front of Cleveland Bay. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

A street party and festival in the city starts at 3pm, before entertainers and musicians lead the crowd to the stadium.

A different type of football

North Queensland Stadium is home to the NRL's North Queensland Cowboys, but soccer fan and local player Mark Gadzikwa hopes Brazil's appearance and performance at the stadium could help curb a "lack of interest" in the round-ball game.

Townsville resident Mark Gadzikwa is both a rugby league and soccer fan. (ABC News: Emily Anderson)

"Brazil has always meant football; there's no better team to do it," he said.

" When you think of football, you think of Brazil. "

Anotida Sandengu has watched soccer since he was five, but this will be his first time watching a team as skilful as Brazil.

Mr Sandengu said he was surprised Townsville was chosen for the international match, which was announced after the World Cup in June.

Townsville locals Anotida Sandengu and Jobe Waring. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

"I wouldn't have called it; I remember I heard the news around the World Cup when everyone was watching soccer," he said.

"It was just really exciting. This is a once-in-a-lifetime event; it probably won't ever happen again." Brazil is the most successful team at the FIFA World Cup, having won five times.

The Socceroos last met Brazil for a friendly game in Melbourne in 2017, where they lost 4-0.

Kick-off in Townsville is 8pm.

World.title: Infantino calls for 'culture of dialogue' amid resignation calls
World.content:
FIFA's embattled president, Gianni Infantino, says he is committed to a fresh culture of openness at the football body that is "not about generating positive headlines".

Two months into a deep rift in global soccer over Infantino's now-dropped $4.2 billion ($6 billion) World Cup sell-off plan, he offered his critics this week an independent review of how FIFA is run and makes decisions.

"I have received positive messages about it from different parts of the world, and it is important that we keep listening to each other," he wrote in an Instagram post from Jeddah in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the Arabian Gulf Cup.

Infantino will chair an October 15 meeting of the 37-member FIFA Council that will also be asked to approve consultation with the 211 member federations and six continental soccer bodies on "how to further strengthen FIFA's decision-making processes".

The 211 members already effectively own FIFA, a Switzerland-based not-for-profit that has at least $5 billion in cash reserves after a financially successful men's World Cup in North America.

FIFA's ruling council includes three vice presidents — European football leader Aleksander Ceferin, North America's Victor Montagliani and Asia's Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa — who have led opposition to Infantino during the furore over his proposal to create a commercial spin-off part-owned by investors fronted by Josh Kushner.

"There must be a culture of dialogue, of listening to each other and respecting one another," Infantino wrote on Thursday, local time, about the council meeting in Zurich. "This is not about generating positive headlines; it is about doing what is right for the game."

Infantino's presidency since 2016 has created most turmoil when proposing multi-billion-dollar commercial plans without fully consulting continental bodies like UEFA, which succeeded in stopping them.

Flying FIFA solo toward close ties to Trump

Gianni Infantino's close ties to Donald Trump have caused tension in the football world. (Getty Images: Chris Brunskill)

FIFA has often seemed an executive one-man leadership as Infantino built closer ties to US President Donald Trump around this year's World Cup. FIFA created a peace prize to award Trump last year and allowed United States striker Folarin Balogun to evade a mandatory ban at the tournament after intervention from the White House.

Infantino's secretive plan to sell at least 20 per cent of FIFA's commercial rights in a deal anchored by Kushner, the brother of Trump's son-in-law, provoked the soccer body's biggest crisis since anti-corruption arrests in 2015 that led to trials in New York.

The 211 national federations were offered $20 million each to approve the creation of the FIFA Forward Enterprise subsidiary. UEFA, North America's CONCACAF and the Asian Football Confederation countered by saying FIFA could afford to give each federation a $10 million dividend just from its reserves.

Now Infantino, who faces an election challenge ahead of a March 18 vote by FIFA members in Morocco, insists he is ready to listen to soccer officials.

"I have never been more determined and committed in doing that," he wrote on Instagram.

"FIFA is always engaged. I am always engaged, and I want to hear how we can continue to grow football for the benefit of everybody, everywhere."

AP

World.title: Incredible catch helps South Africa beat Australia in one-day clash
World.content:
Mitch Marsh could not hide his dismay at how Australia capitulated tamely in their opening ODI in South Africa, who were helped to victory by an incredible catch by Marco Jansen that needs to be seen to be believed.

The Aussies ended up succumbing to a 67-run defeat to the disappointment of their stand-in skipper after a succession of cheap dismissals in a sorry run chase in Durban.

Marsh himself seemed to have laid the foundations for victory with his blistering opening knock of 60, but after he had perished needlessly to the spinning wiles of Kehav Maharaj, none of his team could cement the partnerships to get them anywhere near the hosts' 298-run target.

After watching the world champs collapse to 230 all out off just 41.2 overs, Marsh sighed: "I'm pretty disappointed. South Africa outplayed us. It was a good game of cricket, but we fell well short.

"We had our opportunities. I am probably going to sound like a broken record speaking about having partnerships in our batting, but we weren't able to form many tonight."

Mitchell Marsh got Australia's run chase off to a fast start with a rollicking knock of 60, but his departure was followed by a collapse. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

The South Africans had set a challenging target after being inserted by Marsh, compiling 8-297 thanks largely to a brilliant 112 from Matthew Breetzke and a spectacular 75 off 59 balls from pace-bowling all-rounder Jansen.

Marsh, standing in as skipper again for the rested Pat Cummins, then led from the front in response with his 36-ball pyrotechnics, which featured three sixes, one of which sailed for 104 metres over the dressing room roof at Kingsmead and landed at the roadside.

He shared a blistering opening stand of 90 in just 9.2 overs with Travis Head, but like Head (36), Cooper Connolly, who'd looked supreme in making 38, and Matt Renshaw (44), he got out to an airy shot when the Australians were up with the required rate and under no real pressure.

The superb spinning of the two slow left-armers Maharaj (4-20) and Bjorn Fortuin (2-34) soon put them under that pressure, though.

Discomfited, Josh Inglis got out to a poorly executed reverse sweep on the eighth ball he faced and Australia lost their last six wickets for just 54 to allow the Proteas to draw first blood in the three-match series.

The key moment may have been when Jansen took a sensational running, diving, one-handed catch in the outfield, stretching out his long telescopic arm to scoop up the ball just above the turf to get rid of key man Renshaw off Gerald Coetzee. It left Australia on 7-215, and there was no way back.

So, after the three-match sweep of the Zimbabwe series, this really did feel like a proper test of Australia with the defence of their 50-over World Cup in southern Africa just a year away.

The first part of the reconnaissance mission demonstrated just how much they still have to work on, and the weakness against spin was again shown up even while South Africa had five top-line pace bowlers sidelined through injury.

Matthew Breetzke's brilliant 112 off just 106 deliveries allowed South Africa to post a score of 8-297 in the first innings. (Getty Images: Gerhard Duraan)

Man-of-the-match could easily have been Jansen, with his one wicket, four catches and big-hitting or the superb 36-year-old veteran tweaker Maharaj, but batting at No.4, Breetzke's superb 106-ball knock, before being run out by Connolly, deservedly won the day.

All-rounder Jack Edwards had an uncomfortable debut — 0-56 off 10 overs, followed by scoring five off 15 balls — but there was encouragement again in the display of paceman Nathan Ellis, who, fresh from his outstanding series against Zimbabwe, was again the bowling pick with 3-57.

All-rounder Cameron Green, back in the side after missing the series against Zimbabwe as he recovered from a shoulder injury, had a poor day with the bat, falling for five while trying to belt Maharaj over cow corner and getting caught in the deep.

The opening loss has really put pressure on Australia to turn the series round at The Wanderers in Johannesburg on Sunday, when Cummins is set to be recalled. They haven't won a bilateral series against South Africa since 2014.

AAP

World.title: Socceroos vs Brazil, everything you need to know
World.content:
The Socceroos will play their first internationals since the 2026 FIFA World Cup against five-time world champions Brazil in Queensland this week.

It is the team's first meeting since they played at the MCG in June 2017.

The Socceroos have only ever beaten Brazil once, a 1-0 victory in the 2001 Confederations Cup third-place play-off thanks to Shaun Murphy's 84th-minute strike.

Here's everything you need to know about the Queensland Series.

When are the Socceroos playing?

The Socceroos are back in action on home soil. (Getty Images: Dean Mouhtaropoulos)

The first game is on Friday, September 25 at Townsville's Queensland Country Bank Stadium.

The second is on Tuesday, September 29 at Brisbane's Lang Park.

For both games, kick-off is 8pm AEST, meaning Queensland, New South Wales, Victoria, Tasmania, and the ACT.

In the Northern Territory and South Australia, kick-off is 7:30pm and in Western Australia, it's 6pm.

How can I watch the Socceroos?

Friday night's game in Townsville is available to watch across Network 10 on free to air and Paramount+, you just need to check your local guides.

Tuesday night's game in Brisbane is only available on subscription streaming service Paramount+.

Alternatively, you can follow both games in full on the ABC Sport live blog.

Who is in the Socceroos squad?

Lucas Herrington is back on home soil for the first time since his move to Hull. (Getty Images: PA Images/Annabel Lee-Ellis)

With July's Round of 32 penalty shootout defeat to Egypt in Dallas firmly in the rear-view mirror, coach Tony Popovic's eyes are now gazing forward towards January's AFC Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia.

As such, Popovic has called up seven uncapped youngsters: Dylan Leonard (19 years old), Marcus Younis (21), Kasey Bos (22), Kealey Adamson (23), Yaya Dukuly (23) and Eli Adams (24), while Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek, who both missed the World Cup through injury, return.

Nestory Irankunda will hope to lead the line and test himself against some of the sport's biggest names.

Hull City centre back and Brisbane local Lucas Herrington has had a superb start to life in the Premier League and will look forward to play in front of his friends and family.

Only one player, Sydney FC's Aziz Behich, plies his trade in the A-League Men.

Socceroos squad: Goalkeepers: Patrick Beach (Troyes), Paul Izzo (Randers), Jacob Chapman* (St Mirren). Defenders: Kealey Adamson* (QPR), Aziz Behich (Melbourne City), Alessandro Circati (S.L. Benfica), Milos Degenek (APOEL), Jason Geria (Albirex Niigata), Lucas Herrington (Hull City), Dylan Leonard* (Alemannia Aachen), Harry Souttar (Leicester City), Jacob Italiano (Grazer AK), Kasey Bos* (Excelsior Rotterdam). Midfielders: Paul Okon-Engstler (FC Köln), Jackson Irvine (Cerezo Osaka), Riley McGree (Middlesbrough), Connor Metcalfe (St Pauli), Aiden O'Neill (New York City), Patrick Yazbek (Nashville). Forwards: Eli Adams* (Gamba Osaka), Yaya Dukuly* (NK Celje), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting), Nishan Velupillay (FC Ingolstadt), Tete Yengi (FC Machida Zelvia), Marcus Younis* (Brøndby). *uncapped

Who is not in the Socceroos squad?

Mohamed Touré scored six goals in nine appearances in all competitions for Norwich this season before getting injured. (Getty Images: MI News/NurPhoto/David Watts)

Popovic was dealt a blow by injuries to Mohamed Touré and Alexander Robertson in the last week.

Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Touré, who has been on fire for Norwich in the Championship, has a shoulder injury which could lead to a lengthy lay-off, while Robertson is reportedly being rested by Cardiff after a heavy workload at the start of their campaign.

Several other World Cup players were not selected, namely Cammy Devlin, Awer Mabil, Kai Trewin, Mat Leckie and Ajdin Hrustić.

After the shambolic way his World Cup ended, keeper Mat Ryan has also been dropped, despite playing well for Levante in La Liga.

Cameron Burgess and Jordan Bos are out with long-term injuries, while Cristian Volpato was left out with a hamstring strain.

Volpato was also charged by police over driving with cocaine in his system, a charge he says he will challenge.

Who is in Brazil's squad?

Vinícius Júnior headlines Brazil's squad. (Getty Images: Lars Baron)

Legendary coach Carlo Ancelotti copped a fair amount of criticism for the Seleção's last-16 exit at the World Cup, but just as much flack for his erratic approach to selection.

The five-time Champions League-winning coach was adamant that he would not pick players based on reputation for the World Cup, only to surprisingly select a desperately out-of-form and unfit Neymar Junior, whose only contribution to Brazil's poor performances in the USA was to embarrassingly taunt Norway's goalkeeper Ørjan Nyland after slotting a consolation, stoppage time penalty in their 2-1 defeat.

Neymar has since retired from internationals and Brazil is now firmly on the rebuild.

Brazil squad: Goalkeepers: Hugo Souza (Corinthians), Pedro Morisco (Coritiba), Otávio (Cruzeiro). Defenders: Arthur Dias (Athletico-PR), Douglas Santos (Zenit), Gabriel Magalhães (Arsenal), Jair (Nottingham Forest), Marquinhos (PSG), Matheuzinho (Corinthians), Mauro Junior (PSV Eindhoven), Vitor Reis (Manchester City), Wesley (Roma). Midfielders: Andrey Santos (Manchester United), Breno Bidon (Corinthians), Bruno Guimarães (Arsenal), Danilo Santos (Botafogo), Douglas Luiz (Juventus), Gabriel Bontempo (Santos). Forwards: Endrick (Real Madrid), Estêvão (Chelsea), João Pedro (Chelsea), Pedro (Flamengo), Raphinha (Barcelona), Rayan (Bournemouth), Samuel Lino (Flamengo), Vinícius Júnior (Real Madrid).

"Friendlies are used to have a look at different players … players who I don't know really well," Ancellotti said this week.

Of the 26-man squad, Ancelotti has selected 10 from the domestic Brasileirão Série A, including all three goalkeepers, leaving Liverpool's Alison Becker at home.

There are eight players from the English Premier League in the squad though and a collection of experienced stars from Italy, Spain and France, which Ancelotti said was crucial to Brazil's revival.

"I chose these players — Marquinhos, Gabriel [Magalhães], Bruno [Guimarães], Raphinha and Vini Jr. — to help with this change in direction. They are crucial for the future," Ancelotti said.

Tech.title: Here’s the Tesla Semi… again
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Remember the Tesla Semi? The long-gestating, heavy-duty truck first introduced in concept form in 2017 is finally in volume production as of April 2026 — nearly a decade after its initial introduction. On Thursday evening, the company held yet another event for the Semi to demonstrate to customers and investors that the long wait was finally over.

The event was held at Tesla’s new Semi factory next to Gigafactory Nevada, where the company says it can build 50,000 trucks a year, or 1,000 per week. The purpose was to announce a raft of new (and old) customers for the Semi, including PepsiCo, US Foods, DHL, WattEV, ABF, Einride, IMC, and OK Produce. (Most of these names were leaked ahead of the event by a YouTuber flying a drone over the company’s facility in Sparks, Nevada.) First deliveries of the truck started this week.

Previous Next















1 / 9

But there were still a lot of missing details that could have helped explain why the wait was so long, and where the Semi goes from here. Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers, nor did it update the price of the Semi — which is rumored to be $290,000 for the long range version. In short, like many Tesla events these days, this one was lacking in some key updates.

The trucks were supposed to go into production in 2019 but were delayed for a variety of reasons, including the covid pandemic and a global parts shortage. Tesla delivered a handful of trucks to PepsiCo in 2022, but those units were essentially built by hand on a pilot line.

Back in 2017, the company advertised a starting price of $150,000 for the 300-mile version and $180,000 for the 500-mile one. Tesla never officially updated those prices until today, but Eletrek reported earlier this year that Tesla was quoting customers $290,000 for the 500-mile range version.

Tesla spent the last three years refining the Semi’s design, shaving nearly 1,000 lbs off the weight, and building out a dedicated factory next to its Gigafactory in Sparks. The company revealed the final production design in February 2026, confirming two trims: a Standard Range truck with 325 miles at full 82,000-lb gross combination weight, and a Long Range version with 500 miles of range. In April, Tesla announced that the first Semi had rolled off the line at the new facility, kicking off volume production of the long-delayed truck.

Tesla CEO Elon Musk wasn’t at the event — he was in Washington, DC, attending a state dinner with President Trump and Chinese President Xi — but in a pre-recorded message, he praised the Semi as “the funnest truck to drive.”

“This is really going to be a revolutionary truck,” Musk said, “that is capable of carrying the heaviest loads over very long distances. With ease of recharge, Megacharger that’s capable of a megawatt of power. This is really going to be a phenomenal truck.”

Battery and engineering

Much of the event was devoted to the hardware and engineering that went into the truck. Tesla’s Director of Semi Truck Engineering Dan Priestley emphasized that the 500 mile figure comes from fully loaded trucks rather than tests with a diminishing payload. Tesla Vice President of Engineering Lars Moravy said a Semi carrying a lighter load of around 60,000 pounds could potentially reach about 600 miles. The lower-range truck will have lower mass and be suited to a variety of applications, giving the company multiple Semi configurations rather than relying solely on the long-range version.

Tesla claims the Semi, with its lower energy cost and far fewer parts to maintain, is cheaper to run than diesel. That’s not hard to believe with diesel prices having hit historic record highs, soaring past $6.50 a gallon in the US — nearly double what it cost a year ago. Tesla says the fully loaded truck now consumes about 1,700 Wh/mile, compared with an original target of 2,000 Wh/mile. The efficiency gains allow Tesla to use a smaller, lighter and cheaper battery while retaining the same range.

The Semi is using Tesla’s in-house 4680 battery cells, replacing the purchased 2170 cells used in previous test versions. Tesla says the change, combined with vehicle-efficiency improvements, produces a lower-mass, lower-kWh battery without sacrificing range.

Much of the event was devoted to the hardware and engineering that went into the truck.

The company has also substantially redesigned the powertrain and drive axle since the Semi’s initial reveal. The truck gets a new steel-caged rotor instead of the earlier carbon-fiber-sleeved rotor, a bar-wound stator shared with Cybertruck, and a redesigned drive axle that is about 80 kilograms lighter. Tesla also eliminated the three separate oils used in the original drive axle, leaving no oil in the hub and one common oil for the motor and gearbox, which Moravy says should last more than 250,000 miles.

The hydraulic steering has been replaced by redundant electric power steering that Tesla says provides much greater precision and response. Meanwhile, the truck’s increased wheel cut gives it nearly the turning radius of a Model Y. Tesla specifically designed the system to make tight urban and loading-dock maneuvers easier, Priestley said.

The Semi also shares parts with the newly road-worthy Cybercab, using the same indirect thermal system, including pumps, compressors, and heat exchangers, as the autonomous vehicle. Tesla says the system eliminates long refrigerant lines running to the front of the vehicle and can move heat between the cabin, battery and drive unit to improve efficiency.

Previous Next













1 / 8

Charging and uptime

Over the past year, Tesla has been building up a customer list for the Semi, including PepsiCo, DHL, ABF Freight, and others. Autonomous trucking startup Einride announced a 500-truck order in August, while IMC Logistics said it would buy 50 Semis for California drayage earlier this week. And on Monday, Tesla was selected by “a coalition of the world’s largest cargo-owning shippers” to supply 2,500 trucks for zero-emission freight shipping in California.

Now the challenge will meeting this demand by getting trucks to customers — and quickly. Some of these freight operators have been waiting for years for Tesla to deliver its promised electric trucks, and any more delay will just further damage the company’s reputation.

“This is really going to be a revolutionary truck.” — Elon Musk

Charging will be another challenge, as the Semi requires higher power levels in order to fill its enormous 822 kWh battery pack. Tesla has begun to build out its Megacharger system that can deliver up to 1.2 Megawatts of power per stall. Tesla says it will have more than 30 Semi charging stations representing over 200 megawatt-capable posts by the end of the year, while also supporting customer-installed overnight charging. During the event, Priestley and Moravy kept checking in on a Semi charging at one of the new Megawatt chargers, demonstrating a 3-60 percent charge in about 30 minutes.

Tesla is positioning the Semi as an integrated fleet product, not just an electric truck. The company says its existing fleet has demonstrated more than 98 percent uptime, compared to an average 90-95 percent for diesel-powered class 8 trucks across the industry. Tesla is also building out a dedicated Semi service, mobile service, remote diagnostics and OTA updates around the truck.

The executives demonstrated a number of innovations they said would make for a better driving experience, including driver profiles that follow drivers from truck to truck and range estimates dynamically accounting for changing payloads.

While Tesla didn’t reveal order numbers or starting prices, Musk did say that the “waiting list is significant” and encouraged people to place orders. The company repeatedly emphasized how the Semi is able to achieve a lower total cost of ownership versus diesel, including lower energy costs, reduced maintenance, and less exposure to diesel-price volatility.

“You know, volatility in the oil market and the diesel market goes up and down,” Moravy said. “But typically, we’ve seen in the history of the last 20 years, electricity is pretty flat. And wouldn’t it be great to have a flat cost in your shipping rates?”

Images by Tesla

Tech.title: Microsoft is killing off the ‘Copilot Plus PC’ brand
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Remember when Microsoft wanted everyone to know that “Copilot Plus PCs” were the ones to get, because those were the PCs that that’d have enough built-in AI muscle to get things done? Two and a half years later, Microsoft and Qualcomm seem to be admitting the brand is already dead.

Windows Central’s Zac Bowden reports that even though the new 12-inch Microsoft Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop technically meet the system requirements for a Copilot Plus PC, Microsoft is not calling them by that name anymore. “These are not called Copilot Plus PCs,” Microsoft Surface CVP Brett Ostrom told the publication.

Kedar Kondap, Qualcomm’s SVP of compute and gaming, seemed to agree that the brand’s time is done, telling Bowden that computers that offer the same experiences will “probably” not use that branding anymore.

It’s not surprising to me that Microsoft and its partners would back away. Back in 2024, smart minds pointed out that (almost) every PC would soon contain the basic levels of AI hardware that the brand was supposed to reflect. The flagship feature of Copilot Plus PCs, Microsoft’s Recall feature, wasn’t well received, and Microsoft took flak for constantly annoying Windows users with AI upsells, not to mention the dedicated Copilot keyboard key that you can now finally remap.

Besides, Microsoft’s flagship hardware is now about to have Nvidia chips instead, which will supposedly kick off a new era of personal AI in Windows. On October 7th, when Microsoft hosts a “conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC,” I’m guessing it will have a shiny new brand to replace “Copilot Plus PC.”

Tech.title: Meta employees ordered ‘attorney/client privilege’ hats while fighting child safety disclosures
Tech.content:
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Meta’s lawyers have argued that certain evidence should be withheld from public view on the grounds of attorney-client privilege in the ongoing lawsuits over alleged harm to teens’ safety and mental health. Lawyers suing the company said this week that the label has been applied far too broadly, while pointing to a recently unsealed document showing that the team behind launching Instagram’s Teen Accounts in 2024 put in an order for baseball caps that simply said “a/c priv.”

Image: 4:22-md-03047, document 3509-4

The lawyers suing Meta argue the Project Nido (an internal name for the Teen Accounts team) swag is part of “culture of privilege abuse at Meta” aimed at keeping the research it’s conducted internally on teen harm out of the public eye, an issue that Mark Zuckerberg discussed after internal data on Instagram’s effects leaked in 2021.

US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers already called some of Meta’s privilege redactions “entirely inappropriate” in an order last month.

She pointed out one example where Meta’s lawyers tried to cast a discussion about a slide deck and whether or not to publish certain data as a discussion of attorney legal advice, deciding that based on testimony from the trial, their reticence about publishing was more of a business decision focused on preventing leaks.

Meta de-designated about 65,000 previously withheld or redacted documents in April 2025, after discovery, which the plaintiffs say came too late for them to use in depositions. Now Meta has requested time through the end of this year to re-review other privilege redactions it’s made, while the plaintiffs’ lawyers say a neutral party should be appointed to lead the review, paid for by Meta.

Tech.title: Qualcomm’s new ‘Elite’ sound chip might finally deliver the Wi-Fi earbud dream
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

What if your wireless earbuds — or audio glasses — could stream high-quality lossless audio that doesn’t cut out when you leave your phone on the bedside charger or buried in the couch? Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 is its first to integrate “micro-power Wi-Fi 6E” right into the chip, so they can connect directly to your home Wi-Fi network, and from there to the cloud.

Qualcomm’s old whitepaper shows that it originally required two chips for Wi-Fi earbuds. Now, Wi-Fi is integrated into the main chip. Image: Qualcomm

If that sounds like a familiar promise, it’s probably because Qualcomm promised something similar back in 2023 with the “S7 Pro sound platform” and its Expanded Personal Area Network (XPAN) tech, saying that Wi-Fi earbuds can do what Bluetooth alone cannot. Namely, 24-bit 96kHz lossless audio that can’t fit into Bluetooth’s meager bandwidth.

But that old 7-series platform required a separate Wi-Fi chip to give you Wi-Fi earbuds, and it seems that wasn’t a winning formula for getting makers of incredibly tiny devices to adopt the tech! In fact, we’ve only ever heard of one: Xiaomi’s 2025 Buds 5 Pro, which didn’t get a global release.

Image: Qualcomm

Now that Wi-Fi no longer requires an extra chip, perhaps the idea can take off. Qualcomm says the Elite is also 30 percent smaller, consumes up to 40 percent less power, and has twice the AI processing capabilities of the previous gen chip, all of which should be music to device makers’ ears.

So far, Qualcomm says it’s working with HP on one specific unnamed product, is “working closely with Bose,” and is “pioneering a new category of intelligent hearables” (read: earbuds with built-in cameras) with Cleer.

The camera earbuds. Image: Qualcomm

Tech.title: Microsoft puts Brad Smith in charge of communications
Tech.content:
Communications has never been more important to Microsoft. The company is changing, our industry is changing, and the world around us is changing. And in a media environment that is increasingly fragmented and noisier than ever, we need to continue to be grounded in our mission, earn trust each day, and find new ways to connect directly with all of our constituencies.

I first want to thank Frank for everything he has done for Microsoft. He has made tremendous contributions to the company and to our communications function over the last 17+ years. And he’s been a great source of counsel to our leadership team and to me personally, across the company’s biggest moments.

As Frank prepares to embark on his next chapter, Takeshi, Brad, and I have been discussing the evolution of comms at the company. I have asked Brad to lead the communications function going forward. Few leaders embody Microsoft’s voice as authentically as Brad. He brings a deep understanding of our business, a strong connection to our stakeholders, and a rare ability to communicate complex ideas with clarity, conviction, and trust.

During this transition, Brent Colburn will continue reporting to Brad and will now act as our interim communications leader. The comms leadership team will report to Brent, and Frank will continue to advise Brad and Brent on the transition.

In many ways, the people closest to the work have the best opportunity to shape how Microsoft is understood. We need to give people across the company the tools and support to do it well. And I’m excited about the opportunity to help our engineers, sellers, partners, and others closest to our products and customers become an even bigger part of how we tell our story, all connected by a shared strategy and set of principles. All of you have a critical role to play in making that possible.

We have an exciting fall ahead, with a number of important moments and events coming up and great marketing behind them. It is a real opportunity to bring together our product story, our marketing, and our communications in new ways.

We will learn, we will experiment, and we will evolve. There is a fundamentally new way to think about communications, and this team will be central to building it.

Thank you for everything you do for Microsoft, and for the role you each play in telling our story.

Satya

Tech.title: Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar gives Google’s AI a face
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Google’s new Gemini 3.8 Live update lets users have conversations with the model while watching an animated AI persona respond in real time. The “Live Avatar” will lip-sync and show different facial expressions during conversations, but it’s currently only available to Gemini Enterprise customers.

As noted by Google, Live Avatar can transition between the 97 languages it supports “without degrading video fidelity or introducing visual drift.” One video shared by Google shows its Live Avatar talking in English and Japanese, with its mouth animation lining up with what it’s saying in both languages. It can also pull up information on-screen while it talks.

The launch of Live Avatar comes about a week after Google revealed its new Gemini 3.8 Live model, which the company says “processes visual inputs in near real-time.” Though Google will offer a library of preset avatars for customers to choose from, it will also allow organizations to create their own. Google says output from its Live Avatar comes with its invisible SynthID watermark alongside safeguards to “respect identity.”

Tech.title: Sadly, this $1,549 RTX 5070-equipped gaming PC is a very good deal
Tech.content:
While PC component prices remain high, you can save a good bit of money on a system by purchasing a prebuilt desktop. Walmart has a well-equipped CyberPowerPC gaming PC on sale for $1,549, almost $600 off its original price of $2,139. It’s powered by an Intel Core i7-14700KF processor, and paired with 32GB of 6000MHz DDR5 memory and an Nvidia RTX 5070 Founders Edition with 12GB of VRAM. The case is a CyberPowerPC MA-O1 , an in-house design with extensive cooling options and three dedicated knobs for adjusting internal RGB lighting colors.

While it might not feel like it at first blush, this is a solid value for a gaming PC that’s ready to rock out of the box. The RTX 5070 in this machine is likely to run you upwards of $800 by itself at the moment (it launched in 2025 for $549), and 32GB of fast memory can be $400 or more. For just a small premium, you get those components packed into a nice case with a panoramic glass panel and a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD inside. The whole kit is tested, with a one year warranty for parts and labor. It also includes a keyboard and mouse, so you can start gaming right away once it arrives.

Tech.title: Jensen Huang talks about AI and climate change like a supervillain
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

As Jensen Huang puts it, AI can help fight climate change — but only if it inflicts “an enormous amount of pain and suffering” first.

The Nvidia CEO discussed the future of energy and AI’s impact on our planet in the latest episode of The Ezra Klein Show. But his comments boil down to the same accelerationist spin we’ve seen from a variety of tech leaders as well as President Donald Trump. They promise that AI will be such a gift to humanity that it’s worth the damage caused by data centers currently running on dirty energy.

Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring

Huang’s extreme level of privilege is glaring in the interview. He’s right that there will be pain. People are already suffering from fires and floods exacerbated by climate change. People are already dying earlier because of air pollution from fossil fuels. But Huang, with a net worth of around $192.6 billion, will not pay the price of the pollution his company creates through energy-hungry chip factories and data centers.

Huang tells Klein, after complaining that the US hasn’t built out enough fossil fuel plants, that:

It’s kind of like, in order to save you, they’ve got to hurt you first — that’s the nature of surgery. They’ve got to cut you open to save you. They’ve got to inflict an enormous amount of pain and suffering on you so that they can save you. And so I think AI’s kind of like that.

That’s the bit that gives Thanos energy. Resources are too limited and so after disappearing half of humanity, the Marvel supervillain believes, things will be much rosier. (“I will shred this universe down to its last atom, and then create a new one, teeming with life that knows not what it has lost but only what it has been given,” he tells the Avengers.)

Huang goes on to say:

Over the next several years we have to unfortunately use fossil fuels, because we just don’t have enough sustainable energy to make a difference. And then after that, hopefully, we can transition to that.

For context, nearly every country on Earth agreed to limit climate change when they adopted the Paris agreement in 2015. The accord sets a goal of cutting greenhouse gas emissions in half by 2030 and reaching net zero around 2050. That can only happen with swift transition to carbon-free energy like renewables and nuclear. Here’s just a short list of terrible things getting worse when we stall that progress to pursue advances in AI:

These effects are showing up in Huang’s backyard, even if he’s insulated from them. He mentions in the interview that he doesn’t know what his own address is. However, he reportedly bought a $7.5 million home on Maui in 2004 — before wildfires devastated the island in 2023. That year, an Nvidia spokesperson confirmed with The Verge that the Huangs “have owned the same home in Maui for many years.”

Huang’s property reportedly escaped damage, and the Nvidia spokesperson told me that the Huangs “donated significantly to local relief efforts.” But despite the philanthropy from tech billionaires with residences on Maui, the inferno also inflamed tensions over luxury properties’ hold on Maui’s water supply.

“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community,” Maui County Councilmember Keani Rawlins-Fernandez told me at the time. “It underscores the stark disparity between Indigenous people who want to mālama ‘āina, care for our land, and those who see Hawaii as a vacation destination.”

“Billionaires coming to Maui, buying up large swaths of land as their, I don’t know, seventh vacation home, it’s painful for our community.”

While greenhouse gas pollution from fossil fuels makes wildfires more dangerous by exacerbating hot, dry conditions, climate change isn’t entirely to blame for the flames that razed much of Lahaina on Maui. I reported at the time that previous generations of wealthy land grabbers primed the islands to burn. The US annexed the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1898, egged on by American plantation owners who wanted to evade import taxes. They cleared native vegetation for their businesses, allowing invasive grasses to take hold and make the landscape much more flammable than it used to be.

So when I hear Huang make the case now that there will need to be sacrifices in the name of AI progress, it reminds me that we’ve seen this playbook before. An industry that wants to grow at any cost. And nearby communities and their descendants are just supposed to live with the aftermath.

Huang mentions growing community opposition to data centers in the interview with Klein, and scolds other companies for not spreading the good news with residents about how efficient data centers purportedly are before they start construction. “If they don’t want data centers to be built in their town or whatever it is, then so be it. But if you’re going to build in their town, be sure to go there and let them know what’s coming,” he says.

“I am inevitable,” Thanos notoriously said — and apparently, so are AI data centers.

Even so, data centers don’t actually have to be as polluting as they are turning out to be.

In the interview, Huang also (unfairly) attributes record renewable energy purchases to AI. He blames climate action for stalling the construction of energy infrastructure, presumably for fossil fuels.

I think we just have to acknowledge that we got ourselves really gummed up in climate change and sustainable energy, and as a result, we just didn’t plan enough energy production.

Then he proclaims that AI is “the best opportunity we have” to “turn a corner on climate change, if you want a future that’s sustainable.” He sees AI accelerating demand for clean energy in the long term. But AI already needs a lot of energy now, and fossil fuels are what we’ve got.

“A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable.”

And now, data centers are in turn spurring the development of far more fossil fuel infrastructure. Air pollution associated with AI could lead to up to 1,300 premature deaths and more than $20 billion in public health costs by 2028, according to a study from UC Riverside, Caltech, and the Rochester Institute of Technology.

Nevertheless, “A more polluting AI buildout is not inevitable. It depends on the choices government makes now,” Marc Boom, a senior director of the Environmental Protection Network, a group made up of EPA alumni, said in a recent press briefing on the growing health risks posed by data centers.

It also depends on the attitudes of industry leaders like Huang. If other people’s pain and suffering is the price you’re willing to pay for so-called progress, that says less about what’s possible and more about your own personal priorities.

Tech.title: Lightspeed targets $250M for new India fund, focusing on early-stage AI
Tech.content:
Lightspeed is sharpening its India strategy around AI, targeting $250 million for a new early-stage fund as the venture firm bets the technology will drive the next wave of startups in one of the world’s largest markets.

The Silicon Valley venture firm is already a major investor in AI companies including Anthropic, xAI, and Databricks. In India, it has backed Sarvam AI, one of the country’s leading large language model developers and a startup selected by the Indian government to help develop sovereign AI models.

The new fund, Lightspeed India Partners V, will be half the size of its $500 million predecessor, raised in 2022, and has already secured commitments for 80% of its $250 million target, according to a letter sent to investors on Thursday and seen by TechCrunch.

In late April, Lightspeed disclosed the new fund in a U.S. regulatory filing, though the filing did not specify its target size. Indian media had previously reported that the firm was looking to raise between $300 million and $350 million for the vehicle.

Lightspeed plans to begin investing from the new fund within two months and has designed it around an investment period of roughly two and a half years, per the letter. Until then, it will continue making its final investments from the existing fund.

A Lightspeed spokesperson declined to comment.

Starting with the new fund, Lightspeed is also moving its India funds onto the same fundraising cycle as its global funds for the first time, per the investor letter. The change brings a regional business it established nearly two decades ago more closely in line with the rest of the firm.

The move follows a similar shift by rival firm Accel, which in August raised its latest $550 million India fund alongside new U.S. and Europe funds and a global growth vehicle as part of a coordinated $3.5 billion fundraising effort. It was the first time Accel had raised all four funds simultaneously.

The $250 million fund is sized to match how quickly Lightspeed is currently investing and its shorter investment period, according to the letter. Lightspeed suggested to investors that the smaller size lets it focus on individual deals rather than fund size, and raise its next fund sooner.

The new fund also marks a sharper focus on AI for Lightspeed’s early-stage investment strategy in the region. The investment thesis outlined in the letter anticipates AI creating more value in India than the internet did, with the fund seeking out AI companies across India and Southeast Asia.

India has yet to produce a major frontier AI model developer on the global stage and has attracted far less investment in AI than the U.S. and China. Investors, nonetheless, increasingly see an opportunity for India in the application layer, drawing on the country’s large pool of software developers and its decades-long history as a hub for software and technology services.

The new $250 million India vehicle is a fraction of the capital available across Lightspeed’s global platform. The firm, which manages more than $65 billion in assets globally, raised $9 billion across several new funds last December, the largest fundraising haul in its history. The total included a $980 million early-stage venture fund.

Lightspeed’s dedicated India and Southeast Asia funds represent only part of the capital the firm has put to work in the region. Those funds have deployed roughly $900 million, while Lightspeed’s global funds have invested another $1.6 billion to support companies from the regional portfolio, according to the investor letter.

The decision to dedicate its newest regional fund entirely to AI also marks a sharper thematic focus for Lightspeed in a market where it has historically invested across sectors. Its India portfolio spans businesses including quick commerce, consumer internet, software, and household services.

Lightspeed’s bets in India have included companies such as quick-commerce startup Zepto, audio platform Pocket FM, house-help startup Snabbit, rooftop solar startup SolarSquare, and a range of enterprise software businesses.

The same team that led Lightspeed’s previous four India funds will manage the new fund, per the letter.

Tech.title: Waymo is scaling fast: Here’s what the fleet data shows
Tech.content:
Waymo’s commercial robotaxi ramp-up looks expansive, both in geographic reach and in ridership. And by almost every measure, it is — until you pay attention to where the bulk of those robotaxis are actually showing up.

The numbers over the past two years reflect the kind of commercial rollout you’d expect from a deep-pocketed company like Waymo, which spun out of Google and still counts Alphabet as its majority owner. In September 2024, Waymo was operating in just three cities — Phoenix, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Today, it offers robotaxi service in 15 U.S. cities, with most of those commercial launches occurring in the past year. Ridership has skyrocketed, too, with Waymo now averaging 500,000 paid robotaxi rides every week.

But a closer look at its fleet shows a company concentrating its efforts in just two states. About 80% of Waymo’s roughly 4,000 robotaxis are in California and Texas, and Texas is where the action is now: Waymo’s fleet there has grown by nearly half in the past three weeks, fueled by a new Chinese-built minivan the company is betting will help it scale, even as tariffs drive up its costs.

The other 800 or so vehicles are spread across cities in other states, including Arizona and Florida, another burgeoning hot spot. Most are the familiar white Jaguar I-Pace electric SUVs, but a growing number are the new minivans — a modified Zeekr RT that Waymo has branded “Ojai.”

Waymo’s focus on California is no surprise. It is headquartered in Silicon Valley, and much of its early testing and development work was conducted there. Plus, a segment of the population there is inclined to adopt tech at its earliest stages.

The recent growth in Texas is more interesting. Waymo has increased its Texas fleet by 49% in the past three weeks, according to state vehicle registrations and data from the Texas Autonomous Vehicle Fleet Tracker. As of September 24, Waymo had 1,102 autonomous vehicles registered in the state.

Waymo first launched in commercial service in Austin through a partnership with Uber in March 2025, letting riders hail its robotaxis through the Uber app. Since then, the company has expanded its robotaxi services in Dallas, Houston, and San Antonio.

Waymo’s Texas fleet remained relatively static for most of the summer, inching up from about 600 vehicles in June to more than 700 by the end of August. Then came September, when the fleet surged, driven by an influx of new Ojai minivans, which now make up about a third of Waymo’s Texas fleet.

Expect that share to grow.

The Ojai robotaxi, equipped with Waymo’s sixth-generation self-driving system, is supposed to help Waymo reach mass scale. Its interior is built to withstand heavy use, and it comes with an upgraded rider interface and Google’s Gemini AI, which acts as an in-car assistant for riders.

Strip away that technology, though, and the Ojai is a minivan made by Zeekr, a brand owned by China’s Geely Holding Group (which also owns Volvo). The Ojai is built on Zeekr’s SEA-M platform, a shared vehicle platform designed for uses like robotaxis and delivery vans. The base Zeekr vehicles are shipped to the U.S. without any Chinese connected-car technology on board. Once they arrive, the vehicles are sent to Waymo’s Arizona factory, where they are outfitted with Waymo’s self-driving system.

The Ojai is supposed to drive down costs and ultimately help Waymo reach profitability. For now, though, tariffs are cutting any savings. Under current U.S. trade policy, vehicles built in China face steep import tariffs, raising Waymo’s costs for every Ojai it brings into the country.

Waymo appears willing to absorb that cost. New York-based research firm MoffettNathanson, which tracks Ojai imports using detailed shipping records, said in its September report that Waymo is on track to bring 5,100 of the vehicles into the U.S. by the end of the year.

Where will all those Ojai vehicles go? Texas is certainly on the list. But Florida, where Waymo operates in three cities, and newer markets like Las Vegas will likely see an influx as well.

Tech.title: Nexterity wants to automate the hard, dangerous part of pipefitting
Tech.content:
Lindsey Elliott is big into bolts. At last year’s Bolting Symposium — the 13th annual — she said the highlight was playing Bolting Bingo against the many self-proclaimed “torque dorks” who were in the room.

A former engineer and planner at ExxonMobil, Elliott has spent years thinking about how to improve the infrastructure that moves oil, gas, and petrochemicals. Bolts are what she landed on. Specifically, the bolts that connect sections of pipe (technically called “bolted flange joints”). These bolts require hard, physical work to loosen and tighten and are the source of many pipefitters’ injuries. Like many trade industries, there’s also a labor shortage.

“Those people get really tired when they’re asked to work 12 hours a day for three months in a row,” she told TechCrunch. “I’ve talked to pipefitters across the U.S., across Canada, and just repeatedly have been told North American pipefitting productivity is notoriously low.”

The solution Elliott came up with at her startup Nexterity, which is one of the Startup Battlefield 200 selected to participate in TechCrunch Disrupt, is a remote-controlled robot that can handle this part of the job. It’s the kind of idea that could fundamentally change this particular blue-collar job if widely adopted, making the workers safer and more productive.

Think: more dork, less torque.

The robot comes in two main pieces that fit around a pipe. Powered by batteries, the robot can slide across the pipe once it’s attached and quickly loosen and tighten four bolts at a time.

Elliott said Nexterity has developed a few different configurations of the robot to fit different standard pipe sizes, but they’re all small enough to fit in a Pelican case and be carried by a single worker. That makes them easy to deploy to new sites — flexibility that is crucial to Nexterity’s business model of treating the robot like rental construction equipment.

Elliott said she arrived at this particular design as a result of conversations she’s had over the last few years — not just at the Bolting Symposium, but also with members of the Pressure Vessels & Piping Division of the American Society of Mechanical Engineers.

“What I learned from the people, the torque dorks per se,” she said, “is that 80% of our pipes are between two to eight inches in diameter, or what they call NPS2 to NPS8. And so when you have that much repeatability, you have a fantastic candidate for automation.”

It’s a pretty straightforward idea, but one that Elliott believes has a lot of upside.

“I think it would shock a lot of people just how big this market is,” she said. “I mean, day to day, most of us don’t think about piping infrastructure, but even water, wastewater, water treatment, food and beverage, mining, nuclear, any kind of green and sustainable manufacturing facility — they all use the same kind of piping.”
